AUTUMN, TWILIGHT AND A FIRE GOING OUT, ALL IN ONE MAN

The oldest thing on this scroll and the only one still in its own spelling — including the quarto's famous slip, “Bare rn'wd quiers”, which editors since have read as bare ruin'd choirs. Sonnet 73 by William Shakespeare, who died in 1616 — which is why the whole of it can be printed here

William Shakespeare · 1609 That time of yeeare thou maist in me behold, When yellow leaues, or none, or few doe hange Vpon those boughes which shake against the could, Bare rn'wd quiers, where late the sweet birds sang. In me thou seest the twi-light of such day, As after Sun-set fadeth in the West, Which by and by blacke night doth take away, Deaths second selfe that seals vp all in rest. In me thou seest the glowing of such fire, That on the ashes of his youth doth lye, As the death bed, whereon it must expire, Consum'd with that which it was nurrisht by. This thou perceu'st, which makes thy loue more strong, To loue that well, which thou must leaue ere long. First published in Shake-speares Sonnets (1609). This text is from the 1609 quarto, transcribed from Wikisource's scan-backed text, spelling unmodernised — see it there. William Shakespeare died in 1616, so the poem is out of copyright everywhere. That is the bottom of the scroll. Three hundred and eleven years of it, and thirteen items. Not one of them was a notification. Every text was transcribed from Wikisource and every item names the printing it came from, because these poems exist in several and they differ — which is why The Darkling Thrush is not on here at all. Wikisource’s page for it names no printing and says so itself, and a text nobody can trace is the one thing a scroll built out of dates cannot carry. The headlines and the lines under them are ours and are meant to be funny; the poems are not ours and are not. The Mopery is back up the stairs, and the street is past that. It is very loud out there. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. There is no ambient layer on this scroll at any setting. Paper does not move, and a feed that moved by itself is the thing this room is a joke about. Liner notes · Changelog · a Stimpunks Foundation street.

Job board Hints at every job No score kept Rooms: all of them Somebody has come onto this street and filed everything. Ruled boxes, square corners, a class in the margin, a stamp for a job that is done. It is the only tidy room here and it is tidy the way a form is tidy, which on a street whose whole architecture is that nothing matches is the strangest thing anybody could have built. Every job below sends you to a marker standing in one of the rooms — a small drawing of something lying about in there, drawn in that room’s own colours, because no two rooms on this street look alike and neither do their markers. Open the marker and it gives you a quest code. Bring the code back here. Hand in a quest code Spaces and capitals do not matter. If you followed a link from a marker the code is already in the box — press the button when you are ready, because pressing it is the only thing that makes a noise. Quest code Your browser is not letting this page store anything, so stamps will not survive you leaving. Everything still works; it just will not be here when you come back. Nothing about this is kept anywhere else unless you switch on keeping your jobs in your Profile on the CB. This deletes the jobs kept in your Profile on the CB, and whether they are shown there. The stamps in this browser stay where they are.

Nothing here is scored. No total, no percentage, no streak, no rank you climb, and nothing that expires. The board stamps a job when you hand its code in, a badge is worked out from the stamps, and that is the entire bookkeeping. One job is a perfectly good number of jobs to do. A badge is a set of things done that go together, and nothing else. Most are jobs; two are the shelters’, for rescuing an animal and for adopting one. Each is worked out from what you have already done, every time, and kept nowhere of its own. No badge is rarer or worth more than another, none is secret, none ever asks for more than it did when it was posted, so none can be taken away, and nothing counts how many you have. It certifies nothing: every code is printed in its room and every question gives its answer away, so a badge says where you have walked, and that is all it says. Your stamps stay in your browser unless you ask. Signed on to the CB, you can switch on Keep my jobs in my Profile, by the box above. Then the jobs you hand in are kept there as well, which jobs and nothing about when, they follow you to any device you sign on with, and you can choose to show them, and your badges, to people on the CB. Switching it off deletes them there. Privacy has the rest. The difficulty class is how far you walk. I is on the street, II is through a door off another room, III is off the street altogether — the field past the treeline at one end and the land past its wood, the road past the last streetlight at the other, or the caverns underneath. It says nothing whatever about the person doing it, which is why it is measured in doors. Every job has hints, and some have a question. A question is answered by a sentence already published on the page you are standing on — that is the point of asking. The hints are at the job, the question’s own hints are at the marker, and every question has a “give me the answer” way out. Taking it is a real way through this and not a lesser one. The fanfare does what the dial says, and the words never change. At Gentle handing a code in says its piece and does nothing else. At Regular it chimes. At MAX GLITTER it chimes properly and throws sparks up the page. You get the same sentences at all three. Nothing in here flashes or strobes, at any setting. That is Club Chronic’s rule, and it holds everywhere on this street except in one room: the Rebellion Rave Room has a strobe, and it is off until you switch it on and say yes. The markers are not hidden. They are quiet, which is a different thing: every one is a full-size control in the tab order with a real name on it, and every one opens without JavaScript. A secret only a sighted mouse user can find is not a secret.

Two are not jobs at all but the shelters’: rescuing an animal, and giving one a home.
Handing in any job at all. The house rules say one is a perfectly good number of jobs to do, and this badge is them saying it again. Any job on the board. Yours

Yours Where badges come from, and what we left behind Scouting America’s merit badges are a patch for a list of requirements in one subject. We kept the list, printed in full where you can read it before you start. We left anybody signing it off, because nobody here checks anything. Open Badges is a format for digital badges that its own site calls verifiable and portable: a badge you can take elsewhere and have checked. We left all of that. These do not leave the street, and there is nothing in them to check. Video game achievements are goals laid over a game, shown on a player’s profile; Wikipedia traces them to the iron-on patches Activision posted in 1982 to players who photographed a high score. We kept the fun of hunting them and the profile, if you choose to show them. We left the score they add up to, the rarity and the secret ones.
In the order they were posted rather than sorted by class, because sorting by difficulty would stack the long walks at the bottom and start looking like a ladder. Show Difficulty class Ion the street

The Stoop Somebody has chalked a mark on the kerb outside the guild. Go and look at it. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

The Campgrounds Somebody has left a tent peg in the ground at the campgrounds. The field is past the end of the street, so this one is a walk. Takes two minutes, mostly walking Hint 1 It is not on the street at all. Follow the signpost at the end of it. Hint 2 On the bare ground of the field, not on any of the pitches. Where exactly it is In the grass at the very bottom of the field, below the last pitch. That field has no ambient layer at any dial setting, and the reason is not the same as Club Chronic's: the field is still because quiet is what it is for. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
A candle stub on the windowsill

The Faery Yurt There is a candle stub on the windowsill in the Faery Yurt, pitch 01 in the campgrounds, burnt most of the way down. Take it and leave everything else as you found it. Takes two minutes, mostly walking Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 It is pitch 01, the first thing standing in that field. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the yurt, below everything else in it. That room is Helen Edgar's design and not ours to redesign — the palette, the typefaces, the drawings and every line of its copy came from a mockup she sent. This repo has changed exactly one colour of hers, because her smallest grey failed WCAG on every ground it sat on, and that change is written up in four places. The candle stub is ours, added with Ryan's say-so, and written up in the liner notes for the same reason. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
A bookmark left in a borrowed book

The Reading Room Somebody left a ribbon bookmark in one of the books in the Reading Room, through the oak doors under the Bookshelf in the Faery Yurt. Find it, read the page it marks if you like, and leave the book where it was. Takes three minutes, and a sit-down by the fire Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds, and into the yurt at pitch 01. Hint 2 The bookshelf in the yurt is a door now. Go through it. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the Reading Room, below the last bookcase. The Reading Room is Helen Edgar's, behind her yurt, and holds every book she keeps: the bookcases outgrew the yurt on 2026-10-15 and got a room of their own, with a fire, a sofa, two chairs and candles that stand still. Every spine is a door to its author's page. Nothing in there counts how much you have read. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
A moth asleep on the horn

The Music Room A moth has gone to sleep on the brass horn of the phonograph in the Music Room, through the door by the phonograph in the Faery Yurt. Find it, leave it be, and put a record on quietly if you like. Takes two minutes, and a record if you want one Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds, and into the yurt at pitch 01. Hint 2 The phonograph in the yurt has a door beside it. Go through it. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the Music Room, below the record case. The Music Room is Helen Edgar's, behind her yurt, for anybody who only wants to listen: her whole yarn on the phonograph and every song on it as a record in the case, in a room with nothing else to scroll past. Since 2026-10-18 it is the one place the yarn plays; the yurt keeps its phonograph, with a songbook under it listing every song, and both are written by one tool from one data file. Nothing in there counts what you played. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

The Cinema Somebody has dropped their ticket stub under a seat in the Cinema, through the cinema door in the Faery Yurt. Find it and read what it says; the film it was for is up to you. Takes two minutes, and a film if you want one Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds, and into the yurt at pitch 01. Hint 2 In the yurt, under The Cinema, the oak doors that open onto a galaxy. Open them and step through. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the Cinema, under the last row of reels. The Cinema is Helen Edgar's, behind her yurt: a little picture palace in the Reading Room's colours, where every film she keeps is an old-fashioned reel on a rail, and goes up on the screen when you press it. The projector never flickers. Nothing in there counts what you watched. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Myths & Legends Somebody has left a piece of amber with a tiny beetle caught inside it, in Myths & Legends, through the Alchemist's Arch in the Faery Yurt. Find it and read what it says. Takes two minutes, and a story if you want one Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds, and into the yurt at pitch 01. Hint 2 In the yurt, under Myths & Legends, the arch set with amethyst and amber. Walk through it. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of Myths & Legends, under the shelf of old books. Myths & Legends is Helen Edgar's, behind her yurt, through an arch of amethyst and amber: Stonehenge and its sun, King Arthur and Merlin, the folk of English folklore, and a shelf of old books, where every story says whether it is a story or something known, and where it was read. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Swaying Sweetgrass There is a firefly low in the grass at pitch 02. That room plays the start of a book in its author's own voice and lends you the rest, and it will want you to know how before it lets the firefly go. Takes three minutes, and some reading · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 It is pitch 02, the meadow with the path through it. Where exactly it is Low in the grass at the very bottom of the meadow, below the clearing. That room also carries a correction to our own glossary near the top rather than in a footnote: two of our entries attribute a phrase to Barry Lopez that he never wrote. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

The Solarpunk Hermitage There is a sunflower head drying on a hook outside the hermitage at pitch 03. Three of the four primordial learning spaces are laid out inside that cabin. The fourth is not in there, and the room will tell you where it is. Takes three minutes, and some reading · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 It is pitch 03, the cabin on wheels with the panels on the roof. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the page, below the last of the cabin. It is the only room on this street lit by morning. Every other world here is a dark ground with light applied to it; a cabin that runs on the sun and reads as midnight would be an argument against itself. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Who lit the woodland tea room?

Brew and Stew There is a tea room in a cabin on the Campgrounds, at the edge of the trees, and there is no flame in it anywhere. Go and sit in it, and come back with what gives it its light. Takes three minutes, and a pot of tea if you want one · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 Pitch 04 on the board, the cabin with its window dark. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. Nobody lit it: the light grows in the cabin's own wood, a pale glow in the joints between the logs, in the moss and in the little mushrooms at the foot of the walls, and the stove is shut iron, giving the room its warmth and none of its light. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What is the tree house built round?

The Bough House There is a tree house up in a grove on the Campgrounds, next door to the Faery Yurt. Climb up, and come back with what the house was built round. Takes two minutes, and a song if you want one · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 Pitch 05 on the board, next to the Faery Yurt. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. The tree was there first, and the house was built round it: the trunk comes up through the floor and out through the roof, and two of its limbs curl round the walls and hold the house up. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Which lake is on the cabin wall?

The Emergent Future Worlds Meets Mountain Man There is a log cabin at the top of the mountain that stands over the Campgrounds, with a fire behind glass, a big screen, a wolf on the rug and the whole back wall a window. Take the cable car up, look out of the window, and come back with the name of the lake. Takes two minutes, and a song if you want one · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds first. Hint 2 The sign at the top of the campgrounds' board: the cable car goes up from the pond. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. Lake Geneva: the window opens onto David's own photographs of it, taken in Lausanne in July 2026, and the cabin runs on the mountain's own heat. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Nature’s Contribution Past the campgrounds and through the wood, a stile opens onto a valley in the afternoon, and there are shadows lying across whole fields with nothing standing in them. Go and stand at the stile, and come back with what is casting them. Takes five minutes, and the walk through the wood · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline to the campgrounds, then through the wood. Hint 2 The campgrounds says where the track through the wood comes out. Where exactly it is On the floor of the land's own page, before the sign-off. The clouds: the shadows on the land are the clouds’ own, cast by the sky rather than by anything on the ground, and you are standing in one at the stile, which is why every word on that page stands in the shade while the valley is in the sun. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
How do the keepers see in the dark?

All Needs Met Wildlife Sanctuary There is a sanctuary past the campgrounds where the keepers do a round every night and never carry a torch. Go and look through what they carry instead, and come back with what it sees. Takes five minutes, and the walk through the wood · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline, through the campgrounds' wood, and take the west arm of the fingerpost. Hint 2 The sanctuary is by the wetland. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. Warmth: the keepers' viewer sees heat instead of light, so every resident shows white with their own warmth and nobody is woken by a torch, and nothing in the picture has a colour, because heat has none. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Brighter Days Solar Farm Past the campgrounds there is a solar farm with peppers growing under the panels, and two kinds of pepper answered the same shade in two different ways. Go and find out which one made three times the fruit. Takes five minutes, and the walk through the wood · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline, through the campgrounds' wood, and take the north arm of the fingerpost. Hint 2 Look under What grows under the panels. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. The chiltepin: under the panels it made three times the fruit it made in the open, while the jalapeño made about as much as in the open and lost far less water through its leaves. Neither is the failure case, which is the zine's whole point. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What do the three words not tell you?

Gentle Help Cannabis Farm Past the campgrounds there is a cannabis farm in hoop houses, with a table of strains sold as sativa, indica and hybrid. Go and read under the table, and come back with what those three words turn out not to tell you. Takes five minutes, and the walk through the wood · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline, through the campgrounds' wood, and take the north-west arm of the fingerpost. Hint 2 Read the paragraphs under the table of strains. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. What is in the jar: researchers who looked at tens of thousands of lab results, and others who looked at the plants' genes, found the three words line up poorly with the chemistry, and the THC on a label is often higher than a lab finds. Go by how something sits with you, not by its name. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
Which practice is not on the farm?

All Together Now Farms Past the campgrounds there is a farm where trees, crops and animals share the same fields. The USDA names five ways of farming with trees, and the farm does four of them. Go and find the one it does not, and why. Takes five minutes, and the walk through the wood · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline, through the campgrounds' wood, and take the north-east arm of the fingerpost. Hint 2 Read the five practices under Agroforestry: one of them is drawn with a dashed edge. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. Forest farming: growing crops under a woodland's own canopy. The farm has no woodland of its own, because the wood belongs to the campgrounds, and its page says so rather than leaving the practice off to make the farm look complete. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What does the machine on the counter do?

The Dairy Behind the mixed farm past the campgrounds, the old dairy is a café now, and a steel machine still stands on its counter. Go in and come back with what it does to every drop of milk before anything leaves the room. Takes a few minutes, and the walk through the wood and across the farm · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline, through the campgrounds' wood, take the north-east arm of the fingerpost, and go through the farm to its old dairy. Hint 2 Read the first paragraph under the café's name. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. It pasteurises the milk: heats it enough to kill the germs that make people ill. The CDC says that is crucial for milk safety and that good practice on a farm cannot guarantee safety without it, and Colorado does not allow raw milk to be sold at retail. Difficulty class Ion the street
What will the box not sell?

The Honesty Box There is a farm stand on the street with prices on a board, money in a box and nobody watching. One thing grown on the land past the campgrounds is never on it. Go and find out what, and why a box nobody watches cannot sell it. Takes a few minutes · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the door lit by one lamp under its eave. Hint 2 Read What is not in the box. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. Cannabis: it leaves the land through licensed dispensaries and nowhere else, because you have to be 21 to buy it in Colorado and a box nobody watches cannot ask anybody's age. The hemp rope and cloth are fibre, and they are on the board. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
What is never in the mix?

Wide-Spread Chaos Gardens Past the campgrounds there is a garden sown by throwing seed into the wind. Its mix is checked before it is thrown, because some weeds should never be scattered. Go and bring back the name of one of them. Takes five minutes, and the walk through the wood · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Go out past the treeline, through the campgrounds' wood, and take the east arm of the fingerpost. Hint 2 Read the plant labels under What is thrown. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, before the sign-off. Colorado State University Extension names four noxious weeds to keep out of a seed mix: chicory, dame's rocket, oxeye daisy and yellow toadflax. A pretty mix is not always a harmless one, which is why the garden checks before it throws. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Liner Notes There is a colophon mark at the foot of the liner notes. This street dropped most of the care its sibling sites run on and kept exactly two things. Name the one that is not contrast. Takes two minutes, and some reading · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is one of the pages linked from the pavement at the foot of the street. Hint 2 Go to the very bottom of the credits. Where exactly it is At the very bottom of the page, below the last credit. Contrast survived for a reason that is not the obvious one. This is a Disabled people's organisation, and a glitter-maximalist site that excluded the people it is for would be a self-own of exactly the kind we exist to name. The fix was never to tone it down — it was the dial. Difficulty class Ion the street
What a spider's best answer is

The Garden Somebody has dropped a blank plant label on the path in the garden, which is through the gate in the wall between two of the shopfronts. Pick it up. While you are in there, settle what that room says the garden spider is for, because it is careful about it and the sentence is worth carrying back out with you. Takes two or three minutes, most of it one paragraph · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not behind a shopfront. There is a gate in the wall between two of them, down past the noticeboard. Hint 2 Through the gate is the garden, where every bed is one of the other sites we publish. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the garden, on the path below the hedge and the dial. A glossary exists to give somebody a word for an experience that usually goes unnamed, and a tool that can route them from the experience to the word is doing that job one step earlier. What it must never do is stand in for the page at the other end, which is why that room says out loud that it can be wrong and links the ethics pages where we hold the line. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Zibaldone There is a shopfront on the street with a commonplace book left open on the desk in it. A nib has been put down beside the book. Pick it up, and while you are there settle the question the whole room turns on: one of the quotations in that book had to be traced to a particular printing before it could go in, because the obvious guess was wrong. Takes two or three minutes, most of it one list · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is a shopfront on the street, with the only pale window in the row. Hint 2 The book is open on a desk, and the nib is down at the foot of the page. Where exactly it is Below the attribution slip, at the bottom of the room. Naming the printing is not pedantry, it is the difference between quoting somebody and quoting somebody's editor. A quotation that names only its title cannot be checked by anybody, which is how a misquotation travels for a century in perfectly good faith. Difficulty class Ion the street
The words are not in the hole

The Rabbit Hole There is a shaft at the end of the street with seven recordings hanging in it, all of them of one song or of the record that song came out of. Go down it and count the lyrics. Takes a couple of minutes, and longer if you press something · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is a storefront on the street, not behind another room. Hint 2 The marker is on the wall of the shaft like everything else in there — keep going down past the engravings, the presses and the trail. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. A room can carry a recording without carrying the words to it, and the difference is a legal one rather than a matter of taste. It is also the one place on this street where a room deliberately does less than the page it was built from. Difficulty class Ion the street
What the server says instead of no

The Healing Checkpoint There is a save room on the street with a bed in it and no monsters. It is numbered after an HTTP status code, and that status code has a companion that turns a refusal into a time. Go and find out what the companion is called. Takes a couple of minutes, and as long as you like after that · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is a storefront on the street, not behind another room — although there is also a back stair up to it from this board. Hint 2 The room explains its own number in a section of its own. The answer is a header name, and it is printed in bold there. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. A status code can be a kindness. 429 is the one thing a computer says that blames a rate rather than a person, and the header beside it turns a no into a when — which is most of what anybody at capacity is actually trying to say. Difficulty class Ion the street
The letter that is a hole

The Foundry There is a type foundry on the street. Its own nameplate is set in a face that is not drawn the way the others are, and the room explains what it is instead. Go and read the two paragraphs about it. Takes a few minutes, and a long time after that if you start pulling proofs · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 A shopfront on the street, between the save room and the empty one. Hint 2 The room has a short section about its own display face, under the bench and the proof. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. A letterform can be shaped by what it is cut into rather than by what anybody wanted it to look like. The bridges across a stencil are not styling: they are the only thing holding the middle of the letter in. Difficulty class Ion the street
The joke in the street's own name

Danny the Street This street is named after somebody and the name is a pun in two languages. There is a page about it, reached from a line under the dial on the front page rather than through any door. Go and find out who the joke is about. Takes five minutes, or twenty if you read the whole history · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Not behind a door. It is linked from the front page, in the paragraph under the loudness dial. Hint 2 The page has a section called Where Danny came from, and the answer is in the paragraph that begins with the word pun. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the page, under the dial. The street you are standing on is named after a drag performer by way of a French pun, which means the architecture of this site — rooms that refuse to match, and a street that rearranges itself for whoever turns up — was somebody else's idea first and is credited rather than quietly absorbed. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The far end of the street

The Outskirts The street has two edges. Everybody finds the field past the treeline; far fewer walk the other way, out past the last streetlight, where the kerb gives up and becomes a verge. Go and read the road, and find out what is actually lighting it. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. Leave by the far end rather than the treeline end — the link is under the shopfronts, past the noticeboard and the gate. Hint 2 The answer is in the list at the top of the road, in the item about how far you can see. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the road, under the section about the unlit signs. The street has an edge at each end and they are not the same kind of edge — a field you walk into at one, a road you drive out of at the other — which is also why the guild's class III stopped saying past the treeline and started naming both. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Black Leather Lagoon Down the first turning off The Outskirts there is a drive-in screen standing in black water, and an appreciation of the band it is named after. That appreciation makes a point of something the band deliberately did not have, for years, on purpose. Go and find out what. Takes ten minutes, or an hour if you start pressing the records · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is off the street — out past the last streetlight, then the first turning. Hint 2 The answer is in the appreciation at the top, in the short paragraph that is entirely about a thing that was missing. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the rack of records. A band can remove the part everybody treats as structural and keep going for thirty years, and the missing piece becomes the sound rather than a fault in it. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Sithen Second turning off the road out of town there is a ring of earth standing in a field, and one kind of tree growing on it that people across a whole country decline to touch. A motorway was moved rather than fell one. Go and find out which tree. Takes ten minutes, and there is nothing to press out there · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is off the street — past the last streetlight, then the second turning. Hint 2 The answer is in the documented half of the page, the part about earthworks rather than the part about rules. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about why the door is not opened. There is a tree in Ireland that a motorway was routed around, and the paperwork for that accommodation was a shrug — which is worth holding next to what is usually asked of a Disabled person before anything gets moved. Difficulty class Ion the street

Covenstead There is a kitchen on this street with the good china out and not one cup matching the next. One of the things laid on that table is famous, and the word at the front of it is the whole reason it never hardened into a rule. Go and find out what that word means. Takes ten minutes, and the kettle is already on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with the pale window. Hint 2 It is the second thing on the table, the one first recorded publicly in 1964. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose these all are. The best-known line of a living religious tradition is phrased as advice rather than as an order, and has stayed that way — which is a rarer thing than it sounds if you have spent much time being handed rules that were described to you as guidance. Difficulty class Ion the street
The desks are for sitting at

Dead Tired Society There is a room on this street with the big lights off and the door wedged ajar, where a society of the burnt out meets on the floor. Its standing orders have something to say about the desks. Go and find out who stands on them. Takes five minutes, lying down if you like · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the dark one with a sliver of light in its awning. Hint 2 The standing orders are near the top of the room, just under the drawing of the doorway. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose these are, where the door would swing. A room can make a point of what it will not ask you to do. That one will not ask anybody to stand up — for themselves, for the room, or on a desk — and passing, there, is a whole turn. Difficulty class Ion the street

Laughingstock There is a comedy club on the street, down a ramp rather than a flight of stairs, where the only thing standing in the spotlight is what the comics said. One of them was at a restaurant when the server asked his friend what he would have. Go and find out what the friend said. Takes five minutes, or a full hour if you stay for a special · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with a neon sign in the window. Hint 2 Josh Blue’s lines are in the spotlight near the top of the room, under his name. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the dial, where a set list would be taped down. Talk to the comic, not to whoever came in with them — which is one of that club’s house rules, and a good one for anywhere with tables in it. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Lightbulb Picture House There is a picture house on the street where the house lights never go down, and one of the films on its rack draws autistic attention as something out in space. Go and find out what. Takes five minutes, or four more if you watch the film · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the one with a row of warm bulbs in its awning. Hint 2 It is on the first rack, between Screen One and Screen Two, and the film is the one about monotropism. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the picture house, under the dial, where somebody left them on a seat. Attention that goes deep takes time to come back from. That is monotropism, and it is why a relaxed screening lets you walk in late and leave early. Difficulty class Ion the street

Samefood Cafe There is a café on the street whose kitchen knows its regulars, and whose specials line says what today’s special is — for everybody who walks in. Go and read it. Takes as long as a cup of coffee, the same cup as last time · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the pale one whose awning is a tray of little wells. Hint 2 The specials line is right under the café’s name, above the drawing of the table. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the café, under the section about whose these are, where something slipped off a tray. A special does not have to be one dish for everybody. A café can default to the same thing every time and still make it a different thing for every guest, because it knows its regulars — and for a great many of us the same again is how eating becomes possible at all. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Collection Collection There is a dark gallery on the street full of other people’s collections, each under a lamp of its own, and its house rules say there is one question nobody in there will ever ask you about yours. Go and find out which. Takes as long as it takes to walk past a row of cabinets without counting them · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts — the dark one whose awning is a row of unlit bays. Hint 2 The house rules are further down the gallery, after the cabinets. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the gallery, under the section about whose these are, where a label has come loose. A collection does not have to be counted to count. The gallery shows what people keep, lit the way they choose, with no totals, no prices and no ranking — because a number beside somebody’s things turns something they love into an inventory. Difficulty class Ion the street

Vital Plant Living There is a kitchen on the street whose name over the door is a translation, and the room says so near the top. Go and find out what the old name's first word comes from. Takes about as long as it takes to read a menu board · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the turmeric one whose awning is a row of pots. Hint 2 Near the top of the kitchen, under the lede, there is a panel about where its name comes from. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the kitchen, under the section about whose these are, where something fell off the shelf over the counter. A name can be a translation and say so. Borrowing a word from somebody's faith for a menu that does not keep it would be a claim about the food; saying what the word means in plain English, and crediting where it came from, is the honest version. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Looming Rocks Amphitheatre Third turning off the road out of town there is an open-air stage with something enormous on either side of it, and a lighting rig that points the wrong way. The rocks glow after dark. Go and find out what is actually doing the glowing, and which half of that story the room admits it made up. Takes ten minutes to read, or nine hours if you press everything · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the third turning. Hint 2 It is in the section about what the rocks are, in the paragraph that begins by saying which half is real. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose all this is. A real property of a living thing is doing the work that looks most like special effects — and the room is careful to say which half of its own story is invented, which is the same care the herbarium two areas over takes about naming a plant. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Dance, Punks Fourth turning off the road out of town there is a crowd dancing on an old airstrip, and not one sound of it reaches the verge. Go and find out who decides how loud it is. Takes ten minutes, and nothing plays unless you put a headset on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the fourth turning. Hint 2 It is in the section about why the room is silent, near the top. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. A loud room is an access barrier, and one way round it is to give every person in the crowd their own volume — which is what the dial on every page here is for, too. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

The Small Hours Fifth turning off the road out of town there is a diner with every light on, at an hour when everything else is shut. Something is missing from the clock over its counter. Go and find out what, and why nobody in there minds. Takes ten minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the fifth turning. Hint 2 It is in the heading of the first window you come to. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. Crip time bends the clock to meet the body rather than the body to meet the clock — and some of us are simply awake when the town is not. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

The Repeater Sixth turning off the road out of town, a track goes up to a ridge with a mast on it and nothing lit but two red lamps. Go and find out what the thing on the ridge does with a signal it hears. Takes ten minutes, or as long as you like with the line open · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the sixth turning, and up the track. Hint 2 It is in the second paragraph at the top of the room. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. Far off is not the same as cut off. Signal is a mode of connection in its own right, and no mode sits at the top. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Nothing For Sale Seventh turning off the road out of town there is a lay-by with a ring of cars in it, headlights on, and tables in the middle with everything on them free. Go and find out what the room says it is instead of. Takes ten minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Off the street — past the last streetlight, then the seventh turning. Hint 2 It is the first heading in the room. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the part about whose all this is. Mutual aid goes sideways and charity comes down. Solidarity, not charity, and no proof of worthiness required. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Arlesglad Caverns The street has an edge at each end, and a third one that is not at either end: straight down, by the lift by the stoop or the stair beside it. Go down and read the caverns, and find out what is doing the lighting. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street and not past either end of it. Look for the way down, under the shopfronts with the other things that are not doors. Hint 2 The answer is in the list called What is down here, in the item about light. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the caverns, under the section about where the name comes from. The street has three edges now and only two of them are at an end of it. The caverns are the one you reach by going down, which is also why the guild's class III names all three rather than growing a fourth class for the one that is underneath. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Glow Go Gee Gaws Three floors down in the caverns there is a shop full of glow-in-the-dark toys, every one of them dark until you give it some light. Charge them, and find out which colour lasts longest. Takes five minutes, and a toy or two to hold up to the rail if you want · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns and look for level B3. Hint 2 The answer is in the section called How long a glow lasts. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the shop, under the credit line. A glow-in-the-dark toy does not make light. It keeps some of the light you give it and hands it back, slowly, which is the only light on this street that runs down after you press. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Rebellion Rave Room Out past the last streetlight, an old hangar by the airstrip has the only strobe on the street. Read the walls in the ante-chamber before you go in, and find out how far it goes. Takes five minutes, and nothing needs switching on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is off The Outskirts, past the last streetlight. Look for turning 08. Hint 2 The answer is on the strobe and laser warning, in the ante-chamber. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the hangar, under Whose this all is. The one room on the street with a strobe in it relaxes a rule by holding the opt-in harder than anywhere else: off on every visit, two presses to start it, and Escape stops everything at once. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

The Cooldown Room Beside the rave's ante-chamber there is a small soft room with a vending machine along one wall. Go and sit down in it for a minute, and find out what the machine takes. Takes a minute, and a couch · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is through the other door in the Rebellion Rave Room's ante-chamber, off The Outskirts. Hint 2 The answer is in the section called The machine. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under Whose this all is. A free vending machine does the one thing it was never built for. Taking from it puts nobody in anybody's debt. Difficulty class IIIoff the street
The cellar at the top of the lift

Big Steep Fermentables One floor down under the street there is a cellar with house styles of beer, wine and kombucha. Read how the pours are set out, and find out which one comes first. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press or to drink · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns; this is the first level. Hint 2 The answer is in the introduction to Try our house styles. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the cellar, under the credit line. Every pour on this street says how strong it is before you take it, the same way every play button in its rooms says how long it runs before you press it. The number is what lets somebody decide. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Mycelium Munchies Two floors down in the caverns there is a mushroom farm with a restaurant at the end of it. Read why it is there, and find out what happens to the blocks the mushrooms grew on once they are finished. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns and look for level B2. Hint 2 The answer is in the section called Why a mushroom farm. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line. A mushroom is the fruit and not the thing that grows. The part doing the work is the mycelium, the part nobody sees on a plate, which is a fair description of most of the work on this street. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Stay Frosty Go all the way down: past every level of the caverns to the one at the bottom, where the temperature stops moving. Read the room's rules, and find out what the dial on the page does down there. Takes five minutes, and there is nothing to press · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift by the stoop down to the caverns, and then go to the bottom of its panel. Hint 2 The answer is in the list called What never changes in here. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line. The dial is the street's promise that loudness is yours to hold. In a room with nothing loud in it, the promise is kept by there being nothing to turn down, which is the one setting where Gentle, Regular and MAX look exactly the same. Difficulty class IIIoff the street

Stay Breezy At the very bottom of the caverns there is a room where nothing moves, and a door at the back of it. Go through, and read the house rules of the room full of fans. Takes five minutes, and you can do it without switching a single fan on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is under the street. Take the lift down to the caverns, go to the bottom, and look for the door at the back of the quiet room. Hint 2 The answer is in the house rules, in the one about the ceiling fans. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the credit line. The loudest room in the caverns and the quietest one share a wall, and both keep the same promise from opposite ends: nothing flashes, and nothing happens to you that you did not switch on. Difficulty class Ion the street
The door the radio waits outside

Community Center There is a radio on this street that follows you from room to room once you have switched it on. There is one door it will not go through. Find out which, and why. Takes about as long as it takes to read a noticeboard · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the sage-green one with a hill in its window. Hint 2 Inside, under the front desk, there is a list of how the radio works. The last thing on it is a room. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the section about whose this is, where a leaf fell from the plant on the sill. A room's promise about itself holds even against the street's own furniture. The Healing Checkpoint says it writes nothing down about you, so the radio that remembers where you put it waits outside, rather than the room's promise being quietly narrowed to fit the radio. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
Which channel is the World room's own?

World Past the Garden Spider, through the gate in the wall, is the web it has strung between every room on the street. Find out which channel is that room's own. Takes a few minutes of reading · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is on the street, through the gate in the wall: the Garden. Hint 2 Past the Garden Spider, on its web. Where exactly it is On the floor of the room, under the gardens, before the sign-off. World: the World room's own channel is the CB's World channel, and its own call is the World call, so the room where every other room is listed splits nobody between two. Difficulty class Ion the street
What the middle of the building is open to

Town Hall There is a town hall on the street, a round hall with rooms off it. Go in and find out what the top of its dome is open to. Takes about as long as it takes to look up · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a round hole in its roof. Hint 2 Read the lede, and the section headed Why a hole in the roof. Where exactly it is The gavel is on the floor at the foot of the hall, before the sign-off. A private room and a public record are two different things, and a building can have a place for each: doors round the wall for what has to stay in the room, and the middle open to the sky. Difficulty class IIthrough a door

The Fishbowl Through a door off the Town Hall there is a fishbowl on a sunny sill. Go and find out what the circle in the middle always keeps. Takes about as long as it takes to feed a fish · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Fishbowl's door. Hint 2 Read How a fishbowl goes. Where exactly it is The flake is on the sill at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. A conversation stays open when there is always room to come in. The fishbowl keeps one seat in the middle empty, and whoever takes it is joined by somebody else stepping back out. Difficulty class IIthrough a door

Directors Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' directors, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what the light comes through. Takes about as long as it takes to read a name backwards · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Directors' door. Hint 2 Read Why frosted glass. Where exactly it is The key is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. A room can be private without being hidden. The door is not locked, the directors' names are on the wall, and the glass lets the light through while keeping the detail back. Difficulty class IIthrough a door

Board Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' board, at one long table. Go and find out what every seat at it has in front of it. Takes about as long as it takes to count down a table · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Board's door. Hint 2 Read Why a lamp at every seat. Where exactly it is The pencil is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. A board is a table where every seat counts the same. Nobody's lamp is bigger, and there is no light over the head of the table. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
What lights the room that looks after the street

Moderators Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room for Stimpunks' moderators, above the street at night, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what it is lit by. Takes about as long as it takes to look at a ceiling · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Moderators' door. Hint 2 Read Why the street's own light. Where exactly it is The fuse is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. The room that looks after the street is lit by the street: every shopfront's colour comes up through its window and lies on the ceiling beside the others, none mixed into the next. Difficulty class IIthrough a door

Executive Session Through a door off the Town Hall there is a room where the board meets without staff, with no lamp in it. Go and find out what the one light in it is. Takes about as long as it takes to read a sign · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Go into the Town Hall on the street, and through the Executive Session door. Hint 2 Read Why an exit sign. Where exactly it is The note is on the floor at the foot of the room, before the sign-off. An executive session is the board meeting without staff, and a board that holds one at every meeting never has to mean anything by holding one. Difficulty class Ion the street

Dopamine Dress-Up Den There is a shop on the street for dressing in whatever makes you glad to have it on. Go and find out which colour every rail in it comes in, whatever else it comes in. Takes about as long as it takes to try something on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the lavender one with a strip of patchwork for an awning. Hint 2 Under the stand and the looks off the peg there are house rules, and the first one is about dress codes. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the shop, under the section about whose this is, where something fell off the boa. Dopamine dressing is not the same as wearing colour. It is wearing what makes you glad to have it on, and for a great many people that is black. A room that told them colour was what they needed would be a dress code with a nicer name. Difficulty class Ion the street

Chimera Obscura There is a camera obscura on the street, black inside, where you make one creature out of two animals. Go and find out whose chimera the Pandillo is. Takes about as long as it takes your eyes to get used to the dark · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts, between The Sandbox and Your Room: the black one with a round light in its awning. Hint 2 It is on the wall by the door, under each drawing. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under whose this is, where somebody dropped the lens's cap. Ryan, Chelsea and Inna each chose a chimera years ago, and Becky Hicks drew them for stimpunks.org's About page: a Bearmouse, a Pandillo and a Bunnybadger. They hang on the wall in Chimera Obscura, and its bench can make all three. Difficulty class Ion the street

Community Care There is a shopfront on the street roofed with everybody’s umbrellas, where you can ask for help and offer it. Its channel is for four things. Go and find out the fourth. Takes about as long as a shower lasts · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts, between Chimera Obscura and Your Room: the one with umbrellas for an awning. Hint 2 It is the first heading under the roof, and the cards under it. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, on the dry paving, where somebody left a spare umbrella for whoever needs one. Community Care’s channel on the CB is for asking, offering, receiving and declining, after a line of Vivian Ly’s at Autscape 2020. All four are allowed there, and a no is an answer, not a verdict on anybody. Difficulty class Ion the street
If you only do one thing

Coping There is a shopfront on the street in the eye of a storm, built out of our pages about coping. One of them says what to do if you can only do one thing. Go and find out what it is. Takes about as long as six slow breaths, in for four and out for six · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts, between Community Care and Show Your Work: the one whose awning is a patch of blue sky in a wall of storm cloud. Hint 2 It is under Right now, after the three small things to reach for. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, on the dry floor of the eye, where somebody dropped a packet of seeds. Our Seeds of Cope page says that if you only do one thing, reduce inputs: lower sensory load first, because everything is harder when your nervous system is on fire. Difficulty class Ion the street

Pets There is a shopfront on the street where everybody is down on the floor at the end of the day with the animals asleep, and nobody has switched the lamp on. One of the lines quoted in there says which animals co-regulation is the strongest safety cue for. Go and find out. Takes about as long as a dog takes to turn round three times and lie down · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts, between Coping and Show Your Work: the one whose awning is the sky through a window at dusk. Hint 2 It is under Co-regulation, and why it is not only people. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, on the floor, where somebody's collar tag came off. Our Polyvagal Theory entry quotes NDConnection: co-regulation, the subconscious process of syncing up with a coherent nervous system, is the strongest safety cue for mammals, and that includes cats, dogs and horses as much as people. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Bodymind Booth There is a photo booth on the street with no camera in it, next door to the Dopamine Dress-Up Den. Go and find out the only thing a screen reader hears for an avatar on the CB. Takes about as long as it takes to sit down and pull the curtain · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts, next door to the Dopamine Dress-Up Den: the cream one with a strip of lit frames for an awning. Hint 2 It is in the house rules, and in the words beside the box for what an avatar shows. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the booth, under whose this is, where a strip of frames fell out of the slot. An avatar on this street is a drawing that says nothing about anybody. The only words that go with it on the CB are the ones its owner wrote, and nothing in the booth describes a body for somebody else. Difficulty class IIthrough a door

Fantasy Fancy Dress One faery wing has come loose from its pair and is lying on the floor of Fantasy Fancy Dress, through the curtain at the back of the Dopamine Dress-Up Den. Go and find out what the wings in there do so that whoever wears them can sit back in a chair. Takes a minute or two, and as long as you like trying things on · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is not on the street. It is behind one of the rooms that is. Hint 2 Go into the Dopamine Dress-Up Den and through the curtain at the back. Where exactly it is On the floor at the foot of the shop, under whose this is. Everything in Fantasy Fancy Dress needs somebody to wear it, so it goes on a bodymind, never on the Dress-Up Den's stand, and it is drawn on that bodymind as it is, on its feet or sitting down. Difficulty class Ion the street

Now Playing There is a poster pasted round a column out on the pavement, saying what every room on the street puts on first. Go and read it, and find out the one thing every other gig poster has that this one will not print. Takes about as long as it takes to read a bill standing on a pavement · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the pavement beside the Pebble Board, on a column of its own rather than behind the glass. Hint 2 Under the bill, where the poster says how it is printed. Where exactly it is At the foot of the column, on the pavement, where the paste brush was put down. The poster belongs to all of those rooms at once, so every name on it is set the same size and they run in the order you would walk to them. A gig poster that put one of them in big letters at the top would be ranking our own rooms against each other, on a sheet none of them chose. Difficulty class Ion the street
When does the wall repaint itself?

Plural Mural There is an end wall on the street that will not stay one colour. Go and stand across the road from it, and find out when it repaints itself without anybody asking. Takes about as long as it takes to watch a wall, which is not as long as you would think · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a strip of fresh paint under its capping. Hint 2 Under the list of murals, where the room says how the wall works. Where exactly it is At the foot of the wall, on the pavement, where somebody put the lid down. A picture that changes without being asked is something moving on the page, so the wall only turns over by itself at MAX GLITTER. At Gentle and Regular it holds still until you turn it over, and every mural is in words under it at every setting, because the dial takes away the wobble and never the words. Difficulty class Ion the street
What are you, at the library?

Community Library There is a public library on the street with the sky in its windows, and somebody has left a book on the floor with its date-due slip sticking out. Go and read the room, and find out what the library says you are when you walk in. Takes about as long as it takes to read a reading room's notices, and you can sit down · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with sky in its windows. Hint 2 In the first paragraph under the drawing of the reading room, and again in the praise of the public library. Where exactly it is On the floor at the foot of the room, under the last notice, where somebody put a book down. At the library you are a patron, not a customer. Nothing requires a card, you do not have to buy anything to be there, and nobody checks whether you are being social correctly. That is what makes a library a third place. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
What do you need to find your way through L-space?

L-Space There is a gap in the stacks at the back of the Community Library that is longer on the inside than it is on the outside. Go down it, and find out what you need to find your way back. Takes one gap in the stacks, and as long in there as you like, which is never as long as it felt · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Through the gap in the stacks at the back of the Community Library. Hint 2 In the first paragraph under the drawing, and again in Terry Pratchett's own words further down. Where exactly it is On the floor at the foot of the room, where the string was tied off. In L-space what you need is not a map but a ball of string, because nothing in there is straight. Tie one end to the door you came in by and follow the thread: that is how we think about a library, and how a monotropic mind walks one anyway. Difficulty class IIthrough a door
Why did the Librarian keep his job?

Oook At the far end of the string in L-space somebody has tied it round a banana, and on the other side of the shelf there is a room in the Librarian's own colours. Go and find out why he kept his job when everything else about him changed. Takes the length of a ball of string, and one room at the end of it · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 Through the Community Library's gap in the stacks, and all the way along the string in L-space to the end. Hint 2 In the first paragraph under the drawing of the Disc, and again under why we find him relatable. Where exactly it is On the floor at the foot of the room, where somebody dropped a banana skin. The Librarian kept his job because he was the only one who knew where all the books were. His body changed by accident, he found the new one suited the work, and he declined to be changed back; being the expert is a reason to keep a job that an institution cannot argue with. Difficulty class Ion the street
Who signed for his own books?

Cavendish Coworking There is a house on the street, green throughout, with a shut door onto each of our calls and not one of them locked. Go in, do not open a door, and find out what the man it is named after signed every time he took a book out of his own library. Takes about as long as reading one paragraph, and no call to join · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with its blinds down. Hint 2 In the part of the room about the house in Bedford Square. Where exactly it is At the foot of the room, on the hall floor, where somebody left a note. Henry Cavendish opened his library in Bedford Square for borrowing and signed its register for every book he took, like anybody else. A house can be open without being open-plan: what makes it open is that anybody can find out what is behind each door and when, that the rules apply to the people who run it, and that nothing is locked. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Live Room There is a control room on the street with the red light on and a desk full of sessions, each with its name written on tape. Go in, read the strips, and find out what night of the year one of them was taped on. Takes about as long as reading a few strips, and nothing to play · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a red lamp over the door. Hint 2 On the desk, in the Austin City Limits section. Where exactly it is At the foot of the room, under the desk, where somebody dropped a roll of tape. Leonard Cohen's first time on Austin City Limits was taped on Halloween night 1988, on the I'm Your Man tour, and first broadcast the next year. Every strip on the desk says where and when its session was taped, before the press, alongside how long it runs. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Broadsheet Broadside There is a ship on the street with its ports open and a sheet of paper in every one where a gun would be. Go alongside, turn the first sheet over, and find out who the street is named after. Takes about as long as reading one side of one sheet, and nothing to print · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one that is the side of a ship. Hint 2 On side B of the first sheet on the press. Where exactly it is At the foot of the room, where a sheet came down in the bottom of your boat. The street is Danny the Street's: a living street in DC Comics' Doom Patrol, created in 1990 by Grant Morrison and Richard Case, who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter. Side B of the first sheet says so on the paper, because a printed sheet is the one place a credit cannot be a link somebody follows later. Difficulty class Ion the street

The Doom Scoop There is an ice cream parlour on the street that stays lit after closing, with the news of every morning of the week in its cabinet, a tub to a morning. Go in and find out what flavour Thursday comes in. Takes about as long as reading the lids in the cabinet, and nothing to play · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a row of ice cream tubs in its awning. Hint 2 In the cabinet: every tub's lid names its day and its flavour. Where exactly it is At the foot of the room, on the floor in front of the cabinet, where somebody dropped the scoop. Every morning's tub in the cabinet is a flavour, and the flavour is the day of the week, so Thursday is always vanilla whatever is in it. How far down a tub is scraped says how many mornings old it is, and after a week it is gone. Difficulty class Ion the street

The MUD Room There is a boot room on the street with a whole estuary out of its back door, and the tide out there does not keep time. Go and find out what turns it. Takes a walk down the street, and a look out the back door · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 It is a shopfront on the street, near the far end of the row. Hint 2 The answer is on the noticeboard by the back door, and in the house rules. Where exactly it is Right at the foot of the room, under the guidebook. A world can wait for you. Nothing on the Slake changes until you ask it to. Difficulty class Ion the street
How often will the tree take water?

Pando Calrissian There is a tree on a hillside behind the shopfronts that is everybody's, and it grows as we water it. Go up the hill and find out how often the ground will take another watering. Takes about as long as it takes a watering to soak in · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the gap with a hillside of aspen in it. Hint 2 Under the grove, where the room says how the tree grows. Where exactly it is At the foot of the fence, where the leaves come down. The ground soaks for a minute after every watering, from anybody, before it takes more. It is the whole tree's wait and not anybody's, so nobody is timed, and the tree keeps how many times it has been watered and never who watered it. Difficulty class Ion the street
How many words in a row can one person put up?

The Fridge of Sighs There is a kitchen on the street with a fridge door covered in word magnets, and a sentence on it that everybody is writing together. Go and read the door, and find out how many words anybody can put up in a row. Takes about as long as it takes somebody else to put up the next word · there is a question to answer in the room Hint 1 On the street itself, in the row of shopfronts: the one with a chrome handle down its awning. Hint 2 In the rules about how the door works. Where exactly it is At the foot of the door, where a magnet ends up when it slides. One word each, and never two in a row: once you have put one up, the next is somebody else's. The fridge keeps a scrambled mark of whoever put up the last word, only so it can keep that rule, and the next word replaces it; nothing says whose any word was. Difficulty class Ion the street
How far does the lift take you?

A board is set by somebody with a machine. It is a picture of the railway and it is not the railway. Stimpunks is not one site. There is the big one, and there are the small ones each built to take one kind of weight off it, and every one of them publishes an RSS feed nobody needs an account to read. This room is a hall of indicator boards, one wire per feed, showing what has most recently arrived on each; this street has two, its changelog and the Brass Tacks Board. This room’s channel on the CB hears every new arrival as it comes in, said by The Feed itself a few minutes after it is published. Follow the room on the radio to be told, and talk about what arrived.

Every wire above links its site and its feed. Put the feed in whatever reader you use and the arrivals come to you, on your own time, with no board in between and nothing here deciding what you see first. That is the better version of this room and we would rather you used it. stimpunks.org keeps a feeds page with the lot on it, including the socials and the bookmark archive, which are not up here: a social post has no title, and a board that mixed them in would be a machine with three jobs.
Up the hill, where it all comes from

Every wire in this hall starts somewhere. Out of the back of the concourse and up the hill is The Source: one pool for every repository these sites are built in, and every commit a deposit on it, with its first line and whose hands made it.

The split-flap indicator board is Solari di Udine's machine — the flap boards that stood in railway stations and airports for decades, and the reason a certain clacking noise means something has changed to anybody over about thirty. This room is a picture of one drawn in CSS. It is not one of theirs, it is not affiliated with them, and it makes no noise at all. The sites on the board are Stimpunks Foundation's, several of them built with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms, who is named here rather than folded into our “we”. Penguin Pebbling is hers and Ryan Boren's together. Every title on this board belongs to whoever wrote the page it points at, and this room holds none of their words — only their names, their dates and their doors. The credits are collected in the liner notes.

At Gentle the boards are simply already showing their words, which is what a board does for almost all of its life. At Regular each row settles once as the page arrives — one flap, downward, and then still. At MAX GLITTER they riffle on the way to settling, the way a real board runs through half the alphabet before it finds the letter it wants. Nothing in here flashes, strobes or pulses at any setting, and nothing makes a sound. The words on every row are identical at all three: the dial takes away the clatter, never the arrivals. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes or plays until you say so — and in here, MAX GLITTER is a board that riffles before it settles.

Somebody else already wrote it down. A commonplace book, left open on the desk. People copy lines into it — from poems, from books, from each other — and beside each one they write what it is for. Every line in here says where it came from and how we checked it, because a quotation nobody can trace is just a nice-sounding sentence with a famous name stuck on the end.

Zibaldone is Italian, and it means roughly a heap of things — the name given to the miscellany notebooks Italians have kept since about the fourteenth century, of which Leopardi’s enormous one is the famous example. Merchants kept them. So did poets. They are unruled, unsorted and unfinished on purpose: recipes next to accounts next to a line of verse somebody liked. In English the same object is a commonplace book, which our own glossary has had an entry for since 2022. Montaigne kept one and more or less invented the essay out of it. Marcus Aurelius kept one and it turned into the Meditations. It is not a filing system. It is what you reach for when you cannot find your own words and somebody else’s will do. This room exists because somebody in our community asked for it: a quote bank, quotes for any state of mind. That is what this is. The desk and the rules are ours; the good lines are everybody’s.
What this book will and will not do

A bank of quotations is the most dangerous shape of page on this street, and not for any reason you would notice from the outside. So the rules are in the generator rather than in somebody’s good intentions, and they are written here so you can hold us to them. 30 words is the longest quotation this room will carry, and tools/make-zibaldone.py refuses a longer one rather than trusting anybody to remember. A bank of quotations is the shape of page that turns into republishing somebody’s book one reasonable-looking entry at a time. Where the line is not enough, the book is linked. No song lyrics. Music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel. Nothing musical is hosted anywhere on this street, and a quote bank is exactly where that promise would have been broken in the way that looked most harmless. The tool refuses a song; it is not left to care. Bring us the person talking about the song instead — that we can quote. Every line names its printing, not just its title. These texts differ between printings and a title is not a source. The Dickinson in this book is the proof: it is in the second series, not the first, and the only thing that found that out was going and looking. The Thoreau is the other proof — the version everybody quotes has somebody marching to a beat, and he wrote neither word. Every line says how it was checked, and when. The public domain ones were read out of the transcription named on the card. The ones still in copyright were read off our own published pages, or read in the book itself by the person the card names, who gives the page. An unchecked quotation sitting among checked ones looking identical is the thing this room is built to prevent, so there is nowhere for one to hide. Nothing here is ranked, counted or voted on. No favourites, no most-copied, no top of the bank, no number on a card. A quote bank is the shape of thing that grows one, and this room will never grow a leaderboard — refusing one matters because a leaderboard would turn the one page meant to meet somebody where they are into a popularity contest between other people’s grief. There are no faces in this room. A quote bank for states of mind obviously wants a row of moods you pick from, and the obvious drawing for a mood is a face. A row of happy, sad and angry faces on a Disabled people’s site is the emotion flashcard that autistic people spend their childhoods being drilled with. So each card says what it is for in a sentence about a situation you might actually be in, and you read the ones that sound like your week. The quotations are set in type; only the margins are handwritten. The hand is for the keeper’s own asides. A passage set in a handwriting face is an access failure wearing atmosphere, so the tool refuses one.
I have no more made my book than my book has made me.
