I'm not afraid of storms, for I'm learning how to sail my ship.
I exist as I am, that is enough, If no other in the world be aware I sit content, And if each and all be aware I sit content.
One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.
I took a deep breath and listened to the old brag of my heart. I am, I am, I am.

The spine of this is TASL — Title, Author, Source, Licence, which is Creative Commons’ own shorthand for crediting something you have reused. It is the right skeleton for a photograph, where the thing you are pointing at is one file at one address. A quotation needs three more, marked below: which printing, where you found it, and what it is for. The quotation itself needed Keep it short -- this room's own limit is 30 words, and the reason is on the page. Who wrote it (Author) needed The person, not the person who said it to you. If you do not know, say so here rather than guessing. What it is from (Title) needed The book, poem, essay, talk or post. A chapter or section number if you have one. Which printing needed The edition, year, publisher, issue -- whatever pins down WHICH version of the text this is. Texts differ between printings and this is the field that makes an entry checkable. A link to it (Source) A link to the work itself where there is one. Not a quotation site. Its terms (Licence) Public domain, a Creative Commons licence, all rights reserved, or your own words -- whichever it is. Where you found it The book you were reading, the person who told you, the page you saw it on. This is the field that catches a misquotation, because most of them are copied in good faith off something that was already wrong. What it is for A situation somebody might be in, in your own words. Go down the rabbit hole (embrace serendipity). You have to embrace the accidental. — Ryan Holiday, The 5-Step Research Method I Used For Tim Ferriss, Robert Greene, and Tucker Max, quoted on our own entry

You didn’t mean to be here for three hours. You meant to look up one thing. Welcome to the rabbit hole. You’re among friends. Those two sentences are the opening of our own glossary entry, Rabbit Hole, and this whole room is built out of that page. Read it first if you would rather have the argument straight; everything down here is that argument with the lights turned off. The short version. For monotropic minds — and a great many Autistic and ADHD people are monotropic — the rabbit hole is not a detour. It is the destination. Monotropism describes attention that goes in depth rather than in breadth: everything gets pulled into one blazing interest tunnel, and off you go. The rabbit hole is what that tunnel looks like from the outside. From the inside it looks like flow. Which is why the research rabbit hole is its own genre, and a good one. One citation leads to another. One tab becomes seventeen. One question opens into a whole field you did not know existed. This is not a failure of discipline. It is how knowledge actually gets built — serendipitously, associatively, joyfully. And then you surface, blinking, and need to tell somebody — everybody — everything you found, which is the infodump: the rabbit hole speaking. Cal Newport’s name for the undistracted end of this is deep work, and we have no glossary page for it, so this sentence is where it gets credited and there is nothing of ours to link. Neurodivergent people were doing it a long time before it had a productivity branding deal. Rabbit holes are how some of us learn best. They are how some of us love best. Go deep.

The metaphor is Lewis Carroll’s. Wikipedia’s article on the idiom puts it plainly: going down the rabbit hole means getting deep into something, or ending up somewhere strange — and it does not promise which. The image comes from Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland , 1865, where the whole adventure starts with somebody following a rabbit into a burrow without once considering how they were going to get out again. There is a name for the version of this that most of us do daily. Wikipedia calls it the wiki rabbit hole and defines it as a learning pathway — the route a reader travels by navigating from topic to topic, each one further from where they started than the last. Not a distraction with a cute name. A pathway, with a shape, that people deliberately go looking for. Our glossary entry illustrates that with Glenn Newcomer’s network diagram of a wiki rabbit hole, published on Wikimedia Commons under CC BY-SA 4.0. It is not copied in here, because the drawing beside the argument on that page is doing its job where it is, and this room would only be borrowing it. Go and look at it there.

What we are witnessing is the computational exploitation of a natural human desire: to look “behind the curtain,” to dig deeper into something that engages us. — Zeynep Tufekci, YouTube, the Great Radicalizer, The New York Times, 2018, quoted on our own entry
Be wary of the holes you rabbit

Our own entry says that line, and it is the reason this room is not simply an advertisement for going deep. There is a difference between a hole you dug and a hole that was dug for you. The appetite is the same appetite. What changes is who chose the next thing. A recommendation engine tuned to keep you in the tunnel is not serendipity, it is somebody’s revenue, and the tunnel it builds runs somewhere specific. Monotropic attention is not a vulnerability to be patched — but it is worth knowing that it is valuable to people who do not have your interests at heart. Which is what the rest of this street is for. Stimpunks rabbit holes are meant to take you behind the curtain of the edges inclusively and compassionately, and to hand you back out at the other end with somewhere of your own to go. There is a trail at the foot of this page and every step on it is a page a person wrote. This room has no recommendation engine, no autoplay, no next-up, and nothing that decides for you what comes after. Seven things are offered, all of them named, and nothing reaches YouTube until you press it.

Grace Slick wrote White Rabbit after a childhood of being read Carroll and an adulthood of playing one Miles Davis record until it came out again in something of her own. She has told that story herself, in the Wall Street Journal: she identified with Alice, she went from a planned and bland 1950s into a rock band without looking back, and she called it her own Alice moment, heading down the hole. It is the most famous piece of rabbit-holing in popular music and it is also a description of how a monotropic mind works on something. Anything I love I’m going to cram into my ears, nose and mouth until I use it up, she said, which is the infodump’s cousin. The words to it are not printed on this page, and that is deliberate. Our glossary entry has them; this street says in three places that nothing musical is hosted here, and a quote bank one door along refuses songs outright because song lyric reproduction is a minefield in the United States in a way prose is not. So you get the recordings, credited, and Slick’s own account of writing them, and the words stay where their publisher put them. The two section titles on this page that are her phrases are credited as hers, here. Learning how to learn on his own proved one of the most important lessons of his life. — John Markoff, , quoted on our own entry
What the Dormouse Said: How the Sixties Counterculture Shaped the Personal Computer Industry

Three words of Grace Slick’s, used here as a heading the way our glossary entry uses them, and credited rather than borrowed quietly. The counterculture that produced that song also produced the personal computer, and the book that traces the second out of the first takes its title from the same place. John Markoff’s What the Dormouse Said is about people who learned how to learn on their own, and it makes the case that this turned out to be one of the most important things any of them ever did. Which is the same claim our own pages make about rabbit holes, arriving from a completely different direction. A roaming autodidact is not a person who refused to be taught. It is a person who went and got it.

What it looks like when the head gets fed

Rebecca Wood’s Learning From Autistic Teachers puts the case for taking this seriously as pedagogy rather than treating it as a symptom: Note what those two say together. The first is about the person in the tunnel: a well-timed special interest is not indulgence, it is regulation, and it can head off a meltdown. The second is about everybody else: a hyperfixation that gets to be shared with somebody is a teaching relationship, and an extremely good one. Our white rabbit — also known as Space Bunny — stands for playfulness, curiosity, wonder, hope, and the possibility of expanding what anybody can learn. That is why there is a rabbit on this organisation’s pages at all. It is not a mascot for distraction. It is the thing you follow. So: feed your head. Follow the thing that is going somewhere in a hurry. Read one book cited in every book you read. Keep a commonplace book so you can find it again — there is a whole room of one on this street. And never once consider how in the world you are going to get out again.

This is the Further Reading list off our own glossary entry, in that page’s order, with a line of ours saying what each one is. Each step is further in than the last, which is the only honest way to draw it. Every one of them is a page a person wrote. Monotropism Attention in depth rather than in breadth. The theory underneath the whole room, and the reason a rabbit hole is a destination rather than a detour. Roaming Autodidact The self-teacher the education-technology industry keeps imagining, and who it keeps leaving out. Anti-library The unread books. A shelf of things you have not got to yet is a map of holes you have not fallen down. Created Serendipity You can build the conditions for accidents. Embracing the accidental is a practice and not a mood. Commonplace Book Where what you found in the hole goes so that you can find it again. This street has a whole room of one. Flow The hours that do not feel like hours. What the tunnel is like from inside it. Infodump Surfacing, and needing to tell somebody everything. The rabbit hole speaking — synthesis, enthusiasm and generosity at once. One more, which is not a glossary page and is the best thing on the list: Roll Your Own: Bricolage, Punk, and the Neurodivergent Making Tradition. It is on the entry’s Further Reading too.

Nothing plays until you press play. There are seven buttons in this room and on arrival there is not one iframe on the page and not one request to YouTube. Pressing one builds one frame and leaves the other six alone. Every button says how long it runs before you press it, and the spread in here is the widest on the street: two and a half minutes at one end, sixteen at the other. Nothing in here moves. Not at Gentle, not at Regular, not at MAX GLITTER. There is no tilt on anything, no rotation, no flicker, no strobe. At MAX the wash of daylight from the mouth of the hole is a little stronger and that is the whole of it — the dial has almost nothing to do in this room, because the room was built still. Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. There is no content behind an intensity setting anywhere on this street. Every sentence, every engraving, every credit and every link is the same at all three. Nothing is counted. No progress through the trail, no marks for how deep you got, nothing remembered between visits. A rabbit hole with a completion bar on it would be a curriculum. The words to the song are not here. See above. The recordings are, the credits are, and Grace Slick’s own account of writing it is. A generator refuses a lyric field rather than leaving that to anybody’s memory. Her argument is that rest was taken from people rather than mislaid by them, and that getting it back is something done together instead of scheduled alone. Which is why this is a room and not a feature. A burnout page would tell you what to watch for. A spoon theory page would give you a way to describe the limit. What is on that page and is not in this room

Named rather than quietly left out, because a page built out of somebody else’s page should say what it did not take. In a game it is the room with no monsters in it. A bonfire, an inn, a save point, a bed you can use as many times as you like: your health goes back to full, it costs nothing, and the game stops trying to kill you for as long as you stand there. TV Tropes calls it the Healing Checkpoint. The trope is everybody’s and belongs to nobody; the room is ours. A checkpoint in a game does three things, and this one does none of them. It restores you to full. This one restores nothing, because you are not a health bar. There is no meter in this room, nothing fills up, and nothing is better about you when you leave than when you came in. That is not the room falling short of the trope. It is the room declining a premise the trope smuggles in — that a person is a quantity that runs down and gets topped up. It saves your progress. This one saves nothing at all. No account, no cookie, no local storage, no record that you were ever here. The job board one floor down keeps a list of finished jobs in your own browser, and in your Profile on the CB if you ask it to, and says so; this room keeps nothing, and a checkpoint that remembered you would be keeping a record of how often you needed one. It sits before the hard part. There is no hard part. Nothing is waiting on the other side of this page, there is no next room you are being prepared for, and the way out goes back to the street you came in by. And here is the sentence the whole room is built to protect: rest is not for anything. Not so you can work better, not so you can come back stronger, not so you can be more use to anybody tomorrow. Star Stuff’s zine No. 58 spends a spread refusing exactly that framing, one of our games refuses it in its own code, and our Rest entry never once offers it. A room arguing that rest is owed cannot carry a single sentence saying what it is owed for, so the generator behind this page refuses that vocabulary outright rather than leaving it to anybody’s care.

Because 429 Too Many Requests is the nicest thing a computer says to anybody. It was added to HTTP by Mark Nottingham and Roy Fielding in RFC 6585, in April 2012, and what it means is narrow and precise: the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time. Not that the request was wrong. Not that the sender was wrong. Not that anything is broken. The rate is wrong, and a rate is a property of a situation rather than of a person. That is the difference between a 429 and a 400. A 400 says you made a mistake. A 403 says you are not allowed. A 500 says something inside has fallen over. A 429 says: this is more than can be done at this speed, and that is all it says. Which is a thing a great many Disabled people have spent a great deal of energy trying to explain about themselves to somebody holding a deadline. And the RFC gives the response a way to be kind. Alongside a 429 a server may send Retry-After — not a refusal, a time. Come back then. The door is not shut; the door is on a different clock. Which is crip time with a header name.

The one amenity in this room, and it is the same shape as the spoon drawer in the Playhouse: it hands out the sentences and not the thing itself. Five slips, borrowing the shape of a 429 so you do not have to compose one from scratch when composing anything is the problem. Open one, read it, take it or leave it. Nothing is sent anywhere. There is no form, no endpoint, no fetch and no storage in this room: opening a slip shows you some text, and the copy button — which only appears if you have JavaScript — puts that text on your own clipboard. Where it goes after that is entirely your business. The wording is a borrowing of HTTP’s shape and not a protocol; a real rate limiter is not allowed to send the last one. Retry-After: an hour the smallest one, and the one the RFC’s own example uses 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: an hour Ask me again in an hour and I will have more of an answer. Retry-After: later today for the thing that is real but is not this minute 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: later today Not now. Later today, if it keeps. Retry-After: tomorrow the most useful one, most days 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: tomorrow Tomorrow. I am not ignoring you; I am at capacity. Retry-After: the weekend for the week that has already spent itself 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: the weekend The weekend, or the next one. It will still be there. Retry-After: no date the honest one, and the one a real rate limiter is not allowed to send 429 Too Many Requests Retry-After: no date I do not know when. That is not a no forever, and it is not a yes with a date on it either.

Nothing here is counted. No total, no streak, no minutes, no visits, no record between one time and the next. A checkpoint is precisely the shape of thing somebody gives a counter to, and a number beside a bed would quietly make rest into a quantity you were supposed to be managing. Nothing is stored. Not in a cookie, not in your browser’s storage, not on a server. This page writes nothing down about you at all. Nothing plays and nothing is fetched. There is no video in this room and no sound in it, at any setting on the dial. Nothing flashes. The steam over the water drifts at Regular and at MAX and is gone at Gentle, and that is the whole of what the dial touches in here. There is no flicker anywhere in this room at any setting — Club Chronic’s rule, and it matters most in the room whose entire subject is not being jolted. Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. Every sentence on this page is the same at all three settings. You can stay. There is nothing you are supposed to do next and nobody is waiting for the bed.

Every typeface on this street, and the name of whoever drew it. This is a workshop rather than a shop. It is grey because iron is grey, it is lit through a dirty roof because that is how a workshop was lit before anybody could afford to light one properly, and there is nowhere in it to sit down. Every other room on this street uses a typeface. This is the room where the typefaces are the thing in the window. Put your own words on the bench, or take a passage out of The Playhouse, The Mopery or The Zibaldone, and set it in anything the street owns. Change the size, the leading, the tracking and the measure. Take a weight, a real italic, or the machine slant that is not one. Then pull a proof and print it, with the name of the person who drew the letters on the bottom of the page.

What to set Your own words Typing here moves the picker above to your own words. Nothing you type is stored, sent or remembered, and reloading the page empties it. The face Grouped the way each family’s own record groups it, not the way we would have. Choosing one is what downloads it: nothing here is fetched until you ask for it. Weight Every weight this street declares for this face. Several of these families are one file with a weight axis inside it, declared against two or three weights — the same bytes, genuinely different drawings — and this picker used to drop those, because it asked whether the bytes differed instead of whether the letters did. A weight that came out the same drawings as the regular would be a control that does nothing, so the offered weights are rendered and measured rather than assumed. Upright, italic or slanted An italic is not a leaning roman: it is a second alphabet, drawn separately, often with different letters in it altogether. Where this site holds no italic file the option says so and the machine slant is what is left — which is honest, and is what a phototypesetter did. Case Size 30px A foundry sold type by the size it was cast at. This one is pixels, and it is the only setting here that changes what you can read rather than how it looks. Leading 1.4 The strips of lead a compositor slid between the lines. Multiples of the size, so it stays right when you change it. Tracking 0em Space added to every letter at once. Metal type could only ever have more; this can have a little less. Measure 44ch How wide the column is, in characters. The oldest setting here and the one that does most of the work. Ink and paper Four pairs, and the measured contrast ratio of each one is printed on it. There is no colour picker in here: this is the one room on the street where somebody else chooses the colour of the text, which makes it the one room where an unreadable pair would be ours and theirs at once. Everything offered clears the bar for body text at any size. Printer’s black on proof paper 14.73:1 Vermilion on proof paper 7.77:1 Prussian blue on proof paper 9.86:1 Reversed out, bone on iron 10.65:1 Printing sends the proof and nothing else — not this bench, not the street, not the shelves below. It comes out black on white whatever is on the screen, because paper colour is a screen decision and a printer would spend your toner on it, and it carries a colophon saying what it is set in and who drew that.

Queer without fear. Interdependent and here. Divergent and proud. Living out loud. Stardos Stencil · drawn by Vernon Adams · SIL Open Font License 1.1 — set at 30px, 1.4, 0em, 44ch. Self-hosted from stimpunks.world; the typeface is not ours.

A foundry’s own proof is the characters themselves, and a pangram is the shortest way to see all of them behave. That is The Feed’s refused summary field wearing a type sample. The bench is for your words; ours are here so it is not empty when you arrive.
Why this room is set in a stencil

Every other world on this street chose a display face for how it sounds. This one chose one for what it is. A stencil letter is a hole rather than a mark — a shape cut out of a sheet of metal so that it can be used again and again and come out the same every time — which is the whole idea of type, arriving about four hundred years early and in the wrong material. It is also what actually gets painted on a workshop’s crates and machinery, which is the other reason it is over the door. The bridges you can see holding the middle of an o in place are not a decorative flourish. Without them the counter — the enclosed space inside a letter — would fall out of the sheet, and there is no way round that in a stencil. Nobody drawing type in metal or on a screen has that problem, which is why nothing else here looks like this.
Why nothing here describes a typeface

There is no sentence beside any face saying what it looks like, what it is good for or what century it is pretending to be from, and that is a refusal rather than an omission. Writing a line of appreciation for every family on this street would mean inventing type history at scale, in the one format most likely to be believed — which is the same reason the herbarium two rooms over refuses to name a pressed plant to species. What this room can say truthfully is who drew it, what licence it travels under and which room here sets it, and all three are read off records rather than remembered. The specimen is the description.
An italic is not a slant

A real italic is a second alphabet. It was cut separately, it has different letters in it — look at a single-storey a, or at the way an f descends — and it was never made by leaning the roman over. A machine slant is exactly that leaning: the upright letters pushed sideways by a machine that has no idea what they are. Both are offered here and both are labelled, because the difference is the kind of thing this room exists to show you rather than to tell you. Where this site holds no italic file, the italic option says so and stops being offered. An italic control on a family with no italic is not an error anywhere: the browser answers by inventing one, nothing looks broken, and the room has quietly told you a lie about somebody’s typeface. And the slant is a font setting and never a transform — check-gentle.py reads rotation and skew out of the computed matrix and cannot be asked to take this room’s word for the difference between a tilted page and a slanted letter.
Every face here is self-hosted, and none of it is ours

Reading any page on this street makes no request to anybody’s font service. The files are in this repository, subsetted to Latin, and a face is downloaded only when something actually sets it — which in this room means when you pick it. Nobody who never opens the picker pays for a single one. None of these typefaces belongs to Stimpunks. Every one of them is somebody’s work, released under a licence that asks to be named, and the name beside each face here is verbatim from that family’s own record rather than typed from memory — including where the record credits a studio rather than a person, and including where it disagrees with the fuller credit in our liner notes. Most are under the SIL Open Font License; a few are under the Apache License 2.0, and the shelves below say which is which face by face, because “they are all OFL” is the sort of thing a site says once and stops checking.

Not the faces, not the proofs pulled, not the sizes tried. This is the room on the street most likely to want to boast about how much type it holds, and a number in the window would be out of date the next time somebody adds a face and wrong in a way nobody would notice. There is also no favourite, no most popular and no ranking of one designer’s work against another’s.

The Mopery has a reading nook where The Raven can be set in any face on the street, and it stays exactly as it is. That is one poem in one face inside a library, where borrowing all of them is the joke. This is a bench where any words go into any face at any size in any ink and come out on paper. The two rooms have one list between them and tools/check-faces.py now makes sure of it — before that tool existed, adding a typeface to this site quietly made the library’s claim to hold every one of them false, with nothing anywhere saying so.

Merry meet, and merry part, and merry meet again A covenstead is where a coven meets. Not a temple and not an institution — somebody’s kitchen, in the afternoon, with one window open and the good china out. The group is the whole of the subject. Not one wise person at the front and not a congregation: a handful of people who do not entirely agree, meeting on purpose, to check their own thinking out loud in front of each other. Not one of the cups matches. That is not untidiness, it is the subject of the room sitting on the table.
Merry meet, and merry part, and merry meet again

Read the shape of that rather than the words. It is a greeting with the goodbye already built into it, and then a third clause that undoes the goodbye. The parting is agreed at the door, before anyone has arrived, so leaving is not a rupture and nobody has to negotiate it at the time or perform a reason. That is a better door policy than most groups manage, which is why it is the first thing on this page instead of the last. If you have ever left somewhere early and spent the entire walk home composing the apology, you already know exactly what it is worth. Here the going is assumed. So is the coming back, and the door is on the latch rather than locked.

Every tenet below says whose it is and when it turns up. The line at the foot of each one is ours, written for this room, and is not claimed to be part of anybody’s tradition — the same split the fairy fort up the road keeps, because a reader should not have to tell inherited from borrowed by tone alone. Where the tradition argues with itself, the room says so and does not settle it.
Merry meet, and merry part, and merry meet again

A greeting that contains its own goodbye, and then undoes it. A traditional Wiccan greeting and farewell, in common use. Read the shape of it rather than the words. The parting is built into the hello, so leaving is not a rupture and nobody has to negotiate it at the time. And the third clause settles what the parting meant: going is assumed, and so is coming back. That is a better door policy than most groups manage, and it is the reason this is the first thing on the table rather than the last. If you have ever left somewhere early and spent the walk home composing the apology, you already know what it is worth.
An it harm none, do what ye will

The Wiccan Rede, in its best-known couplet. First publicly recorded in a 1964 speech by Doreen Valiente; the wording varies between published versions. · 1964 The word rede is Middle English for counsel. It is advice, and it has stayed advice for sixty years rather than hardening into a code somebody can be thrown out for breaking. That is rarer than it sounds and it is most of why this room exists: a great many of us have been handed rules dressed as guidance, and the difference is whether anybody is standing over you to enforce it. Note also which way round it runs. The constraint comes first and the permission is enormous.

That what you send out returns to you three times over. Also called the Threefold Law or the Law of Return; a possible prototype appears in Gerald Gardner's 1949 novel High Magic's Aid. · 1949 at the earliest Contested, and the room is not going to settle it: It is not a universal article of faith. There are Wiccans who regard it as an over-elaboration on the Rede, and others who consider it a modern innovation built on Christian morality. It has also been compared to other ethics of reciprocity, including karma and the Golden Rule. We are not going to settle that from out here, and the reason for saying so plainly is that the flattened version is the one that travels. A tidy cosmic ledger where harm is repaid at a fixed exchange rate is a very easy thing for a website to assert in passing, for atmosphere, about somebody else's religion. What is on this table is the argument rather than the verdict.
First Sight and Second Thoughts, that’s what a witch had to rely on: First Sight to see what’s really there, and Second Thoughts to watch the First Thoughts to check that they were thinking right.

Seeing what is actually in front of you rather than what you expected to be there. Terry Pratchett’s, from the Discworld books. The sentence that names it is below. · 2006 It is harder than it sounds, because the expectation arrives first and feels exactly like observation. This street has been caught by that repeatedly and the catches are all in the changelog: a colour that was decided and never rendered, a channel name compared against nothing, a share card built from the wrong meta tag. In every one of them the page looked right to somebody who already knew what it was supposed to look like.
Second Thoughts to watch the First Thoughts to check that they were thinking right.

The thoughts that watch the first thoughts, to check that they were thinking right. Terry Pratchett’s, from the same sentence, and the half our sibling site built its method on. · 2006 Not doubt. Supervision. And this is the half you can build machinery for, which is the only reason this site has any: the contrast checkers, the class checker, the tools that refuse rather than guess. Star Stuff makes the point that matters most, and it is worth carrying here because it is about the limit of all that plumbing: only the second half can be automated. No checker will ever tell you that a beautiful pattern is doing your looking for you.
If I don't help them, who will?
You can’t not help people just because they’re stupid or forgetful or unpleasant. Everyone’s poor around here. If I don’t help them, who will?
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004

I store it in other people. It’s amazing what you can store in other people.
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004

A witch never expects payment and never asks for it and just hopes she never needs to.
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004

Even if it’s not your fault, it’s your responsibility. Witches deal with things.
A Hat Full of Sky, Terry Pratchett, 2004

That the work goes to whoever needs it, including the people who will not thank you for it. The ethic of the Discworld witches, Terry Pratchett’s, collected and argued at length on our own philosophy page. This is the one that makes a coven different from a club. The witches of those books do the unglamorous half of care work, for people who are rude, forgetful or broke, and they keep a ledger that never quite balances on purpose. It is mutual aid with the accounting done out loud, and it is the reason a group that meets to check its own thinking is not merely a seminar.
Only the second half can be automated

That sentence is Star Stuff’s, and it is the most useful thing anybody we publish has said about how this site is built. Second Thoughts you can build machinery for. This street is largely made of that machinery: tools that measure contrast on the page as rendered rather than as written, a checker that refuses a class name two rooms have both claimed, generators that refuse to build rather than guess. Every one of them is a first thought being supervised. First Sight you cannot. No checker will ever tell you that a beautiful pattern is doing your looking for you, that an argument is wrong only in this context, or that a sentence which sounds like solidarity is quietly building a category of people. Those get caught by somebody willing to be disappointed by a finding they liked — and on this site they have been, repeatedly, and the catches are in the changelog rather than tidied away.
What is not in this room

No degrees and no initiation. Nobody is admitted, nobody is examined at the door, and there is no inner circle with the real version in it. A room you have to qualify for is the one thing this street will not build. Nothing is counted. Not visits, not how long you stayed, not how many of these you have read. A place people come back to cannot also be keeping a record of how often they needed to. Nobody is converted. This is a page about what a group of practices says, by people who are not members of them, and it is not an invitation to believe anything. The Wiccan material is somebody else’s religion and is treated as such. No spells, no rituals, no instructions. There is nothing here to perform. What is on the table are ideas about how to treat people and how to check your own thinking, which is the part that travels.

First Sight and Second Thoughts are Terry Pratchett’s, from the Discworld books, and so is the ethic of going to the people nobody else goes to. His words are on this page because they are the point of it. These sentences are the tenets themselves, the way the Rede’s couplet is — an earlier draft of this room named the concepts and sent you elsewhere for the words, which described the thing instead of showing it. Every quotation here names its author, its work and its year, and links to the edition. What is not here is the scene. The short lines above about storing things in other people come out of a long exchange between Miss Level and Tiffany that runs to several hundred words, and that stays where it belongs: quoted properly, at length and in context, on our own philosophy page, which is the better thing to read and is linked rather than raided. tools/make-covenstead.py holds this room to its own limit — wide enough for a defining sentence, not wide enough for a scene — and refuses any quotation that arrives without an author, a work and an edition to point at. The Rede and the Rule of Three belong to living religious traditions, and the second of them is argued about inside those traditions rather than settled. This page says which is which and declines to adjudicate, because a website assembling atmosphere out of somebody else’s faith is precisely the thing that would make this room not worth having. Read off the Wiccan Rede and the Rule of Three on 2026-09-22. est. whenever you got here Peer support, by and for people who are burnt out and people on the far side of it. Nobody here is a professional, nobody is at the front, and nobody is going to fix you, because you are not the thing that broke. It is a room somebody has borrowed after hours, with the big lights switched off and the door left ajar — so that anybody can find it, anybody can leave by it, and nobody has to sit in the light. If tonight is worse than tired: our Help page is a set of doors, and Coping lists crisis lines and warmlines.

They are called standing orders. Nobody is standing. Nobody has to talk. Being here with your camera off and your mouth shut is being here. You may lie on the floor. Most of us already are. The meeting starts when you arrive and ends when you leave, and neither needs announcing. Minutes are not taken. Neither is attendance. Nobody asks how you are doing. If you say anyway, nobody tells you what to do about it — unless you ask, and asking is allowed. Nobody stands on the desks. Most of us have been told to stand up for ourselves quite enough. Nobody in here seizes anything, least of all the day. You can pass. Passing is a whole turn.
What we mean by dead tired
Having All of Your Internal Resources Exhausted Beyond Measure and Being Left with No Clean-Up Crew
The title of Dora M. Raymaker and others, Defining Autistic Burnout, Autism in Adulthood, 2020
What we mean by dead tired
Burnout therefore reflects a failure of relational ecology, not a lack of individual resilience.
Stimpunks, The Ecology of Neurodivergent Burnout
What we mean by dead tired

Not the tired a weekend fixes. Burnout, and autistic burnout in particular: the kind that comes from years of being asked to do more than you could, in places built for somebody else, with nowhere to recover in. The research that defined it was built out of interviews with autistic adults who had been through it, and the title the researchers gave their paper says it better than a definition does. This society is not a clean-up crew either. It is some of the others who were left without one, in the same dark room, which turns out to be a good deal of what a crew was ever for. And it puts the cause where our own writing puts it:
By the door, on the pegs

Everybody comes in carrying something, and there is a row of pegs by the door for it. What wore us out has names, and none of them is yours: every one below is a thing done to people, or asked of them, and not a flaw in the person carrying it. Each peg says what is hanging there, gives one line from somebody who has written about it, and adds one line of ours.
Masking is exhausting. Utterly utterly draining.
Finally Knowing Me: An Autistic Life, Wasting Energy, 2018

On the peg: A plain half-mask with nothing painted on it, hanging by its string. Hang it up. You may need it again on the way out, and nobody in here will pretend otherwise, because the street has not changed while you were sitting down. What nobody in here will do is ask you to put it back on. That is the whole of the difference, and for a great many of us it is the first room it has been true in. Masking, in our glossary →

Researchers hypothesize that decreased social standing leads to stigmatized minority groups being exposed to more stressful life situations, with simultaneously fewer resources to cope with these events.
Monique Botha and David M. Frost, Extending the Minority Stress Model to Understand Mental Health Problems Experienced by the Autistic Population, 2018

On the peg: A rucksack gone out of shape at the bottom, the way a bag does when it has been carried full for years. It is not one heavy thing. It is the stone somebody added this morning on top of every stone from before, carried by the people who were handed the fewest ways to set any of it down. Nobody in here asks why the bag is so heavy. Everybody in here already knows. Minority stress, in our glossary →
Epistemic injustice refers to how people from marginalized communities are denied the opportunity to create knowledge and define their own meaning from their experiences. It’s about who is believed.
Sonny Jane Wise, a post on LinkedIn

On the peg: A lanyard with a visitor's badge clipped to it, although the building was your own life. The badge says visitor. It has said visitor in every room where the subject under discussion was you. In here the expert on your life is the person living it, and the next most expert is anybody else on the floor who has lived something like it, which is what the word peer means and all that it means. Epistemic injustice, in our glossary →
The world demands resilience. We are measured more often by our ability to take the hit and keep going rather than encouraged to stop the world from throwing punches.
NeuroHub Community Ltd, Justice Sensitivity And Autism: What Is It?, 2024

On the peg: A whistle on a cord, worn smooth where somebody kept on blowing it. Noticing what is unfair and not being able to stop noticing is heavy to carry, and it gets described as a flaw in the person carrying it. Nobody in here thinks you are too much about it. You are also allowed to put the whistle down for an evening, which is not the same as agreeing with anything. Justice sensitivity, in our glossary →
No matter the profession, moral injury destroys the capacity for trust and creates an expectation of harm, which leaves few options for the individual to act.
Brianne Kramer, Denisha Jones and Clint Broadbent, The Intensification of Moral Injury in Teachers During the Pandemic, 2026

On the peg: A work apron with a name badge still pinned to the bib. This is the one that comes from being made to do the harm, or to stand beside it, by a place that told you it was your job: a classroom, a ward, a caseload, a helpline with a script. It is not the same thing as being tired, and it does not lift while the place that did it is still open tomorrow. Nobody in here will tell you it was not that bad. Moral injury, in our glossary →
Normal is merely a social construct that controls individuals by enforcing a right way to function, a right way to be, a right way to exist as a human.
Sonny Jane Wise, Normal Is A Social Construct

On the peg: A school blazer on a hanger, cut for somebody else, with the sleeves hanging down past where any hands would be. Behind every other peg on this wall is this one: the idea that there is one right way to have a mind, and that the rest of us are that way done badly. The blazer was never going to fit and it was not cut for you to grow into. Hang it up with the others. Neuronormativity, in our glossary → The wall is longer than this, and nobody has finished putting pegs up. Further along it: the double empathy problem, the disability double bind, affective injustice, spoon theory, shutdown and meltdown. All of them are in our glossary, argued by the people who carried them.
It has come round to you

In a circle like this a talking piece goes round, and whoever is holding it may speak or may pass. Passing is a whole turn, and nobody comes back to you afterwards to check whether you have thought of something. Say it here. It goes nowhere: nothing is sent, nothing is kept, and nobody reads it, us included.
What is not in this room

No advice nobody asked for, and no tips. Not one list of ways to get better. Advice is for when somebody asks, and asking is allowed. No resilience. Nobody here is going to congratulate you on how much you can take. That is how most of us got here. No timeline, and no before and after. Nobody is waiting for you to be better, and nothing in this room assumes you will go back to how you were. Nothing counted. No attendance, no days since, no streak, and no check-in that remembers you came. Nobody at the front. No facilitator with a clipboard and no professional in the corner. The only expertise in the room is having been there. No light you have to sit in. It stays in the corridor. The door is ajar so that it can find you if you want it, and so that you can leave by it if you do not.

Not on this page. A web page cannot sit with anybody, and this one is the sign on the door rather than the room behind it. The people are in our community, by and for neurodivergent and disabled people, which is where our peer support lives, and on the CB Community Care’s channel is where anybody can ask for it. If what is wearing you out is money, mutual aid is the part of Stimpunks that exists because the systems failed us first. Further, and better than this page: Autistic Burnout: The Cost of Masking and Passing · The Ecology of Neurodivergent Burnout · Peer support · Peer respite · Rest

The name is a play on Dead Poets Society, the 1989 film directed by Peter Weir and written by Tom Schulman, about a group that meets away from a school built on conformity in order to resist it. We took the shape of the name and nothing else: no line, no scene, no character and no still. The poets in that title are dead. Everybody here is merely tired, and would like it on the record that merely tired is quite enough. Every line on a peg belongs to whoever wrote it, and is credited to them rather than to our glossary, which is where we found it: Finally Knowing Me, Monique Botha and David M. Tonight: disabled comics, on their own terms Comedy is a form of knowledge. When disabled comedians take the stage, they bring a perspective shaped by daily navigation of a world that was not designed for them — and they do it on their own terms, in their own voice, controlling the frame. They make audiences do their own thinking. Disabled comedians are not inspiring for being on stage. They are comics who happen to be disabled. And these sets map the gap between how disability is publicly discussed and how disabled people actually live, laugh, and relate to their own bodies and communities. From our Campfire Learn Together, Being Disabled Can Be Pretty Funny, where the community watched Josh Blue and Tina Friml together and talked about what their work reveals about disability, identity, and the world.

In this room, the only thing that stands in the light is what the comics said. Everything else — our write-up, our notes, the house rules — is out here in the dark with the audience, which is where it belongs.
“well, fuck cerebral palsy, we could really be helping people.”

Josh Blue has cerebral palsy and is a Paralympian in soccer. He won Last Comic Standing in 2006 and has been touring for over twenty years. His specials center disability without apologizing for it: life with a palsy arm that “has some stuff to do” after dark, a restaurant server who asks his friend “what will he have,” getting put on the disabled list after an injury at the Paralympics, and Botox, which in his telling was developed to help people with cerebral palsy before somebody noticed it would sell. On being put on the disabled list after an injury at the Paralympics. His friend’s answer, in his bit, when a server asked the friend what he would have. On Botox, and on who medical research turns out to be for.
“I don’t suffer from cerebral palsy, I suffer from people”

Tina Friml has cerebral palsy. She frames herself as “the bisexuality of ability” — not fully committed to either side — and names three perks of being a disabled comic: she can never be a hack (“nothing about this is relatable”), CP is the most interesting thing about her (otherwise she is just “a liberal white girl from Vermont”), and nothing she does can fail, because an audience will file all of it under inspiration. That last one is not a boast. It is a critique. She calls it being on “free play” — a baby who cheated death and has been in the bonus round ever since. The social model of disability, compressed into a punchline. One of the three perks of being a disabled comic: she can never be a hack. Not fully committed to either side, which is where a great many of us live. Every line in the light is quoted from our write-up, belongs to the comic who said it, and is 30 words or fewer. The write-up does not say which set each one comes from, and neither do we. The line under each is ours.

Not on the playlist yet, so putting the whole night on will not reach them: Three-Way, Stuart Laws; Is That Guy Still Going?, Stuart Laws. They play from the bill like every other set. The bill takes suggestions. If you know a set by a Disabled comic, working on their own terms, send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. It goes on our playlist first and onto the bill once somebody has watched it, and it is checked to see that it plays and can be shown here before it goes anywhere.

“I suffer from people” — not from cerebral palsy. That is the social model of disability in one sentence. Comedy delivers it where argument bounces off. Even bombing is treated as a TED Talk. Inspiration exploitation means disabled people cannot lose, and that is not a compliment: it removes disabled people from the possibility of being judged on their actual work. “Free play” is the same trap from another angle. It sounds like freedom. It is also a way of being taken out of ordinary life. “Nothing about this is relatable” is not a limitation. It is a position. Comedy from genuinely outside perspectives makes an audience aware of the frame it was inside without knowing it. Asking somebody’s companion “what will he have?” while the disabled person is sitting right there is not a rare failure of manners. It is a routine expression of the assumption that a disabled person at the table is not the one to address. The same person with the same walk gets read as a celebrity, a drunk, or a danger, depending on who is looking. Disability legibility is not neutral. It is shaped by race, gender, class and context. The disability community is the only minority group everyone will eventually join. If that is true, why is it still treated as other, and why is joining it coded as loss? Being around other disabled people — where your disability is the norm, not the exception — changes what you can say, how much energy you spend, and how you move through space. That kind of community is not a luxury. It is a need. From the takeaways of the same write-up, lightly trimmed.

The Campfire ended with questions rather than answers. Three of them, to take home with you: What would it mean for a disabled person to just be bad at something — unremarkable, having a normal day? When have you seen humor do something that more direct advocacy couldn’t? And what are the costs of always having to be funny to be heard? There’s a difference between laughing with a comedian and laughing at the subject of their jokes. How do you read the difference in a room? The rest of them are in the write-up. Campfire Learn Together is where we watch things like this together, and it is open to the whole community.
On the bar: The Daily Tism

Not stand-up, and on the bar anyway. The Daily Tism is a satirical news site in the vein of The Onion, and every story in it is about being Autistic. Sara Gibbs and Elsa Williams founded it in 2024, and it is written by Autistic people for Autistic people — “and the people who like to laugh with us,” in their own words. It turns the usual coverage round the way the sets on the bill turn the usual frame round: Public warned to stop armchair diagnosing celebrities as neurotypical. It makes a sitcom, too. It’s a Superpower?? is an audio sitcom, which they call the first made by a team of Autistic creatives for an Autistic audience: five Autistic people meet at a support group, end up with magic powers they cannot control, and have to save the world from a neurotypical supervillain. The question marks are part of the title. It is made to be heard on headphones, and we think it is really good. Both are The Daily Tism’s and both live on their own site. Nothing on this page reaches it until you follow a link, and the sitcom plays there, from them.

There is no cover and no two-drink minimum, and nothing in here is for sale. The water on the stool is free. The way in is a ramp, and so is the way onto the stage. The mic comes down to whatever height the comic wants it at, and nobody has to sit on the stool. Nobody in the front row is made part of the act without asking to be. Sit wherever you like. Talk to the comic. Not to whoever came in with them. Bombing is allowed. A set that does not land is a set that did not land, and nobody here will turn it into a TED Talk. Nobody is called brave for getting up there. Tell them they were funny, or tell them they were not. Nobody headlines, either. The bill runs in the order the playlist keeps, and a place on it is not a rank. Laughter is loud and arrives without warning, which makes a comedy club one of the harder rooms on any street to be in. Nothing here plays until you press it, the volume is yours, and leaving in the middle of a set is not heckling. Laughingstock is the name of the club. It is nobody’s job.

Every set belongs to the comics who wrote and performed it, who are named on every one, and to the channels that published it. None of them is affiliated with Stimpunks and none of them endorses us. Nothing here is hosted by us: each set is on YouTube, and nothing reaches YouTube until you press play. The playlist is ours, on our own channel. The writing at the top, the takeaways and the questions are ours, from our Campfire Learn Together write-up. The lines in the light are the comics’ own, as that write-up quotes them. The Daily Tism and It’s a Superpower?? are The Daily Tism’s. We link to them and host and play nothing of theirs, and they are not affiliated with Stimpunks either. The name is an ordinary English word for the person everybody laughs at. In here it is the name of the one room where the comic decides what the joke is. The neon is Yellowtail, by Astigmatic, under the Apache License 2.0, and it sets the club’s name, the comics’ names and nothing you have to read. Everything you do read is Bricolage Grotesque, by Mathieu Triay, under the SIL Open Font License — bricolage being making do with whatever is to hand. More in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and in here, MAX GLITTER is the water on the stool going sparkling.

Every screening is a relaxed screening. The house lights stay up. A lot of us found out who we were from a video. Somebody on a screen described a life that turned out to be ours — the textures, the plans that fell apart, the conversations that went sideways for no reason anybody would name — and something switched on. This picture house is named for that moment, and for the short film on its first screen that calls it a lightbulb moment. Most of what is showing here was made by the people it is about. Every screen is one of our own playlists, and every film on them has a card on a rack saying who made it, how long it runs and what is in it, before you press anything.
Every screening is a relaxed screening
Awareness says: Donate to the awesome organizations that have all the pretty puzzle pieces and all the pretty blue lights!
Amy Sequenzia, I Don’t Want Your Awareness, as quoted in our Acceptance entry
Every screening is a relaxed screening

The house lights stay up. Nobody sits in the dark who did not ask to. The captions are on. Every screen here asks for them before the film starts, and you can switch them off in the player. Nothing plays until you press it, nothing plays before the film you chose, and the volume is yours. Move, stim, rock, pace, flap, hum, sit on the floor, lie across three seats. Nobody shushes anybody. Bring your ear defenders, or borrow the pair hung on the seat in the second row. Come in late and leave early. You can walk out in the middle of a film and walk back in at the end of it, and nobody will ask why. Every film on a rack tells you what is in it before you press play — how long it runs, and anything you might want to know first, from a panic attack to a sponsor segment. Every screen has a rack under it, and every rack folds away if you would rather not scroll past it. Nothing in this building is blue. Every April, autism charities run by parents and professionals light landmarks up blue, and autistic people have been saying for years what they think of it — one of them, below, better than we could. The bulbs here are warm on purpose, there is no puzzle piece anywhere in the place, and the ornament over the screen is the gold infinity — Autistic UK’s, from Au, the chemical symbol for gold.

← back to the street on the street · the same table as last time · no need to order A café on the street, the same as last time

Today’s special: your favourite. In the window: one divided plate, with pesto pasta in the big well on the left, nooch popcorn along the top right, cheese in the well below it, and the peanut butter in a small well of its own. On the right of the plate, a mug of coffee. On the left, the apple slices in a ramekin, to go with the peanut butter on the plate; on Ryan’s list they are one thing, and they meet when whoever is eating them decides they meet, and below them Ronan’s ketchup in its own ramekin, touching nothing, which is how Ronan has every red thing. Nothing on the table touches anything else, and every food on it is off a regular’s tray further down. A café for samefoods and safe foods, and for anybody whose plate has ever been treated as a problem somebody else had to solve. The kitchen knows its regulars: it keeps what each of them has, the way they have it, and it is ready for the day their samefood changes with the season, so the menu is whatever the regulars ask for and nothing on it changes unless somebody asks. Nobody here will ask you to try a bite of anything, nothing on your plate touches anything else unless you want it to, and the light over the table is the same at every hour, so that nothing on the plate ever looks different from last time.

We default to structure, separation and predictability, and every guest is accommodated individually. You are never regarded as fussy, picky or too much: you are quietly and professionally accommodated. The house fits itself to you, never the other way round, and nobody’s way of eating is anybody else’s rule. The same again is always on. Nobody asks whether you would like to try something different today. Samefoods have seasons. If yours changes, or you put one down for a while and come back to it years later, the kitchen still has it, and nobody asks why. Nothing touches unless you want it to. Every plate in here is divided for whoever needs it, every bowl is yours to fill the way you eat it, and every plate is the same plate and every bowl the same bowl. And if you do not mind your food touching, nobody here minds for you. Some of us need everything apart and some of us do not care at all, and both are the same again. Anything can come in a ramekin of its own, if you ask. Ronan, a Stimpunk, has every condiment that way and red things always, touching nothing else, so his ketchup comes in its own — and that is Ronan’s way, not the house’s, so nobody else’s ketchup has to. The same brand, the same shape, the same way. We can tell the difference as well, and nobody in here will tell you that you can’t. Nobody comments on your plate: not what is on it, not how much, and not how often you have had it. Nothing is hidden in anything. What it looks like is what it is, all the way through. Nobody has to eat with anybody. A table for one is a whole table. Nobody finishes your samefood without asking. Our glossary calls that a tragedy, and in here it is treated as one. Nobody in here is a picky eater. Selective, sensory, hypersensory, or simply somebody who knows exactly what they need: all of it is welcome, and none of it needs explaining.
This café gets its menu from our glossary, and the menu is three words long. Each one is on a plate of its own.
A samefood often needs to be prepared in a very specific way, eaten in a ritualistic manner, or may only be a specific brand.
C.L. Lynch, 7 Cool Aspects of Autistic Culture, NeuroClastic, 2019Read against NeuroClastic's own page on 2026-09-23, byline from the page's own metadata.

Eating the same food, often, sometimes for weeks or months at a time, made the same way every time and sometimes only one brand of it. It is how a great many of us eat, and plenty of us say it brings peace. Samefoods have seasons, too: one can carry you for months, get put down, and come back years later, and the kitchen here keeps every one of them. Nobody has an opinion about any of it. Samefood, in our glossary →
These foods are not boring to me. They are the reason I can sit at a table at all.
Kari Burroughs Kraakevik, Safe Foods, Thinking Person’s Guide to Autism, 2026Read against Thinking Person’s Guide to Autism’s own page on 2026-09-23.

A food you can reliably eat, especially when everything else is hard: the texture, the taste, the smell and the predictability are all right, and it asks nothing unexpected of you. Our glossary puts it plainly: safe foods are about access, and for many of us they are how eating becomes possible at all. Safe food, in our glossary →
Food aversion is okay. It’s not something I’m trying to cure.
Matthew Broberg-Moffitt, Color Taste Texture, Penguin Publishing Group, 2023Read off our own Food Aversion entry, which quotes the book; not checked against a copy of the book from here.

A body saying that a food is not safe, through its texture, its taste, its temperature, its smell or its colour, and meaning it. It is neurobiological rather than a mood, and nobody in here argues with it. Our glossary entry is careful about where it sits beside ARFID, and is the better place to read about that than a menu. Food aversion, in our glossary →
If you only eat a specific brand of frozen breaded chicken nuggets, you find comfort in the knowledge that what you are going to eat is both familiar and unproblematic.
Matthew Broberg-Moffitt, Color Taste Texture, Penguin Publishing Group, 2023Read off our own Samefood entry, which quotes the book; not checked against a copy of the book from here.

One book, because one is the right number of books for a counter to have. Color Taste Texture Recipes for Picky Eaters, Those with Food Aversion, and Anyone Who’s Ever Cringed at Food by Matthew Broberg-Moffitt · Penguin Publishing Group, 2023 · ISBN 9780593538593 A cookbook that starts from acceptance rather than correction. Our glossary calls it a compassionate, validating and accessible guide, and recommends it to our community, which is why it is the one book on this counter. The recipes are for the people its subtitle names, and the stance is the one this whole café is built on: the plate is not the problem, and neither is the person eating from it. Find it in a library Its Open Library record From an independent bookshop

Our community’s own samefoods, each person’s on a tray of their own and each food in a well of its own, with a bowl of whatever is their samefood of the moment. They are written down exactly as they were given — lowercase, brands and all — and they are being collected a few at a time in our community’s Discord, so there are more people to come and more trays to set. A tray changes whenever its person says so, because samefoods come and go and come back.

Nobody’s list is tidied, corrected, sorted or ranked, nothing is added up across the trays, and nothing on one tray is compared with anything on another. Every list comes down the moment the person whose it is asks, and coming down means gone rather than hidden. If you would like a tray of your own, tell us in our community.
What is not on the menu

No calories, no nutrition labels, and no sorting of anybody’s food into good and bad. No ‘just one bite’, and no ‘they will eat when they get hungry enough’. Our Food Aversion entry says what that second one can do, and it is not nothing. Nothing smuggled into anything else. A plate you cannot trust is a plate you cannot eat from. No recipes and no tips about eating. There is a book on the counter by somebody who knows, and a menu that does not change. Nothing counted: not how many of us drink coffee, and not how many times anybody has had the same again. No surprise dish. A new one goes on the menu only when somebody asks for it — a regular, or somebody walking in for the first time — and the kitchen keeps it from then on, the way that person has it. Nothing is ever put in front of you that you did not order, and nothing comes off the menu because somebody else got bored of it.

Every quotation belongs to whoever wrote it, and is credited to them rather than to our glossary, which is where we found most of them: C.L. Lynch at NeuroClastic, Kari Burroughs Kraakevik at Thinking Person’s Guide to Autism, and Matthew Broberg-Moffitt, whose book is on the counter. The lists on the trays belong to the people whose names are on them, and the way about red things and ramekins is Ronan’s own. The words round all of it, and the drawing of the table, are ours. Every quotation in this café is 30 words or fewer, names who said it, where and when, and says beside it how it was checked. tools/make-samefood.py refuses a longer one, and refuses the vocabulary of correcting somebody’s plate, a tally, and advice about eating, in the room’s own voice. It also walks every coordinate of the drawing of the table and refuses anything on it that touches anything else. Further, and better than a menu: Samefood · Safe food · Food aversion · Bodily autonomy · Neuroception and Sensory Load The type is Fredoka, by Milena Brandão and Hafontia, for the café’s name and headings, and Inclusive Sans, by Olivia King, for everything you read: a face drawn so that no letter can be taken for another, which is this room’s rule about plates arriving at the size of the alphabet. Both under the SIL Open Font License. More in the liner notes.

A cabinet of our people’s collections. The house brings the furniture; the light is theirs. In the picture: the gallery from the doorway, dark, with the cabinets standing apart on the bare floor. Ryan’s pens, paper and ink: a writing box open on a little table, with a daylight desk lamp on an arm, lit; Ryan’s perfume: a tall cupboard with its door ajar, with a strip light inside the door, switched off, because there is nothing in it yet; Norah and her husband’s leather swatches and stamping tools: a pegboard on the wall over a bench, with no lamp yet, because the lamp is Norah and her husband’s to choose; Chelsea’s house plants: a plant stand in three steps, with no lamp yet, because the lamp is Chelsea’s to choose; Helen’s books and rocks: a chest of shallow drawers with books along the top and one drawer pulled out, with no lamp yet, because the lamp is Helen’s to choose. Some of us keep things. Pens, and the inks that go in them; perfume; the swatches and tools a trade is made of; plants on every sill; books, and rocks. This is a gallery of our people’s collections, one cabinet each, and every cabinet has a lamp of its own chosen for the thing it lights. There are no house lights. What you can see in here is exactly what somebody has decided to show you.
Some special interests are short lived, and some last the lifetime of the person; but, however long they last, they are intense, delightful, and a vital part of autistic culture.
C.L. Lynch, 7 Cool Aspects of Autistic Culture, NeuroClastic, 2019. Read against NeuroClastic's own page on 2026-09-23. Special Interest, in our glossary.
Many of us identify with the items we love, and even feel a degree of empathy for them, as if they were alive.

Devon Price, Unmasking Autism, Harmony Books, 2022. Read off our own Object Personification entry, which quotes the book at pages 169 and 170; not checked against a copy of the book from here. Object Personification, in our glossary.

Nobody in here needs a reason, and nobody is asked for one. But the things we keep have a way of being more than things, and two of our glossary entries say why better than a label could. A special interest is a whole way of paying attention, and a collection is often what one looks like from across a room: And object personification: the pen that would be lonely in the drawer, the rock that is glad to be back on the shelf. That is not a mistake about pens and rocks. It is care, and it is ordinary, and in here it is how everything on display is treated.

One per collection, in the order they arrived. Each owner is named the way they asked to be, and anything that reached us through somebody else says so on its label. A cabinet with nothing in it yet stands with its lamp off, and its label is exactly as easy to read as the lit ones: an empty cabinet is not a lesser one, it is one that is waiting. Ryan’s

Nobody asks how many. A collection is not a number, and nothing in here is counted: not the pens, not the plants, not the cabinets. Nothing is priced, valued or called rare. What a thing might fetch is none of our business, and a page that listed what people own with a price beside each thing would be a list for somebody else to shop from. Nothing is ranked. No best cabinet, no biggest collection, and nobody’s pens set against anybody else’s. Every cabinet has its own lamp, and no two lamps in here are alike. The owner chooses it. The house only ever guesses at the furniture. A collection can be anything somebody keeps on purpose. It can stop for years, sit in a drawer, and start again, and nobody asks why. Nobody explains their collection to anybody. “What is it for?” is not asked in here. The pictures are of things, never of people. A photograph with a person in it belongs on the polaroid wall, which has its own promises and its own consent record. Nothing in a picture says where you live. The location a phone writes into every photograph is stripped before a file comes anywhere near this site, and every frame is looked at for an address, a letter or a view out of a window before it goes up. Nothing is filtered or cropped. A photograph is made smaller so the page loads, and that is all that is done to it. The lamp’s colour goes round the picture and never over it. Everything comes down when you say so, one thing or the whole cabinet. It comes out of the repository too, and nobody asks whether you are sure.

Send the photographs, and that is the whole job. Phone pictures are fine, badly lit is fine, the desk behind them is fine. You do not have to title anything, describe anything or caption anything: the house does the describing, and says it did. That is the opposite of the polaroid wall, on purpose. The wall asks you to write the words for a picture of yourself, because a description of a person is theirs to write and nobody else’s. A description of a pen is not a description of anybody. It is work, and work is exactly the thing that stops people sending a picture at all, so in here the house takes it. The describing is done by Claude, an AI, looking at each photograph, and every cabinet says so on its label. It writes only what it can see: colour, shape, what a thing is made of, what it is standing beside. It does not name a maker or a model from what a thing looks like, because a guess on a label reads as a fact. If a name is printed on the thing and can be read in the picture, it can go on the label; otherwise the name is yours to give, and yours wins over anything the house wrote. Reach us through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community, say whose collection it is and how you want to be named, and it goes in a cabinet. To take anything down, the same routes, and the word remove is enough.

Every collection belongs to the person whose name is on its cabinet, and so does every photograph of it. The photographs are not under this site’s Creative Commons licence and carry no licence onward at all, so that taking one down stays possible: a Creative Commons licence cannot be revoked, and “it comes down when you say so” would otherwise be a promise the licence contradicted. Every quotation belongs to whoever wrote it: C.L. Lynch at NeuroClastic, and Devon Price, whose book we have read only as far as our own glossary quotes it, and say so beside the line. Every quotation in this room is 30 words or fewer, names who said it, where and when, and says beside it how it was checked. tools/make-collection.py refuses a longer one; refuses a photograph that still carries any metadata, that nobody has described, or that nobody has looked at for a person or an address; refuses a maker’s name in words Claude wrote unless it can be read in the picture; refuses a filter on any photograph; and refuses two cabinets with the same lamp. Further, and better than a label: Special Interest · Object Personification · Monotropism · Infodump The type is Gloock, by Duarte Pinto, for the room’s name and every label’s heading — a sharp, high-contrast serif of the kind a museum cuts its labels in — and Hanken Grotesk, by Alfredo Marco Pradil and Hanken Design Co., for everything you read. Both are on the Foundry’s shelves.

Build your own bowl or wrap, or have one of ours. On the shelf over the counter, cut through the middle like everything else in here: scallions, with their white bulbs showing under the soil; cilantro, lacy and many-lobed; garlic, a whole bulb in the soil with its cloves drawn in; ginger, tall and narrow-leaved over a knobbly rhizome; a chili plant with its red chilies hanging; carrots, feathery on top and one orange root going down; red potatoes, three of them in the soil under the leaves; flat Italian parsley, broader-leaved than the cilantro; a leek, its white shaft half under the soil; and a small lemon tree with lemons on it. Every pot on it is something in the pantry, and where the part the kitchen uses grows underground, you can see it under the soil. Everything in here is plants, and everything in here is drawn the way a cook sketches a dish to show what is in it: cut straight through the middle, so you can see every layer sitting on the one under it. Build your own bowl or wrap out of the pantry below, or start from one of the combos on the board, each standing on a flavour base from somewhere in the world. The pantry is Ryan’s own, the list he cooks from at home, so these are a real kitchen’s shelves rather than a menu somebody imagined. When you have built something, copy it and take it shopping.

This room was going to be called Ital Plant Livity, and both of those words are Rastafari’s. Ital comes from vital with the v taken off, so that the word begins with I, which Rastafari speech does to a great many words; livity is the life Rastafari hold is in everybody. Rastafari has been a big influence on Ryan, and the playlist on the stereo is still called Ital Plant Livity and is full of songs about Ital food. But this kitchen is not Ital, so it does not say it is. Many people who keep Ital avoid food with anything added to it, and some avoid added salt; this pantry has three kinds of salt, MSG, soy sauce and things out of packets. And how Ital is kept varies from one person to the next, which is not ours to settle from outside. So the name over the door says what it means in plain English, and the songs say the rest in their own words. Ital, on Wikipedia, which is where the lines above were checked.

Plant-based cooks on YouTube, chosen by Ryan and in the order he listed them, with the last month of what each one has put up, shorts and all, newest first under each cook. A machine refills it every morning and the older ones go off the end, so nobody here watched these first: Ryan chose the cooks, not the videos. Nothing plays until you press play, and every video says how long it runs before you press it. Each one plays where it hangs, or goes up on the telly. The titles are the cooks’ own, as they wrote them, capitals and emoji and all. If a title says what a dish will do for you, that is theirs to say; the house rule that nobody in here tells you what a bowl does for your body is ours.

Everything in here is plants. Every bowl, every wrap, everything at the counter. Everything touches. The sauce runs into the rice and that is the idea. If you need your food kept apart, Samefood Cafe is a few doors along, and nothing on a plate in there touches anything. Vital means alive. Nobody in here will tell you what a bowl does for your body, and nothing on the board is good for you or bad for you. It is food. Nothing is weighed and nothing is counted: no portions, no numbers on anything, no favourite of the week. The builder keeps nothing and sends nothing. Copying puts your ticket on your own clipboard and nowhere else, and closing the page empties the bowl. No claims about anybody’s cooking. A flavour base is where a kitchen somewhere starts from; what you build on it is yours. Hot peppers, everything. Nooch, everything. Those two are Ryan’s, and they are on the house.

The pantry is Ryan’s, the list he cooks from for himself, written down as he gave it, including his names for its sections and his list of pairings, trinities and go-tos, which is where every flavour base in the builder comes from. Where a line of his held several things it is split into them, and a thing on his list twice is in the builder once. The combos, the notes on them and the drawings are ours. The words Ital and livity are Rastafari’s, and the songs on the stereo belong to the musicians named beside them. tools/make-vital.py builds this room out of one data file. It refuses a combo that brings in anything the pantry does not keep, and a combo that stands on no flavour base. It refuses the word Ital anywhere on the menu. It refuses the vocabulary of authenticity, of wellness and of counting in the room’s own voice. And it refuses a pot on the shelf that is not on the menu, and anything you can tick that the drawing of your bowl would not know how to draw. The type is Bagel Fat One, by Kyungwon Kim and JAMO, for the kitchen’s name and its headings, and Be Vietnam Pro, by Lâm Bảo, Tony Le and ViệtAnh Nguyễn, for everything you read: open, round-shouldered and easy going down a long list, which is most of this page.
