CB sign-on at the front desk The street’s community center, a quiet room in sage lime plaster. One big window faces north onto a hillside, so the light is soft and the same all day and no sun lands anywhere, and a deep seat is built into the bay under it, with a cushion, a folded throw and a plant on the sill; there is a radio on the front desk. This is where you get started in our community: how to join the CB with an invite and a username of your own, just below. The radio is the CB, a chat channel patterned after citizens band radio, and this is the only place it is switched on. Sign on with your username and your password and it rides along in the corner of your screen, on every page of the street, until you sign off. Our community talks on the CB and in the forums, which are the CB’s too, for whatever needs longer than a day. Every room on the street, and who is in each, is on the World room’s web, past the Garden’s spider. On the wall by the desk is the community service board: every way there is to give something to a room on this street, and how.

Ask to join. Go to the Stimpunks Community page and request to join, with the join form. It takes a few minutes, and you share only what you are comfortable sharing. As part of that, you are given an invite to Stimpunks.World: a link, or a code. A moderator can give you one too. Open the invite’s link. It opens the joining page with the code filled in. If you were given a code on its own, type it in there. Choose your username and a password of your own, eight characters or more, and an email address for password recovery if you want one. Then press Join. Keep the recovery code the joining page shows you then. It is shown once, and it is the way back in if you forget your password: write it down, or keep it where you keep your passwords.

From the moment you join, your username signs on with your own password and nothing else, so nobody else can be you. Next time, sign on at the front desk, below, or with Get on the CB on the bar in the bottom right corner of any page. Account, on the radio in the part called You, is where you change your password, add, change or take off your email address, or delete your username. On the CB with the old starter password? It was retired on 21 October 2026, when every username on the CB came to be claimed. The radio asks you to claim the username you are on as, with a password of your own, before anything else: press Claim and your username, and keep the recovery code it shows you. Your pets, avatars and everything else kept under the username stay with it. Signed off already? Ask a moderator for an invite.

Now that you are on, you can chat on the CB, post to our forums, fill in your profile, and much more. Here are some quests you can go on: Post an introduction in the forums’ Introductions, saying as much or as little as you like. Adopt a pet from Rescue A Cat, Rescue A Dog or Rescue Small Animals. Your pets live in Profile on your radio. Collect badges by doing jobs from the Adventurer’s Guild: jobs that go together make a badge. Collect patches lying about the street and on some shop counters, and sew them onto your battle jacket. Where the patches are, in Profile, lists them. Make your profile your own with a profile card, avatars from the Bodymind Booth, and a theme for your radio. Scroll down this page for the CB’s house norms and the community service board, with everything else there is to do and give here.

Sign on with your username and your own password. New here? You join with an invite, on the joining page: Getting started, above, says how to get one. A moderator whose username on the moderators’ list is not claimed yet claims it there, with the moderators’ password. Your username Your password Forgotten your password? Gave an email address for recovery? We send a reset code to it, from our team’s mailbox, usually within ten minutes. It works for an hour, in the form below. The answer here is the same whether or not the address is the one on your username, so it tells nobody anything about anybody’s address. Your username The email address on it Then use the code, or the recovery code you were given when you joined, or a reset code from a moderator, and choose a new password. Your username Your recovery code, a reset code we emailed, or a moderator’s A new password The same again You are on the channel as . Once you are on, Account on the radio is where your username is kept: its password, its email address for recovery, and the way to delete it. Signing on keeps your username, a pass and where you put the radio in your own browser. What the channel keeps, for how long, and what it never keeps are all on the privacy page.

Every button and switch on the radio, named the way the radio names it, is in the CB guide. These are the things worth knowing first. Open is on and closed is off. While the radio is open and the tab is in front of you, it listens to the channel every few seconds. Fold it away, or look at another tab, and it stops listening altogether. Notifications only if you ask for them. The radio has no chimes, no badges and no unread count, and nothing is saved up for when you come back. Notifications, under Your radio, can switch a device on to be told when somebody @mentions you, when there is a message in a room you follow, when a call starts, or about everything on World, even with the site closed. Each is off until you switch it on, and Privacy says what that keeps. A picture can go with a message. Press Picture beside Transmit, pick a screenshot or a photo, and say what is in it if you like. The radio redraws it before it goes, which takes off where it was taken and anything else the camera wrote into it, and it goes when its message goes. Press a picture to see it larger, and Download keeps a copy on your own device; the same norm as a screenshot applies to passing it on. A message can be long. Up to 2,000 characters, and it keeps its lines: Enter sends and Shift and Enter starts a new line. The box grows as you type, and you can drag its corner to make it taller. A little Markdown works: **bold**, *italic*, `code`, three backticks on a line of their own round a block of code, > at the start of a line for a quote, and - or 1. for a list. A link’s words are always its address, so [words](an address) stays as you typed it. Copy on a message puts its words, as they were typed, on your own clipboard. Be seen here, if you like. In any room, Be seen here on the radio shows you, by your handle, to anybody else signed on who has switched it on in that room, and shows them to you, with the names of everybody in that room’s call, so you can see who is there before you join. Names only, and no count. It also puts you on Who’s online, beside World and This room, where anybody signed on can see who is around and which room they are in, and go there; typing @ in Teleport finds somebody the same way. While it is off you are on nobody’s list. Your browser remembers it until you switch it off. A profile card, if you claim your username. Press somebody’s handle, on the channel or on Who’s online, and their profile opens: their card, and their avatars, pets, badges and battle jacket as they have chosen to show them. Edit my profile card, in Profile, fills in yours: a theme and a banner, a decoration round the avatar you wear, a frame round your profile and an effect over it, a face for your name, a nameplate on Who’s online, your pronouns, a few words about yourself, links elsewhere and your favourite room. Whatever you fill in is shown to anybody signed on, and nothing on it says when you joined. Privacy has the whole of it. From an icon to the whole window. − and + on the bar take the radio down and up through an icon of a CB set, which is still listening and shows nothing else; Small, which is the bar and the newest message and still listening; Normal; Large, which is wider and taller, for long messages and pictures; and Full, the whole window, for when you want only the CB. Press the icon to open the radio again. A hundred messages, for two weeks, unless a channel says otherwise. The latest hundred are all there is on a channel; once it is full, the newest pushes the oldest off, and every message is deleted two weeks after it was sent, unless our administrators have set that channel otherwise, which the radio says under In this channel, so people in every timezone get to read it. Take off on a message you sent takes it off the air sooner, for everybody, with its picture and its reactions. It cannot be put back. Edit changes the words of a message you sent; it then says edited, and the words it had before are not kept. The forums are the CB’s too, for what needs longer than two weeks. The forums keep topics for weeks or months, in categories, and only a claimed username can read or write in them. Take to the forums, under a message’s three dots, starts a topic with messages from the channel, copied exactly as they are on the channel. What they keep. The same sign-on writes on the chalkboard. Plural Mural has a chalkboard at the foot of its wall, Helen Edgar’s idea, and only people signed on here can chalk a note on it. It is not the channel: anybody walking past can read it, signed on or not, and a note stays up for seven days, where a message on the channel stays two weeks. It sits in the bottom right corner. Drag it by its bar to put it somewhere else, or press Move, the six dots, and use the arrow keys; Home puts it back in the corner. It remembers where you left it. It reads aloud if you want it to. With the radio open, a screen reader hears new messages as they come in, and the switch New messages to a screen reader turns that off. Speak new messages aloud is for everybody else: switch it on and the radio reads each new message out, handle first, in your own device’s voice, with a burst of squelch as the station keys up and the tail as it lets go, like a voice coming over the air. At the Gentle setting you get the words without the static. It is off until you turn it on, it never reads what was already on the channel when you tuned in, and folding the radio away stops it. A screen reader user with both switches on will hear everything twice. There is one room it stays out of. The Healing Checkpoint, room 429, promises that it writes nothing down about you, and a radio that listens to a server and remembers where you put it would make that untrue. So the radio waits outside that door and is there again when you come out.

Our covenant is the floor. Everything in the Stimpunks Covenant applies on the channel, as it does in every Stimpunks space. A reaction names who pressed it. React on a message puts a heart, an otter, a penguin or any other emoji under it with your handle beside it, and pressing it again takes yours back. Nobody is shown a count, only names, so a reaction is a person saying something small, not a score. A username is somebody’s, and only theirs. Every username on the CB is claimed, and signs on only with its owner’s own password, so a message under a name came from whoever holds that name’s password. It says nothing more about who they are. BASE is the one mark, and it means a moderator: only our moderators can send it, each under their own username off the moderators’ list. Nobody can type it or tick it; only the server puts it there. World, or this room. The radio hears one channel at a time. World is the one the whole street shares. This room is the room you are standing in, heard by whoever else is tuned to it there, and walking into another room tuned that way hears that room’s channel instead. Every channel keeps a hundred messages, each for two weeks, unless our administrators set it otherwise, and the radio says which. Every room has a call. Join this room’s call opens voice and video for the room you are in, for people signed on to the CB. The rooms off the Town Hall for our directors, board and moderators are the base’s: anybody can walk in, and their channel and call are for the base alone. Camera and microphone start off, and camera off and microphone off is a fine way to be in a call. The base station moderates, and is the only one who can record a call or turn on transcription; before doing either, say so in the call, and a recording or transcript is shared only if everybody in it has said yes, the same as a screenshot of the channel. Anybody can share a YouTube video in the call for everybody to watch together; whoever shares it plays and pauses it for everybody, and while it plays with its sound on, Jitsi mutes your microphone, so unmute to talk over it. For watching at your own pace instead, use the room’s own players and the CB’s spots. Anybody in a call can share a screenshot or a photo there with Share file; it goes to 8x8, not to us, so share nothing with somebody else in it unless they have said yes, the same as a screenshot of the channel. It is a room, not a private line. Everybody on the CB can read the channel. Say what you would say in a room with people in it. What is said here stays here. That goes for pictures too. The channel forgets after two weeks; do not carry it off in a screenshot, a repost or a forum topic unless everybody in it has said you can. That is the covenant’s own privacy norm, on the one channel of ours built to forget. If somebody takes what you said to the forums anyway, Take my message out there takes it back. Nobody has to answer. A notification is the reader’s own choice, never a summons, and an @mention is not a deadline: nobody is waiting on you. A message into a quiet channel is fine, a quiet channel is fine, and you can leave without saying goodbye. Plain words are fine. Say ten-four and breaker-breaker if you like them. Nobody needs to know the codes. A room on the street is a link. Type # and the start of its name, like #den, pick it from the list, and everybody on the channel sees it as #The Den, linked. Arrow keys move through the list, Enter or Tab picks, and Escape leaves your # alone. A room’s full address works too, like stimpunks.world/the-den.html. An address on another site is a link that says it is leaving. Write it out with https:// and it opens in a new tab, with the site it goes to after it, like ↗ example.com. Check that name before you follow it: a handle proves nothing about who sent it. A link can have words of its own, [words](an address), and one to another site still has its site after the words, so check that name too. A place in a film is a button. Watching something together, type @ and the time, like @34:12 or @1:02:03, or press Add my spot to put in where your film has got to, which film it is and which room you are in. Everybody sees it as a button that moves the film on their own page to that place, and the room as a link to go there. Following that link takes you to the film’s play button, ready to start at that place when you press it. If a spot names a room or a film, it only moves that film in that room, and anywhere else it tells you where that spot is instead. It does not press play, so anybody taking a break can catch up when they come back. A time without the @, like 7:30, stays words. Hosting is a beacon, not a remote. Press Host this film while you watch something, and everybody on the channel sees where you are in it and in which room, with a Catch up button if they are in the same room, and a Follow switch that keeps their film in step with yours, at their own volume. Nobody’s film moves unless they press one of those themselves, and pausing your own film stops following, so taking a break and coming back is always fine. One person hosts a room at a time. Keep the password inside the community. It only changes if there is a problem, and everybody is signed off when it does. If something is wrong, tell the base. Say so on the channel, or reach us privately. The base station can take any message off the air, as you can take off your own. If it keeps happening, the password changes, which signs everybody off at once, and that is the only other lever there is.

The Stimpunks Covenant is where our community norms live, and it is longer and better than anything this room could say about them. It starts from the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1, which every Stimpunk agrees to abide by, and adds what we have learned since: no proselytising, prosocial ways of settling conflict, and how to repair harm when it happens. Read it on stimpunks.org, where it is kept up to date, rather than here, where it would not be.

The ash pigeonholes on the wall by the desk have a slot for every room on the street that takes something in from our community. Each slot says what the room takes, what it asks of you and how to send it, and points at the room’s own words, where the full terms are. Nothing on this board sends anything, and neither does the CB: the radio forgets after two weeks and everybody signed on can read it, which is the wrong place for somebody’s photograph. Everything here goes the way its own room says, and you do not need to be signed on to the radio for any of it.

The Polaroid Wall, in Enid’s Room A photograph of you, for the wall in Enid’s Room. Say how you want to be named, and what you want said about the picture, or nothing at all. The yes has to be yours. A young person’s yes is their own, and a parent’s does not stand in for it. It goes up as you sent it: nobody crops it or filters it. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How the wall takes one, and gives it back

The Collection Collection Photographs of something you collect, for a cabinet of your own under a lamp you choose. Choose the lamp, and say why it suits what it lights. No two lamps in there are alike. The house writes the titles and descriptions and says it did, so you do not have to. Nothing is counted, priced or called rare, and nothing in a photograph may say where you live. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How to put something in a cabinet

The Playhouse A recording of you yelling, badly, hoarsely, briefly, whatever comes out, for the yell button. Say how you want to be named, or stay anonymous. The room says whose yell it is out loud when it plays. A voice identifies you as surely as a face does, so it keeps the Polaroid Wall’s promises, and one message takes it down. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. The Playhouse’s own terms for a yell

The Pebble Board A song, a poem, a picture, a joke, a recipe: anything you would bring somebody because it made you think of them. The board is what one gathering brought each other, and a new edition goes up after the next one. Whoever keeps that edition decides what gets pinned. Bring it to a gathering in our community. What a pebble is

The Zibaldone A short line for the commonplace book, for any state of mind. Thirty words at most, and never a song lyric. Say who said it, which printing it is in, and where you found it. The attribution slip in the room writes that out for you. Say what you are unsure of. It is checked against a printing before it goes in, and a line nobody can place stays out. Send it however you already talk to us: the contact page, our community, email, a text message. The attribution slip

The Zine Table A page for the next issue, or an idea for one. One sheet, black and white, legible out of a bad printer. On paper, by photo, by voice note or by AAC: any way you have of getting a sentence out counts as writing. Your name goes on it the way you spell it. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. What the zine table asks for

The Broadsheet Broadside An idea for the press’s next sheet: a manifesto somebody on this street would want to pin up, or a memento of a room worth handing over. In words. Every sheet is written for the press, so an idea is an idea for a sheet rather than a sheet printed as it arrives. A sheet says what we hold and never what you must do. One sheet, both sides, and its credits and its licence on the paper. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. What the press takes

Samefood Cafe The foods that carry you right now, for a tray of your own. Written exactly as you give them, capitals and spelling and all. Nobody’s list is tidied, sorted or compared with anybody else’s. Say how you like it served, if you do. It comes down the moment you ask. Tell us in our community. The trays as they stand

The Dopamine Dress-Up Den What you wear, in your own words, for a look on the peg with your name on it. Words, not a photograph: the pieces, the prints, the colours, and how they feel if you like. Your words go beside the look exactly as you give them. If something you wear is not on a rail yet, the house draws it and hangs it up. Say how you want to be named. Nothing is rated, and it comes down the moment you ask. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How the Dress-Up Den takes a look

Show Your Work Something you are making, writing, learning or fixing, finished or not, for a card on the bench. Where it lives, how you want to be named, and what state it is in. Your words go on the card exactly as you give them. A photograph of it if you like, under the polaroid wall's rules: a description in your own words, and the yes of whoever took it and anybody in it. In progress is welcome. Finished is not required. It comes down the moment you ask. Send it however you already talk to us: the contact page, our community, email, a text message. How Show Your Work takes a piece of work

Plural Mural Something you would like painted on the end wall, in words, for the house to paint and put up in turn. Words, not a picture: what is on it, what it says if it says anything, and the colours. The house paints it. Nobody real is painted on the wall. Your words go beside the mural exactly as you give them. Say how you want to be named. Nothing is voted on, and it comes down the moment you ask. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How Plural Mural takes a mural

The rooms with a screen in them A recommendation for a room with a screen in it. Laughingstock: a set by a Disabled comic, on their own terms. The Lightbulb Picture House: a film about being Autistic, ADHD or otherwise neurodivergent, best of all made by the people it is about. Looming Rocks: a whole concert played outdoors, filmed. The Live Room: a whole session played in a studio, filmed. Black Leather Lagoon: something spooky for the Halloween playlist on the drive-in screen. The Solarpunk Hermitage: a documentary for the campfire. Every one is checked before it goes up: that it plays, that it can be shown here, and how long it runs. A film for the Picture House is watched first, so its card can say what is in it before anybody presses play. A recommendation is a suggestion rather than a booking, and the choosing stays with whoever keeps that room’s list. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community.

The rooms that keep a playlist A song for a room that keeps a list of them. Dance, Punks: something to dance to on the airstrip. Vital Plant Living: a song about food for the stereo. Club Chronic: a song for Chronic Neurodivergent Depressed Queer Punk, the playlist on the stage. Nothing musical is hosted here, so a song goes in as a link to where it already lives, and no lyrics go on any page. Every one is checked to see that it plays and can be shown here before it goes in. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community.

The Doomscroll A poem of doom, for the scroll behind the Mopery’s library. Public domain everywhere, not only in the United States: its author has to have been dead more than seventy years. Say which printing it comes from, because poems change between printings. Send it however you already talk to us: the contact page, our community, email, a text message. The scroll and its rule

Your Room An idea for the empty storefront with the keys in the door, or a room you built for it with your own AI. One paragraph is plenty: what it is for, who walks into it, and what it looks like when they do. Built with your AI from the prompt on that page? Send a share link, or the file, with the note your AI put at the top. No form, no application, and no portfolio. A room here does not expire, and it comes down if you say so once. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. How to submit your room, and what happens next

Chimera Obscura An animal the shelf does not have yet, or a part no animal on it has, for everybody to make chimeras out of. Ask in the suggestion box, signed on to the CB. A moderator answers it: done, or not doing, and why. It gets drawn the way every part there was, as code, and goes on the shelf for everybody. That takes days, not seconds. Only real animals: no people or parts of people, and no character somebody owns. Drop it in the suggestion box in The Sandbox, signed on to the CB, or send it through the Stimpunks contact page. How Chimera Obscura takes a request
An idea, a feature or a bug

The Sandbox A suggestion, a feature request or a bug report, about any room on the street, the CB included. Half an idea is fine, and so is a bug you cannot quite describe. Your handle goes on it, anybody can read it, and a moderator answers it in replies under it: done, or not doing, and why. You can reply too. Somebody else’s already there? Press Me too on it: the box names who a suggestion affects, never how many. A screenshot can go with it, with a sentence saying what it shows. Anybody can see it, so look at all of it first. A security problem does not go in the box, where everybody can read it: send it privately. Drop it in the suggestion box in The Sandbox, signed on to the CB, or send it through the Stimpunks contact page. How the suggestion box works
A new shop, pitch or turning

The street, the campgrounds and the Outskirts An idea for somewhere new: a shopfront on the street, a pitch in the campgrounds past the treeline, or a turning off the Outskirts past the last streetlight. Say what it is for, and which way it goes. The campgrounds are for being somewhat apart, at peace, with the street still in reach. The Outskirts are for crowds, noise and staying out late, and for getting as far off as you can. Helen Edgar’s question helps: would it be just as happy on the campsite? Then it is probably a pitch. No two rooms here look alike, so say what the light is like in there, if you know. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. The street as it stands

Anywhere on the street A name spelled wrong, a credit missing, a quotation we cannot back up, a colour you cannot read, a button you cannot reach. Anything you cannot read, reach or press is a fault in the room, not in you. A correction is written up in the changelog and stays on the page it was made to, rather than being quietly swapped. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page. A security hole goes privately on GitHub instead. The changelog, where corrections go

Anything with you in it Your photograph, your voice, your tray, your cabinet, your look, your page, your name in a credit. It comes down when you say so. One message, no reason needed. Coming down means gone, not hidden. Send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. What this site keeps about you

A pull-down map of where our community lives, as each of us chose to say on the Join form: a city, a region or a country, and never a name. The number on a pin is how many of us are there. We draw it here ourselves, from Natural Earth’s world, so looking at it asks no other site for anything. The whole world. Zoom in to pull crowded places apart: the pins stay the same size as the world grows under them. You can also drag the map to move it, pinch it or hold Ctrl or Cmd and scroll on it, and double-press a spot to zoom in there. Press a pin to see where it is. Every place on the map is listed in words below. Every place on the map, in words The world is Natural Earth’s, public domain. Places are found with OpenStreetMap: © OpenStreetMap contributors. What the map keeps. To be on it, give your city when you join, or ask us.

The CB was Ryan’s idea: a simple chat patterned after citizens band radio, one password shared with the community, no alerts until the community asked for notifications, a short history cleared daily until people in other timezones needed two days of it, and a radio that floats on the screen once you are on. It is the one thing on this street that talks to a server, and the only thing that sends anything anywhere, and the privacy page says in plain words what that server keeps. The room’s look answers a request from our community for something softer and quieter, and leans on 14 Patterns of Biophilic Design, by William Browning, Catherine Ryan and Joseph Clancy for Terrapin Bright Green (2014). The type is Varela Round, by Joe Prince, for the room’s name and headings, and Radio Canada, by Charles Daoud, Coppers and Brasses, Alexandre Saumier Demers and Jacques Le Bailly, for everything that is read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records rather than typed. The window, the seat and the radio on the desk are ours. Everything is credited in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

The street’s town hall, at noon. It is one round room under a dome, and the top of the dome is open to the sky, so the sun comes down through the hole and lies on the floor as a single disc that moves round the hall through the day. This is where Stimpunks meets to run itself, and the doors round the wall go to the rooms where that happens. Every one of them is open to walk into. What changes from door to door is who can talk once you are in.

The Fishbowl A room for community Fishbowl Meetings for anyone with CB access. Anybody can walk in, and anybody signed on to the CB can talk there. go in Directors A room for Stimpunks Directors to meet. Anybody can walk in. The radio and the call in there are for moderators with the director role, and for administrators. go in Board A room for Stimpunks Board Members to meet. Anybody can walk in. The radio and the call in there are for moderators with the board or director role, and for administrators. go in Moderators A room for Stimpunks Moderators to meet. Anybody can walk in. The radio and the call in there are for any moderator. go in Executive Session For those with the board role only. Anybody can walk in. The radio and the call in there are for moderators with the board role, and nobody else: not even an administrator. go in A patch: Interdependence. Left on a seat in the open middle of the hall. Interdependent and here, the street’s own line: we need each other, and nobody here is ashamed of it. Signed on to the CB, pick it up and it goes on the battle jacket in your Profile, sewn on with every other patch on the street, whatever its shape.

Anybody can walk into any room here, signed on or not, and read everything on its walls. The Fishbowl is the CB’s. Anybody signed on at the Community Center can tune the radio to it and join its call. The rooms for our directors, our board and our moderators are for moderators, who sign on with their own password, under a username on the moderators’ list. The Moderators’ room takes any of them; the Board room, the ones with the board role or the director role, because directors join board meetings; the Directors’ room, the ones with the director role; and an administrator can go into any of them but one. Executive Session is the board role and nothing else, because an executive session is the board without staff, so the administrator key does not open it. In those rooms the radio only comes in with the people the room is for: for everybody else it waits outside the door, and is there again in the hall. That is a lock and not a curtain. The street’s server hands each of those rooms’ channel, its call and any film hosted in it to the people the room is for and to nobody else, whatever a browser asks for, and nobody else’s radio hears that anything is going on in there. Who holds which role is kept in the street’s settings, not published here. The house norms are the CB’s, at the Community Center, and our covenant applies in every room of this building.
Why a hole in the roof

Some of what gets said in a town hall has to stay in the room it was said in, and the rooms round this wall have doors for that reason. The hall in the middle is open to the sky. Our bylaws are published in full: our accountability pages on stimpunks.org carry the bylaws and a transparency log. A private conversation and a public outcome are two different things, and this building has a place for each.

The rooms, and the one line on each door, are Ryan’s, from his brief of 2026-09-29. The hall, its drawing and every other word here are ours, and nothing in the drawing is a picture of any real building. Forum is Denis Masharov’s and Gelasio is Eben Sorkin’s, both under the SIL Open Font License. More in the liner notes.

A room for community Fishbowl Meetings for anyone with CB access.

A fishbowl is a conversation for a lot of people that only a few hold at a time. A small circle in the middle talks. Everybody else sits in a wider circle round the outside and listens. One seat in the middle is always left empty, and anybody from the outside can come in and take it; when they do, somebody in the middle gets up and goes back out, so there is always a seat free. Nobody is called on, nobody is on a panel, and the circle is never closed. It suits a big group with one thing to talk through, because it keeps the talking small and the listening wide. James Carrier’s introduction at PeopleShift is where this room started, and it also says that some people find a format this loose and this level a little daunting. That is a fair thing to feel, and the outer circle is there for it.

The middle is whoever has their microphone on. Everybody else is the outer circle, and listening there is a whole way to take part. There is always an empty seat. To come in, raise your hand in the call or say so in the chat, then unmute when there is room. When somebody comes in, somebody goes out. Stepping back is a thing you choose, and nobody needs a reason for it. Typing is talking. Something written in the call’s chat can be read into the middle, if you ask; you do not have to speak to be in the circle. Nobody is put on the spot. Nobody has to come into the middle, and nobody is asked to.

The call in here is for people signed on to the CB. Anybody can come in and look around; to talk, and to be in the circle, you need the CB, and the Community Center says how to get on it. You are not signed on to the CB in this browser. Sign on at the Community Center, then come back and the way in is here. The call is run by 8x8’s Jitsi as a Service. Your camera and microphone start off, the name you are called by goes to 8x8 inside your pass into the call, and while somebody is in the call we keep their name in it, until they leave. What goes where.
Why a bowl on a sill

Because it is a fishbowl: a small round world you can see all the way into from outside, with a ring of stones on the gravel that always has one gap in it and a wider ring of shells round the foot of the glass. The sun comes through the water and lands on the gravel and the sill in bright tangled lines, and that is all the light the room needs. Nothing in here moves, at any setting.

For those with the board role only.

It is the board meeting without staff. A board closes the door for part of its meeting to talk through what cannot be talked through with everybody there: a review of the chief executive’s work, what staff are paid, a concern about somebody’s conduct, a conversation with the auditor. Sometimes the chief executive is asked to stay for part of it, and sometimes an adviser is asked in for one item. BoardSource’s guide to executive sessions, which this room is built on, recommends: Holding one at the end of every regular board meeting, so that having one never has to mean something is wrong. A written policy for when the board goes into session and who stays. A confidential record of who was there, what was decided and how the vote went. Telling the chief executive what was concluded, if they were not in the room. Ending the session once its business is done, and not holding closed sessions for what belongs in the open meeting. Those are BoardSource’s recommendations, not a Stimpunks policy. What our board has adopted is on our accountability pages.

Mix it, layer it, clash it. Nothing here comes in a size. Dopamine dressing is wearing what makes you glad to have it on: colours, textures and styles chosen for how they make you feel rather than for how well they help you blend in. Our glossary sets it beside unmasking, and it is often what happens when somebody stops dressing to pass. This is a shop on the street for it. There is a wooden valet stand in the middle of the floor and rails of clothes round the walls: put something on your head, something over the top, something underneath, the bottom half and your feet, in any print and any colours, and nothing has to go with anything. If you have drawn your bodymind at the Bodymind Booth next door, bring it in and everything on the stand goes on you instead. Through to Fantasy Fancy Dress At the back of the shop, through a curtain, is Fantasy Fancy Dress: faery wings, animal ears, tails and paws, jewellery and beads, onesies and dress-up suits. There is no dress code. Our Dress Codes entry is about what dress codes do to people, and it has a school in it that banned black clothing on the grounds of mental health. So nothing in here is required and nothing is turned away, and black is a colour in here too: every rail comes in all black, and choosing it is as much dopamine dressing as choosing all the colours there are. Nothing comes in a size, and nobody is measured. Nothing here is sold. The clothes hang on a stand rather than on a drawing of a person, because a drawing of a person is a body, with one shape and one skin and one gender, handed to everybody who walks in. Whoever is wearing these is you. The only body this room ever shows is one you drew yourself at the Bodymind Booth next door and brought in. No rail is for men or for women. A gown hangs on the same rail as a T-shirt, and a big wig beside a beanie. All the colours there are is borrowed from the title of our course, Neurodiversity and Gender: You Hit So Hard With All the Colors That There Are. How it feels counts as much as how it looks. Every garment on the rails says how it feels and how it goes on and comes off. Ryan wears Thai fisherman pants for sensory and comfort reasons first, and his own field guide says all of his outerwear has a means of escape, so every jacket in here says how you get out of it; it also says the knot on the pants is not accessible to everybody, so every other bottom half does up without one. Our Why Sheet for a hoodie makes the same argument to a school. Nothing has to go with anything. This street says on its front door that clashing is not the same as illegible, and in here that is the whole shop. Florals on patchwork on stripes is an outfit. Nothing is too much and nothing is too little. The dial never takes anything off the rails. The sequins, the boa and the big wig are all here at Gentle. The dial changes how much the room moves, which in here is only the rainbows on the wall, and only at MAX GLITTER; nothing flashes, and nothing sparkles on its own. Nothing is rated, and nothing is kept or sent unless you ask. No score, no like button, no best-dressed. The rails keep nothing, and the copy button puts what is on the stand on your own clipboard, for you to take wherever you want it: a shopping list, a message, nowhere. Keep it as an avatar, signed on to the CB, sends what is on the stand, or on your bodymind, to your Profile, and only when you press it, and Open my strip only asks your Profile for the ones you kept. Closing the page empties the stand. Dopamine is in the name because that is what people call it. Nothing in here claims a colour does anything to anybody’s brain chemistry. It is a word for a feeling you already know, and the only one who can say what gives you it is you.

The room and its name are Helen Edgar’s idea. She suggested a Dopamine Dress-Up Den for the next shopfront, and the rails are the brief Ryan wrote from it: his own wardrobe first, which is Thai fisherman pants in bold florals, bold blocks and patchwork, button-down shirts in all sorts of colours, a haori over the top, and beanies and slouchy beanies in a staggering array; then Helen’s cardigans and flowing dresses; and then the rest of our community, some of whom take it further, with a veritable drag show of colour and variety. Helen’s look was relayed by Ryan rather than given by her, the witchy prints on it are the house’s guess, and she has the final say on it. The haori and the pants are named plainly. A haori is a Japanese jacket worn over a kimono, usually tied at the front with two short cords, and Thai fisherman pants are made so wide in the waist that one pair fits anybody, wrapped round and tied. The street is Danny’s, and Danny repaints On the wall now: Queer without fear. A rainbow in six broad bands, red through violet, arching up from the foot of the wall on a navy ground scattered with small cream stars, and across the top a cream banner with its ends notched, painted in navy capitals: QUEER WITHOUT FEAR. This is the end wall of a building on the street, and it is never painted the same way twice. The street is Danny’s, and Danny rearranges what is on them for whoever turns up, so one day the wall is a rainbow and the next it is a hillside with its roots showing. At MAX GLITTER the wall repaints itself every three minutes, one mural dissolving into the next, and you can keep the one you like up for as long as you stay. At Gentle and Regular it holds still until you turn it over yourself. Every mural is on the list below at every setting, in words, with a button to put it up.

Leaning against the foot of the wall, on the pavement and not on the paint, there is a chalkboard for leaving a note to whoever comes by next. It is Helen Edgar’s idea, after the board at her floatation tank place. The chalkboard needs scripts to read it. A note, chalked up as Anybody who walks past can read this board, signed on to the CB or not, for seven days. Write what you would write on a board in the street. Writing on the board takes a username on the CB, which you join with an invite: get started or sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Reading it takes nothing. Anybody can read it, and only people signed on to the CB can write on it. It is a board, not a feed: a note is there, and then it is not.

Knowledge is infrastructure. Access to it is mutual aid. This is our library, with the doors open and the sky in the windows. Books of the edges, zine walls, music, bookmarks, and things you can borrow and have, made by and for neurodivergent and disabled people. Nothing requires a card. You do not have to buy anything to be here, or explain yourself, or be social correctly. Libraries are already the most radical institution most people use without thinking about it: you borrow something, you give it back, and somebody else borrows it. No one owns it. Everyone benefits. At the library you are a patron, not a customer.

Third places are the places between home and work that belong to everyone and ask nothing of you except that you turn up. No transaction, and no role to perform. Libraries are the third place, and especially for neurodivergent people, who get pushed out of so many other rooms: quiet corners for deep focus, tables for gathering, open floors for wandering, and nobody checking whether you are doing any of it properly. You can be there without performing being there. That is third places in our glossary, and it is Cavendish Space too: caves, campfires and watering holes, under one roof. We wrote about what makes one work for us in Neurodivergent Libraries.
The America I loved still exists at the front desks of our public libraries.

Librarians are kind of upside-down cops: public employees who are stepping in wherever the rest of our services have failed.

Librarians are doing the work the rest of our institutions walked away from. They are social workers, tech support, a safe harbour and the defenders of intellectual freedom, often in the same shift, without much money and more and more under political attack. They also, quietly, know where everything is. — Kurt Vonnegut, A Man Without a Country , 2005 Read off our Library page, which cites the book on WorldCat. Not checked against the book. — Cory Doctorow, They Want to Kill Libraries , 2022 Read off our Library page, which links the essay. Not checked against the essay.

Libraries are infrastructure, and not as a figure of speech. They hold a town together the way its roads and its water do, except that what they carry is knowledge, and safety, and the chance of walking out as somebody different from who walked in. Eric Klinenberg calls them social infrastructure in Palaces for the People, and we think that undersells them. Built with public money. Open to everyone. No dress code and no cover charge. They are worth defending.
Books are for use. Every person his or her book. Every book its reader. Save the time of the reader. A library is a growing organism.
— S. R. Ranganathan, The Five Laws of Library Science , 1931

A librarian in Madras wrote the whole job down in five sentences in 1931, and they still read like a manifesto. — S. R. Ranganathan, The Five Laws of Library Science , 1931 Read off our Library page, which gives the laws as Wikipedia does. The book's record was resolved on Open Library; the 1931 printing itself was not checked, so this is the wording as Wikipedia gives it, which may not be Ranganathan's word for word. The fourth one is the one we would carve over the door if the door were ours to carve: save the time of the reader. A library that makes you queue, fill in a form and prove who you are before you may look something up has forgotten it.

Borrowing is not only a way of running a building full of books. It is an ethic: a way of sharing what sustains a life that needs neither wealth, nor competition, nor owning anything for ever. Murray Bookchin named the principles under it usufruct, the freedom to use what is held in common without using it up; the irreducible minimum, the level of living nobody falls below whatever they put in; and complementarity, differences without a ladder in them, each of us a small part of something bigger than the sum. We call it the library economy, and tool libraries, clothing libraries and seed libraries are already running on it. What if we ran more of the world this way? Ours is the Things Library.

Mass distorts space. Enough books distort it into something you can walk along. A library is not just a building full of books. It is a place in L-space: every library, everywhere, joined to every other through the sheer weight of what is in them. Knowledge is power, power is energy, energy is matter, and matter is mass, which is Terry Pratchett’s arithmetic, from the Discworld books, and mass bends the space around it. Enough books bend it into something you can walk through. What you need to find your way is not a map. It is a ball of string. — Terry Pratchett, Guards! Guards! , 1989 Read off our Library page, which quotes the passage it comes out of at length. Not checked against the book.
So, while the Dewey system has its fine points, when you’re setting out to look something up in the multidimensional folds of L-space what you really need is a ball of string.

— Terry Pratchett, Guards! Guards! , 1989 Read off our Library page, which quotes the passage it comes out of at length. Not checked against the book. That is how we think about a library. Not a catalogue. Not a curriculum. A space you move through by following a thread, finding what you need on the way to something else, and getting home again because you tied one end to the door. People ask it about a big shelf of books as if it were an accusation. They have misunderstood what a library is for. An unread book is not a failure. It is a resource, a future you got ready for, and the books you have not read yet are the most honest part of any collection: the part that says there is more to know. That is the anti-library. Neurodivergent people often build our libraries this way. We follow threads, we collect ahead of a hyperfocus that has not arrived yet, and we buy the book because something in us knew it before the moment to read it came. That is not disorganisation. It is monotropism working across time, and in L-space it is how the shelves get so heavy. — John Waters Read off our Library page, WHICH GIVES IT NO SOURCE, and we could not trace it from here. It is here on that page's word, and it says so under the quotation.

We call our reading lists Books of the Edges because of where we live. Disabled and neurodivergent people are always the edge cases. The middle of the world is built for some people, with its neat categories and its smooth timelines, and real life happens at the edges: in the breaks, the mismatches and the overlaps, where systems fail to account for how complicated people are and where new worlds come from. The name is from Octavia E. Butler, whose disabled narrator in Parable of the Sower calls her philosophy Earthseed: The Book of the Living, after the Books of the Dead. L-space is the one place where every edge of every library meets every other.

Not many people these days remarked upon the fact that he was an ape.

A Discworld homage, from a library that finds him relatable Our library has a guide. He lives in the stacks of Unseen University, climbs the shelves with prehensile hands and feet, and communicates mainly in Oook. He was transformed by a magical accident and refused to be changed back. He kept his job because he was the only one who knew where all the books were. We find him relatable. He is Terry Pratchett’s, from the Discworld books, and this room is a thank-you note. — Terry Pratchett, Guards! Guards! , 1989 Read off our Library page, which quotes the whole passage and gives it as pages 3 and 4. Not checked against the book.

Not the ape. The rest of it. His body changed, suddenly and not by his choice, and he found the new one suited the work better than the old one had: shelves are easier to climb with four hands, and a librarian who can sort books with his feet is ahead of one who cannot. So he declined to be put back. Every offer to fix him was an offer to take away something that worked, made by people who assumed they knew what he ought to want. Nobody else got to decide that. And he kept his job because he was the expert: the only one who knew where everything was, which is a better reason to keep a job than most, and a reason an institution cannot argue with however much it might like to. On a Disabled people’s site that is not a joke about an animal. It is a librarian who was told what he should want to be, and said Oook.

The world he looks after the books of is flat. Two of Henry Cavendish’s houses were kept for opposite things. At Clapham Common, then outside London, he worked: a red-brick house whose drawing room he made into a laboratory, with a forge in the room next to it, an observatory upstairs and an eighty-foot ship’s mast in the grounds for a telescope. Nobody needed to be let in to see that something was going on there: the mast alone told the neighbours that the new resident was different. In Bedford Square he kept his library, and he opened it for borrowing, at all seasons of the year, with a librarian to look after it. Anybody shown round it, his biographers write, would have concluded it was a house of knowledge. It was green throughout — green moreen curtains, green fire screens, green chair covers — and its mahogany blinds were lined with green transparent canvas: they could be down, and you could still see through them. It had rules, and the rules were his too. He signed the register for every book he took out of it to Clapham, like anybody else, and when the librarian died he gave a day a week to checking books out himself. That is the house this room is built after. A place can be open without being open-plan. What makes it open is that anybody can find out what is behind each door and when, that the rules on the door apply to the people who run the house, and that nothing is locked. Our meetings are where the Stimpunks team does its work, and the team goes in by the same doors you do. Everything on this page about Cavendish’s houses is from Christa Jungnickel and Russell McCormmach’s Cavendish: The Experimental Life, chapter 11, “Places” (second revised edition, 2016), read on 2026-09-25. The line about the librarian is their report of Thomas Young’s.
It is not true, however, that he wanted to remove himself entirely from the company of his peers; he just wanted to stand off to the side, soaking everything in.
Steve Silberman, NeuroTribes, p. 25, as our Cavendish Space entry quotes it
Perhaps the most important form of control over one’s space is authority over who comes in and out
Annie Murphy Paul, The Extended Mind, as our Cavendish Space page quotes it

Cavendish Space is our name for psychologically and sensory safe space: caves for quiet reflection, campfires for learning together, watering holes for peer connection. We named it after Henry Cavendish, the eighteenth-century natural philosopher who discovered hydrogen, as Steve Silberman tells his life in NeuroTribes. Cavendish needed his cave. He also needed, now and then, a small set of his peers — the Royal Society’s Monday Club was his campfire — and he came to it on his own terms. A door is how you get to do that. Our page on Cavendish Space quotes Annie Murphy Paul on why a place to work needs doors: Here that authority is yours, on the doorstep. You decide whether to knock, and once you are in, the call will let you keep your microphone and camera off and stand off to the side, which is what the man the house is named after would have done. Next door in spirit: body doubling, which our Watering Hole Hangs welcome, and whose nature cams run up the street in the Jungle Room. The calendar with everything on it is on our events page.

← back to the street on the street · the control room · the red light is on A recording studio on the street

Sessions played in a studio rather than at a gig, and the band on the other side of the glass. A session is a band playing a room with nobody in it but the people making the recording — or a room with a small crowd in it, sitting down, that the band can see the faces of. A television studio, a radio station’s live room, somewhere with a desk and a sheet of glass. It is the nearest a record gets to being played in the room you are sitting in. That is why a room of them is worth having here. No queue, no crowd to stand in, no volume that somebody else chose, and you can stop in the middle and nobody sees you leave. On the desk so far: Austin City Limits, a television studio with a crowd in it, and two radio stations’ live rooms, KEXP’s and KCRW’s. Under the desk, the last month off each of those studios’ own channels, refilled every morning. Anybody else with a live room is welcome next.
While the red light is on

Nothing plays until you press it. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press a play button, and pressing one plays that video and no other. Anything can go up on the glass. Every strip, on the desk and in the month under it, plays where it hangs, or its second button puts it on the glass over the desk instead, saying how long it runs before you press it. Taking it off puts the glass back as it was and plays nothing. Every strip on the desk says how long before you press it, and where and when the session was taped. Where a video is not the whole session, the strip says that too, because a runtime is only honest if you know what it is the runtime of. The month under the desk says how long and when each one went up, and not where it was played, because nobody here has looked. The desk is not a chart. Nothing here is ranked, rated or counted. The sessions are in the order they were patched in, the month is in the order the studios put things up, newest first, and neither order is an argument about which is better. The red lamp is steady. It does not flash at any dial setting, and nothing else in the room does either. A light that can put somebody on the floor has no business in a room anybody is meant to enjoy. Nobody is drawn in the live room. The only people in there are the players, in their own sessions. The glass. The live room is lit and nobody is in it. Any session on the desk, or anything in the month under it, can go up here with the button under it, and nothing loads until you press one.

← back to the street on the street · alongside, at the waterline · the ports are open A broadsheet press on the street

Manifestos and mementos, served across your bow. A broadside is two things. It is a large sheet of paper printed on one side and posted up where people will see it — proclamations, ballads, political views, advertisements — and it is the side of a warship, with every gun along it. Both definitions are Wikipedia’s, in print and at sea, read on 2026-09-25. This shopfront is the second, seen from a boat at the waterline, and what comes out of its ports is the first. Ours are printed on both sides, which strictly makes them broadsheets, and that is where the press gets its name. The form is the Stimpunks broadsides’, which whysheet.press prints: one sheet, made to be carried into a room and handed to somebody. Side A carries one thing you can read across the room, to pin up. Side B does the work, to hand over. And theirs is Alfie Kohn’s, whose Why Sheet was a single double-sided sheet laying out a case briskly.

One sheet, both sides. Every broadside prints to exactly one sheet, side A then side B, on a page that fits both A4 and US Letter, so it comes out of a printer in any country uncropped. Print this page, or press the button over a sheet, and nothing else comes out with it. Ink on white, on the screen as well. What you see here is a preview of the paper and not the paper, and it is drawn the way the paper will come out: white, because that is what comes out of a printer. Two inks to a sheet, and no two sheets share a pair. The pair is what tells two sheets apart face down in a stack. Every ink is measured on white before it goes on the press. Living out loud, and the rest of it

The rest of the masthead, and what it commits us to. Every line here is a promise somebody can check against the street. Living out loud The glitter is real, and so is the dial. Every page carries Gentle, Regular and MAX GLITTER. Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. Access is the premise, not the brake. A loud site that shut out the people it is for would be the thing we exist to name, so how loud it gets belongs to whoever holds the dial. Nothing plays until somebody presses. Every play button says, before the press, how long the thing runs, or that it runs until somebody stops it. Plucky pluralism, for human organisms Many worlds at once, and a body in every one of them: stretch, flap, eat, drink, pee, and a fan blowing on you in a cool room. Organisms, not output. Nobody on the street is counted, ranked or scored, and nothing measures how much of it anybody got through. Rest is owed, not earned. The street has rooms for it, and none of them says what rest is for. Becoming and belonging, with ribald songing Belonging comes first and is never in question. Becoming comes after and is never finished, which is why nobody here counts the rooms: the street keeps growing. Ribald means the rooms may be bawdy, rude and funny. Songing means music everywhere, with the writers named on every cut and nobody’s words used without their say. What this is not: neutral, finished, a design system, or a claim to speak for every Disabled or neurodivergent person. If the rooms stop matching these words, the sheet is what is wrong. Daily news, usually bad. Every morning a timer reads the channels Ryan keeps an eye on and fills a tub in the cabinet with what they put out between five the morning before and five that morning. That is the morning edition. The newest stands at the front with the scoop in it; the six mornings before it are behind it, each a flavour of its own and each a little more scraped out than the last. A week, and then it is gone. The eighth morning is not kept, not archived and not moved to a back page. It goes, and it is still on the channel that posted it. Up the street is the Doomscroll, whose whole shape is a roll with no end to it. This one has a bottom, and you can see it from the door.

Nothing plays until you press it. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press a scoop, and pressing one plays that video and no other. Every tub has a screen of its own at the top. Any video in that tub plays where it is, or goes up on the screen, bigger, with the second button under it. Taking it off leaves the screen empty again. Every scoop says how long it runs before you press it, when it went up and whose channel it is on. A short is the shape of a phone, because that is the shape it plays in. Nobody here watched any of it before it went up. A timer filled the cabinet. What it asked about every video is whether it plays, whether it can be shown on this site and how long it runs. A video whose channel will not let it be shown on another site, or that YouTube shows only to signed-in adults, is a door out to YouTube rather than a screen in here, and it says which. The headlines are the channels’ own, word for word and capital for capital, and some of them shout. Rewriting somebody’s headline would be putting words in their mouth. Nothing is ranked and nothing is counted. No views, no likes, nothing trending and no most-watched. The sources are in the groups Ryan put them in and the order he listed them, and each one’s scoops are in the order they went up. A feed only reaches so far back. A channel’s feed carries its newest uploads and nothing older, so a channel that posts a great deal between two mornings has the earliest of them left off. Where that has happened, the tub says so on that channel rather than looking complete. Every time is Mountain time, the street’s own clock.

Nothing else on this street is news. The Healing Checkpoint has a bed made up and asks nothing of you for it, the Latibulum is a burrow under the hill for when you have had enough of being findable, and the Jungle Room is live cameras on waterholes, where most of the time nothing happens at all.

The sources are Ryan Boren’s, in his groups and his order: the independent news, the late-night shows and the YouTubers he watches. Every video is its channel’s, every headline is written by whoever posted it, and every scoop names the channel it is on. None of these channels, shows or sites is affiliated with Stimpunks, and none of them endorses us; a source being in the cabinet is not Stimpunks vouching for everything on it. The full list, with links, is in the liner notes. The room’s name is lettered in Leckerli One, by Gesine Todt, and everything else is Onest, by Dmitri Voloshin and Andrey Kudryavtsev, both under the SIL Open Font License. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and in here nothing moves at any setting. The news does enough of that, and the loudest thing in the room is whichever scoop you put on.
