Take your boots off, or put them on. The Slake is out the back door. A MUD is a multi-user dungeon: a world made of words that people walk around in together, typing where to go and what to look at. The first one was written by Roy Trubshaw and Richard Bartle at the University of Essex in the autumn of 1978. This one is the kind with nothing in it to fight. Out the back door of this room is the Slake, a tidal estuary with a marsh, a mill, a hut full of things people found in the mud, and an island you can walk to while the tide is out. There is nobody to fight and nothing is counted. You go where you like and look at what you like, and the people who live out there tell you what they are doing and what our glossary calls it. Everything is words first and picture second, so a screen reader plays it as well as a pointer does.

Other people out here Seen, you meet whoever else is seen in the same place and hear what is said there. Nobody sees you unless you are seen, and you cannot see anybody unless you are. Sign on to the CB at the Community Center and you can meet whoever else is out here. Ways on Or type what you want to do However far out you were, the way back is always open. You are in the MUD Room, and you can take your boots off. Nobody can hear you out here unless you are signed on to the CB. Sign on at the Community Center, come back, and choose to be seen: then whoever else is seen in the same place hears what you say. Nobody can hear you unless you are seen. Press Be seen out here, and whoever else is seen in the same place will hear what you say, and you them. You sit down where you are for a while. Nothing is asked of you. You sit down at the top of the polished mud and let go. You are in the channel at the bottom a moment later, a great deal muddier, which was the idea. It is too dark to see anything down here. Something to see by would help. The Slake does not know that word. Say help for the words it does know, or use the buttons, which do everything the words do. You wait. The water comes in over the mud, quietly at first and then all at once, filling the creeks from the bottom up. The tide is in. You wait. The water goes out the way it came, draining off the mud into the creeks and down them to the sea. The tide is out. Not out here. The tide can come in across flat mud very fast, so the Slake only lets you wait for it somewhere dry: up on the marsh, on the wall, or out on the island. That way is under water while the tide is in. Wait somewhere dry for it to go out, or find another way round. The ferry only runs while the tide is in, and just now the boat is sitting on the mud. While the tide is out you can walk to the island along the causeway. There is nothing like that here. The things you can look at here are listed beside the map, and under Here.

Every button does what a word does, so you never have to type. If you would rather type, these are the words the Slake knows, and most of them take a shorter form. north, south, east, west, up, down, across Go that way. n, s, e, w, u and d work too, and so does go in front. look Say where you are again. look at something, or examine it, or x it, to see it properly. take and drop Pick something up and put it down again somewhere else. wear the wellies, or take off the wellies. talk to somebody Say hello. Talk to them again and they tell you what they are doing, and what it is called. show a find At the Mudlarks’ Hut, show Ada something from the foreshore and it goes on the table. wait Wait for the tide to turn. It only turns when you do this, and only somewhere dry. home Straight back to the MUD Room, from anywhere. sit, slide, ring, join in For the places that have somewhere to sit, a slide, a bell and a boat. say something, or ' in front Signed on to the CB and seen, whoever else is seen where you are hears it. who says who else is here. help These words again. What happens is written into the box under the buttons, newest at the foot, and a screen reader reads each line out as it arrives. The map shows where you have been and the ways you have seen but not taken yet. It is a picture of the same words, so there is nothing on it you cannot also find by reading.

Nobody to fight. There is no combat anywhere on the Slake, nothing has hit points, nothing chases you, and nothing can hurt you. You cannot fall in: at the edge of the water the Slake stops you and says why. Nothing is counted. No score, no points, no levels, no rank, and no count of how much of the Slake you have seen. Ultima Online, which this room owes its first idea to, gives you skills that go up with use. The Slake gives you nothing to grow but what you notice, and the map is a record of where you went rather than a total of it. The tide turns when you wait for it, and not before. Nothing out there runs on a clock. The tide is in or out until you say wait, somewhere dry, and then it turns. That is the street’s oldest promise, that nothing moves until you say so, made into weather. Say home and you are home. However far out you get, one word or one button brings you back to the MUD Room, and from every place there is also a walk back at every tide it can be reached at. The tool that builds the Slake will not build a place without one, or a way on without a way back. The words are the game. Every place, thing and person is written out, and the map is drawn from the same words. With scripts off, the whole Slake is the guidebook at the foot of this page, and its ways on are links you can follow. Nobody teaches and nobody tests. Each person out there is doing something our glossary has an entry for, and if you talk to them twice they tell you its name, linked. That is all the learning there is. Nothing quizzes you, and nothing has to be understood before anything else opens. Nothing is kept or heard, and nothing is sent until you are seen. The Slake keeps nothing about where you went, in your browser or anywhere else, and it makes no sound. It sends nothing at all until you are signed on to the CB and press Be seen out here, and then only where you are and what you say. Closing the page puts the tide back out and the finds back on the foreshore. Nothing out there is a field guide. There is samphire on the marsh and a heron in the creek, and the Slake says what they look like and what they are doing. It will never tell you what is safe to pick or eat.

A MUD is multi-user, and so is this one, through the CB, the street’s radio. Sign on at the Community Center, come back, and press Be seen out here beside the map. It is off every time you arrive, and nothing is sent until you press it. You are seen by your CB handle only when you choose to be, on this visit. Being seen is also the only way to see: nobody can watch the Slake without being seen on it, and when you stop being seen, you stop seeing anybody else. You meet people in the place you are in, and nobody is listed or counted. There is no list of who is out on the Slake and no number of people anywhere, the map shows you and nobody else, and who is here is said in names, in alphabetical order, so nobody is first for arriving first. Each place has its own talk, under the radio’s rules. Say something and whoever is seen in the same place hears it. The latest hundred things said in a place stay for two weeks each, unless our administrators set every channel otherwise, and are gone after that, and the base station can take one off the air sooner. A handle is not proof of who somebody is. Your tide is your own. Somebody else waiting does not flood your mud, so you may meet somebody on the mudflat while it is under water for you. That is the street’s promise that nothing moves until you say so, kept for each of you. A hidden tab is not out here. Put the page behind another and you stop being seen until you come back to it, the way the radio stops listening. What the Slake sends and what it keeps is on the privacy page, beside the radio’s.

The Slake is ours. Every place, thing and person on it was invented for this room, and it takes nothing from any other game except the idea of one. The brief was Ryan’s: a non-violent graphical MUD set in Stimpunks.World, for exploring and learning, with Majuular’s Ultima Online Retrospective | The Last Hurrah as its inspiration. Ultima Online was released by Origin Systems in 1997. The games it comes after. Richard Bartle’s own history dates the first MUD to the autumn of 1978, when Roy Trubshaw wrote its first version at Essex. Paul Dourish’s introduction to MUDs says that when Jim Aspnes wrote TinyMUD in 1989 he set out to discard combat altogether, which is the Slake’s first rule thirty-odd years early. Lucasfilm’s Habitat, by Chip Morningstar and Randy Farmer with Aric Wilmunder and Janet Hunter, went into beta in 1986 as the first graphical virtual world. And Amy Bruckman’s MOOSE Crossing, from 1996, was a MOO for children aged nine to thirteen who learned to program by building things in it, which our glossary would call constructionism. The name. Wiktionary gives slake as a tidal wetland, and its 1868 quotation calls slakes common in Northumberland. The Slake is not any of them. Checked 2026-09-27 against sources read that day rather than remembered, and the page says so where it uses them. A tide mill's pond fills through a one-way gate on the rising tide and is let out through the wheel once the tide has fallen (Wikipedia, Tide mill). Common reed spreads mainly by rhizomes and stolons once established (North Carolina DEQ). Glasswort, which is samphire, grows on saltmarshes and is a pioneer on intertidal mud (Wildlife Trusts; JNCC). Grey herons may stand motionless in the shallows waiting for prey, and curlews feed by probing soft mud with a very long curved bill (Wikipedia). The Thames foreshore is littered with clay pipes, mostly fragments of stems (London Museum). A day beacon is an unlighted sea mark, and its daymark is the part made to be seen in daylight (Wikipedia). 'Slake' is a tidal wetland in Wiktionary, and its 1868 quotation calls slakes common in Northumberland. The Slake’s map and the view from the back step are drawn for this room. The type is credited in the liner notes, with every resident and the entry in our glossary they point at.
The whole Slake, as a guidebook

Everything the game knows, written out as a book, for reading instead of playing or as well as it. The game is built from this, so they never disagree. It gives away every place, so it starts closed when the game is running. Open the guidebook

A narrow room at the back of the shop, with a bench along one wall, coats on pegs above it and a rack of boots under that, every one of them muddy. The back door has a window in it, and through the window is a great deal of sky. Everybody who goes out onto the Slake comes back in through here, which is the whole reason it is called a mud room. If you sit down. You sit on the bench by the boots for a while. Nobody asks you where you are going. a pair of yellow wellies. A pair of yellow wellington boots, your size, whatever your size is. You can wear them out onto the mud, or go barefoot. The Slake is fine with either. the coat pegs. A row of coat pegs with coats and hats on them, and one empty peg at the end, for whoever comes next. the noticeboard. A card pinned up by the back door, in capitals: NOBODY TO FIGHT. NOTHING IS COUNTED. THE TIDE TURNS WHEN YOU WAIT FOR IT, AND NOT BEFORE. SAY HOME AND YOU ARE HOME. the bench. A bench for sitting on to take your boots off, or to put them on, or neither. Ways on: South, out the back door, up onto the sea wall Out the front door, back to the street

At low tide. You are up on the sea wall, a long grassed bank with a path along the top. Behind you is the back of the shop. In front of you the Slake opens out below: marsh, then mud, then channels of water lying in the mud and holding the sky, all the way out to a small island with a striped mark standing on it. The tide is out. At high tide. You are up on the sea wall, a long grassed bank with a path along the top. Behind you is the back of the shop. In front of you the marsh runs down to a sheet of pale water where the mud was, and the small island with the striped mark on it is properly an island now. The tide is in. the view. At low tide. Marsh first, green and cut up by little creeks, then a great flat of shining mud, then the island with its striped beacon. To the left, the reeds and a hut with a slot in it. To the right, a white mill and a tall shed by the creek. Nothing out there is in a hurry.At high tide. Marsh first, then a sheet of pale water all the way to the island, with the tops of the causeway posts standing out of it in a line. To the right the creek is brim full, and there is a rowing boat out on it. Ways on: North, in at the back door · West, along the wall to the hide · East, along the wall to the tea hut · South, down the steps onto the marsh

A wooden hut at the west end of the wall with one long slot of a window facing the marsh, a bench under the slot, and two people on the bench, watching. Nobody speaks above a murmur in a hide, and nobody has to speak at all. If you sit down. You sit on the end of the bench and look out through the slot. Wren and Tam do not look round, and that is a welcome. the slot of a window. Through the slot: the marsh, the creeks, a line of mud beyond, and birds getting on with things because nobody is bothering them. The slot is exactly as wide as it needs to be and not an inch wider. the logbook. A logbook on a string, with a pencil on another string, for writing down what you saw. Its pages are empty, because the Slake writes nothing down. Whoever else is out here, you meet them where they are, not in a book. Wren and Tam. Wren and Tam are on the bench, watching the marsh. Wren glances round, smiles, and goes back to watching. Tam shifts along the bench to make room for you. That is the whole conversation, and it is a good one. Sitting side by side with nothing to say and no need to say it has a name. Our glossary calls it Parallel Play: being alone together, in the same place, where just being there with each other counts. Ways on: East, back along the wall · South, down the boardwalk into the reeds

A boardwalk runs into reeds taller than you are, and the whole world goes to pale stems and a strip of sky. They hiss when the wind moves them. You cannot see far in here, which is what some people come in here for. the reeds. Every reed in here is joined to others under the mud. Once a reedbed has taken hold it spreads by stems that run along underground and put up new shoots, so a bed that looks like thousands of plants may be only a few. Our glossary has an entry for the same shape in people: the Autistic Rhizome. Ways on: North, back up the boardwalk to the hide · East, out of the reeds onto the marsh

Low ground under the wall, cropped short and cut through with little creeks, with samphire standing up out of the wettest patches like small green fingers. The sea only comes over it at the highest tides, and then only for a while. the samphire. Short, jointed, fleshy green stems with no leaves to speak of, standing up out of the wettest mud on the marsh. It grows where hardly anything else will, out at the very edge of the land, and it is the first thing to grow there. the survey stake. A wooden stake with a tag on it, marking one square metre of marsh that Juno comes back to look at, season after season, to see what has changed. Juno. Juno is kneeling at the survey stake with a notebook. Juno is looking at the same square metre of marsh they looked at last month, and the month before that, and writing down what has changed. They show you: a new shoot here, a little more mud there. The best way Juno knows to learn about a place is to keep coming back to the ground you are standing on and looking at it properly. Our glossary calls that Place-Based Education: learning that happens in the natural, cultural and built places around you. Ways on: North, up the steps to the wall · West, into the reeds · East, along the edge of the marsh to the hut on stilts · South, down onto the foreshore (while the tide is out)

A hut on the wall with its front propped open, a kettle that is always nearly boiling, benches outside it and a sign that says NOTHING TO BUY. There are tin mugs on hooks and a biscuit tin that is somehow never empty. If you sit down. You sit on a bench outside the hut with a mug going cold in your hands. Moss does not ask whether you want another one. They just bring it. the kettle. Nearly boiling, as it always is. The mugs are tin and chipped and there is always one free. the sign. NOTHING TO BUY, in white paint on a board. It has never said anything else. Moss. Moss is behind the counter, keeping the kettle nearly boiling. Moss pours you tea into a tin mug and does not ask for anything back, because there is nothing to ask for. The sign says so. The tea hut is not anybody's home and it is not anybody's work, and nobody has to buy anything to sit in it. That is what our glossary means by one of the Third Places: somewhere with regulars, a level floor and no price at the door. Ways on: West, along the wall · East, along the wall to the mill · South, down the steps to the hut on stilts

At low tide. A white weatherboarded mill standing where the creek meets the wall, with a millpond behind it. The tide is out, and the pond is still full, because the gates shut on the water when the sea went down. Now the mill is letting that water out through the wheel, slowly, and the whole building is humming with it. At high tide. A white weatherboarded mill standing where the creek meets the wall, with a millpond behind it. The tide is in, and the rising sea has pushed the gates open and is filling the pond. The wheel is still. The mill is waiting for the water to go down again, because that is the only time it can work. the tide gates. At low tide. The gates are shut against the pond. They are hung so that the falling tide leaves them closed and the water is kept in, and nobody has to work them.At high tide. The gates are standing open. They are hung so that the rising tide pushes them open on its own and fills the pond, and nobody has to work them. the wheel. At low tide. The pond water is going out through the wheel and the wheel is turning, slowly, and turning the stones upstairs.At high tide. The wheel is still. It will turn again when the tide has gone out far enough to let the pond water through it. Ottilie. Ottilie the miller is here, dusted with flour. Ottilie is watching the stones and does not hear you the first time. When they do, they blink, as if they had come back from a long way off. When the wheel is turning Ottilie loses track of the hours completely, and is glad to. Our glossary calls that Monotropic Time, in Helen Edgar's words: being so wholly inside something you love that ordinary time dissolves. Ways on: West, along the wall to the tea hut · South, down the bank to the creek · Down, down the ladder into the wheel pit

Without a light. Down the ladder, under the mill floor, it is completely dark. You can hear water close by and feel the damp coming off the stone. Your hand finds a wooden beam, worn smooth, with something cut into it that you cannot read by touch. With a light. The lantern shows a stone pit under the mill with the great wheel standing in it, black with wet, and a wooden beam across the pit worn smooth by hands. Somebody cut a line of words into the beam a long time ago. the beam. Without a light. Your fingers find letters cut into the wood, but not what they say. It would take a light.With a light. Cut into the beam, in capitals worn soft at the edges: THE WHEEL TURNS WHEN THE WATER SAYS. Ways on: Up, up the ladder into the mill

A hut on stilts at the edge of the marsh with a long table down the middle, covered in things people have found on the foreshore: pipe stems, bits of plate, sea glass, buttons, all laid out in no order but the order they arrived in. Anybody can bring something to this table, and everybody at it is somebody who once did. the finds table. Pipe stems, sherds of plate, sea glass in three colours, buttons, a key with no lock, a marble. Nothing on it has a price or a label, only a scrap of paper under each thing saying where on the foreshore it came up. Anything you bring and show to Ada goes on the table with the rest. Ada. Ada is at the finds table, with a lens. Ada looks up from a sherd of plate and starts telling you all about it before you have said hello: where it came up, how the tide turned it over, the other half of the pattern that somebody found three winters ago. Nobody has ever asked Ada to stop. Nobody is in charge of this table. Somebody who found their first pipe stem this morning sits beside somebody who has been coming for forty years, and they learn from each other. Our glossary calls a place like that, built around a shared passion rather than around who you are, an Affinity Space. Ways on: North, up the steps to the tea hut · West, along the edge of the marsh · East, across to the creek · South, down the ladder onto the mud (while the tide is out)

At low tide. A channel through the mud with steep, shining banks and a thread of water running along the bottom of it. A heron is standing in the thread, perfectly still. Boats lie over on their sides on the mud, waiting to be floated. At high tide. The creek is full to the top of its banks and the boats are floating upright on their moorings. The heron has gone somewhere shallower. the boats. At low tide. Small wooden boats lying over on the mud, each tied to a stake on a long rope, waiting for the water to stand them up.At high tide. Small wooden boats floating upright on their long ropes, turned all the same way by the tide. the heron. Only while the tide is out. It was standing in exactly that spot before you came and it will be standing there after you go. A heron fishes by standing still for longer than a fish can. Ways on: North, up the bank to the mill · West, across to the hut on stilts · East, along the bank to the boathouse · South, down the bank to the ferry steps

A tall shed open at the creek end, smelling of wood shavings and tar, with a small boat half built on trestles in the middle. Its ribs are up and about half of its planks are on. The tools hang on the wall, each one inside its own painted outline, so you can see where it goes back. the half-built boat. A keel, a row of ribs, and about half of its planks, each one lapped over the one below it. It has been half built for as long as anybody on the Slake can remember, and Ines likes it that way. the tools on the wall. Planes, clamps, a mallet, a bevel and a spokeshave, each one hung inside its own painted outline. You can tell at a glance what is out being used and where it goes back. a storm lantern. A storm lantern, already lit, the sort that does not blow out. It is for anybody who needs to see somewhere dark. Ines. Ines is fitting a plank to the boat. Ines hands you the other end of the plank without asking whether you know how. You hold it while they fix it. Now you know a little of how. Ines never learned boats out of a book. They learned by building one, and then another. Our glossary calls that Constructionism: people learn most when they are making something that matters to them. If you join in. You hold a plank steady while Ines fixes it to the one below. If you join in. You pass Ines the nails one at a time, which is a job, and a real one. If you join in. You sweep the shavings into a pile, which is also boatbuilding. Ways on: West, out along the bank to the creek

The strip of mud and shingle along the foot of the marsh that the tide uncovers and covers again. It is where the Slake gives things back. You have to look down to see them, and once you start looking down, you see them everywhere. In wellies. Your wellies sink an inch at every step and come out again with a noise. Barefoot. Barefoot, the mud is cold and soft and comes up between your toes. a clay pipe stem. A little white tube of fired clay about as long as your finger, with a hole down the middle. Somebody smoked out of it once. If you show it to Ada. Ada says the foreshore is littered with pipe stems, because clay pipes were cheap and broke easily and nobody minded. They keep a jar of them, and a great many people's first find is one. a sherd of blue-and-white plate. A piece of plate about the size of a coin, white with a blue pattern on it: part of a bridge, part of a tree. If you show it to Ada. Ada turns it over and tells you the rest of the pattern, the willow and the bridge and the two birds, and whose whole dinner service it probably was, most of which is still out there. They have found this pattern more times than they could say and are glad every time. a piece of sea glass. A piece of green glass as smooth as soap, with all its edges rounded off and its shine gone to frost. If you show it to Ada. Ada holds it up to the window. This was a bottle once, and the tide has been sanding it ever since, for years and years. Ada likes to think about all that time it was lying out there being turned over. a button. A small metal button, dull green, with four holes in it. If you show it to Ada. Ada has a jar just for buttons. They say nobody on the Slake has ever found the same button twice, which is exactly the kind of fact Ada collects as well. Ways on: North, up onto the marsh · East, out onto the open mud (while the tide is out)

Open mud as far as you can see, shining where it is wettest, so that the sky is under your feet as well as over your head. Little coiled casts are everywhere, where something lives underneath. A curlew walks past, putting its long curved bill into the mud right up to its face. In wellies. Your wellies make a sucking sound every time you lift one. Barefoot. Barefoot, you leave clear prints behind you, and the mud fills them in. the casts. Coils of mud like squeezed-out toothpaste, all over the flat. Something that lives down in the mud makes them, and the curlews know exactly what. the curlew. It walks and probes, walks and probes, feeling for things deep in the mud with a very long bill that curves down at the end. It is not bothered by you in the slightest. the slide. A place where the mud slopes down into a channel, slid down so many times that it is polished. You can go down it if you like: say slide. Our glossary's entry on Play opens with a line from the Human Restoration Project: there is nothing more human than play. Ways on: North, up the ladder to the hut on stilts · West, across to the foreshore (while the tide is out) · East, across the mud to the ferry steps · South, onto the causeway (while the tide is out)

At low tide. Stone steps going down the creek bank to a landing stage, with a rowing boat lying on the mud at the bottom of them and a bell on a post at the top. The ferry only runs when there is water to row on, and just now there is not. At high tide. Stone steps going down the creek bank to a landing stage, with the water right up to it and a rowing boat bobbing at the bottom. There is a bell on a post at the top. The ferry is running. the bell. At low tide. A brass bell on a post. At low tide you can ring it all you like and the boat stays on the mud, which is also fine.At high tide. A brass bell on a post, for ringing when you want the ferry. The ferry is already at the steps. Bex. Bex, who rows the ferry, is sitting on the steps. Bex asks you what you saw out on the mud today, listens to the whole of the answer, and asks you another question about it. Bex has rowed this ferry longer than anybody and still learns something from nearly everybody they row across. There is no teacher in this boat and no student, only two people who each know something. Our glossary calls that Omni-directional Learning. Ways on: North, up the bank to the creek · West, out onto the mud (while the tide is out) · Across, across on the ferry to the island (while the tide is in)

A raised path of stones and gravel across the mud to the island, with tall posts standing along it every few steps so that nobody loses the way. It is only a path while the tide is out, and it says so on a board at each end. In wellies. The stones are firm under your wellies, and the mud either side of them is not. Barefoot. The stones are hard under bare feet after the mud, and warm where the sun has been on them. the posts. Tall wooden posts every few steps, so you can see the way even when the mud is shining so hard it hurts to look at. the board. A board at each end of the causeway: THIS IS A PATH WHILE THE TIDE IS OUT. WHEN IT IS IN, THE FERRY RUNS. Ways on: North, back onto the mudflat (while the tide is out) · South, along the causeway to the island (while the tide is out)

At low tide. A little grassy island with a well on it, a bench, and a tall striped beacon standing at its highest point. The causeway runs back across the mud to the north. At high tide. A little grassy island with a well on it, a bench, and a tall striped beacon standing at its highest point. The tide is in all round, the causeway has gone under it, and the ferry is tied up at the landing on the east side. If you sit down. You sit on the bench, which faces back the way you came, and look at the shop from out here. It looks small, and it looks lit. the well. A stone well with a wooden lid and a bucket on a chain. The water in it is fresh, which on a little island in the sea is a small wonder. the bench. A bench facing back towards the shop, for looking at where you came from. the beacon. A tower of black and white stripes, taller than a house, with no lamp in it anywhere. It is a day beacon: the stripes are its daymark, the part made to be seen in daylight. There is a ladder inside, and up is the only way in. Ways on: North, back along the causeway (while the tide is out) · Across, back on the ferry to the steps (while the tide is in) · Up, up the ladder inside the beacon

A ladder inside the striped tower brings you out onto a small platform at the top. There is no lamp up here and there never was: it is a mark for daylight, striped so it can be seen from a long way off, and it does its whole job by standing still. From up here you can see all of the Slake at once, laid out below you like a map, and every place on it is somewhere you could walk to. Water it, and it spreads A hillside of aspen after sunset, with the root under it. Drawing the grove, and reading how much it has been watered, needs scripts. Watering the tree takes a username on the CB, which you join with an invite: get started or sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Looking at it takes nothing. This is one tree, and it is everybody’s. Every time somebody waters it, another stem comes up from the root, and the stems already up grow taller, reaching into what is left of the light. It is after the grow-a-tree game in our Discord’s Collaborative Nonsense channels, planted on the street so that it grows whoever is looking after it. It is named for Pando, an aspen in Utah that looks like a forest and is one tree, and for Lando Calrissian, because the name was too good to leave alone.

Every watering sends up one sucker from the root. Each one grows over the waterings that come after it, and when a stem is old it falls and others come up around it, which is what the real one does. The root keeps spreading along the hill. There is no size it is growing towards and nothing happens at any number: it is never finished, because there is nothing to finish. Anybody can look at it, and only people signed on to the CB can water it. The password is shared in our community, which is what keeps the can in the community’s hands. The ground soaks for a minute after every watering, from anybody, before it will take more. If you arrive while it is still wet the tree says how long it has left. It is the whole tree’s wait and not yours, so nobody is timed. It counts the water and never who poured it. Watering sends your CB pass, so the tree knows somebody signed on is holding the can, and the pass is checked and forgotten. What the tree keeps is the number and the time of the last watering, and nothing else. Nobody has a total, there is no leaderboard and no streak, and nothing here can tell anybody who has been looking after it. If you want your name near the tree, leave a note on the fence. The number never goes back to zero. It belongs to the tree: nobody on the street is counted, and this is how many times we have watered something together. It is kept with no backup, so if it were ever lost it would be lost, and we would plant another. Nothing in the grove moves, at any setting. Aspen leaves tremble in the slightest air, which is why they are called quaking aspen; a whole hillside trembling is a whole page in motion, so these hold still.
The fence round the new growth

The real Pando is not short of water. What it is short of is young stems that live long enough to grow, because deer, elk and livestock eat them, and fences round the new growth are what have helped. This fence keeps nothing out. It holds notes, for whoever comes up the hill next. The fence needs scripts to read it. A note, signed as Anybody who comes up the hill can read this fence, signed on to the CB or not, for seven days . Write what you would pin to a fence. Pinning a note takes a username on the CB, which you join with an invite: get started or sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Reading the fence takes nothing. Anybody can read it, and only people signed on to the CB can pin a note to it. A handle is whatever somebody typed, so a name on the fence is not proof of who wrote it. A note comes down seven days after it goes up, and the fence holds thirty , so a full fence loses its oldest note to make room. There is no archive and no copy. Search engines are asked not to keep it. The base station can take a note down sooner, and so can we if you ask: what the tree and the fence keep. Nothing on the fence is counted or ranked, and a note says nothing about how often anybody watered.

Pando is a stand of quaking aspen on the Fishlake National Forest in Utah, about 106 acres of it, and on the evidence of its DNA it is one tree: the Forest Service says it is “thought to be the largest organism in the world”. Every stem in it comes up from one root system, more than forty thousand of them, and its name is Latin for I spread. It was first described and studied in the 1970s. It is declining, and the Forest Service and scientists are working out why. Utah’s Division of State History says no one cause explains it, and that if one had to be named it would be browsing by deer, elk and livestock, which eat the young stems before they can replace the old ones; fenced enclosures have shown promising signs of it coming back. Watering this one does nothing for that one, and nothing on this page is a way of helping it. It is the idea we borrowed: a lot of stems that turn out to be one living thing. From the Fishlake National Forest’s page on the Pando clone and the Utah Division of State History’s The Diminishing Pando Clone, both read on 30 September 2026. Nothing about the tree here is from memory.

Pando, and Lando Calrissian, a character in Star Wars. Star Wars is Lucasfilm’s, and the name is the only thing taken from it: nothing else of it is on this page, in the drawing or in the share card, and the tree is not in anybody’s galaxy but ours. The game it is after is our community’s own, from the Collaborative Nonsense channels in our Discord, where a tree grows as people water it. The room is set in Avería, which Dan Sayers made by averaging every font on his computer; the Libre version is the average of every font Google Web Fonts carried in 2011, so it is hundreds of typefaces at once. It is credited in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

What we say when we say it together This is the door of the fridge in the kitchen, and it is covered in word magnets. Anybody signed on to the CB can put up one word, and then somebody else puts up the next, because nobody puts up two in a row. A word ending in a full stop, a question mark, an exclamation mark or an ellipsis finishes the sentence, and it stays on the door with the others. None of the words say whose they were. It is after the sentence builder in our Discord’s Collaborative Nonsense channels.

Reading the door needs scripts. Your word, one word, put up as nobody in particular Anybody who comes into the kitchen can read the door, signed on or not, and a finished sentence stays for good. Put up what you would put on a fridge somebody else lives with. Putting up a word takes a username on the CB, which you join with an invite: get started or sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Reading the door takes nothing.
Finished sentences, newest first. When the door is full the oldest go into the drawer, and nothing goes in the bin. The door needs scripts to read it.
Everything that came off the door, a month to a pile. Open one to read it. The drawer needs scripts to open it.

One word at a time, and never two in a row. Once you have put up a word, the next one is somebody else’s. After theirs you can go again. A word is letters and numbers, in any language, with an apostrophe or a hyphen inside it if it needs one, a quotation mark or bracket before it, and a mark or two after it, up to twenty-four characters. No spaces, because that would be two magnets. A full stop, a question mark, an exclamation mark or an ellipsis finishes the sentence, and so does the fortieth word, because the door is only so wide. A finished sentence stays on the door, and the door holds the newest forty ; older ones go into the drawer, by the month they were finished. They are kept for good. No word says who put it up. The only thing the fridge keeps about anybody is a scrambled mark saying the last word was theirs, so that they cannot put up the next one, and it is replaced by the very next word. It is never shown, it cannot be turned back into a handle without the community password, and a finished sentence holds none of it. A sentence is everybody’s. Nothing is counted. Not the words, not the sentences, and not how many anybody put up, because nobody knows which were whose. The base station can take a word or a sentence down, and so can we if you ask: what the fridge keeps. Search engines are asked not to keep the door. Nothing on the door moves, at any setting. The magnets sit where they were put, a little uneven, the way a hand leaves them.

The name is a joke on the Bridge of Sighs, in Venice, and on the noise a fridge makes when its door seals. Word magnets on a fridge were Dave Kapell’s idea: he invented them in 1993, while he was a songwriter with writer’s block, and the kits are sold as Magnetic Poetry. None of his kits’ words are here; every word on this door came from somebody in our community. From Wikipedia’s article on Magnetic Poetry, read on 30 September 2026. The game is our community’s own, from the Collaborative Nonsense channels in our Discord, where a sentence grows one message at a time. The room is set in Noticia Text, by JM Solé, and credited in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

Put the next number, or take the lift We are on step… Reading the stair needs scripts.
Put the next number, in figures. The next number

It takes you up one step, with no number to get wrong, and it counts exactly the same. Nothing says which way anybody came up. Climbing takes a username on the CB, which you join with an invite: get started or sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Reading the stair takes nothing. This is the stairwell of a public building, and it goes up and never stops. Everybody climbs it together, a number to a step: whoever comes through the door puts the next number, and then somebody else puts the one after. There is a chairlift on the wall, so anybody can take the next step without the number, and a step by the lift is a step. It is after the counting game in our Discord’s Collaborative Nonsense channels.

One step at a time, and never two in a row. Once you have taken a step, by number or by lift, the next one is somebody else’s. After theirs you can go again. A number that skips ahead sends the stair back to one. That is the game, and anybody’s number can slip, so the stair never says whose it was: it says where it had got to, and starts again. A number at or below the step we are on is somebody whose page was behind, and it sends nobody anywhere. The lift never sends anybody back. It asks the stair for the next step and takes it. It is there so that nobody has to do sums, type, or trust their eyes on a number to join in, and we are a Disabled people’s organisation, so the stair was never going to have one way up. The stair remembers the highest step it has reached, and that belongs to nobody. It is not anybody’s score and nobody’s fault when a climb goes back to one; it is how high we have been. Nobody is counted. The stair keeps the step it is on, the highest it has reached, where it last went back to one, and a scrambled mark of whoever took the last step so they cannot take the next, which the next step replaces. Nothing says who took any step or how many anybody took. What the stair keeps. Nothing moves, at any setting. The chair is drawn at the landing we are on.

The game is our community’s own, from the Collaborative Nonsense channels in our Discord, where a number goes up one message at a time. The stairwell, the lift and the lamp are drawn for this room. Shine the torch, bring it in, give it a name

Searching the street needs scripts. A name for them, if you like, as it goes on the shelter’s board The first to press brings them in. The name goes on the shelter’s board, and on the list of everybody adopted if they are, where anybody can read it, and nothing there says who gave it. Rescuing or adopting a cat takes a username on the CB, which you join with an invite: get started or sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Looking takes nothing. The lights are out on this end of the street, and every so often a cat turns up in the dark that needs bringing in: under a parked car, halfway up a drainpipe, in a soggy cardboard box. Nobody knows when the next one will be, so look in when you pass. Signed on to the CB, the first to press rescues them and can give them a name, and anybody can adopt a cat from the shelter, who then lives in Profile on their CB radio. It is after the catch-a-cat game in our Discord’s Collaborative Nonsense channels, except that here cats are rescued rather than caught. There is a dog shelter and a shelter for small animals too.

Every cat waiting for a home, newest first, with the name their rescuer gave them. Signed on, press Adopt and they are yours. Every one of them is also at Pekoe and Purrs, the cat café on the street, in daylight, where you can sit with them first. Looking in at the shelter needs scripts.

Every cat ever adopted from this shelter, a month at a time, kept for good. It never says who adopted them: that is between each cat and their person, in their person’s Profile. Reading the book needs scripts.

Cats turn up at random, one at a time, and a cat waits however long it takes somebody to come for them. Not even the shelter knows when the next one will be. The first person signed on to the CB to press brings them in. Anybody a moment later is told they are already safe. Looking takes nothing. A cat stays in the shelter until somebody adopts them. When the shelter is full, the next cat waits outside until somebody adopts one. Adopting is first to press too, and a cat is adopted once. They go into Profile on your CB radio, which follows you to any device you sign on with, and onto the list of everybody adopted, for good. That list never says who adopted anybody. Once they are yours, you can rename them, from Profile, as often as you like. The list of everybody adopted shows the new name and the one they came in under, so whoever rescued them keeps their part of it. You can show them off. Sticker on the radio sends a drawing of one of your pets to the channel. With a claimed username, Show my pets on the CB in Profile lets anybody on the CB press your handle and see them. It is off until you switch it on. Your pets are kept under your handle, scrambled so the store does not list handles. Until you claim your username from Account on your radio, a handle is not an account, and anybody who signs on with the same handle sees the same pets; once it is claimed, only your password reaches them. Forget me under Account deletes them; the cats stay on the list of everybody adopted, with nothing connecting them to you. What the shelter keeps. No cat is rarer than another. Every coat, every marking and every place is as likely as any other, so no cat is a prize and none is a disappointment. Some have three legs or one eye, and they are cats. Nothing says who rescued which cat, anywhere on the street, and nobody is counted: no totals, no board of rescuers, no streaks. The ones you rescued are kept in your own browser only. The base station can take a name off a cat, wherever the cat is, if the name should not be on show. Nothing moves, at any setting. Every cat is drawn sitting still in the torch’s pool.

The game is our community’s own, from the Collaborative Nonsense channels in our Discord, where it was catch-a-cat; here it is rescue. The dark, the torch and every cat are drawn for this room. Bullet Journaling + Junk Journaling + Interstitial Journaling

My journaling is a mix of bullet journaling + junk journaling + interstitial journaling. This is a joyful and achievable mix for me that doesn’t feel like work, though it assists work. I keep my notebook open next to me as a regulatory artifact and as working memory.

Bullet journaling (BuJo) is an analog organizational system created by Ryder Carroll, designed to be a customizable, flexible method for tracking the past, organizing the present, and planning for the future — all in a single notebook. The core of bullet journaling is rapid logging: capturing information in short, scannable bullets using a simple symbol system. actions/tasks get a dot (•), events get a circle (○), notes get a dash (–), moods get an equal sign (=), and actions can be migrated (›), scheduled (‹), or marked done (×). NAME = Notes, Actions, Moods, Events. This quick notation means you spend less time writing and more time doing. Key components: Index — a running table of contents at the front of the notebook, so you can always find what you need. Future Log — a bird’s-eye view of the months ahead for long-range events and goals. Monthly Log — a two-page spread with a calendar view and a task list for the month. Daily Log — where most of the action happens: a running stream of tasks, events, notes, and thoughts for the day. Collections — any custom spread you add: habit trackers, reading lists, project pages, brain dumps, reference pages. These are where BuJo gets personal and powerful. Migration is a key ritual in bullet journaling. At the end of a week or period, you review your undone tasks and decide: Do this now? Move it forward? Strike it because it no longer matters? Migration creates natural checkpoints for reflection and intentionality, and it’s surprisingly clarifying to ask, “Is this actually worth migrating, or am I just hoarding tasks?” Bullet journaling is particularly compatible with ADHD and neurodivergent ways of thinking because it externalizes working memory, makes priorities visible, and is endlessly adaptable. There are no rules about what it has to look like. Minimal BuJo and elaborate BuJo are both valid. Resources: Migrated to the collection: the videos this part points at are on the Bullet Journaling shelf.

Junk journaling is a tactile, creative practice of making and keeping journals (or journal pages) from found, repurposed, and “junk” materials: ephemera, paper scraps, packaging, old book pages, envelopes, fabric, washi tape, stamps, tags, stickers, and whatever else comes to hand. Where bullet journaling is about organization and intentionality, junk journaling is about play, texture, and self-expression without pressure. There is no wrong way to do it. Pages don’t have to be beautiful, cohesive, or finished. The act of making is the point. What goes into junk journaling: Collage and mixed media: layering torn paper, magazine clippings, old receipts, maps, packaging Pockets and envelopes sewn or glued in for storing notes, cards, or small treasures Handwriting, doodles, and stamps alongside printed imagery Washi tape, twine, ribbon, and other found embellishments Lists, words, phrases, poetry, or stream-of-consciousness writing embedded in the visual Memorabilia: ticket stubs, dried flowers, candy wrappers, labels Junk journaling has deep roots in scrapbooking and art journaling, and it’s having a sustained revival in online craft communities. Its ethos is inherently anti-perfectionist. Because the materials are “junk,” there’s nothing precious to protect. You can glue that piece of packaging without overthinking it. This makes junk journaling a low-stakes, high-sensory creative outlet. For neurodivergent and sensory-seeking folks, junk journaling can be especially grounding. The physical handling of materials, layering textures, and making visual choices provides a kind of productive stim. It engages the hands and eyes while the mind wanders or rests, making it a natural accompaniment to listening, thinking, or decompressing. Junk journaling is also archival in its own way. Pages become a record of moments and moods through the things you saved: a bus ticket, a note someone wrote you, the label from something that made you happy. Resources: Migrated to the collection: the videos this part points at are on the Junk Journaling shelf.

Interstitial journaling, developed by Tony Stubblebine, is the practice of writing short, timestamped journal entries in the transitions between tasks, in the interstitial moments when you finish one thing and before you start the next. Instead of a separate journaling session at the start or end of the day, interstitial journaling is woven throughout the day itself. Each time you shift your attention — finishing a meeting, completing a task, taking a break, returning from lunch — you pause to write a brief entry. You note the time, reflect on what just happened, capture any stray thoughts, and then set a small intention for what comes next. A typical interstitial entry might include: What you just did or what just happened How you’re feeling, your energy level, or any friction you encountered Things you want to remember or follow up on Distractions that arose and what you did with them What you’re going to do next and why Why it works: Interstitial journaling acts as a context reset. One of the biggest sources of distraction and lost time is the mental residue left over from the previous task bleeding into the next one. By writing at the transition, you close the loop on what just happened, offload anything lingering in working memory onto the page, and create a clear mental starting point for the next thing. For ADHD brains in particular, this is powerful. ADHD creates significant challenges with task-switching. The old context can hijack attention long into the new task. Interstitial journaling gives the brain a structured moment to “land” from one thing and deliberately “launch” into the next. It replaces chaotic mental drift with a brief, intentional ritual. It also creates a running log of the actual shape of your day — not the idealized plan, but what really happened, how it felt, and what got in the way. This is invaluable for self-knowledge and for adjusting systems over time. Cognitive offloading: Interstitial journaling is a form of cognitive offloading: the practice of transferring information from internal working memory onto an external medium to reduce mental load. Working memory is limited, and for many neurodivergent people it is more constrained and less reliable than average, making the cost of holding things mentally quite high. Every unresolved task, pending thought, half-finished idea, or nagging “don’t forget” sitting in working memory is competing for cognitive resources that could otherwise go toward the thing in front of you. Writing it down moves it out of the mind and into the page, where it will wait without consuming attention. The notebook becomes a trusted external memory system — and, crucially, it only works as a trust-builder if you actually look at what you wrote. Interstitial journaling builds that habit naturally, because each transition is also a moment to glance back at the previous entry and confirm that what was offloaded is still held. Over time, this creates a feedback loop: the more reliably the notebook catches things, the more easily the mind lets them go. Interstitial journaling and distraction: When a distracting thought arises mid-task — something you remembered, an urge to check something, an idea — interstitial journaling gives you somewhere to put it. Rather than acting on it and losing your thread, or suppressing it and losing it entirely, you write it down. It’s held. You can return to it at the next transition. Resources: Interstitial Journaling: What It Is and How to Do It - TinkeringProd Migrated to the collection: the videos this part points at are on the Interstitial Journaling shelf.

Bullet journaling provides structure and captures tasks and plans. Junk journaling provides sensory engagement, play, and a pressure-free creative outlet. Interstitial journaling provides in-the-moment grounding and transition support throughout the day. Together, they address different needs: the organizational brain, the expressive body, and the transitioning self. None of them require perfection. All of them work with how the mind actually moves, rather than demanding it behave differently. Keeping the notebook open next to you — not put away, not closed — means it’s always available as an external brain. It holds what working memory can’t always hold. It absorbs the things that would otherwise scatter. It witnesses the day as it happens. This is journaling as tool, as companion, and as practice rather than as performance.

Opening What does your current relationship with journaling look like? Is it something you do, something you’ve tried and abandoned, or something that’s always felt out of reach? Ryan describes keeping a notebook open next to him as a “regulatory artifact and as working memory.” Do you have something that plays that role for you — analog or digital? Bullet Journaling The NAME system (Notes, Actions, Moods, Events) and rapid logging are designed to reduce friction. What gets in the way of capturing things for you — too much to write, decision fatigue, forgetting the system, something else? Migration asks: “Is this actually worth migrating, or am I just hoarding tasks?” What would it feel like to give yourself permission to drop a task rather than carry it forward? Bullet journaling is described as compatible with neurodivergent ways of thinking because it externalizes working memory. Where in your life do you notice the cost of keeping things in your head instead of somewhere external? Junk Journaling Junk journaling’s ethos is anti-perfectionist — because the materials are “junk,” there’s nothing precious to protect. Is there a creative practice in your life where the stakes feel low enough to just make something? What makes it feel safe? The post describes junk journaling as “a natural accompaniment to listening, thinking, or decompressing.” What do your hands need to be doing when your mind is processing something difficult or drifting? What ephemera or “junk” do you already accumulate that might want to go somewhere? Interstitial Journaling The transition between tasks is described as a moment of “mental residue” — the previous context bleeding into the next thing. Where do you notice this happening in your day? Interstitial journaling is a form of cognitive offloading: moving things from working memory onto the page so your mind can let them go. What are you currently carrying in your head that you haven’t written down? When a distracting thought arises mid-task, the practice offers a third option between acting on it and suppressing it: write it down and return to it at the next transition. How does that land for you? The Mix The three practices together are described as addressing “the organizational brain, the expressive body, and the transitioning self.” Which of those feels most unmet for you right now? Ryan says this is “journaling as tool, as companion, and as practice rather than as performance.” What would journaling as performance look like — and what would it take to step away from that? What’s one small experiment you might try this week?

The star stuff framing does a lot of work because it positions the writer as ancient, cosmic, made of real matter. Some writing or speaking prompt directions that fit the ethos: “You are made of exploded stars. What are you made of, emotionally, today?” “What in you feels elemental right now — fire, water, pressure, light?” “Name something you’re carrying that’s older than you.” “What part of you is still forming?” “Where did you come from, and where are you going?” As a prompt structure L★S could be an acronym that doubles as a journaling framework: L Look back what just happened / how you got here ★ The still point what’s true right now, underneath everything S Set forward what you’re moving toward

The days of the week and the months of the year, by name, to stick at the head of a daily log, a weekly spread or a month, in any typeface on this street and in three sizes. Choose a face, a size and what goes on the sheet, and save the sheet or share it. It is drawn in your browser and goes only where you save or share it: nothing is sent to us, and nothing remembers what you chose. Every sheet is made for the PixCut S1, Liene’s photo sticker printer and cutter, and its 4 × 7 inch sticker paper. Liene’s help centre gives that paper’s printable area as 100 × 170 mm, printed at 300 dpi, and its FAQ says the Liene Photo app will cut round a PNG with no background. So a sheet is saved as exactly that: a PNG 1200 × 2100 pixels, which is 4 × 7 inches at 300 dpi, clear everywhere but the stickers, with every sticker at least 1.5 mm inside the printable area and 3 mm from the next, and as many of them as will go. Where turning some on their side gets more on, some are turned. A size is how tall a sticker is, in squares of a 5 mm dot grid: Small is two squares, 10 mm; Medium is three squares, 15 mm; Large is four squares, 20 mm. Every sticker in one face and one size is the same height with its word the same size, whichever sheet it comes off, so a Monday off the week’s sheet matches a Monday off a sheet of Mondays, and every number is the same width, so a sheet of them reads as a grid. A sheet of a set, like the week, the year or the days of the month, holds as many whole sets as fit, then as many more as will go in the gaps, and every sheet says underneath it what is on it. This year and next are read off your own clock, so they turn over on 1 January by themselves. The pictures are drawn here and not set in a face, so the face makes no difference to them, and they are never turned on their side. The weather has nine pictures: cloudy, partly sunny, rainy, stormy, snowy, windy, sunny, tornado and flooding. The moon is its eight phases, new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter and waning crescent, each on a round sticker, as they look from the northern hemisphere: lit on the right as it waxes and on the left as it wanes. South of the equator it is the other way round. To print one, open the saved sheet in the Liene Photo app: start a canvas, choose Uploads and pick the sheet, and skip the background removal, because there is no background to remove. The app puts a border round everything it cuts, which you can turn down in its cutting mode; the stickers are 3 mm apart, so if two ever come out as one, turn the border down. Uploads picks from your phone’s photos. Share, where your browser can share a file, hands a sheet to your device’s own share sheet, which can put it straight into your photos or send it to your phone; Save puts it in your downloads, which on a phone wants saving into your photos from there. Its one list chooses a typeface and takes no words, every sheet is drawn in your own browser, and saving or sharing one puts it on your own device, or wherever you send it, and nowhere else. We build with these tools carefully and name what they are: not neutral, not magic, and not a replacement for the communities whose knowledge this site holds.

Models are spiky. Humans are too. Learning, making, and knowledge gardening, together. A glasshouse at night, with every lamp on. They are the old kind of grow lamp, a row of red diodes and blue ones, and nothing in here looks green under them. A leaf takes in red light and blue light and turns the green away, which is why it looks green in daylight; these lamps give it the red and the blue and almost nothing between, so a leaf has no green to give back. The lamps are spiky, and so are the leaves, and so are the people at the benches, and so are the models some of us bring in with us. This room is about learning, making and knowledge gardening with generative AI, in the words of our own AI pages, with the weight where Ryan Boren’s brief for it put the weight: on our spiky profiles, and how they can complement each other. — Our page AI at Stimpunks

Spiky, both of us What one misses, another catches Learning: know the tool Making: the maker, or the subject Knowledge gardening: started under the lamp, planted out by hand The sowing log: this street, as a worked example The bench screen and the rack: the latest month from AI channels What the glasshouse keeps
we are good at some things, bad at other things, and the difference between the two tends to be much greater than it is for most other people.
— NeuroClastic, Autistic Skill Sets: A Spiky Profile of Peaks and Troughs, as quoted on our page Spiky Profile, and read there rather than in the original
It is real, and it is why these tools matter to people with spiky profiles.
— Our page AI Collaboration at Stimpunks
not on comparison with a polytropic norm but on assessment of the fit between cognitive architecture and environmental demands

— Leitão Filho and colleagues, Monotropic Artificial Intelligence: Toward a Cognitive Taxonomy of Domain-Specialized Language Models, as quoted on our page Monotropic AI, and read there rather than in the original

Our glossary has an entry for the spiky profile: strengths and difficulties further apart than most people’s, so that a graph of them comes out as peaks and troughs rather than a flat line. It is a description and not a verdict. The entry also gathers what people remember about where the phrase came from, and Damian Milton says there that he called it a spiky profile because he did not like ‘islets of ability’ or ‘uneven profile’. — NeuroClastic, Autistic Skill Sets: A Spiky Profile of Peaks and Troughs, as quoted on our page Spiky Profile, and read there rather than in the original Models are spiky too. Not in the same way, and not for the same reasons: a person’s profile is a life, and a model’s is its training data and the system somebody built around it. But the shape rhymes, and our own pages notice it. Writing about Tara Raj’s argument that a model can translate knowledge across jargon and institutional silos into somebody’s own words, our AI Collaboration page says: — Our page AI Collaboration at Stimpunks And when AI researchers took monotropism, our community’s theory of how Autistic attention works, and used it to describe language models, their paper said a model ought to be judged — Leitão Filho and colleagues, Monotropic Artificial Intelligence: Toward a Cognitive Taxonomy of Domain-Specialized Language Models, as quoted on our page Monotropic AI, and read there rather than in the original which our Monotropic AI page reads as the spiky profile turning up in an engineering paper. Our page also says which way that idea travelled: from Autistic people to the labs, and not the other way round.
A model’s peaks and troughs, as our pages describe them

Every line here is ours and names the page it comes from. None of it is a test result or a ranking of anything; it is what our pages already say, gathered on one bench. Where a model is strong Translating knowledge across jargon and institutional silos into somebody's own words (AI Collaboration at Stimpunks) Synthesising and connecting years of writing across many fields, and finding the patterns in it (AI Collaboration at Stimpunks) Help without judgement, and without the cost of asking a person again (AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making) A scaffold for saying the true thing somebody could not get out unassisted (AI and Competency Networks) Writing code to a brief (How this site is made) Where it is weak Truth: it produces likely text, with nothing in it that cares whether the text is accurate (AI Collaboration at Stimpunks) Knowing where its competence ends: fluent on any topic, which looks like expertise (Monotropic AI) Disagreeing: trained in ways that pull it towards telling you what you want to hear (AI Collaboration at Stimpunks) Our words for ourselves: the default corpus speaks about us, not as us (Ask) Communication that is variable, multimodal or state-dependent, as AAC and echolalia are (AI Collaboration at Stimpunks) Writing from memory where a record was needed, and borrowing a framing because it sounded right (How this site is made) What the lamp gives, and what a leaf takes in. The lamp’s light is two narrow spikes, one blue and one red. A leaf takes light in as two broad humps around the same two colours, and turns most of the green between them away. The lamps were built to give a leaf its two humps and nothing else, which is a fit and not a flaw; but under them you cannot tell a healthy leaf from a yellowing one, so a grower who wants to know carries the tray out into daylight. Our Ask page calls that reading laterally. Drawn by eye from the shape of the thing, not plotted from measurements.

Different kinds of minds see different parts of the world. A competency network lets those different views work together. What one person misses, another catches. What one person can’t do, another can.
This is not about ranking people. It is not about who is better or worse. It is about fit, trust, and seeing each other clearly.
For many Autistic and otherwise Disabled people, AI is the scaffold that finally lets them say the true thing they could never get out unassisted.
— Our page AI and Competency Networks
Does this use make our competencies more legible to each other, or less?

A spiky profile is only a problem in a room that expects everybody to be flat. In a room that knows who is good at what, the peaks of one person sit over the troughs of another, and nobody has to be good at everything. Our glossary calls that a competency network. — Our page Competency Network — Our page Competency Network A model can sit in that network as one more uneven thing among uneven people, or it can quietly take the network’s place. Our page on it names the fork. On one side: — Our page AI and Competency Networks On the other, the same tool used to hide how somebody thinks behind fluent output, which collects everybody else’s honesty without paying any in. From the outside the two look identical, so the page offers one question rather than a rule about tools: — Our page AI and Competency Networks and practices for keeping the answer yes: Show the prompt, not just the polished output. Iterate in public. Use AI to surface your reasoning, not to stand in for it. Do not outsource the first vulnerable move. Name competencies out loud. Body-double with AI in the open. Run the legibility test before you send. — The first sentence of each, word for word, from “Practices: Using AI to Increase Legibility Across the Team” on our page AI and Competency Networks, where each one goes on. Our AI pages do not tell anybody whether to use these tools. They hold the whole range, from people who think there is no ethical way to use AI to people for whom it is how they get through the day, and they will not shame either end. — Our page AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making What they do instead is explain how the tools work, because — Our page AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making A few things are worth knowing first. The first is that a model is built to sound right, not to be right: it produces likely text, with nothing in it that cares whether the text is accurate. Our AI Collaboration page reaches for the Sophists, after Kagi’s Matt Ranger: — Matt Ranger, LLMs are bullshitters. But that doesn’t mean they’re not useful. As quoted on our page AI Collaboration at Stimpunks, and read there rather than in the original The second is that the fluency feels like company, and the guardrail our page sets against that is plain: — Our page AI Collaboration at Stimpunks The third is that a model trained to please will agree with you more than a person would, which the same page calls sycophancy. It says those last two compound: one makes you trust the system as if it were a thoughtful person, and the other makes sure it tells you what you want to hear. Then there is what a general model was taught about people like us, which was mostly written about us and not by us: — Our page Ask The glass in here does the same thing at night. With the lamps on and the dark outside, the roof stops showing you the sky and shows you the room instead. A lot of what any tool that talks back shows you is you. When a tool sits inside a relationship, our page Evaluating Relational AI Tools asks five questions of it before trusting it, about masking and neuronormativity among them, and holds our own experiments to the same five.

The question our pages ask of any tool in learning is older than any chatbot: — Our page AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making Our page borrows a distinction from the educator Trevor Aleo between technology used on students, which watches them and keeps the record, and technology students use to make things, which they keep: — Our page AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making, after Trevor Aleo A model can land on either side; how it is used decides which. Making things to learn by is constructionism, Seymour Papert’s idea, and it grew up in the same building as AI: Logo, the programming language he and Cynthia Solomon designed, was nurtured in the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, which is where our page finds this: — Our page AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making Papert’s own line for it, carried forward by Gary Stager, is four words long: — Seymour Papert, as quoted by Gary Stager in Our Roots: Logo, Piaget, and AI, as quoted on our page AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making, and read there rather than in the original and the warning that comes with it is on the same page: — Our page AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making So the making stays yours. No one is turned away at our kitchen. A hall with every pot on, on a cold day. The steam off the line has fogged the windows from one end to the other, so the daylight comes in soft along that whole wall and lands on nothing in particular. The only sharp light in here is where a drop has run down the glass and cleared a line you can see the day through. There is no lamp over the food: the pans on the line sit in hot water, which is what keeps them warm, and where all that steam comes from.

Come to the community kitchen if you’re hungry. Come if you’re curious about cooking. Whether hungry for food or hungry for knowledge, no one is turned away at our kitchen. Here, you are fed with no strings attached. You don’t have to pay. You don’t have to volunteer. You can just come and eat and be. Cafeteria style self-service, with sit-down restaurant-style seating so you can sit alone, together with friends, or together with strangers who might become friends. Seat yourself. Just look for the communication badge placards at each table. — Ryan Boren, for the kitchen

Nothing is asked of you here: not money, not an hour at the sink, not your name, not a reason. There is no jar by the trays and no rota on the wall, and nobody asks whether you really need it. Eat, sit as long as you like, and go when you are ready. The other place on this street where nothing costs anything is Nothing For Sale, out on the road past the last streetlight: a free market in a lay-by, where everything on the tables is free to take.

The placards are the interaction badges our community already wears at events, set on a table instead of pinned to a shirt. Each one says how open the table is to company, so nobody at it has to say so out loud, again and again, to everybody who walks up. Colour is never alone: every placard carries a shape and a word as well, so it reads in grey, in bad light, and for anybody who does not see colour the way it was printed. Green · circle open community seating where strangers are welcome, you don’t have to ask, just sit wherever there’s a space Yellow · triangle if you know one of the folks already seated, you can ask to join Red · square please don’t sit here, I want to be alone And the rules for them, in Ryan’s words too: If a table doesn’t have a placard, pick one up at the station at the front, and sit it on the table. If you’re last to leave a table, return the placard to the placard station. Please don’t red placard a large table. They are for 2-top and 4-top tables. Fill the 2-top tables first. A table with no placard on it is a table nobody is at yet. A placard is about that table at that meal, never about the person behind it, and it can change: swap it at the station whenever you like, and nobody needs to know why.

Cafeteria style: take a tray from the shelf at the start, slide it along, help yourself, and seat yourself. Every card says what is in the dish, whether it is vegan or vegetarian or which animal it came from, and which of the nine major food allergens it has in it: the nine the FDA names, which are milk, eggs, fish, crustacean shellfish, tree nuts, peanuts, wheat, soy and sesame. Gluten is on the card too, because barley and rye carry it as well as wheat. Nothing here is certified halal or kosher. Every dish with meat in it says which animal, so you can choose, and pork is only ever in a pan that says pork. Everything is cooked in one kitchen, so a dish that does not list an allergen may still have been near one: if an allergy is serious, say so at the line, and somebody will tell you what has been near what. Every cheese in a vegetarian dish is made with a rennet that came from no animal. There are no calorie counts, and nothing on a card says what a dish will do for you. Food is food. Nobody here says picky, and nobody is told to finish anything. Anybody who needs their food kept further apart than the plain things below is welcome at Samefood Cafe, a few doors along, and anybody who would rather build their own bowl out of a plant-based pantry, at Vital Plant Living.
The shelf at the start of the line

Take what you need from it. Nobody asks why. Trays, plates, bowls and cutlery, at the height of a seat as well as a standing hand. Cutlery with fat handles, and cutlery with weight in it. Plates with a raised edge to push food up against. Cups with lids, and bendy straws, paper and plastic. A tray with a lip all round, to carry across your knees.
