The line and every table are built to work from a wheelchair. Every number here is out of the 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, as the U.S. Access Board publishes them, and each one links to its section there. The tray slide runs the whole length of the line, with its top between 28 and 34 inches (710 and 865 mm) off the floor, so a tray slides along at the height of a seat. ADA 904 Every pan, shelf and dispenser on the line is in reach from a seat: nothing higher than 48 inches (1220 mm) and nothing lower than 15 inches (380 mm). The standard asks this of at least half of each kind of self-service shelf. Here it is all of them. ADA 308, ADA 227 Every table top is between 28 and 34 inches (710 and 865 mm) high, with clear space under it up to 27 inches (685 mm) and at least 30 inches (760 mm) wide, for knees and a wheelchair. ADA 902, ADA 306 Every aisle is at least 36 inches (915 mm) wide. ADA 403 There is room to turn a wheelchair right round, a circle 60 inches (1525 mm) across, at both ends of the line and by the placard station. ADA 304 The standard asks for at least one seat in twenty at a dining surface to be built this way. Here it is every seat, so there is no wheelchair table, and nobody has to sit wherever the wheelchair seat happens to be. ADA 226 And what no standard measures: Help on the line is offered, never assumed. Ask for a hand with a tray, a ladle or a lid, and somebody gives it; nobody takes your tray off you to be kind. If the line is more than you have in you today — standing, waiting, carrying, choosing quickly — sit down anywhere and say so, and somebody brings the week’s board, and then the plate. At every table one place has no chair in it, and every chair lifts out, so anybody can sit anywhere. The whole week is on this page, so you can choose before you arrive rather than at the counter with people waiting behind you.

Hungry for knowledge counts too. The teaching kitchen is at the back: a counter at table height with room under it for knees and a wheelchair, a mirror angled over it so everybody can see the cook’s hands, and a screen beside the mirror. There is no sign-up, and nobody takes a register. Every class is written here in full, to follow at your own pace, in here or at home. Each one says how long it takes before you start, what it sounds and smells like, and that all of it can be done sitting down. Nothing is graded, and nothing ends in a certificate.

An onion, a carrot and a pepper cut small, which is how most things start Hands on 15 to 20 minutes In all 15 to 20 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like The knife on the board, a steady knock. Cut onion stings the eyes and nose for a few minutes; goggles hang on a hook by the counter, and nobody says a word about them. You need: A cutting board on a damp cloth, and a sharp knife: a blunt one needs more force, and force is what makes a knife slip. Or kitchen scissors, or a chopper you press down on. What goes in: An onion, a carrot, a pepper. Put the board on a damp cloth so it stays where you put it. Cut the onion in half from the root to the tip and peel off the papery skin. Lay each half flat side down: anything lying on a flat side cannot roll. Curl the fingertips of the hand holding it under, knuckles forward, so the flat of the blade rests against your knuckles and your fingertips are behind them. That is the claw. Cut by pushing the knife forward and down, and move the claw back a little after every cut. For something round, like a carrot, cut a thin slice off one side first, so it lies flat. Then do the same. If a knife is not for you today, kitchen scissors cut spring onions, herbs and peppers well, and a chopper you press down on does an onion in seconds. Frozen chopped onion and bags of cut vegetables count as cooking. Nobody checks.
A pot of rice, and a pot of beans

Plain rice for four, and black beans from a tin or from dry Hands on 10 minutes In all rice in 30 minutes; beans from dry take a night’s soak and 1 to 2 hours more Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like A quiet one. A lid that rattles means the heat is too high, which is the pot telling you to turn it down. You need: A pot with a lid that fits, a sieve, and a fork. What goes in: 1 cup of long-grain white rice, 1½ cups of water, salt. A tin of black beans, or a cup of dried ones. Oil, garlic, cumin. Rinse the rice in a sieve under the tap until the water runs nearly clear. Put it in the pot with the water and a pinch of salt, and bring it to the boil. Turn the heat to its lowest, put the lid on, and leave it for 15 minutes without lifting the lid. Take it off the heat and leave it covered for 10 minutes more, then loosen it with a fork. Brown rice wants more water and about twice as long; its bag says how much. Beans from a tin: drain and rinse them, and warm them in a pot with a splash of water, a little oil, salt, a crushed clove of garlic and a pinch of cumin. Beans from dry: soak them overnight in plenty of water, drain them, cover them with fresh water by a couple of inches, and simmer them until they are soft all the way through, which takes 1 to 2 hours depending on the bean. Salt them near the end.
Soup out of what is there

A big pot of vegetable soup, about six bowls Hands on 20 minutes In all 50 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like Onions in oil hiss, then go quiet and sweet-smelling. The blender at the end is loud for about a minute; skip it and the soup is a chunky one, which is also soup. You need: A big pot, a wooden spoon, and a stick blender if you want it smooth. What goes in: 2 tablespoons of oil, an onion, 2 carrots, 2 sticks of celery, 2 cloves of garlic, 2 potatoes, a tin of chopped tomatoes, 4 cups (1 litre) of vegetable stock, salt and pepper, and whatever else is in the drawer. Chop the onion, carrots and celery small, and cook them in the oil over a medium heat with a pinch of salt for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring now and then, until they are soft but not brown. Add the garlic, chopped, and cook it for a minute. Add the potatoes in small cubes, the tomatoes and the stock. Bring it to the boil, then turn it down and simmer it for 20 to 25 minutes, until a piece of potato is soft when you poke it. Taste it. A soup tastes flat until it has enough salt: add a little, stir, taste, and add again. Blend it, or don’t. Soup keeps in the fridge for a few days. Reheat it until it is steaming hot all the way through. Another way: With chicken: stir in cooked chicken at the end and heat the soup until it is steaming hot all the way through, to 165°F (74°C). Safe temperatures, from FoodSafety.gov: Leftovers, of any kind: 165°F (74°C); Chicken, turkey and other poultry, all of it: 165°F (74°C).
One tray, one oven, and a chair

Roast vegetables with chickpeas, or with chicken thighs, for two to four Hands on 15 minutes In all 45 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like The oven ticks as it heats, and the tray spits a little. It smells of roasting from about twenty minutes in. Oven gloves that cover the forearm hang on the hook by the oven. You need: A big baking tray, oven gloves, and a food thermometer for the chicken. What goes in: 4 potatoes or sweet potatoes, 3 carrots, 2 peppers, an onion, a tin of chickpeas, 3 tablespoons of oil, salt, pepper, and paprika or cumin. Heat the oven to 425°F (220°C). Cut the vegetables into pieces about the same size as each other, so they are done at the same time. Toss them on the tray with the oil, salt and spice, and spread them out in one layer. Piled up, they steam instead of browning. Roast them for 20 minutes. Drain the chickpeas, pat them dry, and scatter them over. Turn everything over with a spatula, and roast it for 15 to 20 minutes more, until the edges are brown and the potatoes are soft. Most of this is waiting, and all the waiting can be done sitting down. Another way: With chicken: leave out the chickpeas and lay 4 chicken thighs on the vegetables from the start, skin side up. They are done when a thermometer in the thickest part says 165°F (74°C), which is FoodSafety.gov’s number for chicken. Safe temperatures, from FoodSafety.gov: Chicken, turkey and other poultry, all of it: 165°F (74°C).
Eggs, and a scramble without them

Scrambled eggs, or a tofu scramble, for one or two Hands on 10 minutes In all 10 minutes Sitting down All of it. The teaching counter is at table height, with room under it for knees and a wheelchair. What it is like A quiet one. The butter or the oil sizzles softly; if it spits, the pan is too hot. You need: A non-stick pan and a flat spatula. What goes in: 3 eggs, a knob of butter or a spoon of oil, salt. Or a block of firm tofu, half an onion, a pinch of turmeric, salt and pepper, and black salt if you have it. Beat the eggs in a bowl with a pinch of salt. Melt the butter in the pan over a low to medium heat, and pour the eggs in. Push them slowly from the edges into the middle with the spatula, and keep going until there is no runny egg left: FoodSafety.gov says to cook eggs until the yolk and the white are firm. For the scramble without eggs: soften the chopped onion in the oil, crumble the tofu in with your hands, and add the turmeric, which is for colour, and salt and pepper. Cook it for 5 to 8 minutes, stirring, until it is hot and catching a little at the edges. A pinch of black salt at the end makes it smell of eggs, if that is what you want. Safe temperatures, from FoodSafety.gov: Eggs: Cook until the yolk and the white are firm. The temperatures the kitchen cooks to, off FoodSafety.gov’s chart What Inside, at the thickest part Chicken, turkey and other poultry, all of it 165°F (74°C) Ground meat and sausage 160°F (71°C) Beef, pork, lamb and veal steaks, roasts and chops 145°F (63°C), then rest 3 minutes Fish 145°F (63°C), or cook until the flesh is no longer translucent and separates easily with a fork Eggs Cook until the yolk and the white are firm Egg dishes, such as a frittata or a quiche 160°F (71°C) Leftovers, of any kind 165°F (74°C) Every hot dish on the line is cooked to these too, and leftovers are heated to 165°F (74°C) before they go back out.

The last month from cooking channels Ryan chose, in the order he listed them: their videos and their shorts, newest first under each. A machine refills it every morning and the older ones go off the end, so nobody here watched these first. The titles are the channels’ own, as they wrote them, and some of them say things about food and bodies that nobody in this kitchen would. The house rules are ours, not theirs.

Nobody is turned away, and nobody is asked for anything: not money, not work, not a name, not a reason. Nobody is counted. No tally of meals, no count of who came, and nothing that remembers you were here. Every dish says what is in it before you take it, and which animal, if it has one. The vegan pan is first, every day. Nothing plays until you press play, and every video says how long it runs before you press it. Coffee, tea, tea sandwiches, and cats from the shelter, waiting to be adopted. A café with a window at every height. Somebody cut them all to the size of a cat, from one down at the floor for watching feet go by to a round one up under the eaves, so every cat in here has a window of its own, and every window lays a small square of day on the wall beside it. The light in the room is all of those squares at once. The cats were found out on the street in the dark; in here every one of them can be seen whole, in daylight.

The cats are at Rescue A Cat, the shelter on the street. This room reads who is there each time it opens, and needs scripts to do it. The café is wider than a phone: scroll the picture sideways to see all of it, or meet everybody from the list under it. in the window under the eaves in the round window at the top on the top step of the shelves on the glass bridge across the ceiling on the glass bridge, near the left end in the middle of the glass bridge on the glass bridge, near the right end on top of the cat tree in the high cubby near the top of the shelves in the little round window high up the cat tree high on the shelves in the square window in the middle of the wall in the hammock under the bridge in the arched window in the low cubby halfway up the shelves halfway up the cat tree on the second step of the shelves on the long ledge, by the window end on the long ledge, over the first table on the long ledge, over the second table on the long ledge, by the cat tree on the bottom step of the shelves on the lowest platform of the cat tree in the basket under the shelves on the floor by the low window, watching feet go by on a chair at the first table under the first table on the other chair at the first table on a chair at the second table under the second table on the other chair at the second table on the floor by the hatch, hopefully in the cardboard box in the far corner

If you adopted a cat at Rescue A Cat, you can let them out in the café for a while, among the cats still waiting for homes, and anybody who comes in can meet them. They stay yours, and you can take them home whenever you like. Their card says they have a home, and never whose. Up to three of yours can be out at a time, and the cats waiting for homes come first: when every place in the café is taken, yours wait at home, or at the door, until one is free. Sign on to the CB, at the Community Center, and the cats you have adopted are here to let out. You have no cats yet. Every cat at Rescue A Cat is waiting for a home, and adopting happens there.

Every cat in here came from Rescue A Cat, the shelter on the street. The shelter sends every cat still waiting for a home, and any cat in here who has one has been let out for a while by their person, which you can do too (your own cat, above). The café keeps no list of its own: each time it opens it reads the shelter’s, so a cat adopted this morning has already gone home, and a cat brought in an hour ago is already here, finding somewhere to sit. Press a cat to meet them: their name, what they are like, where they were found and when they came in, all in the shelter’s own words. Adopting happens at the shelter. Every waiting cat’s card has a link to that cat’s own card there, where anybody signed on to the CB can adopt them. The café is not told who adopted whom, and does not ask. Where a cat goes is up to the cat. The shelter wrote down each cat’s mood when they came in, and that is all the café goes by: a cat who watches everything from the top of the cupboard stays up high, a cat who is only interested in food stays down on the floor and the chairs, where the crumbs are, a cat who went straight for a lap stays near the tables, and a cat who fell asleep before the door shut finds somewhere soft. Three legs, one eye, a kink in the tail: none of it decides where a cat may go. A cat with three legs gets to the top of the tree like anybody else. You can pick a cat up and put them on your lap, unless they want to be left alone, which is allowed. The shelter wrote that down too, and the café keeps to it: those cats have no button for picking them up. Sit near them instead. One cat to a lap: picking up another means the first hops down and goes somewhere they like. Look down and you see your lap under the café’s blanket, which it lends to anybody with a cat on them, because claws, and your table with whatever you asked for from the menu. At MAX GLITTER the cats wander about by themselves, now and then, one at a time, the way cats do. At Gentle and Regular they stay where they are until something moves them: wave the feather wand, roll the crinkle ball or put down a box, and whoever is interested goes after it. A cat who is asleep, or wants to be left alone, is not interested, which is allowed as well. The words say who went where at every setting; only the moving changes.

A telly hangs by the hatch, and the rack under it holds films from other cat cafés, most of them in Japan, picked by Ryan, in his order. Each one plays where it hangs, or goes up on the telly with the button under it. Nothing loads from YouTube until you press play, and every button says how long the film runs before you press it. Every item on the board says what is in it, whether it is vegan or vegetarian or which animal it came from, and which of the nine major food allergens the FDA names it has, and gluten. Every drink says how much caffeine it has, in words: decaf is never quite none, chocolate carries some, and a tisane brewed from flowers or leaves that are not tea has none. The house milk is oat, so every milk drink is vegan as it comes, and soy or dairy is there if you ask. Everything is made in one kitchen, behind the hatch, so if an allergy is serious, say so there, and somebody will tell you what has been near what. Nothing here is certified halal or kosher; the two sandwiches with meat in them say which animal. And every cup, mug and pot in here is the same teal mug, because the regulars knock things off tables, and the good china would not last an afternoon.

Let the cats come to you. A cat who walks away has said no, and that is the end of it. A cat who would rather not be picked up is not picked up. The shelter wrote it down, and the café has no button for it. No cat sits on the hatch, and none goes into the kitchen. The food is made behind the wall, because cats and kitchens do not mix. Nothing in here makes a sound. The purring is the cats’ business. Nobody is counted: not the cats, not the cups, and not you.

Nothing about you. Your lap and your table live in this page and nowhere else, and are gone when you leave it. The café’s own scripts store nothing in your browser: they read the shelter’s list when the room opens, and send nothing anywhere unless you are signed on to the CB and have cats of your own to let out, when they ask which of yours are out and say which one you let out or take home. A pint, something from the stove, and a table that fits you. Made like McAnally’s, in Jim Butcher’s Dresden Files. A pub a few steps down from the street, with a ramp beside the steps as wide as they are. The only light in here is the street’s. It comes in at the top of the walls, through thirteen small windows set at the level of the pavement, and most of it reaches the tables by way of thirteen old mirrors, each hung at its own height and tipped its own way. So it lands in patches, none the same shape and none in a row, a little dimmer and a little green, which is what old mirror glass gives back. Nothing in here is lit warm: the stove is shut, and nobody lights a lamp. Thirteen of everything, and no two alike: thirteen tables of thirteen heights, thirteen stools along a bar that meanders, thirteen carved columns standing where they stand, and thirteen ceiling fans. There is no television, no games machine and no jukebox, only a player piano. Nobody has to order anything to sit down.
From a seat at the south end, at the height of somebody sitting down, which is where most people in a pub are. Drawn from the plan below, so the two cannot disagree.

The tables are all different sizes and heights, scattered round the floor. That is an access feature as much as a look: when no two tables are the same height, one of them is likelier to be yours. The columns are wooden, each a different thickness, standing where they stand, and each is carved with a nursery tale. They break the room up, and they never block it: the plan above walks every way between them. The Twelve Dancing Princesses: a row of shoes, every pair worn through. The Enormous Turnip: a turnip as big as a barrel, and a line of everybody pulling at it, down to a mouse. The Golden Goose: a goose, and a line of people stuck to it and to each other. Jack and the Beanstalk: a beanstalk, climbing the whole of the column to the ceiling. Stone Soup: a pot over a fire, with hands round it, each holding something to put in. The Bremen Town Musicians: a donkey, a dog, a cat and a rooster, standing on each other's backs. Tables 1 and 4 are by it. The Princess and the Pea: a stack of mattresses all the way up the column, and one pea under the bottom of them. Table 3 is by it. Goldilocks and the Three Bears: three chairs, three bowls and three beds, no two of them the same size. The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse: two mice at a table, one of them putting on a coat to go home where it is quiet. Rapunzel: a tower, which is the column itself, with a window at the top and hair let down from it. The Fisherman and His Wife: a fish in a rough sea, and a hut on the shore. Tables 8 and 9 are by it. The Three Billy Goats Gruff: three goats crossing a bridge, and something under it. Table 12 is by it. The Elves and the Shoemaker: a workbench at night, and small shoes finished on it by morning. Table 10 is by it.

A player piano, which plays a roll of punched paper by itself, and the only music in the pub. It plays only when somebody presses a roll, and one roll at a time, and every roll says how long it runs before you press it. Each is a recording of a real roll, kept on its own page on Wikimedia Commons, where it is public domain, and nothing is fetched from there until you press. Every composer on the shelf died more than seventy years ago, so the music is free everywhere, not only in the United States.

What our page adds is the radical part, and the radical part is what this room is for.

Neutral ground. Nobody in here has to be anybody’s host or anybody’s guest, and nobody starts anything. You never have to order anything to sit down, and nothing on the board has a price. Every pint says how strong it is before you order it, and the alcohol-free one comes first, in the same glass, at the same size. Nobody buys a round for anybody, and nobody asks what is in your glass. Fetch your order from the bar, or say so and it is brought to you. Nobody asks why. Sit where you like, and as long as you like. Nothing behind the bar has a screen. The piano is a player piano, and it plays only when somebody presses a roll, one roll at a time. Nothing in the pub moves, at any setting, the fans included. Nobody is counted: not the pints, not the rounds, and not you.

Nothing about you. The table you sit at and what is on it live in this page and are gone when you leave it. The pub’s own scripts store nothing in your browser and send nothing anywhere. Every card says what is in it before you order it, and every pint how strong it is. Nothing plays until you press a roll, and nothing is fetched from Wikimedia Commons until then. Every roll says how long it runs first.

The brief is Ryan Boren’s, of 2026-10-05, and so is the name. The pub it is made like is Jim Butcher’s: McAnally’s, Mac and everything else in The Dresden Files are his, and nothing here is affiliated with him or his publishers. Ryan’s brief pointed at the Dresden Files fan wiki’s page for McAnally’s, and nothing here is drawn from it: the room is built from the books’ own passages, which Ryan quoted from his copies, and every quotation names its book. The tales on the columns are old and nobody’s; what is carved on each, and every word on the board, are ours. The piano’s rolls are recordings on Wikimedia Commons, each public domain on its own page and named on its card. The measurements are the 2010 ADA Standards’, read on the Access Board’s page. The drawings are Claude’s, written as code. Set in Amarante and Brygada 1918. Where each thing was read is in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and in this pub, nothing moves even then.

Everyone is welcome in this sandbox. Come in curious. Pull up a patch of sand, try things, break things, and share what you notice. We’ll meet you in the middle. Bring whatever spoons you can spare for ideas and fixes. However many that is, it’s enough.
“The sandbox metaphor derives from the concept of a child's sandbox—a play area where children can build, destroy, and experiment without causing any real-world damage.”
In software, a sandbox is a fenced-off place to run something you don’t trust yet, so that if it breaks, nothing else breaks with it. The name came from the playground.
Dig with the spade, tip out a bucket, bounce the ball. Or build a castle and burn it down. Nothing has to turn into anything, nothing is saved, and nothing can be lost. Just play Build, if you like

Got an idea for the sandbox, or found something that didn’t work? We’d love to hear it. Half an idea is fine. Some places to start: Something that confused me was… Something I broke was… Something I’d add is…

Anybody signed on to the CB can drop something in: a suggestion, a feature request, or a bug report, about this room or anywhere on the street, the CB included. Your handle goes on it, for everybody to see. A picture can go with it, a screenshot of a bug most of all, and with any reply too. Each is redrawn in your browser, which takes off anything a camera or a phone wrote into it, each needs a sentence saying what it shows, and anybody can see it in the box, so look at all of it first. Anybody can read what is in the box, signed on or not. Our moderators answer each one, in replies under it with their own username on each: done, or not doing, and why, or a question while it stays open. Whoever dropped it in can reply too, as often as it takes, and edit or take down their own replies. A not yet can become a yes. You can be told when a moderator replies to yours: switch on When a moderator replies to a suggestion of mine under Notifications, in Your radio on the CB. Me too says it affects you too. Anybody signed on can press it on somebody else’s suggestion, to put their handle beside it, and press it again to take it back. It is not a vote: the box names who a suggestion affects, and never says how many. It stays until it is taken down, by whoever dropped it in or by any moderator. Nothing in the box is counted, ranked or voted on. What the box keeps. A security problem is not for the box, where everybody can read it. Report it privately: SECURITY.md says how. Signed on to the CB as . Your handle goes on whatever you drop in, for everybody to see. To drop one in, sign on to the CB: press Get on the CB on the radio in the corner of your screen. You join with an invite and a username of your own, and the Community Center says how. Not on the CB? Write to us instead, or fix it yourself.
Reading the box needs scripts. Without them, or without the CB, write to us instead.

Every room on this street is a file in one public repository, and so is every tool that builds and checks them. If you would rather fix a thing than describe it, you can. Your own copy is a sandbox too: nothing you break there reaches the street until Ryan Boren or Helen Edgar merge it. Most of the street is built with Claude, Anthropic’s AI, and it can help you too. It reads the street’s rules, in CLAUDE.md, before it changes anything. You do not need to be a programmer. You do need some spoons, a GitHub account, and a computer you can install things on. Take the steps at whatever pace suits you; nobody is waiting.

A Mac, a Linux computer, or Windows with WSL: the street’s tools are Bash and Python scripts, so on Windows we run them inside Linux. A GitHub account. And these, which the setup script in a moment checks for you: Git, and Python 3. Node.js 22 or newer. Google Chrome or Chromium. Every check looks at the pages through it, the way a visitor’s browser does. GitHub’s own gh, for making your copy and sending a change back. The GitHub website does both too. Only for particular jobs, and the script says when: cwebp and ffmpeg for new photographs and recordings, and Pillow for the Collection Collection.

Your copy is called a fork. With gh, these make it and put it on your computer, with the street’s own copy named upstream so you can keep up with it: gh auth login gh repo fork Stimpunks/Stimpunks-Love --clone cd Stimpunks-Love Without gh: press Fork on the repository, then git clone your fork’s address and cd into it.

tools/setup.sh It checks for everything above, installs the one library the CB needs with npm, and says in plain words what is missing and how to get it. It installs nothing else and never asks for your password. Run it again whenever you like.

Claude Code is Claude working in a folder of code: it reads the files, runs the tools and makes changes, and asks before anything it is not sure of. It needs a Claude Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise plan, or an Anthropic Console account; the free plan does not include it. Install it, then start it in your copy: curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash claude Other ways to install it, Windows included, are in Anthropic’s setup guide. Or use the Code tab of the Claude desktop app and choose your copy’s folder: it shows you the street as you change it. Either way, Claude reads CLAUDE.md first: the street’s rules, and how a change from your own copy comes in.
See the street on your own computer

npx -y serve . -l 8919 Then open http://localhost:8919 in your browser. There is no build step: every page is a file, served as it is. The CB does not run there, so the radio says it has no signal and the suggestion box says it cannot be read. To try the CB too, see Running the CB yourself.
Make your change, on a branch of its own

git switch -c a-short-name-for-your-change Then ask Claude for what you want, in your own words. Small is good. Every room is its own world, on purpose, and a change that makes two rooms look more alike is probably the wrong change: CLAUDE.md says why, at length. Some things are somebody’s to decide, like Helen’s Faery Yurt, or the sand in this very room. If Claude says a change is somebody else’s call, ask in your pull request rather than making it.

tools/check-all.sh It runs every generator and every checker in the one order that works, and stops at the first refusal. It looks at every page at every setting of the dial, so it takes a while. When a tool refuses, fix what it says; never loosen the tool. Files it changes are generated files catching up with your change, and they go in with it. Then add a line at the top of changelog.html saying what you changed, with your name on it if you want it there.

Look at what you are sending first, then send it: git status git add -A git commit -m "What you changed, in a sentence" git push -u origin HEAD gh pr create --repo Stimpunks/Stimpunks-Love That opens a pull request: your change, with a note saying what it is and why. Ryan Boren or Helen Edgar reads it, and may ask a question or ask for something to change. Merging publishes it: stimpunks.world is rebuilt from the repository within a minute or two. What you send is under the street’s licence, CC BY-SA 4.0, like everything here. Photographs and recordings of anybody’s voice are not, and need that person’s own yes on record first, so talk to us before sending one. A security problem goes privately: see SECURITY.md.

The street changes by itself every morning, when the Feed and the racks refill, so a copy a few days old is behind. This catches yours up: git fetch upstream git merge upstream/main tools/check-all.sh If the merge says a generated file conflicts, like feed.xml, sitemap.xml, llms.txt, a share card in og/, or anything between :begin and :end markers, do not fix it by hand. Take either side, finish the merge, and run tools/check-all.sh, which writes it again from its sources. The board in the suggestion box and these steps are the street’s, written by Stimpunks with Claude and filled in by tools/make-sandbox.py. Everything else in this room is its maker’s, as the credits say.

Two animals, one creature, thrown onto a white table by a lens in the roof. It is dark in here on purpose. A camera obscura is a room painted black inside, so that the only light in it is what comes through one opening and makes a picture on a surface; in this one the opening is a lens in the roof, and the surface is a round white table. A chimera is one creature made out of more than one animal, and whatever you make here appears on that table in full colour. The room began with Norah asking for an otteraccoon, an otter and a raccoon at once, so that is what is on the table when you walk in.
Otteraccoon The body, head, mouth, arms, feet and colours of an otter; the ears, tail and markings of a raccoon.

Pick two animals, then choose which one each part comes from. Bring another animal to the bench to take parts from it too, one for every part at most. Toss picks two for you. Start from one of these The animals on the bench Its name The name it suggests is the body’s animal and then the animal that gave the most other parts. Change it to anything you like. Its sayings, one to a line Up to five lines, each up to 80 characters, in your words. A familiar says one when you press it, and now and then in a speech bubble when it may move by itself. They go with it when you take it with you or keep it in your Profile. Take it with you and it follows you from room to room as your familiar, sitting wherever there are no words. It stays where you put it unless the dial is at MAX GLITTER or you let it move. Press it to move it or send it home. Your browser keeps it, and nothing is sent anywhere. Signed on to the CB as . Keep this chimera in your Profile, with its name, and you can send it as a sticker from the radio and show it in your profile. Sign on to the CB, at the Community Center, to keep a chimera in your Profile and send it as a sticker. Mutual aid, peer support and any other help, asked for and offered among people who get it. Overhead, everybody’s umbrellas, open and tied to one another and to the shopfronts either side, so that between them they make one roof. It is raining on top of it. Under here it is dry. This is the room where you ask. Its channel on the CB is for asking for mutual aid, for peer support and for any other help you need, and for offering it to whoever asks. Nobody here is a professional, and nobody needs to be: everybody under these umbrellas is a peer, which means somebody who has been somewhere like where you are. To ask, sign on to the CB and tune the radio to This room while you are in here, or open Community Care on the chat page, under Community. If you are not on the CB yet, the Community Center says how to get an invite. This channel is people, and it is not a crisis line. If tonight is worse than a hard day, our Help page is a set of doors, and Coping lists crisis lines and warmlines.
It’s much easier to practice asking, offering, receiving, and declining among people who “get it”!
Vivian Ly, Collective Community Care: Dreaming of Futures in Autistic Mutual Aid, Autscape 2020, read on our Community Care page

That is the whole of what the channel is for, and all four of them are allowed here. The line is off a slide in Vivian Ly’s talk at Autscape 2020, which our own Community Care page carries, and which is here to press as well. On Autscape’s own channel. The questions at the end were left out of the upload, as its own description says. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press it.

Say what you need, in your own words, as much or as little as you like. Nobody asks you to prove it, to say how you came to need it, or to have tried everything else first. Asking is not a weight on the room: it is how the people who want to show up find out where to stand.
Offer what you can spare, when you can spare it, and on your own terms. Nobody keeps track of who offered and who did not, and an offer that turns out to be more than you have can be taken back.
Take what is offered without paying for it in gratitude. Thanks are welcome and never owed, and nobody keeps a note of who has had help, or how often.
Either side can say no. An offer that does not fit can be turned down, an ask can go by, and nobody is asked for a reason. A no is an answer, not a verdict on anybody.
Vivian Ly, Collective Community Care: Dreaming of Futures in Autistic Mutual Aid, Autscape 2020, read on our Community Care page
It’s about moving from a rights-based frame to a justice-based one: not accommodation as charity, but care as infrastructure. Not self-improvement, but survival as a shared project.

Mutual aid is people meeting each other’s needs directly, sideways rather than downwards. Nobody in here is the giving kind or the needing kind, because most of us are both, often in the same week, and the umbrella you are standing under today is not the one you brought. Stimpunks also makes mutual aid grants and creator grants to neurodivergent and disabled people. Those are the Foundation’s, by application, in scheduled rounds, and they cannot cover anything urgent; their own pages say whether they are open, who they can reach and what they cannot pay for. Asking in this channel is asking the community, not applying, and you can do both.

Peer support is typically defined as a non-clinical, mutuality-based relationship between folks who share lived experience

It was championed first by the people who built kinship over the fact that they’d been othered, not by nonprofits and politicians playing the respectability game

I believe people first and foremost do mutual aid and peer support because that’s what it means to show up for each other in relationships

provide care and support, without imposing interaction or forcing others to perform to a specific measurable outcome

Peer support, and where it comes from

Many schools have run peer support models in the past where neurodivergent young people have been ‘buddied up’ with a neurotypical peer. However, often the goal of this is to help the neurodivergent person ‘learn’ neurotypical ‘social norms’.
Salvesen Mindroom Research Centre, NEST (NEurodivergent peer Support Toolkit), read on our Peer Support page
Peer support, and where it comes from
A common thread in the experiences of older autistic adults (aged 50+) was the importance of universality; being ‘in the same boat’.

Norris, Harvey & Hull, citing Hickey et al. (2018), Post-diagnostic support for adults diagnosed with autism in adulthood in the UK: A systematic review with narrative synthesis, 2025, read on our Peer Support page
Peer support, and where it comes from

The preference was for autistic-led peer support. However, individuals acknowledged that being autistic does not inherently provide the knowledge or skills necessary for the role, and that this requires training and/or experience.
Norris, Harvey & Hull, Post-diagnostic support for adults diagnosed with autism in adulthood in the UK: A systematic review with narrative synthesis, 2025, read on our Peer Support page
Peer support, and where it comes from
Autistic adults desired peer support not as a substitute for specialist services such as mental health support, but working alongside them.
Peer support, and where it comes from

Tuesday Ferguson wrote that for our blog in 2024, as a youth peer support worker, about what becomes of peer support when it turns into a job inside the systems it grew up resisting. The whole essay is better than anything this room could say about it. What the room takes from it is where peer support comes from: So nobody here is assessed, referred or signed up for anything. Peer support in a channel is somebody saying that happened to me too, and this is what helped, and staying. Nothing has to come of it that anybody else can measure: Our glossary’s entry on peer support starts by naming the version this is not: Nobody in here is buddied up with anybody to learn how to pass. The research the entry gathers says what Autistic people kept asking for instead, and it is honest about what being a peer does not give you: This room keeps that second line. Being a peer is not the same as knowing what to do, nobody in here is pretending to be a service, and the entry says what peer support is for beside the rest:

I am often struck by the dangerous narcissism fostered by spiritual rhetoric that pays so much attention to individual self-improvement and so little to the practice of love within the context of community.
bell hooks, as our Community Care page quotes it, naming no work
We gotta keep each other alive any way we can ’cause nobody else is goin’ do it.
Larry Mitchell, as our Community Care page quotes it, naming no work
Community care is the refusal of that story.
I am fighting for an interdependence that embraces need and tells the truth: no one does it on their own and the myth of independence is just that, a myth.
Mia Mingus, Changing the Framework: Disability Justice, read on our Community Care page
Self-care is birthed by and through community care.
Talila A. Lewis, a post on Twitter, read on our Community Care page
The parts we need to survive are scattered All amongst us.
Tinu Abayomi-Paul, a post on Twitter, read on our Community Care page
Our mutual entwinement must be careful, spacious and supple, with no single knot tied too tight.
Sophie K. Rosa, Radical Intimacy, Pluto Press, pages 172–173, read on our Community Care page

Our Community Care page opens with those two, and then with the story the dominant culture tells about care: that needing help is weakness, that independence is a virtue, and that your survival is your own problem. That is what the umbrellas are. Nobody brought enough for everybody, and nobody had to. Every umbrella is tied to the ones beside it and to the shopfronts either side, nothing else holds the roof up, and not one of them keeps anybody dry by itself. The ties are drawn from a line of Sophie K. Rosa’s, which our page carries too:

No proving it. Nobody asks for a diagnosis, a story, a reason or evidence, and nobody decides whether a need is real. No sorting. Nobody here is the deserving kind or the other kind. Everybody under the umbrellas is somebody who might ask. No ledger. Help puts nobody in anybody’s debt. Nothing records who gave and who got, and receiving costs nobody a performance of gratitude. Nothing counted. No total of what was asked or what was given, no list of who helped, and no wall of thank-yous. Nobody at the front. No professionals, no caseworkers, no intake and no forms. The only expertise in the room is having been there. Nobody owes an answer. An ask can go unanswered and an offer can go untaken, and neither is a verdict on anybody. If an ask goes by, asking again is allowed. Not a crisis line. Our Help page is a set of doors, and Coping lists crisis lines and warmlines. Nobody here is on call.
Who reads the channel, and for how long

Everybody signed on to the CB can read this room’s channel, so say only what you would say in a room with all of them in it. It keeps the house norms, like every channel. Unless our administrators set this channel otherwise, every message on it goes two weeks after it was sent, and the radio says what it keeps, first under In this channel. For an ask that needs longer, Mutual aid in the forums keeps a topic 3 months after its last post, and Coping keeps one 1 week. A direct message is between two people, and it is not end-to-end encrypted. One that breaks the house norms can be reported, which is the one way it reaches a moderator.

This is a coping toolkit for getting through hard moments in a hard world.
Struggling in unjust conditions is not a personal failure. You are not broken. The system is.

Getting through hard moments in a hard world: what to reach for, why it works, and why cope is not an insult. All the way round, a wall of storm cloud, white where the sun lands on its tops and slate at its foot, where the rain is. Straight up, clear sky. On the floor of the eye it is dry and still and the sun is out, and a few doors stand on it with nothing round them. The storm has not gone anywhere. This room is the eye of the storm. The storm is the hard world: paperwork, punishment, noise, people, and systems built for somebody else. It is still there, all the way round, in plain sight, and nothing in here pretends otherwise, because that is the difference between coping and denial. In the middle of it there is a patch of still air, clear sky straight up, and room to breathe. The room is built out of three pages from our Regulation and Coping hub on stimpunks.org: Seeds of Cope, small things to reach for; The Science of Cope, why they work; and Cope Is Not an Insult, a manifesto taking the word back. This is a summary of them in our own words, with their lines quoted where they say it best. The pages are the better thing, and they go further. Its channel on the CB is for talking about coping: what is going on, what helps, what did not. Sign on and tune the radio to This room while you are in here, or open Coping on the chat page, under Community. If you are not on the CB yet, the Community Center says how to get an invite. This is not clinical advice and it is not a crisis line. If you are in danger, or feel like you might hurt yourself, call your local emergency number. Our Help page is a set of doors to support, and Coping on stimpunks.org lists crisis lines and warmlines.
Pick one. Do it imperfectly. Tiny is valid.
Dim the lights, or switch the overheads off. Headphones or earplugs. A different position: sitting, lying down, leaning, on the floor. Fewer tabs, fewer voices, fewer tasks.
In for four seconds and out for six, six times over, the breath out longer than the breath in. A hum, a sigh or a yawn. Cold water on your face or your wrists.
If you only do one thing: reduce inputs. Lower sensory load first. Everything is harder when your nervous system is on fire.

Hands pressed together hard for ten seconds. A blanket wrapped round you, or deep pressure. Rock, pace, flap, stim, which our page grants permission for in as many words. A stretch of the jaw, the shoulders, the hands. Every page on this street has two things in its dial for exactly that. I need a bodymind break lays a calm screen over whatever page you are on, with nothing moving on it, and the crisis lines on it. Feeling overwhelmed? Escape to a low-stimulation mode lays a few quiet colours over every room on the street at once and stops everything moving, until you press it again. Both are at the foot of this page.
Not everything is psychological. A lot of it is sensory, social, and systemic.

Feeling bad / stuck / flooded? Is this sensory load? What helps: reduce input, change environment, add pressure, step outside Is this transition / task-switching pain? Seeds to plant ahead, or grab in a storm
These are small, repeatable interventions. You can plant them ahead of time, or grab them in a storm.
Stim is regulation. Let your body do its job.

Change the room: another chair, another corner, another light. Fewer sounds, fewer things to look at, fewer obligations. Somewhere to go without having to explain, and a small kit to carry, with earplugs, sunglasses, gum, something to fidget with and water.
Permission to leave. You don’t need to justify your nervous system.

Writing instead of talking, which our page says is often the great social equalizer. Less performing: drop the eye contact, the small talk, the masking. Being together without talking, which our page calls parallel presence. And an exit line written ahead of time, from the words further down.
Sometimes you’re not “overthinking.” You’re stuck in a loop because your attention won’t release and your body won’t downshift.

One small change in the body: stand up, drink water, open a window. Write the thought down once and park it. Walk to a beat, tap, rock, count steps. Give the thought seven minutes on a timer, and then stop. Or move over to a safe special interest, a softer focus that can bring you back. Our page reads the loop through monotropism, and our glossary has a word for it, the monotropic spiral.
Pressure: weighted blanket, tight hoodie, firm hug (if wanted).

Temperature: cold water, a warm drink, a heating pad. Orientation: five things you can see, four you can feel, three you can hear. Breath: a long breath out, humming, sighing. Hands: something to squeeze, palms pressed together, lotion rubbed in slowly.
If your life is being squeezed by paperwork, punishment, sorting, surveillance, and “standards,” you may be reacting normally to abnormal conditions.

Our page’s reframe is that this is a mismatch, not a moral failure. Ask who benefits from the rule as it is written. Broken systems, not broken people. Ask for support, which you deserve without humiliation rituals, and remember that refusing can be a way of protecting yourself.
After a meltdown/shutdown/panic spike, your job is gentle recovery — not “getting back to normal.”
Plan one lily pad. What makes the next transition safer?

Fewer demands: cancel what you can, put off what you can. Water, food and rest, which are not optional. Quiet and predictability, because our page says routine is medicine. Repair the shame, in our page’s words: my nervous system did what it had to do. A lily pad is our glossary’s word for a place to land between one thing and the next.
Use these as-is. Edit them. Make them yours. The point is to reduce effort in the moment.
I need a moment to regulate. I’ll return when I’m able.
I’m hitting sensory overload. I’m going to step out.
I’m not okay right now. Can you stay nearby and be quiet with me?
I need fewer questions. Please give me time and space.
I work/learn better with breaks. I’m taking one so I can come back regulated.
Written is easier for me than verbal. Can we switch to text/email?
Every one of them from Stimpunks, Seeds of Cope.
Coping is not imaginary. It is neurobiological.
The body notices threat before thinking does
These are not personality flaws. They are adaptive responses.
The body notices threat before thinking does
The body notices threat before thinking does

Our page starts from Stephen Porges’ Polyvagal Theory and his word for it, neuroception: the body moves into survival before reasoning has caught up. Fight, flight, freeze, fawn. Withdrawing, stimming, pacing, shutting down, seeking comfort and seeking connection are all, on our page, ways of steadying the autonomic nervous system.
Trauma symptoms are not random. They are adaptations that once increased survival probability.

After Bessel van der Kolk and Judith Herman, our page reads trauma as a body-level answer to overwhelming stress. Hypervigilance is adaptive under threat, dissociation protective under overwhelm, and avoidance saves energy under danger.
Coping behaviors often emerge to lower allostatic load.

Bruce McEwen’s allostatic load is the wear chronic stress leaves on a body. Sleep changes, sensory tolerance narrows, emotional bandwidth shrinks, executive function declines. Reducing light, seeking sameness, limiting social demand and controlling the environment are, our page says, attempts to rebalance.
They are not “malfunctioning.” They are regulating.

Repetitive movement, eating the same food, avoiding eye contact, needing parallel presence. Our page says autistic burnout research increasingly frames burnout as a stress injury, built out of masking, overextension and sensory overload, and coping as protection against it.
If removing fluorescent lights reduces shutdown, the problem was lighting — not character.
If written communication reduces panic, the problem was phone culture — not fragility.
Coping behaviors frequently expose structural flaws.
The social model of disability says difficulty does not come from impairment alone. When an environment overloads a body, the body adapts, and coping is often an answer to inaccessible design.
Coping is not delusion. It is prerequisite to change.
Coping is not the enemy of change. It is what keeps people alive long enough to build it.

Internet culture uses copium to mean fooling yourself. Our page answers that regulation is the first step towards higher-order thinking: without it, learning declines, reasoning narrows and social capacity collapses. Co-regulation is how one nervous system steadies another. Our entry for it opens with Trauma Geek’s definition: Most of what gets written about it is about people: a parent and a baby, a teacher and a child, a friend who sits with you while it passes. It is not only people. Mammals do it with each other, with their own kind and with other kinds, and the lines our Polyvagal Theory entry quotes say so in as many words: The same definition says what a safe enough person is like: Leave out the face and the voice, and that is a dog asleep against your legs, or a cat purring on your chest: breathing slow and deep, eyes half shut, heart steady, and glad of you close. Lie still beside that for long enough and your own body starts to keep time with it.

Why it matters so much to so many Autistic people

For a lot of Autistic people an animal is the easiest company there is, and the most settling. An animal does not want eye contact or small talk, does not take a stim for something wrong with you, and never needs anybody to mask. It says plainly what it wants, its day has the same shape every day, and you can be with it without doing anything at all. Being with somebody does not have to mean doing something together, or even being in the same room. Helen Edgar writes about co-regulating in ways that suit each person’s physical, social and sensory needs: A cat asleep in the next room counts. So does a dog who follows you from room to room and lies down wherever you stop, which our Body Doubling entry has a word for, and which leaves room for a pet: An animal is sensory company too. A dog leaning its whole weight on your legs is deep pressure, stroking fur is a stim, and a purr is a sound with no words in it to work out. Our Seeds of Cope puts co-regulation in its cope map, among what helps when fear, shame or trauma comes up, and our Glimmers entry has this among the small moments that bring peace, joy or connection:
Do not pet, feed, or otherwise distract a service dog. Please approach their handler before interacting.
Midwest FurFest, Accessibility Services , read on our Event Access Guide page

It is not only Autistic people. Plenty of people talk to the dog when they cannot talk to anybody, get up in the morning because the cat wants feeding, and go outside because the dog does. People have lived alongside animals for far longer than anybody has been writing it down, and a body that settles with a warm animal against it is one of the oldest kinds of company there is. Not everybody can live with an animal: allergies, rent, money, a body that cannot manage the walks, or an animal who died and is still missed. The animals on this street need none of that. Anybody can visit them, nothing about them costs anything, and none of them will ever need walking at six in the morning. And a dog in a harness may be working. The work of folks in our community, out in the daylight before it is finished. A garage seen from the driveway with its door rolled up and the day coming in off the street, so the floor is lit by the door and the back wall is in shade. Over the bench at the back, a card is pinned up for every piece of work on it, with a blank one at the end. Beside them the tools hang on their shadow board, each inside the outline painted round it, and one outline is empty because its tool is out being used. At the far end of the bench, a box of cards stands with their backs to you. This is a garage with the door rolled up. Inside is the work of folks in our community: the drafts, the half-made things and the projects with the seams still showing, put out where the people who love the same things can find them. Nothing has to be finished to be in here. There are three places to show your work here, for three lengths of time: this room’s channel on the CB for today, Show your work in the forums for the longer write-up and the conversation after it, and the bench for as long as you want your work out on the street.
Share what you love, and the people who love the same things will find you.
Austin Kleon, Show Your Work!, read on our Show Your Work page
Show your work and your process. Showing your work creates serendipity and creates a scene.
created serendipity: the more connected you are, the more ideas seem to find you, not the other way around.
The Principal of Change, 3 Obvious Ways Twitter Promotes Literacy, read on our Show Your Work page
The best way to get started on the path to sharing your work is to think about what you want to learn, and make a commitment to learning it in front of others.
Austin Kleon, Show Your Work!, read on our Show Your Work page

That is the whole of the idea, and it is Austin Kleon’s, from his book Show Your Work!, which our own Show Your Work page is built round. Showing your work is not showing off the finished thing. It is letting people see the making: the draft, the false start, the thing you are learning as you go. The serendipity is the point. Work kept in a drawer meets nobody. Work left out where people can see it meets the people who love the same things, and they turn up with the piece you were missing, or a question that sends you somewhere better, or just to say they have been making something like it too. And it does not wait until you know what you are doing. Kleon’s way in is to learn out loud:
Scenius stands for the intelligence and the intuition of a whole cultural scene. It is the communal form of the concept of the genius.
Brian Eno, The Technium: Scenius, or Communal Genius, read on our Scenius page
great ideas are often birthed by a group of creative individuals—artists, curators, thinkers, theorists, and other tastemakers—who make up an “ecology of talent.”
Austin Kleon, Show Your Work!, read on our Show Your Work page

Being a valuable part of a scenius is not necessarily about how smart or talented you are, but about what you have to contribute—the ideas you share, the quality of the connections you make, and the conversations you start.
Austin Kleon, Show Your Work!, read on our Show Your Work page
If you want to get, you have to give. If you want to be noticed, you have to notice.
Austin Kleon, Show Your Work!, read on our Show Your Work page

A garage is where the story of the lone genius usually starts: one person, the door pulled down, coming out years later with the finished thing. Brian Eno’s word for what really happens is scenius, and Kleon took it up: So the door is up. Nobody in here is a genius, and nobody has to be: what makes a scene is people looking at each other’s work, borrowing, answering and adding, and that only happens when the work is out where the scene can get at it. It runs both ways: Showing your work is half of it. Looking at somebody else’s, and telling them what it set off in you, is the other half.
Most of what we make, we make in the dark.

Tell us these, and the house puts a card up for it: Where your work lives: an address anybody can open, a repository, a page, a shop, a post. CB radios, the way people talk on them, where they came from, and the long haul. Night on the interstate, from the driver’s seat of a rig in the middle of a convoy. Nothing in the picture is lit except the lights themselves: three red lamps in a row high on the back of the trailer ahead, a red lamp at each of its top corners and its tail lamps low down; the same red smaller and smaller up the lane, as far as the front door; down the side of the rig in the next lane, a row of amber lamps along the bottom and another along the top; across the median, three amber dots at a time over the hedge, which are trucks coming the other way; three amber dots in the mirror, which is the back door; and on the dash, the radio, its red readout on 19. Breaker Breaker is a shopfront for the citizens band: the radios, the talk on them, where the band came from, and the truckers who kept their sets on. It is lit the way a convoy is at night. Every light in here is a marker lamp, which shows where the edge of something is and lights nothing round it, and that is what those lamps are for. In the United States and Canada a vehicle over 80 inches wide carries three amber identification lamps across the front and three red across the back, at the middle and as high as they will go, and more at its corners and along its sides, so anybody can see how wide, how tall and how long it is in the dark. Truckers who fit more than the law asks call them chicken lights. You see the shape of every rig on the road, and nothing of what it is carrying. This street asks every play button in its rooms to say how long a thing runs before you press it. The road asks every rig to say how big it is before you reach it. It is the same courtesy.

On a CB everybody in range shares one channel, and only one radio can send at a time: you press the button on the microphone to talk and let go to listen. So before you say anything you ask for the channel. Breaker is the asking, often with the channel’s number, breaker one-nine, and then you wait for somebody to come back to you before you go on. Nineteen is the channel the interstate keeps on. Highway talk was once on 10 east of the Mississippi and on 19 west of it, and 19 won in most places: 10 sits right beside channel 9, which the FCC has kept for emergencies since 1969, and 19 does not. People called it the trucker’s channel. The radio on the dash in the picture is on it.

The citizens band is named for who it was for. When the Federal Communications Commission began its personal radio services in 1945, it was to give citizens a band of their own to talk on, for their families and their businesses and for flying model aeroplanes, and the first handsets made for it sold mostly to farmers and the Coast Guard. The band everybody now means by CB, on 27 MHz, came in 1958 with 23 channels, and the 40 channels a set has now came in 1977. That set it apart from amateur radio, the hams’ band, which asks you to pass an exam before you transmit; in the United States, until February 2007, the exam took in Morse code. The citizens band asked only for a licence you bought, twenty dollars in the early 1970s and four from March 1975, and a call sign to go with it. At the height of the craze a great many people ignored all that and made up a name for themselves instead, a handle. On 28 April 1983 the licence went altogether. The band belonged to whoever switched a set on. That is the word this street took. Citizen is what everybody who lives here is: a room somebody brings to the street takes the street’s conventions as they arrive, which Your Room calls part of being a citizen here, and a convention anybody dislikes goes to the Town Hall, where conventions are talked over and can change. Our CB takes an invite to join, from stimpunks.org’s Community page, and once you are on it nobody is more of a citizen than anybody else. Everybody goes by a handle they chose, and nobody on the channel is ranked or counted.
From the citizens band to ours
Similar to Internet chat rooms a quarter-century later, CB allowed people to get to know one another in a quasi-anonymous manner.

From the citizens band to ours

The CB on this street, the radio in the corner of every page once you are signed on, is a chat channel patterned after citizens band radio. It was Ryan’s idea, and this is what came across: A handle You are on the channel as a name you chose, and everybody on it knows you by it. A channel everybody shares, and one of your own World is the channel the whole street shares, the way 19 is the one everybody on the interstate leaves on. Every room has a channel of its own too, this one included, the way a town on the CB used to keep a home channel, so people from there could find each other without crowding the calling channel. Channel 19 At its smallest, the radio is a drawing of a CB set on its own case with its readout on 19, and until 26 September 2026 the bar said CH 19 where Teleport is now. The squelch Switch on Speak new messages aloud and every message keys up with a burst of static and lets go with a tail of it, which is the sound a CB makes. At the Gentle setting you get the words without the static. Off is off Open and in front of you, the radio listens. Fold it away and it sends nothing, like a set switched off. On the air, then gone A CB keeps nothing: once something has been said, it has gone by. Ours keeps a hundred messages, each for two weeks, unless our administrators set a channel otherwise, and Take off takes one off the air. Reading the mail Listening without saying anything is fine on ours as well. Nobody is counted, and you are on Who’s online only if you press Be seen here. BASE BASE beside a name is one of our moderators, after the base station, the CB set at home rather than out on the road. Routing around the face to face

Another community that enabled autistic people to make the most of their natural strengths in the early and mid-twentieth century was amateur radio. By routing around the face-to-face interactions they found so daunting, even people who found it nearly impossible to communicate through speech were able to reach out to kindred spirits, find potential mentors, and gain the skills and confidence they needed to become productive members of society.

Steve Silberman, NeuroTribes: The Legacy of Autism and the Future of Neurodiversity (2015), pages 223–224, read on our page Written Communication Is the Great Social Equalizer, which quotes it from the Kindle edition, and checked against it word for word.
Routing around the face to face
Written communication isn’t a lesser substitute for speech. It’s a medium with its own power — one that neurodivergent people helped build, because they needed it.
Our page Written Communication Is the Great Social Equalizer.

Amateur radio and the citizens band are different services, and Steve Silberman is writing about the first of them: Steve Silberman, NeuroTribes: The Legacy of Autism and the Future of Neurodiversity (2015), pages 223–224, read on our page Written Communication Is the Great Social Equalizer, which quotes it from the Kindle edition, and checked against it word for word. Our page Written Communication Is the Great Social Equalizer. A radio you can talk on without being seen, a channel you can listen to for as long as you like before you say anything, and a name you chose for yourself: none of that was made for Autistic people, and a great many of us have found a home in it all the same, on the air and later in text. The channel on this street is text first for that reason, and you can stay on it reading the mail for as long as you want. The Repeater, past the last streetlight at the end of the Outskirts road, is the street’s other radio: a mast on a ridge that hears everybody, built on our Shared-Signal Space entry.

CB slang grew up alongside the ten-codes the emergency services used, and the truckers of the 1970s made it a language of their own. Here is some of it. Some of the list it comes from names people unkindly, women, sex workers and people speaking another language among them, and none of that is here.

Breaker I would like the channel. Often with its number: breaker one-nine. Then you wait for somebody to answer before you go on. Handle The name you go by on the air, which you choose. What’s your handle? asks somebody theirs. 10-4 Message received. Also yes, I agree: that’s a big 10-4. Four, or foe, for short. Copy, copy that I heard you, and I understand. Got your ears on? Is anybody listening? Or, with a handle in front of it, are you? 10-20, your 20 Where you are. What’s your 20? My 20 is the truck stop at the next exit. Reading the mail Listening without saying anything, which is allowed. 10-10 Going quiet but still listening: 10-10 on the side. Wall to wall and treetop tall Coming in loud and clear. Five by five says it too. Alligator station All mouth and no ears: somebody who talks and never listens. A hot mic keeps the channel to themselves. 10-36 The right time, please. 10-100 A restroom break. 3s and 8s Best wishes, borrowed from the 73 and 88 of the amateurs’ Morse code: best regards, and hugs and kisses. Good buddy Somebody on the channel you are friendly with. The word of the 1970s. 10-7 Signing off.

Front door, rocking chair, back door A group of trucks running together: the front door leads and watches ahead, the back door brings up the rear and watches behind, and the rocking chair is everybody between, who can ride easy. Hammer down Foot on the gas pedal, all the way. The hammer lane is the fast lane. Double nickels A 55 mph speed limit. Chicken lights Marker lights beyond what the law asks for, on a truck dressed up with chrome to match. Go-go juice Fuel. Hundred-mile coffee is very strong coffee. Watering hole A truck stop. A nap trap is a rest area. Gator A long strip of tyre on the road, which from a distance looks like an alligator lying in the sun. Comedian The median, the strip down the middle of the highway. Thick stuff Bad weather: fog, heavy rain or snow. Yardstick A mile marker. Bobtail A truck running without a trailer. Flip-flop The trip back the other way, and going home. Stack of bricks Home. I’m heading back to my stack of bricks.

Smokey, a bear A state trooper, after Smokey Bear’s hat, which looks like a highway patrol’s. Bear in the air Police in a plane or a helicopter. Kojak with a Kodak A police officer running radar. Chicken coop A weigh station, where the scales are. County mountie A county sheriff or deputy.

Mile High Denver. Shakeytown Los Angeles. Flagtown Flagstaff. Bat City Austin. Guitar Town Nashville. All of it from Wikipedia’s List of CB slang, read at revision 1381092654 on 2026-10-24, under CC BY-SA 4.0, and put into our words.

After the oil crisis of 1973 the United States brought in a 55 mph speed limit across the whole country, and fuel was short and rationed. Truckers, many of them paid by the mile, used their radios to find the stations that had fuel, to warn each other about speed traps, and to organise the blockades and convoys of a strike in 1974 against the new limit and other rules on the trade. By the middle of the decade the sets had spread far beyond the trucks. The First Lady, Betty Ford, went by First Mama, and Mel Blanc talked on the air in Los Angeles as Bugs or as Daffy, in their voices. Truck-driving country is the country music of all that: trucks and truck stops, CB radio, roads, weather and loneliness, and Wikipedia’s article calls it, at least partly, an oral history of trucking. Terry Fell put out Truck Drivin’ Man in 1954, and Dave Dudley, Red Sovine and Jerry Reed are in it. So is C. W. McCall, a truck-driving country singer whom Bill Fries, an art director at an Omaha advertising agency, made up for a series of bread commercials and recorded with Chip Davis. Convoy went to number one in January 1976. Fries retired to Ouray, Colorado, and was its mayor from 1986 to 1992. Dale Watson put out The Truckin’ Sessions in 1998, a whole record of truck-driving songs, and two more after it. He went to truck driving school around the time his first album came out, got his commercial driver’s licence, and often drives the band’s bus on tour.
