There is a storefront on this street with nothing in it, and it is empty on purpose. It is not scenery and it is not “coming soon” — it is a room we are not going to decorate, because it is not ours to decorate.

One Disabled, Autistic, neurodivergent or otherwise stimpunk person gets a page on this street. You get: A room of your own at stimpunks.world/<your-room>, linked from the front door beside all the others. Your own stylesheet. Not a theme, not a template with your colours swapped in — a blank CSS file and a room that is allowed to contradict every other room on the street. That is the whole architecture here. Your name on it, spelled and pronounced how you say, linked where you want it linked. Help building it if you want help, and none if you don’t. Describe the room and we will build it; or take the files and do it yourself; or anything between. To take the keys: build it with us or build it with your AI, then send it to us. You do not need to know how to make a web page for either. What happens next says what we do with it and how long that takes.

Four things, and they are the same four every room here already honours. They are not editorial control — nobody is going to tell you the room is too much. What every room on this street keeps, and why none of it is negotiable The rule Why it is not negotiable The dial works Gentle mode has to turn your room down without taking any of it away. It is the promise the whole street makes at the front door. Text clears 4.5:1 Clashing is not the same as illegible. Be as ugly as you like; be readable while you do it. Nothing autoplays Sound, video, motion: on press, never on arrival. No exceptions, including for a very good song. Credit what you didn’t write Attribution is a licence, not a house style. Quote anything; name whose it is.

Some things turn up in every room on the street: the dial, the sign-off at the foot of the page, a job marker on the floor, the CB bar in the corner. As new ones develop, they arrive in your room too, without us asking first. That is part of being a citizen here. They are the street’s furniture and not a redesign: your room’s look, its drawings and its words stay yours. If you don’t like one, bring it to the Town Hall, where the street’s conventions are talked over from time to time and can change.
What we are not going to do
Edit your room for tone. Ask you to be more positive, or more palatable, or more professional. Take it down because somebody complained that it was weird.

Tell us what the room is, and we build it with you. These are the questions to answer. Skip any you like, and if you do not know an answer yet, say so and we will suggest something for you to react to. What the room is for, and who walks into it. What it looks like when they do, and where its light comes from (a lamp, a window, a screen, the floor, nowhere at all). Rooms on this street are told apart mostly by their light, so let that decide the palette. What should be in it: words, drawings, songs or videos, anything to press. What it must never do. Your name as you want it credited, how to say it, your pronouns if you want them shown, and where your name should link. One paragraph is plenty. There is no form and no application, and you do not need a portfolio or a reason to deserve it. How to submit your room says where to send it.
Build it with your AI, if you like

You can also design your room in conversation with Claude, or whichever AI you use, and send us what it makes. Copy the prompt below into a new chat. It asks you the same questions as the list above, then builds the room as one web page you can look at and keep changing until it is right. Claude calls that page an artifact, and other AIs have their own names for it. When you are happy with it, send it to us the way How to submit your room says. How this site is made is the best short account of how rooms here work, if you or your AI want to read it first. It also says how we use an AI ourselves. You do not need an AI, and the room is yours either way. The prompt tells the AI to use your own words for anything about you and not to write your story for you. One thing to know first: whatever you tell an AI goes to the company that runs it, so tell it only what you are happy for that company to have. Nothing on this page sends anything anywhere. The prompt is text you copy.

I'd like your help designing my own room on Stimpunks.World (https://stimpunks.world), a website run by Stimpunks, a Disabled people's organisation. The site is a street of rooms, and no two rooms look alike: every room is its own visual world with its own colours, typefaces and light. How the site works is explained at https://stimpunks.world/design.html, and the offer I'm answering is at https://stimpunks.world/your-room.html. If you can read web pages, read both. Make my room look like nothing else on that street. FIRST, ASK ME ABOUT THE ROOM. Ask a few questions at a time and let me skip any of them: - what the room is for, and who walks into it - what it looks like when they do, and where its light comes from (a lamp, a window, a screen, the floor, nowhere at all). Rooms on this street are told apart mostly by their light, so let that decide the palette. - what should be in it: words, drawings, songs or videos, anything to press - what it must never do - my name as I want it credited, how to say it, my pronouns if I want them shown, and where my name should link Use my own words for anything about me. Don't write my story for me. If you draft words, show them to me as drafts I can change. If I don't know an answer yet, pick something and let me react to it. THEN BUILD IT as a single self-contained HTML page I can preview and we can keep changing together. HOW THE PAGE HAS TO BE BUILT, so the street can bring it in: 1. One HTML file with lang="en", a that is the room's name, a <meta name="description"> of one short sentence saying what the room is (it goes on the room's door and its share card, so keep it under 200 characters), one <h1>, and headings in order. Put class="room-SLUG" on <body>, where SLUG is a short name for the room in lowercase with hyphens. Everything the room shows goes inside <main>. 2. All the CSS goes in one <style> element. Every selector starts with .room-SLUG, apart from :root. Every class name starts with a short prefix of two or three letters followed by a hyphen (for example "xy-"), and so does every @keyframes name. Declare every solid colour once, as a hex custom property on :root that uses the same prefix (for example --xy-ground), and use var() everywhere else, in the CSS and in any SVG fill or stroke. A translucent colour for a shadow can be written as rgba(). Set the room's ground (background-color) and text colour on .room-SLUG itself, and a link colour on .room-SLUG a: the street's own furniture (the way back to the street, the loudness dial and the sign-off at the foot) sits in your room and takes those. 3. Typefaces from Google Fonts only, under the SIL Open Font License or the Apache License 2.0. You may load them from Google Fonts for the preview; the street hosts its own copies. 4. No other external files at all: no scripts, stylesheets, images, trackers or embeds from anywhere else, and no <img>. Draw pictures as inline SVG or CSS. Don't use an image generator: nothing on this street comes from one. If I want a photograph in the room, leave a clearly marked space for it: an element with data-photo="a-short-name", role="img" and an aria-label describing the photograph, and list its name under Photographs in the notes. I'll send the photo separately, named to match, and only one I took myself, with the say-so of anybody in it. The street puts it in that space. 5. THE DIAL. The street sets data-intensity="gentle", "regular" or "max" on <html>, and the room has to honour all three: - gentle: nothing moves. No animation, no transition, no rotation or skew. Every word and every thing is still there. Gentle turns the room down and never takes anything away. - regular: motion only on hover or keyboard focus. - max: ambient motion is allowed. At every setting, nothing flashes or strobes (never more than three flashes a second). Until the street sets the attribute, follow prefers-reduced-motion. Add a small preview dial with three buttons so I can try all three settings. Put its markup, its styles and its script each in their own element marked data-preview-only, so the street can remove it cleanly and put its own dial where yours was. 6. CONTRAST. Every piece of text must reach at least 4.5:1 against the colour actually behind it. Put text on flat colour, never directly on a gradient, pattern or picture. Choose a link colour for every ground a link sits on, and make the keyboard focus ring clearly visible on each of those grounds. Next to each colour in the CSS, note in a comment which colours it is used with and the ratio. 7. NOTHING PLAYS BY ITSELF. No <audio>, no <video>, no iframes. For each YouTube video or TIDAL track I want, put a <button type="button" data-media="LINK"> saying what it is, who made it and how long it runs (like 3:45). A TIDAL button also says that without a TIDAL account it plays a preview. The street turns those into its own press-to-play players. Anything that isn't a single YouTube video or a single TIDAL track, just link to it. 8. NOTHING IS SENT OR KEPT. No forms, no fetch, no cookies, no localStorage, no analytics. Any script is small, plain JavaScript in one <script> at the end of the page, with no onclick-style attributes, and the room still reads completely with scripts switched off. Anything meant to be found is reachable by keyboard and by a screen reader. Nothing is hidden with display:none or shrunk to a tiny target to make it a secret. 9. It works at 360 pixels wide with no sideways scrolling. Every meaningful picture has alt text, and decoration is aria-hidden. 10. CREDITS. Add a section at the foot of the room under a heading with the word Credits in it. Name every quotation (who, which work, which year, and a link), every typeface and who designed it, every song, and anything else borrowed. Don't quote anything you can't source. If you're unsure of a source, say so rather than guessing. Say in the credits that the room was built with your help, and name which AI you are. LAST, put this comment at the very top of the file, filled in in exactly this shape: one "Key: value" to a line, each item of a list on its own line starting with "- ", and "none" wherever there is nothing. The street's import tool reads it. <!-- FOR THE STREET Name: my name as I want it credited Link: where my name links, or none Pronouns: as I want them shown, or none Say it: how to say my name, or none Slug: the same SLUG as in room-SLUG Prefix: the two or three letters every class and colour starts with Light: where the room's light comes from, in one sentence Typefaces: - each family, exactly as Google Fonts names it Media: - title | who made it | link | how long it runs Photographs: none, or a line about them - the data-photo name of each space a photograph goes in Words: which words are mine and which you drafted Built with: which AI you are, and who makes you Could not do: anything I asked for that these rules did not allow, or none --> Keep improving the page with me until I say it's done.
However you made it, send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. Nothing on this page sends anything: what goes, and where, is up to you.
If we are building it with you

Send your answers to the questions under Build it with us. A paragraph is plenty, and a list is fine. If you want a photograph in the room, say so and we will ask you for it separately. It has to be one you took yourself, with the say-so of anybody in it.
If you built it with your AI

Send the page. A share link from your AI is easiest, because the contact page takes a link. If you have the file instead, tell us through the contact page and attach the file when we write back, or send it to us in our community. Keep the note at the top. The prompt has your AI put a note at the very top of the file, starting FOR THE STREET. Our import tool reads it, so leave it in. Send any photographs separately, named to match the spaces your AI left for them. Only ones you took yourself, with the say-so of anybody in them.

We write back. We are a tiny team of chronically ill, neurodivergent people, and our contact page says how that goes: we do our best to reply within a week, and sometimes we take a week or two off for self-care. If you have not heard from us within a week, send it again. Real messages do get lost among the spam, and we want to hear from you. Then we build it with you, or bring it in. Built with us: we make a first draft from your answers, show it to you, and change it with you until it is yours. Anything about you stays in your own words. Built with your AI: a tool measures your page against the four rules above and everything else the prompt asks for. If anything falls short, we send you every reason at once, so you can change it with your AI and send it again. We fix things with you, not around you. Then it opens. Your room gets a door on the street, a share card, a place on the map, a job marker on its floor, and what the street brings in. We credit you in the room and in the liner notes, the way you asked to be credited. If you would rather your name were nowhere else, say so. If you built it with an AI, the room says so, the same way How this site is made says how we use one ourselves. Its opening goes in the changelog. How long it takes, after we write back, depends on how many rounds the room needs. A room built with your AI that meets every rule the first time is mostly plumbing for us. A room we build with you, or one that needs a few changes, takes as many rounds as it takes. Nobody is on a deadline, you included. Changing it later. Send a new version the same way, or tell us what to change. A room built with your AI is brought in again whole, so the new version replaces the old one, and the street’s furniture stays where it was.
A note on what happens if it goes quiet

A room here does not expire and does not need maintaining. If you stop updating it, it stays up exactly as you left it, with your name on it. If you want it taken down, say so once and it comes down, no conversation required. A gift with conditions attached is not a gift. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

Nothing has come down off the board yet. When the next gathering pins a new edition up, this one moves down here and keeps its own page. An empty rack is what a board that has had one edition actually looks like.

A pebble is anything you bring somebody because it made you think of them. Gentoo penguins do it with stones; we do it with songs, art, poems, quotes, photographs, recipes, and whatever else was in our hands that day. The locution is Amythest Schaber’s and Stimpunks documented it; Helen Edgar wrote it up at Autistic Realms. We share our soul samefoods. We share our SpIns. We share our fandom. We share artifacts of our constructionism. We share joy, sorrow, anger and pride, the silly and the serious, our truth and our lived experience. We share to remember and we share to forget. We share to cope, and to make a community out of it. This is show-and-tell. The board rotates when there is a new gathering, not on a clock. Nothing here plays until you press it, and every label says how long it runs before you do. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Gentle takes the scatter out of the cards and leaves every one of them, and everything written on them, exactly where it was.

News, notices, events, celebrations, and anything meant to last The Pebble Board is what our people bring each other, edition by edition. This board is for what has to stay put: news, notices, events, celebrations and posts, each on a brass plate tacked to an old copper wall gone green, and kept until it is taken down. Anybody can read it. Our moderators post on it, and every post carries the username of the moderator who put it up, so you always know who to ask about it. It has a feed of its own, for feed readers.
You are signed on as a moderator, so you can post. Your username goes on the post for everybody to see. You can edit your own posts afterwards, and any moderator can take any post down.
Reading the board needs scripts. The feed has every post without them.

Anybody can read it, signed on or not, and its feed carries every post to feed readers, so search engines may find them too. Only a moderator can post, signed on to the CB as a moderator, and their username is on the post, public, for good. The moderator who posted it can edit it, and the post says it was edited and when. Any moderator can take any post down, picture and all. Posts stay until they are taken down. There is no other copy and no archive, and nothing on the board is counted: no views, no likes, no most-read. A post is words, written in Markdown: headings, lists, quotes, tables, code and links. A link goes to an address on the web, an email address, or somewhere on the street, and a link off the street shows where it goes. Nothing typed into a post becomes code on the page. A post can carry a picture. It is redrawn in the moderator’s browser first, which takes off everything a camera writes into a file, the place it was taken first; it needs a description; and the moderator says that everybody recognisable in it has said yes to it being here. It goes when its post goes. What the board keeps.

Ryan’s idea, for the things the CB forgets after two weeks and the Pebble Board was never for. The wall, the plates and the tacks are drawn for this board. It is set in Bellefair, by Nick Shinn and Liron Lavi Turkenic, and Merriweather, by Sorkin Type, and credited in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

In the order you would reach them walking down the street and out past either end. Every name on it is the same size, because there is no headliner.

What is on first is read off each room’s own page, every time the poster is printed: the first thing in there you can press, with its name and its running time exactly as that room prints them. Where a room puts on a playlist, the poster says so, and says what the room says about it: that it runs until you stop it, or that it starts somewhere random. Stimpunks is not one website. It is a knowledge garden, and this is the part of it you can walk out into: one bed for every site we publish, the path going wherever you like, and a gate at the bottom back onto the street.

Ideas spread sideways rather than down. A filing system runs subjects, then categories, then articles, which is exactly right for an encyclopedia and wrong for us. Our own page about the garden grows the other way instead: experiences first, then concepts, a glossary, patterns, recipes, environments, systems — each layer out of the one underneath it. Autistic Rhizome is the shape that describes, and it is a term in the glossary it describes. Nothing needs to be read in order. Skimming, skipping and stopping partway are all fine here. That sentence is on the garden’s own page and it is not a courtesy; a knowledge base that only works if you start at the top is a knowledge base for people who are not tired. It grows unevenly, and some of it lies fallow. The glossary and the pattern language have years in them; other regions are sparse, and a few are left alone for a season while the work moves elsewhere. A garden with no fallow ground is a catalogue — our words, on that page, and worth repeating in a room that could easily pretend every bed is thriving. When an idea outgrows a page it gets a site of its own. Which is what this room is a list of. Every bed below links straight out, because each of those is already somewhere, and a shopfront on this street promising a room you never arrive in would be a lie about the architecture. The working library behind it is not public, and the garden is. That shelf holds our own copies of other people’s work — things we can cite and cannot redistribute — next to private notes. What gets published is the writing that grows out of the shelf rather than the shelf. Everything linked from this page is open to anybody, with no account and no paywall. Nothing in here is ranked, counted or scored. No bed is the biggest, the best or the busiest, and no bed says how much its site holds. A number like that is wrong within the week and looks authoritative in the meantime, and a garden measured by volume is an inventory. tools/make-garden.py refuses both, so this stays true after we have forgotten we meant it. How the whole thing is actually tended is written up in three places, each answering a different question: the field guide to the system opens with what happens to everything we know when the person holding it is unavailable; the garden as curriculum reads it as a course of study rather than a filing cabinet; and start your own knowledge garden is the version written for you instead of for us. That last one is down the path.

One per site, in the order our own feeds page puts them in, which is not a decision this room gets to make. Beside each bed is the habit of growth it keeps, and every habit is different: that is what tells the drawings apart, rather than a colour of their own. Some of these were made with other people, and every bed says so on its face.

stimpunks.org The garden itself, and the one the others were built to take weight off: a glossary kept in public, a pattern language grown out of lived experience, recipes for the environments those patterns ask for, and the frameworks that came out of all three. Its own page about the garden says nothing there needs to be read in order, and means it. What is growing here: A rhizome, running sideways under the bed and coming up in several places at once. That is the shape our own page gives this knowledge, and Autistic Rhizome is a term in the glossary it comes up in. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation, and everybody whose writing the glossary credits by name.

starstuff.earth Zines, field guides and broadsides that start from something settled in physics, cosmology, chemistry or biology and let it carry an argument about belonging — not as loose metaphor, but as the same pattern showing up at more than one scale. Its about page calls itself the public flowering of this garden, which is its phrase and not ours. What is growing here: An umbel coming into flower: one stem, and every ray of it opening at the same height. It is the bed in flower because that site said it was. Grown with A collaboration between Stimpunks and More Realms, where a great deal of it was grown from seed.

queering.earth A cabinet of mounted sheets on queerness, illness and the natural world, with an accession register that publishes its own corrections rather than quietly fixing them. One of the sheets in it is about Monotropa uniflora, the ghost pipe, which makes no chlorophyll of its own and lives by what it is connected to underground. What is growing here: That plant, which is why this is the one bed in the garden with no green in it at all. It is carried by its outline and by the threads running out of it, the way the things in it are. Grown with Built with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms, who is named on the sheets she wrote rather than folded into our “we”, and with contributions credited on the cabinet's own pages.

cavendish.space Caves, campfires, watering holes, the library of what we have worked out, and the habitat that holds all four — plus the Cavendish Cards deck, which lets somebody point at a picture instead of explaining, and the room sheets for working out which zones a real room can already hold. Everything there is free and CC0. What is growing here: The one bed with something built over it, because that site is about the structure: a frame changes what a bed can grow, which is the whole argument for zoning a room rather than telling somebody to cope in it. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation. The three primordial spaces are David Thornburg's, from From the Campfire to the Holodeck; the name comes from Henry Cavendish by way of Steve Silberman's NeuroTribes; and Ira Socol's home of opportunity is on that site's origin page beside them.

penguinpebbling.app A card game about bringing somebody a small thing for no reason, and about what that does. No winners, no pressure to perform, and you can leave whenever you need to. There is a cabinet in our arcade built on the same practice that deliberately takes nothing from that deck — the deck is the better thing and it is here. What is growing here: Runners: the plant reaches sideways and puts a new plant down beside itself, roots and all, without being asked for anything back. That is pebbling rather than trading. Grown with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms and Ryan Boren of Stimpunks, together. The locution the practice is described in is Amythest Schaber's.

whysheet.press One-page arguments, openly licensed and editable, made to be printed and carried into a room where somebody is about to be talked over. You tick the sheets you need and the press hands back a single correctly paginated PDF with the citations intact. Nothing is uploaded and no account is kept. What is growing here: A seed head gone dry, which is the only bed here whose point is that you take it away. What it grows into somewhere we will never see is the intended outcome rather than a side effect. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation, and the researchers, lawyers and self-advocates each sheet cites on its own face.

stimpunks.world The street you are standing on, and the loud half of the same lung. No single design system, no two rooms alike, credits scrawled in the margins, and a dial that lets you decide how much of it happens. The street is that way and the liner notes say where everything in it came from. What is growing here: A scramble: nasturtiums over the edges of the bed, out onto the path and up whatever is standing near them. Nothing in this bed has been kept in its row. Grown with Stimpunks Foundation, with a pitch in the campgrounds that is Helen Edgar's own room and a community board kept by Norah Hobbs.

monotropicmap.org Twenty places a monotropic person goes, drawn as an island you can walk — attention tunnels, rabbit holes of research, infodump canyon, burnout whirlpools, the forest of joy, awe and wonder — with a second tool for drawing your own. Some of those places are where the good work happens and some are weather that other people make. What is growing here: A tendril: the stem puts out a feeler, finds something, and holds on. Tendril Theory is one of the places on that island, which is why this bed grows the thing the theory is named after. Grown with Helen Edgar's map of her own Autistic and ADHD experience, published with Stimpunks. Monotropism is Dinah Murray, Wenn Lawson and Mike Lesser's.

Through the ivy at the side, and not ours. Both of these are Helen Edgar’s — the grounded one, and the wilder ground beyond it — and they are here because so many of the beds above have her hands in them that a garden pointing only at itself would be a courtyard. Nothing over there is tended by us, nothing over there is on our feeds page, and neither of them is a bed: tools/make-garden.py refuses a plot that turns up on our own roster exactly as firmly as it refuses a bed that does not. You can see as far as the ivy and no further, which is why every drawing here stops where the ivy runs. That line was a woven fence for an afternoon, and Helen asked for ivy and stars instead. She was right about more than the picture: a fence says kept out, and ivy says this is as far as we can see. What it marks is the edge of what we know, never the edge of where anybody may go — which is the opposite reading, and the right one on a page about somebody else’s work.

autisticrealms.com Helen Edgar's own site, and the grounded one: neuro-affirming resources, reading lists, glossaries of the language to use and the language to avoid, and signposting for families, educators and Autistic people who have arrived without the words yet. Her own page sets out what the work is for as being, belonging and becoming, in that order, and she writes as an Autistic advocate, author and consultant who spent twenty years teaching in SEND early years and primary settings before any of this. Monotropism, flow and burnout are where she goes deepest. What is growing there: A nurse tree, which is planted to take the weather off whatever is growing under it until that can stand in its own light. The shelter is the work and it is not the same work as the growing — which is her argument rather than our metaphor: her page says young Autistic people need to feel accepted and understood first, and that the conditions come before the flourishing. Tended by Helen Edgar, who is a colleague and not a corpus. Her site is hers, her name is on her own writing there, and nothing of hers is folded into our “we” on this street either. morerealms.com The wilder ground past it, and hers as well. There is a spider in this garden that will answer questions about it. It is grounded in the garden itself — the glossary, the patterns, the frameworks — so the words it reaches for are the ones we planted: monotropism, the double empathy problem, spiky profiles. That matters most for somebody who does not have the word yet, because you cannot search for monotropism if nobody has ever told you it exists. It can also be wrong. Generative AI can misstate, confuse, and confidently produce things we did not say, and scoping it to our own garden reduces the source of the distortion rather than the possibility of it. So every trail it puts you on ends at a page a person wrote: follow the link, read laterally, and treat what it says as a starting point rather than as us. A spider is a guide to the garden and never a replacement for it, and its best answer is an entrance. Those are our own sentences, from the page it lives on, and how we hold that line is written up at AI Collaboration and AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making. Ask the garden →
Start a garden of your own

None of this needs our budget, our tools or our people. The steps below are the short version of Start Your Own Knowledge Garden, and they degrade gracefully: most of the value is in the first one, which needs no software at all, and each later one only adds convenience on top of something that already worked. Stop wherever it stops being useful. A half-built garden is a garden, not a failure — and the opposite framing is how these things die, because a tool that only pays off once you have finished configuring it gets abandoned during configuration, on a bad day, by exactly the person who needed it.
Make a garden. No tools required.

One folder. Everything you read, save or write goes in it, untouched. One index file, listing what is in the folder with a line about why each thing is there. A habit of adding to both. That is a garden — no app, no subscription, no AI — and the line about why this is here is a small act of synthesis repeated hundreds of times, which is where the learning actually shows.

Not to tidy a filename, not to fix a typo. Every derived thing — summaries, categories, indexes — lives somewhere else and points back at the original. That single rule is the difference between provenance you can cite and a pile you have been quietly rewriting.
Put it in git, for mercy.

Not for collaboration and not really for backup. Once every version of your thinking is recoverable you stop being careful with your own work in the way that stops you working. Version control is mercy, made structural. The template arrives as a repository already, so check with git status before running git init anywhere — and check which folder you are standing in first, which is the one mistake on that page with real consequences.
Let something else write the index.

Past a few dozen files, keeping an index by hand stops being fun. The template ships a script that walks your originals and writes it for you. The index is disposable and the sources are not: if it comes out wrong, change the configuration and run it again, and never hand-edit a generated page, because your edits get silently overwritten — which is worse than being refused.
Make it searchable, when filenames stop being enough.

A library you cannot search is half a library, and a filename is a terrible index of meaning. The payoff is finding things by what they mean: somebody in distress does not arrive knowing your vocabulary, they arrive saying it hurts. Filling the Garden is the one-click version of the whole thing, including clipping an article into your library with its source and date intact, and it needs no terminal either.
Why the garden is off the street

None of it was planned as a system. It accumulated, the way a garden does, and then we went back and named what had grown — which is also the honest account of this street. The difference is that every bed out here belongs to a site that had to leave: an idea gets big enough that a page cannot hold it, somebody builds it somewhere of its own, and what stays behind is a label saying where it went. The gate at the bottom of the hedge is the one you came in by. The street is back through there, and it is a great deal louder than this. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes or plays until you say so — and out here the only thing that moves at all is the leaf shadow.

If you adopted a dog at Rescue A Dog, you can let them off the lead on the Run for a while, among the dogs still waiting for homes, and anybody who comes by can meet them. They stay yours, and you can take them home whenever you like. Their card says they have a home, and never whose. Every dog on the Run came from Rescue A Dog, the shelter on the street. The shelter sends every dog still waiting for a home, and any dog out here who has one has been let off the lead for a while by their person, which you can do too (your own dog, above). The Run keeps no list of its own: each time it opens it reads the shelter’s, so a dog adopted this morning has already gone home, and a dog brought in an hour ago is already out on the grass. Where a dog goes is the shelter’s word for its mood, and nothing else. A dog who wagged the whole way in is out on the grass waiting for the ball; a dog who leans on everybody is on the porch, near the chairs; a dog who went straight for the radiator is flat out in a patch of sun; a dog who fell asleep before the door shut is on a bed, or in the shade. A dog with three legs gets to the far end of the field like anybody else. And a dog who wants to be left alone is left alone: nobody calls that dog over, and there is no button for it. Press a dog to meet them: their name, what they are like, where they were found and when they came in, all in the shelter’s own words. Adopting happens at the shelter. Every waiting dog’s card has a link to that dog’s own card there, where anybody signed on to the CB can adopt them, and the Run is not told who adopted whom. Nobody gives a command on the Run. Nobody is told to sit, nobody is trained, and nobody is a good boy or a bad dog. A dog who brings the ball back is playing, and a dog who does not is also playing.

Most people have three kinds of cone in the eye. Dogs have two, which is what Jay Neitz, Timothy Geist and Gerald Jacobs found in 1989, and it means a dog sees in blues and yellows and greys. In 2017 Marcello Siniscalchi and his colleagues tested dogs themselves rather than their eyes, and the dogs could not tell red from green. Stanley Coren’s account of what that looks like is that green, yellow and orange all come out yellowish, blue and violet come out blue, blue-green comes out grey, and red comes out a very dark brownish grey. So everything the Run paints itself is a blue, a yellow or a grey, and the tool that builds the room reads every one of its colours to make sure. The grass is the yellow a dog sees it as. The sky is blue, which is one of the colours a dog has. The porch roof is slate and the boards are straw. The shadows are not blue: they are the grass’s own yellow, darker, because this is summer grass under clouds going over and not snow. The dogs are the one thing on the Run not drawn in a dog’s colours. A dog here is the same dog it is at the shelter and in the Profile of whoever adopts them, drawn by the same file in its own coat, chocolate and golden and brindle and all. The ball is blue, because on green grass a dog can find a blue ball and loses a red one. That is Marcello Siniscalchi’s own advice, given to Live Science when the 2017 paper came out, rather than something the paper tested, and we would rather say which it is. And the commonest colour blindness in people is red-green, the same pair a dog cannot tell apart, so on the Run nobody who has it is missing anything the room has put there.

Every truck does one thing, several ways, and leads with a vegan way of doing it, the same size as the rest. Every item says what is in it before you ask for it, whether it is vegan or vegetarian or which animal it came from, and which of the nine major food allergens the FDA names it has, and gluten, worked out from what is in it. The Truck Stop is the second of the lots side by side where the buildings stop, and it serves both its neighbours. Through the gate at the left-hand end of the back fence is the Run, where the dogs from the shelter are out: its treat tin is filled from the treat truck here. Through the gate at the right-hand end is the Green, with a porch of its own to carry a cold drink to. Past the Green is the Pile.

Everything is free, and nobody keeps count of how many times you came back. Sit anywhere on the porch, for as long as you like. Nobody clears a table that somebody is still at. The treats are for dogs, and every bag says so. Nobody at a hatch asks why you want what you asked for. Nothing is counted: not the tacos, not the cups, and not you.

A wood, a pond, and a boardwalk round it, just after the rain. It has just stopped raining. There is no sun on the Green, so nothing casts a shadow, and everything that is wet holds a line of the pale sky along its top edge: every leaf, every board, every rail, the rim of every bed. A wood stands all round, there is a pond in the middle with the last of the rain still putting rings on it, and a wooden boardwalk goes round the pond in a meandering loop, built so anybody can go round it, with beds of herbs and flowers and vegetables all along it. It starts and ends at the covered porch, where you are.

The boardwalk goes from the porch, round the pond, and back, and every stop on it has a resting place beside the boards. Here is every stop, in the order you come to them. Nothing on the trail is counted: not your steps, not the laps, and not how long you take.

Where the trail starts and ends, under a roof, with the rain still running off its edge in a line of drops. The trailhead sign is on the post by the steps, and the steps have a ramp beside them as wide as they are. You might notice: The drip off the gutter, and the smell of the wet boards.

A raised bed at the first turn of the boardwalk, its rim at the height of a seat, planted with things that smell when you touch them. Planted: rosemary, thyme, sage, lavender, chives, mint, in a pot of its own, because mint runs. You might notice: Brush the rosemary and your hand smells of it for an hour. The lavender is heavy with water and bent over the rim.

Three long raised beds along the boardwalk, every one 27 inches high, the height the University of Minnesota's extension service gives as comfortable for gardening from a wheelchair. Everything in them was planted to be eaten, and anybody may pick what is ripe. Planted: tomatoes, runner beans up canes, courgettes, kale, chard, peppers, lettuce, strawberries along the edge. You might notice: Wet tomato leaves, which smell green, and beads of water standing on the kale.

A wide landing over the water, with a rail along the edge at the height of somebody sitting. The last of the rain is still putting rings on the pond, and there are lily pads at this end. You might notice: Frogs, now that it has stopped. The rings spreading and crossing each other.

Where the boardwalk crosses the pond's outflow, a little stream that runs into the trees. The bridge rises one inch in every twenty on each side, the steepest the trail ever gets. You might notice: Water going over stones, louder than usual after the rain.

A shallow dip below the boardwalk where the water off the boards and the porch roof runs to, planted with things that like their feet wet. It is full now, and will be dry again by tomorrow. Planted: rushes, sedges, irises, marsh marigolds, ferns at the shady end. You might notice: Standing water with the sky in it, and the rushes bent over by the rain and straightening.

A long bed on the far side of the pond, planted for bees and butterflies. Nothing is flying yet: they wait for it to dry. Planted: coneflowers, bee balm, black-eyed Susans, asters, goldenrod, milkweed. You might notice: The coneflowers' heads full of water, and the bee balm bowed over under the rain it is still holding.

Where the boardwalk goes back in under the trees, a bed of things that grow in shade, and the softest things on the Green to touch. Planted: ferns, hostas, moss, wild ginger, foamflower. You might notice: Every leaf over you still dripping. The moss is cold and soaked through.

A bench with a back and arms, on a resting place beside the boards, with room beside it for a wheelchair. You can see the porch from here, and the pond through the trees. You might notice: The quiet, which is mostly the drip.

On the post by the porch steps. The boardwalk is built to the U.S. Access Board’s standard for trails, section 1017 of the Architectural Barriers Act standards, and section 1017.10 asks a sign at the start of a trail for exactly these, so that somebody can decide before they set off. Everything on it is true of every part of the trail. Length 1,100 feet, one loop, back to the porch Surface boards laid across the way you walk, with gaps no wider than half an inch, and a strip of grit on every board, because they are wet Tread width 60 inches all the way round, and never less than 60 Running slope 1:48 usually, and 1:20 at the steepest, on the bridge Cross slope 1:60 usually, and 1:48 at the most Resting places a resting place at every stop, 60 inches long, beside the boards, with a bench that has a back and arms and room for a wheelchair beside it

Every bed along the boardwalk is raised, with its rim at the height of a seat, so nobody has to kneel in the wet to reach it. The vegetable beds are 27 inches high, which the University of Minnesota’s extension service gives as a comfortable height for gardening from a wheelchair. Everything in them was planted to be eaten, and anybody may pick what is ripe; nobody minds, and nobody keeps count. Every plant here is named by its common name only. A Latin name typed from memory reads as if somebody had looked, and nothing on this page was looked up in a key. Everything that is eaten on the Green was planted in a bed to be eaten, and that is the only thing on this page about eating anything.
A covered porch – allowing learning to stay outdoors in any weather – was essential.

Pallets, plywood, rope, an old piano, a slide off a playground that closed, and a den roofed in bubble wrap. Everything on it is whatever you say it is. A lot of sand with a big tree at one end and a heap of everything on it: pallets, plywood, tree stumps, an old upright piano, a metal slide, buckets, shovels, ropes, old chairs, fabric, duct tape, and pots of tempera paint, which has got on most of it. In the middle is a den, pallets stood on end for walls and a roof of bubble wrap, and every bubble throws a ring of light on the sand under it. The light has no colour in it, anywhere on the Pile: all the colour is paint.

Take anything off the Pile and say what it is now. A pallet can be a wall or a raft or a ladder, and a bucket can be a drum or a hat, and nobody here tells you which. Paint the last thing you put down, or knock it all down and start again. Nothing you make is kept, and nothing is scored. Take and make it Paint the last thing you put on

The idea is a Danish landscape architect's, Carl Theodor Sørensen's, who wrote in 1931 about a junk playground where children could make their own world out of what was lying about. (Adventure playground, Wikipedia) The first was set up in Emdrup, in Denmark, during the German occupation. Wikipedia's article on adventure playgrounds says 1943, and its article on Sørensen says 1940; we have not read anything that settles it. (Adventure playground, Wikipedia) Lady Allen of Hurtwood, a landscape architect, brought the idea to Britain after the war, to the bomb sites, in a book of 1946 called Why Not Use Our Bomb Sites Like This? There the name changed from junk playground to adventure playground, to make it easier for councils to say yes to. (Adventure playground, Wikipedia) They are staffed by playworkers, and playwork, in Wikipedia's words, is the work of creating and maintaining spaces for children to play. (Playwork, Wikipedia) The one at the Berkeley Marina opened in 1979 and is still there. (Adventure Playground, the City of Berkeley) The Land, at Plas Madoc in Wales, seven miles south of Wrexham, has been open since 2011, and Erin Davis made a film about it, The Land, in 2015. (The Land (adventure playground), Wikipedia, and Erin Davis's page for her film The Land (2015)) The Yard, on Governors Island, is New York's only adventure playground, and grown-ups stay outside the main area so the children can play their own way. (The Yard, play:groundNYC) The idea under all of them has a name, the theory of loose parts, from the artist Simon Nicholson in 1971. (Simon Nicholson, Wikipedia) Simon Nicholson’s sentence is the one the theory is quoted by: Simon Nicholson, in How NOT to Cheat Children: The Theory of Loose Parts, Landscape Architecture 62, 1971, as Wikipedia's article on him gives it: Simon Nicholson. The Pile is for anybody, at any age. Nothing on it has been made safe, and nothing has been made dangerous on purpose: how high you climb is yours to decide.

Not everybody wants a shopfront. The street is a row of them shoulder to shoulder under a marquee that shouts at you, and some of us would rather be out at the edge of town with a stream going past. So the street stops here and the field starts, and the field has pitches on it, and a mountain standing over it with one home at the top.

Nothing out here moves. Not at Gentle, not at Regular, not at MAX GLITTER. The dial still works and it still governs every pitch, because each pitch is its own world and sets its own noise — but this field has nothing for it to turn up. An area that exists for people who want quiet cannot have a loud setting and mean it. You can arrive and leave without telling anybody. There is nothing to sign, nothing to join, and nothing that notices you came. Read the sign before you go in. A pitch is somebody’s own place and it looks like them, not like this field and not like the street. The signs below say what is inside so that walking in is a decision rather than a surprise. The mountain is the campgrounds’ too. It stands over the far side of the field, and the way up is a cable car from the bottom station by the pond: level with the platform at both ends, so a wheelchair rolls straight on, and it goes when somebody presses the button and not before. A track goes up from the same place for anybody who would rather walk, in long zigzags with a bench at every turn. What is at the top is somebody’s home and not a lookout. Its sign is first on the board, because the mountain is the first thing you see from anywhere on the field. The stream is the boundary. Past it is woodland and we have not drawn a map of it. That is on purpose too. One track goes through it, and comes out at a stile onto open land: Nature’s Contribution, where the street’s food and power are grown and the wildlife is left room.
The Emergent Future Worlds Meets Mountain Man

A log cabin at the top of the mountain, at night: a fire behind the glass of the stove, LED strips in a colour you pick, a big screen with David’s own playlist on it, a lake under a full moon through the window, coffee on the stove and sweets on the table, one wolf asleep on the rug and the pack outside on the warm ground, where a hot spring steams. It runs on the mountain’s own heat, and the cable car goes up from the pond. A candlelit yurt at the edge of the woods, warm the way this field is not. A reading room of old books through the bookcase door, fairy lights strung low across the canvas, a regulation nook, three animals with opinions, and a window at the far end that does not look out onto the field. Danny the Street rearranges themselves for whoever needs sheltering, and for some of us that shape is not a street. A row of lit storefronts is a wonderful place to be and an exhausting place to live, and a site that only had one of those would be telling its own quiet people that the loud room is the only room. So the street kept its doors and grew an edge. Out here the type is bigger, the ground is cold, and there is exactly one thing to read at a time. The street is still there when you want it. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so — and in this field, nothing moves even then.

Helen’s candlelit yurt on Stimpunks.World, pitched at the edge of the woods. Lots of books, music, Faeries, candle light and weird thoughts and happenings..... This is my yurt, pitched at the edge of the woods in the campgrounds of Stimpunks.World, with a stream tracing the trees; follow the fairy lights from the treeline and you will find it. It is always night here, the good kind of night, candles lit along the shelves and fairy lights strung low across the canvas so the whole room glows amber instead of going properly dark. The sofas are too soft to sit in properly (you sink, and then you stay), the beanbags were claimed by a hamster some time ago, and the ivy worked its way in through the window frame years back and was never asked to leave. The flap of the door is always open. Come in, take your shoes off, and stay as long as you need to. Like More Realms, the looser, weirder realm beyond Autistic Realms, this is not a place of conclusions or answers. It is a place to wander, to feel, to think sideways, and to deep dive monotropically into other ways of experiencing the world. There is no map, but there are threads, glimmers, and soft, weird spaces to explore… HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. In here MAX lights the fairy lights and turns the record, and makes the stars sparkle behind any portal door you open and the amber and amethyst glow in the Alchemist’s Arch; nothing else in the yurt moves unless you ask it to, below. Faeries drifting across the page, and ivy and mushrooms growing very slowly round its edges. Each stays still until you press it, whatever the dial says, and pressing again clears it. Nothing flashes, and nothing is remembered: next time both are off.

Through the Alchemist’s Arch, set with amethyst and amber, is a room of the old stories: Stonehenge and its sun, King Arthur and Merlin, the boggarts and hobs and black dogs of English folklore, a wheel of crystals, a herbery with a cauldron, and the old books that wrote them down. Through the Alchemist’s Arch →Stonehenge and its sun, Arthur and Merlin, the folk under the hill, and the old books of fairies and myth. Inside, too: the Crystal Wheel, photographs of crystals round a circle, with what each one really is and the meanings people have given it; and the Herbery, herbs with their myths and folklore to gather into a basket and stir into brews and stews, made of words. The amethyst cave: Anya Gallaccio’s The Light Pours Out Of Me Amethyst is a violet quartz, coloured by traces of iron, and the birthstone for February. It has long been held to be a calming stone, kept for peace of mind, clear thinking and restful sleep. Wishing you a magical glimmer day. The bowl in the hollow stump: leave one

The bowl needs scripts to read it. Anybody who comes to this door can see what is in the bowl, signed on to the CB or not, for seven days. A pebble, left as : what it is, in your words Where it is, if it is somewhere else (you can leave this empty) Leaving a pebble takes a username on the CB, which you join with an invite: get started or sign on at the Community Center, then come back. Taking one takes nothing. Anybody can see the bowl, and only people signed on to the CB can leave a pebble in it. A handle is whatever somebody typed, so a name in the bowl is not proof of who left it. A pebble goes seven days after it is left, and a full bowl lets its oldest go to make room. The base station can lift one out sooner, and so can we if you ask: what the bowls keep. A link shows its whole address, so what you read is where it goes. Nothing here is counted: not what was taken, not what was left, and not who came to the door. Leaving a pebble is the only footprint there is, and nobody has to leave one.

The yurt itself sits on a small campsite off the main street, tucked into the woodlands with a stream tracing the edge of the trees. Follow the fairy lights from the treeline and you will find the door. The neighbours on the campgrounds, from the pond, down a pebble path or up the cable car: David Gray-Hammond’s Emergent Future Worlds Meets Mountain Man at the summit, Jess’s Bough House at pitch 05 and Ryan Boren’s Solarpunk Hermitage at pitch 03. Go and visit. Out in the wider world, my writing lives in two places. Autistic Realms is where I share grounded, practical support for families, educators, and those navigating Autistic ways of being. More Realms is where things are looser, weirder, more speculative.

Every book I keep, a fire that has caught, and a chair that is yours while you are in it. The yurt got too full of books, so they have a room of their own now, through the bookcase door. It is lit by the fire and by candles that never flicker, the walls are claret and the arches go up to points, and there is a sofa and two chairs turned to the hearth. Take any book off a shelf and it opens its author’s page. Nobody will ask what you are reading, or how far you have got. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. In here MAX turns the record on the gramophone; nothing else moves at any setting unless you ask it to, below, and the candles stand still. Faeries drifting between the bookcases, and ivy and mushrooms growing very slowly round the edges of the room. Each stays still until you press it, whatever the dial says, and pressing again clears it. Nothing is stored.

One case for each kind of book, alphabetical inside each by surname, and every spine a door: press one and it opens the author’s page on Wikipedia, or their own site where Wikipedia has none. Two of the cases are mine: what I have written and what has cited or carried it, and the ebooks and training packs at Autistic Realms. The last case is the artists whose paintings cannot hang in the gallery back in the yurt because their work is still their own. Want to borrow a book rather than meet its author? Ryan lends his: every book on his shelves in the cave at the Solarpunk Hermitage, across the campgrounds, has a link to borrow it or read it.

Just the music, with nothing to scroll past: the phonograph, the records, and a chair in the dark. If you came for the songs and not for the rest of the yurt, this is the room. The phonograph is in here with both my playlists on it, and every song on them stands on a shelf as a record you can take out and put on. The window is open on the night, the candles never flicker, and the raven on the sill does not mind what you play. Nothing starts until you press it. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. In here MAX turns the record; nothing else moves unless you ask it to, below, and the candles stand still. Faeries drifting between the candles, and ivy and mushrooms growing very slowly round the edges of the room. Each stays still until you press it, whatever the dial says, and pressing again clears it. Nothing is stored.
