Old stones, old kings, and the folk who live under the hill. Come through the arch. The amethyst and the amber set in it light this room, and nothing in here is a flame. It is where I keep the stories this island has told itself for a very long time: the stones on Salisbury Plain, Arthur and Merlin, the boggarts and hobs and the black dog in the lane, and the old books that wrote them down. Where a story is a story, and where something is known, I try to say which. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. In here MAX makes the amber glow and the amethyst glint; nothing else moves, and the sun over the stones only moves when you press a season.

Stonehenge stands on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire, and it was built to face the sun. Press a season to turn the drawing to it. Turn to the sun Midsummer sunrise Midwinter sunset At midsummer, standing in the middle of the circle, you see the sun rise just to the left of the Heel Stone, the big stone outside the circle, along the line of the Avenue. (English Heritage, Celestial Stonehenge) At midwinter, looking the other way, the sun would once have set between the two uprights of the tallest trilithon. Half of that trilithon has fallen, so the view is gone, but the line is still the same. (English Heritage, Celestial Stonehenge)
What is known about the stones

It was built in stages: first a round ditch with banks inside and out, about 3000 BC, and the great stones put up about 2500 BC. (English Heritage, Building Stonehenge) Most of the big sarsen stones came from West Woods, on the Marlborough Downs, about 15 miles to the north. That was found in 2020 by matching their chemistry. (English Heritage, 2020) The smaller bluestones came about 150 miles, from the Preseli Hills in south-west Wales. (English Heritage, Building Stonehenge) The Altar Stone came further still: in 2024 it was traced to north-east Scotland, at least 700 km (about 435 miles) away. (Aberystwyth University, on Clarke et al. in Nature, 2024) The druids did not build it. It is more than 2,000 years older than anything written about druids. John Aubrey in the 1600s and William Stukeley in the 1700s were the ones who linked it to them. (English Heritage, Archaeologists of Stonehenge) On the summer solstice English Heritage lets everybody in to the stones for free, and streams the sunset and the sunrise online. (English Heritage, Summer Solstice 2026)
Wiltshire The largest stone circle in Britain, with a village built partly inside it. (English Heritage)
Wiltshire, near Avebury The largest artificial mound in Europe, probably finished around 2400 BC, and nobody is sure what it was for. (English Heritage)

the Ridgeway, Oxfordshire A Neolithic long barrow, a tomb older than Stonehenge's stones. The story, written down in 1738, is that if you left your horse there with a coin, you came back to find the coin gone and the horse new shod, by Wayland the smith. (Wikipedia, citing Francis Wise)
the Ridgeway, Oxfordshire A horse cut into the chalk hillside about 3,000 years ago, in the late Bronze Age or early Iron Age. (Wikipedia)

Most historians today do not think King Arthur was a real person. What there certainly is, is a story that grew for a thousand years, each storyteller adding to it, and places across the land that say he was here.

About 829. The Historia Brittonum, a history of the Britons traditionally said to be by Nennius, lists twelve battles fought by Arthur, the last on Mount Badon. (Wikipedia) Mid-900s. The Welsh Annals give one line to Camlann, the strife “in which Arthur and Medraut fell”. (Wikipedia) About 1136–38. Geoffrey of Monmouth writes the first full life of Arthur: Uther Pendragon, Arthur's birth at Tintagel, Merlin, the last battle, and Arthur carried away to the isle of Avalon. Most of it seems to be his own invention. (Wikipedia) About 1170–90. In France, Chrétien de Troyes brings in Lancelot, and is the first writer to tell of the Holy Grail. (Wikipedia) 1485. William Caxton prints Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur, the great English telling that most later versions grow from. (Project Gutenberg, Caxton's note) Today. Most historians do not think Arthur was a real person; he is a figure of story and folklore, and a very long-lived one. (Wikipedia)
The enchanter, who in Geoffrey's story brings the stones of Stonehenge over from Ireland, and arranges Arthur's birth. (Geoffrey of Monmouth, in Giles's Old English Chronicles)

In Malory an arm clothed in white samite rises from the lake holding Excalibur. Malory has two swords: the one Arthur pulls from the stone, which breaks in a fight, and Excalibur from the lake. (He calls Arthur's sword Excalibur once before the lake too.) (Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book I)

A lady of the lake whom Merlin falls for, and who shuts him under a great stone from which he never comes out. Malory gave her the name Nimue; the French romances called her Viviane. (Wikipedia, and Malory, Book IV)
Sir Gawain and the Green Knight
A late-1300s poem by an unknown writer: a green giant walks into Camelot at Christmas and asks for a beheading game. It survives in only one manuscript, now in the British Library. (British Library)
Cornwall Geoffrey set Arthur's birth here. In the 1230s Richard, Earl of Cornwall built a castle on the island, very likely to make Geoffrey's scene real. (English Heritage)
Somerset After a great fire at the abbey in 1184, the monks said in 1191 that they had found the grave of Arthur and Guinevere. Historians mostly see it as a way of raising money. (Wikipedia)
Somerset A great hill fort, lived in from the Neolithic to the Iron Age, that John Leland wrote down in 1542 as Camelot, from what local people said. (Wikipedia)
the Great Hall, Winchester A real round table hangs on the wall, but tree rings date it to the late 1200s, probably made for Edward I. Henry VIII had it painted as it is now. (Wikipedia)
Some of England’s fairies, goblins and stranger things, where they are said to be found, and the old book or play that tells of them.
all over England A mischief-making household spirit who leads travellers astray and cards the wool while people sleep. Shakespeare put him in A Midsummer Night's Dream. (Wikipedia)

Lancashire, Yorkshire and the north Spirits that can be a helpful house spirit gone sour, or something lurking in a field, a marsh or a lane. One old Lancashire belief: never give a boggart a name, or it can no longer be reasoned with. (Wikipedia)
northern England, the Midlands and the Borders Small hairy helpers who do the farm's work at night. One lived in Hob Hole at Runswick Bay in North Yorkshire. (Wikipedia)
Scotland and the north of England Household spirits who work in the house while everybody sleeps, and vanish for good if you give them clothes. (Wikipedia)

Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex and the Fens A great black ghost dog with burning eyes. On 4 August 1577, in a storm, a black dog was said to have burst into the churches at Bungay and Blythburgh; the door at Blythburgh still has scorch marks people call the devil's fingerprints. (Wikipedia)

the River Wear, County Durham John Lambton, heir to the estate, fished a small worm out of the river and threw it down a well. It grew into a monster that wrapped itself round a hill, and he came home from the Crusades to kill it, and brought a curse on his family. (Wikipedia)
Windsor Great Park A ghostly huntsman with antlers who walks round an old oak in Windsor Forest. The first written telling is in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor. (Wikipedia)

carved in churches all over England A face made of leaves, or with leaves growing from its mouth, carved in churches mostly from the 1200s to the 1400s. The name was given by Lady Raglan in 1939; what the carvings meant is still argued about. (Wikipedia)
marshes and bogs A strange light over the marsh at night that leads travellers off the path. It has many names: jack-o'-lantern, friar's lantern, hobby lantern and hinkypunk. (Wikipedia)
Devon and Cornwall, on the moors Small folk of Dartmoor and the West Country. If they lead you round in circles you are pixy-led, and the old answer is to turn your coat inside out. (Wikipedia)
the Cornish tin mines Little people underground who knock on the rock, to warn of a fall or to show the miners where the tin is. (Wikipedia)

Lancashire, Cheshire, Shropshire and Staffordshire A river hag hiding under the green weed on a pond, told of to keep children back from the water. Round Liverpool her name is also a word for duckweed. (Wikipedia)

the sky on stormy nights, all over Europe Phantom huntsmen and hounds riding through the sky. In England they were seen in 1127, written down in the Peterborough Chronicle, and Devon has its own Wisht Hounds. (Wikipedia)

Suffolk A small little black thing with a long tail who spins five skeins a day for a girl, and will have her for himself unless she can guess his name: England's own Rumpelstiltskin, first in Joseph Jacobs' English Fairy Tales. (Jacobs, English Fairy Tales)

Each card has a story on the front. Turn it over for what is actually known. Merlin brought the stones of Stonehenge over from Ireland. What is known That is Geoffrey of Monmouth's story, written in the 1130s. But stones really did travel a long way: the bluestones about 150 miles from Wales, and the Altar Stone more than 400 miles from Scotland. (English Heritage) The druids built Stonehenge. What is known No. It is more than 2,000 years older than any written mention of druids. The idea comes from John Aubrey and William Stukeley, in the 1600s and 1700s. (English Heritage) King Arthur's Round Table hangs in Winchester. What is known A round table hangs there, but tree rings date it to the late 1200s, hundreds of years after any Arthur could have lived. (Wikipedia) Arthur and Guinevere are buried at Glastonbury. What is known The monks said they found the grave in 1191, seven years after a fire had burnt their abbey and they needed money to rebuild. Most historians think that was the point. (Wikipedia) The Green Man is an ancient pagan god hidden in Christian churches. What is known The carvings are real and lovely, but the name and the pagan god idea came from Lady Raglan in 1939, and the evidence for it has since been taken apart. (Wikipedia) Black Shuck burst into Bungay church in 1577. What is known A pamphlet of 1577 does tell of a black dog in the storm at Bungay. The name Black Shuck is not in it; it was first printed in 1850. (Wikipedia) Amethyst keeps you from getting drunk. What is known That is where its name comes from: Greek amethystos means “not drunken”, and people really did believe it. It does not work. (Wikipedia) Amber is the tears of the sun's daughters. What is known In Ovid, Phaethon's sisters weep until they turn into trees, and amber drips from the branches and hardens in the sun. Amber is really fossilised tree resin, sometimes with tiny insects caught inside it, so the story was nearly right about the trees. (Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book II, in Riley's translation)

Eight festivals round the year: four old Gaelic ones on the quarter days between, and the two solstices and two equinoxes. They are old, but gathering all eight into one wheel is modern, from Gerald Gardner and Ross Nichols in the 1950s and 60s, and the names Litha, Ostara and Mabon were given by Aidan Kelly in the early 1970s. (Wikipedia) Samhain, around 31 October. Summer's end, when the old stories say the door to the other world stands open. Yule, the winter solstice. The longest night, and the sun's turn back towards spring. Imbolc, around 1 February. The coming of spring, and the ewes in lamb. Ostara, the spring equinox. Day and night of equal length. Beltane, around 1 May. May Day and the start of summer, with bonfires. Litha, or Midsummer, the summer solstice. The longest day, and the sunrise over the Heel Stone. Lughnasadh, or Lammas, around 1 August. The start of the harvest. In England it was Lammas. Mabon, the autumn equinox. Day and night equal again, and the harvest in.

Every stone below is a real one, photographed by somebody who shared the picture, and every meaning is an old belief or a story people tell, not medicine. (“There is no peer-reviewed scientific evidence that crystal healing has any effect”: Wikipedia, Crystal healing) The Crystal Wheelpress a stone

Fill a pouch here, as many as three, and draw the string: it tells you what is in it and what it might bring, out of each stone's old belief or lore. A possible outcome, in this room's telling, and never a promise. It sends nothing and keeps nothing; to keep a crystal, take it with you from its card. Put in up to three crystals Amethyst Citrine Garnet Moonstone Labradorite Lapis lazuli Turquoise Rose quartz Clear quartz Smoky quartz Obsidian Tiger's eye

Birthstone for February (GIA) What it is A violet variety of quartz, coloured by iron impurities and natural irradiation. (Wikipedia) Big producers include Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul), Artigas in Uruguay, Zambia and Thunder Bay, Ontario. (Wikipedia) Heated, amethyst turns yellow-orange or brown and can pass for citrine. (Wikipedia) Old tradition Its Greek name, amethystos, means not drunken: people believed it kept the wearer sober, clear-headed and quick-witted. (GIA) Photograph by Gonzalo Devia, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

Birthstone for November (GIA) What it is A transparent yellow variety of quartz; the name comes from citrus, by way of French citron (lemon). (Wikipedia) Natural citrine is rare: most 'citrine' sold is heated amethyst or smoky quartz. (Wikipedia) Most citrine, natural or heated, comes from Brazil. (Wikipedia) Old tradition People believed citrine could soothe tempers and calm the wearer; it has also been called the 'merchant's stone' or 'money stone' from a superstition that it brought prosperity. (GIA) Photograph by Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

Birthstone for January (GIA) What it is Not one mineral but a group of silicate minerals (almandine, pyrope, spessartine, grossular, andradite, uvarovite). (Wikipedia) Used since the Bronze Age as gemstones and abrasives. (Wikipedia) The name likely comes from Latin granatum, pomegranate, whose red seeds look like garnet crystals. (Wikipedia) Old tradition Some believe garnet brings the wearer good health, wealth and happiness. (GIA) Photograph by Moha112100, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

Birthstone for June (GIA) What it is A feldspar whose milky blue glow (adularescence) comes from light scattered by thin alternating layers of orthoclase and albite. (Wikipedia) The commonest moonstone is adularia, named for Mt Adular in Switzerland, where this specimen comes from. (Wikipedia) Most commercial moonstone today comes from Sri Lanka; the most valuable blue ones historically came from Myanmar. (Wikipedia) Old tradition The Romans believed it was made of solidified rays of the Moon; Hindu mythology says solidified moonbeams, and it was linked with Roman and Greek lunar deities. (GIA) Photograph by Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

What it is A calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar, first identified in Labrador, Canada (type area Paul's Island near Nain). (Wikipedia) Its play of colour is called labradorescence, from very thin layers that form only when the rock cools very slowly. (Wikipedia) Spectrolite is a richly coloured kind found at Ylämaa, Finland, in 1940 while fortifications were being built. (Wikipedia) Old tradition A story told in Nunatsiavut, on the Labrador coast: an angakok trapped the northern lights in the rocks, and a hunter's harpoon set some of them free. The colours left behind in the stone are labradorite. Told by Jason Sikoak. (Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami, Inuktitut Magazine) Photograph by Parent Géry, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

What it is A rock, not a single mineral: mostly lazurite, with pyrite, diopside and calcite. (Wikipedia) Mined at Sar-i Sang in Badakhshan, Afghanistan, for more than 6,000 years. (Wikipedia) Ground into ultramarine, the blue Renaissance painters such as Titian and Vermeer used. (Wikipedia) Old tradition In Mesopotamia it became the chief material for magic stones; it was used in Tutankhamun's funeral mask. (Wikipedia) Photograph by Hannes Grobe, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

Birthstone for December (GIA) What it is A blue-to-green hydrous phosphate of copper and aluminium; copper gives the blue. (Wikipedia) The name is Old French for 'Turkish': it reached Europe through the Ottoman Empire, though it came from Persia. (Wikipedia) It almost never forms single crystals; it fills veins and nodules in rock. (Wikipedia) Old tradition From the 1200s it was believed to keep the wearer from falling, especially off a horse. In Tibet it is believed to bring good fortune and protection. (GIA) Photograph by Robert M. Lavinsky, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

What it is A pink, translucent variety of quartz that grows as masses, never as well-formed crystals. (Wikipedia) Its pink comes from microscopic fibres of a silicate related to dumortierite; it used to be blamed on rutile. (Wikipedia) It formed at 400-700 °C in the quartz cores of pegmatites. (Wikipedia) Modern crystal lore No older tradition about it was found. Crystal sellers today call it the stone of love. (a crystal seller's page) Photograph by James St. John, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

What it is Pure quartz, traditionally called rock crystal or clear quartz, is colourless silicon dioxide. (Wikipedia) Quartz is the second most common mineral in the Earth's crust, about 12% by mass. (Wikipedia) A quartz crystal keeps time in quartz clocks and watches (the crystal oscillator, 1920s). (Wikipedia) Old tradition The Greeks called it krustallos, from kruos 'icy cold': some believed it was supercooled ice, and Pliny the Elder thought it was ice frozen for ages. The idea lasted until the 17th century. (Wikipedia) Photograph by Didier Descouens, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

What it is Brown to black quartz, coloured when natural gamma radiation from surrounding rock activates aluminium colour centres. (Wikipedia) Cairngorm is a smoky quartz from the Cairngorm Mountains of Scotland, used in Scottish jewellery and kilt pins. (Wikipedia) Flat panes of smoky quartz were used as sunglasses in 12th-century China. (Wikipedia) Modern crystal lore It was not important in older tradition. Crystal sellers today call it a stone for grounding and cleansing. (a crystal seller's page) Photograph by Rob Lavinsky, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

What it is Volcanic glass, formed when silica-rich lava cools too fast for crystals to grow. (Wikipedia) Not a true mineral, because a glass is not crystalline; sometimes called a mineraloid. (Wikipedia) It breaks to edges sharper than steel scalpels; Lipari, where this piece comes from, was a Neolithic source of obsidian blades traded widely. (Wikipedia) Old tradition Some Aztec priests used obsidian mirrors to conjure visions and make prophecies; they were linked with Tezcatlipoca, 'Smoking Mirror'. (Wikipedia) Photograph by Ji-Elle, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

What it is Quartz grown in parallel with altered amphibole fibres, mostly turned to limonite; that gives the silky shifting band (chatoyancy). (Wikipedia) It forms by the alteration of crocidolite; sources include South Africa, Australia, India, Namibia and Brazil. (Wikipedia) Usually cut as a cabochon (a smooth dome) to show the shifting light. (Wikipedia) Old tradition In some parts of the world it is believed to ward off the evil eye. (Wikipedia) Photograph by Marek Novotnak, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons; resized, and cropped to a circle on the wheel. Back to the wheel

Herbs that have been hung, strewn, given and told about for a very long time, each with what it is and the story that comes with it. Gather one and it goes in the herb basket in your Profile, on the radio; tip two or three into the cauldron and the book will tell you what you have stirred. The brews and stews in this room are stories, stirred out of words. None of them is a recipe, and nothing on this page is to eat or drink.

What it is An evergreen shrub of the mint family, with needle-like leaves and small pale flowers, from the Mediterranean. (Wikipedia) Its old Latin name, ros marinus, means sea-dew: Elizabeth Kent wrote in 1823 that it grows best by the sea. (Wikipedia) Old tradition Rosemary stands for remembrance. Ophelia says so in Hamlet, mourners have tossed it into graves, and in Australia sprigs of it are worn on Anzac Day. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is A small culinary herb of the mint family from around the Mediterranean, perhaps first grown in the Levant. (Wikipedia) The grayling, a fish, was given the name Thymallus for the faint smell of thyme on it. (Wikipedia) Old tradition The ancient Greeks burnt thyme in their temples, believing it a source of courage. In the Middle Ages it went under pillows to keep nightmares away, and into gifts for knights, for courage. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is Mints have square stems and leaves in opposite pairs, and spread by runners above and below the ground, so far that some are counted invasive. (Wikipedia) The whole mint family is named after it, and takes in basil, rosemary, sage and oregano. (Wikipedia) Myth In Greek myth the nymph Minthe, of the underworld river Cocytus, was turned into the garden mint by Persephone, or by her mother Demeter. Its other old name, hedyosmos, means sweet-smelling. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is A tender herb of the mint family, from tropical Asia and Australasia, grown as an annual where winters are cold. (Wikipedia) Its name comes from the Greek for the royal plant, perhaps because it went into royal perfumes. (Wikipedia) Folklore In Portugal a pot of bush basil, with a poem and a paper carnation, is given to a sweetheart on the feasts of Saint John and Saint Anthony. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is Bay laurel is an evergreen tree or large shrub of the Mediterranean, with smooth, scented leaves used in cooking. (Wikipedia) Many other plants are called bay or laurel because their leaves look or smell like it. (Wikipedia) Myth Its Greek name is daphne, after the nymph who escaped Apollo; in Ovid's telling she became a laurel tree. A wreath of bay was the prize at the Pythian Games, held for Apollo. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is A group of 47 species of the mint family, from Spain and the Mediterranean east to India. (Wikipedia) Its name probably comes, by way of Old French, from Latin lavare, to wash, after the blue infusions of it used for bathing. (Wikipedia) History In Roman times its flowers sold for 100 denarii a pound, about a month's wages for a farm labourer. Queen Elizabeth I is said to have prized a lavender jam at her table. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is There are over three hundred species of rose and tens of thousands of cultivars, most of the species native to Asia. (Wikipedia) The sharp points on a rose stem are commonly called thorns but are prickles, hooks that help it climb over other plants. (Wikipedia) Myth Sub rosa, under the rose, means in secret: in Roman myth Cupid gave a rose to Harpocrates, god of silence, so he would keep Venus's secrets, and banquet rooms were carved with roses as a reminder. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is Elders are fast-growing shrubs and small trees, with wide flat clusters of small cream flowers, elderflower, and then berries, elderberry. (Wikipedia) Watchmakers have used elder pith to clean their tools before fine work. (Wikipedia) Folklore Cut an elder down and the Elder Mother, a spirit in it, would take her revenge; it could only safely be cut while chanting a rhyme to her. Some say elder keeps witches away, others that witches gather under it. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is A plant up to a metre tall with small whitish flowers and feathery leaves; millefolium, its old name, means thousand-leaved. (Wikipedia) Yarrow has been found with Neanderthal burials, which suggests people have had it near for 60,000 years. (Wikipedia) Old tradition In China dried yarrow stalks are used in I Ching divination, and yarrow and tortoiseshell are counted lucky. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

What it is Hundreds of species of thorny shrubs and small trees of the rose family, also called the May-tree, whitethorn and quickthorn. (Wikipedia) The Glastonbury thorn, in Somerset, flowers twice a year. (Wikipedia) Folklore In Gaelic folklore the hawthorn marks the entrance to the otherworld and belongs to the fairies. A lone thorn is unlucky to cut, except in bloom, when it is cut and dressed as a May bush. (Wikipedia) To the cauldron

Every herb brings something out of its own story, and the cauldron tells you what a mix might bring: a possible outcome, in this room's telling, and never a promise. Tip in two or three herbs Rosemary Thyme Mint Basil Bay Lavender Rose Elder Yarrow Hawthorn
The book of brews and stews

Brew of Remembering, a brew of Rosemary and Bay. For an evening of telling old stories out loud, so nobody in them is forgotten. Brew of Small Courage, a brew of Thyme and Basil. For the moment before a door, a phone call, or the first word in a full room. Under-the-Rose Brew, a brew of Rose and Mint. For a secret kept kindly: the kind that is somebody else's to tell. Elder Mother's Brew, a brew of Elder and Hawthorn. Ask the Elder Mother first, and leave the lone thorn standing. Sea-Dew Brew, a brew of Rosemary and Lavender. Sea air and clean washing, for a room that wants airing. Yarrow Stalk Brew, a brew of Yarrow and Thyme. Stir it while you wonder, and let the stalks fall where they fall. Underworld Stew, a stew of Mint, Rose and Bay. Minthe, Daphne and the rose that kept a secret: three stories of plants and gods, simmered together. Fair Folk Stew, a stew of Hawthorn, Elder and Yarrow. Set out a bowl under the thorn, and do not wait up. Windowsill Stew, a stew of Basil, Thyme and Rosemary. Everything growing on the sill, for an ordinary Tuesday. Moonlight Stew, a stew of Lavender, Rose and Elder. Pale flowers only, stirred after dark. Every fact and story about a herb was read on the page it links to, on 2026-10-25; the book is this room’s own.

Books of fairies, myth and legend that are old enough to belong to everybody now, each one free to read online. The Golden Bough James George Frazer, 1890, cut to one volume in 1922. An enormous gathering of magic, ritual and myth from all over the world, starting from a sacred grove in Italy where a priest-king guarded a golden bough. A famous and fascinating book, but Frazer's big theories, of a dying and rising god behind every myth, are now largely set aside by scholars. Read it as an old book, not as fact. There is a fairy fort out past the last streetlight, Sithen, where the rules nobody will say out loud about the fair folk are written down plainly, and on the street the witches of Covenstead keep their kitchen. The rest of the yurt is back through the arch.
← back to the campgrounds pitch 05 · up in the grove · next door to the Faery Yurt A tree house in a grove

Jess’s, up among the autumn leaves, with the tree growing up through the middle of it. The tree was here first. The house was built round it, so the trunk comes up through the floor and goes out through the roof, and two of its limbs curl round the walls as if they were holding it up, which they are. It is autumn up here: the leaves have turned gold, rust and crimson, a few are still green, and the ones that have let go lie deep round the foot of the ladder, and round a fairy door at the foot of the trunk, arched, with a round window, a gold knob, a step up to it and a toadstool beside it: the right size for whoever lives in a tree. The last of the afternoon sun is still in the top of the grove after the ground below has gone into shade.

This is Jess’s. She founded GROVE and runs it: mentoring, interest groups and a programme called BEING ME, for Autistic young people, by Autistic adults, based in the UK and open to young people anywhere. A tree house in a grove, for somebody whose work is called one. Visit GROVE at gr0ve.org
Ben is a tiny black dog, and this is his tree house too. He is on the platform in the drawing, by the door.

There is one record up here and it plays on repeat: press it once and it goes round, from the top every time it ends, until you stop it. Nothing plays until you press. Let Me Touch You For Awhile, by Alison Krauss & Union Station, written by Robert Lee Castleman, from their album New Favorite (2001). 3:23, on YouTube, via AlisonKraussVEVO.

From the foot of the ladder a pebble path runs across the grass, past a pond with swing seats beside it, one of them a platform swing a wheelchair can roll onto, a hammock, and a playground for pets, to the Faery Yurt, and another runs on across the field to the Solarpunk Hermitage. The pond and the playground are on the campground between the pitches, and belong to nobody’s: every home stays its own. The neighbours on the campgrounds, from the pond, down a pebble path or up the cable car: David Gray-Hammond’s Emergent Future Worlds Meets Mountain Man at the summit, Helen Edgar’s Faery Yurt at pitch 01 and Ryan Boren’s Solarpunk Hermitage at pitch 03. Go and visit.

The brief is Jess’s, passed on by Helen Edgar on 2026-10-17: a tree house in a grove, with the tree growing up through it and wrapped round it, in autumn colours, Ben, one song on repeat, and a link to GROVE. The name was ours, chosen for a house in the boughs of a grove, and is Jess’s to change. The drawing and the words here were written for this room. What GROVE does was read off GROVE’s own site on 2026-10-17. The song’s title, artist and length were read off its own page on YouTube, and its writer and album off MusicBrainz, the same day. Set in Merienda, by Eduardo Tunni, and Overlock, by Dario Manuel Muhafara, both under the SIL Open Font License. Every source is in the liner notes. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? A meadow, and almost nothing done to it. One path goes in, cut so that somebody using wheels can get to the middle, and at the middle there is a ring of stones with a fire in it and benches round the fire. That is the whole build. The rest is grass doing what grass does. what is growing here
Left alone is a decision, not a gap in the plan

Every other pitch in this field is a building. This one is a field inside a field. Nothing here is landscaped, nothing is arranged for looking at from a particular spot, and there is no best time to come. The argument for that is not that nature is nice. It is that a place you keep turning up to will tell you things, and will go on telling you for as long as you keep turning up — and that this is a relationship with obligations running both ways rather than a view with a bench in front of it. Our own glossary calls the learning half of this place-based: the natural, cultural and built environment as the text, and knowledge that belongs somewhere rather than everywhere. The other half is on Nature and on Offline — fresh air, daylight, large muscle movement, and the freedom to stim while you are out in it.
A correction we owe, kept where you can see it

Hold out your hands and let me lay upon them a sheaf of freshly picked sweetgrass, loose and flowing, like newly washed hair. Golden green and glossy above, the stems are banded with purple and white where they meet the ground. Hold the bundle up to your nose. Find the fragrance of honeyed vanilla over the scent of river water and black earth and you understand its scientific name: Hierochloe odorata, meaning the fragrant, holy grass. In our language it is called wiingaashk, the sweet-smelling hair of Mother Earth. Breathe it in and you start to remember things you didn't know you'd forgotten.
Robin Wall Kimmerer, Braiding Sweetgrass Also on our own Nature.
A correction we owe, kept where you can see it

Our glossary attributes a framework called reciprocal ethical unity to Barry Lopez. Star Stuff went and read the essay for The Place Knows You’re There and he never wrote the phrase. What he wrote was “living in some sort of ethical unity with a place”, and the hedge was doing work: he was being careful not to sound more certain than he was about somebody else’s relationship to the ground. Fusing that with a question he asks two paragraphs later turned a hesitation into a term of art. We did it, and this room is quoting from the pages where we did it, so it says so here rather than further down. That zine also takes apart the sentence most people meet reciprocity through — as long as we protect nature, nature will protect us, which is Jessica Hernandez’s father’s teaching, reported by her. If you have spent your life being offered belonging on terms, you hear a contract in those first three words, and the flinch is correct and aimed at the wrong sentence. Nothing is being withheld. Walk far enough out of a relation and it does not start refusing you; it just cannot reach you. And the attention this asks for is attention some of us get assessed for. The first thing Lopez names is paying intimate attention — one deep channel going a long way into one thing rather than a thin layer over everything. Read from where we are standing that is a description of monotropism. Same attention, different name, depending on who is doing it and whether anybody thought to ask what it was for. Robin Wall Kimmerer, Braiding Sweetgrass Also on our own Nature. the way in
One path, and it is everybody’s path

A meadow is not automatically anybody’s. Left completely alone it is a place for people who can wade through waist-high grass over uneven ground, which is a smaller group than it sounds and not the group this organisation is for. So there is a path, and the path has a specification, because “accessible” without one is a word in a brochure. Firm, stable and still a natural surface. Compacted stone dust, not asphalt. You can get a chair or a rollator down it in the wet, and it still sounds like ground under you. Wide enough to turn round on, and wide enough for two people to go in side by side, because arriving somewhere alone because the path was single file is its own kind of exclusion. Somewhere to stop that is not the destination. There are places to sit along it, not only at the end. A route that only rewards you for finishing is a route designed by somebody who never needed to stop. It says how long and how steep before you set off, the same way every press-to-play control in this street’s rooms says how long it runs before you press it. Deciding needs the number in advance. It is the only path. Not a step-free alternative round the back past the bins. One way in, and it is this one, and everybody uses it. Past where the path stops, the grass is grass. We have not drawn a map of the rest of it, the way the field above has not drawn one of the woodland. That is on purpose too. the clearing

Native scholar Greg Cajete has written that in indigenous ways of knowing, we understand a thing only when we understand it with all four aspects of our being: mind, body, emotion, and spirit. I came to understand quite sharply when I began my training as a scientist that science privileges only one, possibly two, of those ways of knowing: mind and body. As a young person wanting to know everything about plants, I did not question this. But it is a whole human being who finds the beautiful path. That September pairing of purple and gold is lived reciprocity; its wisdom is that the beauty of one is illuminated by the radiance of the other. Science and art, matter and spirit, indigenous knowledge and Western science — can they be goldenrod and asters for each other? When I am in their presence, their beauty asks me for reciprocity, to be the complementary color, to make something beautiful in response.

Herbal teas, soups and stews, and bread, in a cabin in the woods. Everything on the board is vegan. A cabin at the edge of the trees, and nobody lit it. The light grows in the wood: a pale glow along the joints between the logs, in the moss on the sill and in the little mushrooms at the foot of the walls, enough to read by and never enough to throw a shadow. The stove is shut iron, so it gives the room its warmth and none of its light. There is no flame in here anywhere, and nothing in here moves, at any setting: you come in off a dark field into a room that is lit by itself, and sit down.

Everything on the board is vegan, and every card says what is in it and which of the nine major food allergens the FDA names it has, and gluten. Every tea is a tisane, made from flowers, leaves, roots, seeds or fruit and none of the tea plant, so none of them has any caffeine. There is no honey, so every tea comes with maple syrup on the side. Nothing on the board is a remedy. A cup of chamomile here is a cup of chamomile, and nothing on a card says what it will do for you. Nothing was picked in the wood either: the herbs come from the cottage garden and the jars on the shelf, and the mushrooms in the soup were grown on a farm. Everything is made at the one stove, so if an allergy is serious, say so there, and somebody will tell you what has been near what.

David’s: a fire behind glass, lights in a colour you pick, a big screen, a lake under a full moon through the window, a hot spring steaming outside the door, and the wolves. You come in by the door on the left and the whole back wall is a window. Below it the lake is lying under a full moon, with the moon’s path across the water, the mountain’s own shoulder between you and it, and, on the warm ground just outside the glass, the pack, lying in the snow where the hot spring’s steam goes past them. Inside, the walls are logs, and the room is lit three ways at once: the fire behind the glass of the stove, with the coffee pot on top and a shelf of cups above it; the LED strips along the top of the walls and under the big screen, in whichever colour you pick, the whole rainbow among them; and the moon. A corner sofa runs along the right wall, a high-back sofa sits under the window, two high-back armchairs face the stove and the screen, every one of them piled with cushions that wear whichever colour the strips are and change when they do, bean bags in bright colours lie about the floor, and the low table between them has the crisps, the sweets and a bowl of rainbow sweets on it. The oil diffuser is on the side table by the stove, with its shelf of oils beside it. The big screen is on the right wall with a speaker standing either side of it. One wolf is asleep on the rug by the stove. Nothing in here moves until you press the switch, and the words beside it say what did.

This is David Gray-Hammond’s (he/they). He works with Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, and he knows Jess, whose Bough House is down on the field, and others in the Stimpunks community: those are Helen’s words for him, passed on with the brief, and so are his name and his pronouns. Everything he makes is on one page of his own, which was read for this room: his books, his podcasts (Autistic Identity With NeuroHub, The Mycelial Mind, and A Multitude of Drops, a series on philosophies of Autistic identity), PhiliaSense, his one-to-one and professional services, the online communities NeuroHub Community runs, and The Wider Existence, the newsletter he writes with Helen. Everything David makes, at david.neurohubcommunity.org David, with the Diversity Power List honours, in front of the NeuroHub wall.

Everything in the cabin is on one switch: the fire, the LED strips, the diffuser, the big screen’s plate and the speakers go on together and off together, and the words beside the switch say which it is. When they come on, the fire burns and the diffuser’s wisps rise, at Regular and MAX; at Gentle they are lit and still, and the words are the same. The switch remembers nothing and sends nothing: come back and the cabin is as you first found it. The lights are yours to colour. Next colour steps the strips through the cabin’s colours one press at a time, at every setting: teal, magenta, lime and periwinkle, and then the whole rainbow, red to violet. At MAX GLITTER there is a second button that lets them drift from one colour to the next on their own, round the rainbow, slowly, until you stop them, and it never flashes: a colour takes seconds to become the next one. The diffuser has a shelf of oils beside it, and Change the scent steps through them, saying which is in: lavender, chamomile, tea tree, orange blossom, chocolate, marshmallow and cupcakes. A scent here is a smell and nothing else; nothing says what any of them does for you. Without JavaScript the cabin is as drawn, everything on and still, and the buttons do not appear.
The hot spring, and what runs on it

Outside the door the snow stops at a ring of stones and the ground is water: a hot spring, steaming in the cold, with a shelf of rock along one side to sit on and a step beside it at seat height, so a wheelchair transfers straight onto the shelf and back. The mountain is warm inside, and the cabin runs on that: the spring’s water goes through pipes under the floor before it reaches the pool, and a small geothermal plant in the hut behind the cabin makes the electricity for the lights, the screen and the speakers out of the same heat. No wire comes up the mountain. The stove is for the look of a fire and the warmth of sitting in front of one, and the coffee. Ryan’s Solarpunk Hermitage down on the field runs on the sun; this runs on the ground. The spring is water, hot. Nothing here says what it does for a body, because that is the sentence every hot spring on the internet is sold with, and it is not one this street makes. One wolf lives inside, asleep on the rug by the stove with its tail over its nose, and the rest of the pack lives on the mountain and comes as far as the stones. The warmest ground on the whole mountain is the strip where the pipes run from the spring to the cabin, and that is where they lie, in the moonlight, with the steam going past them. They are the mountain’s and not the cabin’s: nobody feeds them, nobody names them, nobody counts them, and they go when they want to. All Needs Met, past the campgrounds’ wood, is where the land is left to the wild things on purpose; up here it was never anybody else’s to leave. You can hear them. The button below makes the pack howl: one wolf starts and the others join, and it lasts about five seconds. The howl is made in your browser, out of nothing but arithmetic, when you press and not before; it is not a recording of any wolf, nothing is fetched, and the loudest it can be is a little under the speakers’ own ceiling. And you can hear real ones. Beside the made howl there is a recording of wolves howling, from Wikimedia Commons, made by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and in the public domain; the button says how long it runs, it plays from Commons when you press, and nothing is fetched before that. The cable car, and the way down

The way up is a cable car, from a bottom station by the pond on the field to a top station on the snow beside the cabin. It hangs on its wire down the left-hand edge of this page: Send the cable car, in the row under the drawing, sets it running up and down the wire and stops it again, and pressing the car itself takes you back down to the campsite. Land kept for wildlife, for food and for power at once, where every part of it feeds the others, and the street. The track through the campgrounds’ wood comes out at a stile, and the land opens out in front of you: a whole valley of it, in the afternoon, under a big sky with the clouds coming apart. The shadows lying on the fields are the clouds’. Nothing on the ground casts them, and they go over whole fields at once with edges as soft as the cloud. You are standing in one at the stile. Out in the sun there is a wetland with a low barn beside it, three hoop houses, rows of solar panels with sheep under them, a farm with trees growing through its fields, and a stretch of ground at the far side that somebody seems to have sown by throwing it.

In words: the wood stands dark on both sides of the stile. Out in front, a wetland with reeds and a low barn with a ramp to its door lies to the west, by the trees; three white hoop houses stand in the next field; in the middle distance, rows of dark solar panels on posts catch a line of sun along their tops, with sheep grazing underneath; to the east there is a red barn, rows of trees with crops between them, and corn; and at the far east the ground is speckled all over with flowers of every colour. Cloud shadows lie across the fields, one over the hoop houses, one over the flowers and one on the fields nearest the stile, softer at the edges than anything else in the picture.
A white fingerpost stands by the stile with an arm for every place on this land, and each arm says which way. Under each one, what is there, and what the land there is doing. WEST

A wildlife preserve for whatever lives here already, and a sanctuary for animals who are disabled or were abandoned. At night the keepers go round with a viewer that sees warmth instead of a torch, so nobody is woken. The land here is left to wildlife. NORTH-WEST

Cannabis grown in hoop houses among the plants that grow well beside it, and a farm that would rather teach you how to be careful than sell you anything. Harm reduction, from our own pages. The land here is shared with companion plants. NORTH

Solar panels on posts high enough to walk under, with peppers growing in their shade and the farm's sheep grazing between the rows. It powers everything out here and much of the street, though every place out here has panels and a battery of its own as well. The land here is shared with crops and sheep. NORTH-EAST

A mixed farm and its agroforestry: nut trees with crops between them, the Three Sisters, sheep, goats and chickens, and a café in the old dairy where everything edible out here ends up on the menu. The land here is shared between trees, crops and animals. EAST
An ornamental garden and a food garden, sown by throwing the seed and letting whatever suits the ground win. Nothing in rows. The land here is shared between flowers and food.
Our analysis suggests that if increased demand for food and energy is met without co-locating sectors, it is not possible to meet conservation and development goals.

Ryan’s brief for this land was a paper: “Balancing land use for conservation, agriculture, and renewable energy”, in Nature Communications this year. It divides each country’s land between wildlife and the things people need from land, food and power among them, and compares three ways of planning it: putting development first, putting nature first, and planning for both at once. Planning for both at once is the one this land is built on, and the paper is plain about why somebody has to: Co-locating means more than one use on the same ground, and most of this land does that. The panels stand over peppers and sheep, the farm grows trees, crops and animals in the same fields, the cannabis grows among the plants that grow well beside it, and the chaos gardens are flowers and food at once: And some of it is not shared at all. The sanctuary’s preserve is left to whatever lives there, because the paper is just as plain that sharing ground is not the whole answer for wildlife: So the land does both, on purpose: some of it shared, some of it left alone, and all of it planned together, which is the paper’s own summing up. It is a story, and the paper is careful about how far its own maps go, so we are too: nothing on this land is a model of anywhere real, or a plan for anybody’s field. The name comes from the same paper. Among the things its conservation targets protect are what it calls nature’s contributions to people: clean water, pollination, shelter from the sea, somewhere to be outside. Out here the contributions run every way, people to land as well as land to people, and the table below says where each one goes.

Every place out here gives something to another, and most of what the land grows goes to the street, through the honesty box on the street or the café in the farm’s old dairy. The sun powers all of it: the solar farm runs the land and much of the street, and every place out here has panels and a battery of its own as well, so none of them goes dark if another does. Cannabis leaves only through licensed dispensaries, never through the honesty box, because a box nobody watches cannot ask anybody’s age. And nothing leaves the sanctuary but its manure: its residents are not stock. A wildlife sanctuary: a preserve left to whatever was here first, and a home for good for animals who are disabled or were abandoned. It is after dark, and the keepers are doing their round. They do not carry a torch, because a torch wakes everybody, so they carry a viewer that sees warmth instead, and this is what it shows: every resident white with their own warmth, the cold night black around them, and nothing in the picture with a colour, because heat has none. All needs met is what the picture means. Somebody fed and sheltered and settled is warm, and you can see it from across the yard without waking them.

In words: the sky and the wetland are black. Reeds stand round the water a shade lighter, a heron is white in the shallows, bats are small white shapes over the water and a muskrat is a white smudge on the bank. At the trees behind, a deer stands white at the edge. In the yard, Duke the duck is by the pond, two hens are close together, Juniper the goat has her head down on three legs, Clover the rabbit sits with her head on one side, Hollis the dog lies facing the barn, Mabel the pig is a big white shape near the fence, and Bramble the sheep stands beyond her. The barn’s doorway glows, Otis the owl is white on his perch inside the wire of his mews, and the keepers’ hut has a bright window.

Everybody in the yard came here because somewhere else would not keep them, and they live here for good. Nobody here is brave, or sad, or a lesson for anybody: they are a goat, a hen, a dog and the rest, getting on with it. What follows is how each one came, how they get about, and what they like, and it is all ours: they are this story’s animals, not anybody’s real ones.
A goat. Came from a farm that would not keep a goat with three legs. Gets about on three legs, and she is the first to the hay every morning. Likes the bale by the barn door, which nobody else gets.

A hen. Came with a crate of hens nobody wanted any more. Gets about without seeing: she knows the run by the wire under her feet and by the other hens' voices. Likes the same dust bath in the same corner every afternoon.
A dog. Came after somebody left him at the side of a road. Gets about without hearing: he watches, and the keepers talk to him with their hands. Likes lying where he can see the door.
A pig. Came from a family who were told she would stay small, and she did not. Gets about wherever she likes, slowly. Likes the wallow, and having her back scratched with a broom.

A great horned owl. Came with a wing that healed the wrong way after he flew into a fence, so he cannot go back to the wild. Gets about by hopping and climbing, and by gliding from his high perch to the floor of his mews. Likes being left alone in the daytime.
A sheep. Came from a flock that was being split up, with one eye. Gets about keeping the rest of the flock on the side she can see. Likes having her chin scratched, and nothing else touched.
A rabbit. Came after she was let loose in a park in the spring. Gets about with her head on one side, which is how she has always held it. Likes a cardboard box with two doors.
A duck. Came from a pond where the others would not let him on the bank. Gets about with a wobble on land, and dead straight on the water. Likes the shallow end of the pond, and Pip.

Past the yard the wetland is left to whatever was here first. There is no path into it and nobody goes in: you look from the edge of the yard. Some of the neighbours, and when you might see them from there: Great blue herons, standing in the shallows at dawn and dusk. Red-winged blackbirds, on the reeds all spring. Chorus frogs, calling from the wetland after rain. Muskrats, in and out of the bank at night. Mule deer, at the edge of the trees at first light. Coyotes, passing through, and not stopping. Little brown bats, over the water on summer evenings. Dragonflies, over the shallows in the heat of the day. Plain names only, and nothing here tells you how to find or tell any of them apart. This is their home, not a field guide.

Connection You can come and sit in the yard. Anybody who wants to come to you will, and anybody who does not is not called over. Conservation The preserve is left to whatever was here first. There is no path through it: you look from the edge of the yard, and the wetland gets on with being a wetland. Education The keepers will tell you about anybody here, if you ask, and the screen in their hut has a month of films from people who look after animals and the wild all over the world. Manure Composted behind the barn, and carted to the cannabis farm's beds and the chaos gardens. It is the only thing that ever leaves.

Cannabis grown among the plants that grow well beside it, and a farm that would rather help you be careful than sell you anything. The cannabis grows in hoop houses, long tunnels of milky plastic over hoops, and in the afternoon the whole skin glows: the light comes through all of the arch at once, every leaf is lit from above and from both sides, and the only shadow is a soft one under each plant. The plants are in flower. The flowers are the sticky tops, with their orange hairs and a frost of resin over them, and the frost is where the plant makes what people come to it for. Between the cannabis grow basil and dill, marigolds and alfalfa, and at the far end the doorway is a square of brighter light.

In words: you stand on the path down the middle of a hoop house. The hoops arch overhead, pale against the glowing plastic, closer together towards a bright doorway at the far end. On both sides cannabis plants stand in their beds, tall at the front and smaller further back, with big fan leaves of seven narrow leaflets and pale green flowering tops dotted with orange hairs and white frost; two of them have purple flowers. Along the edges of the beds, by the path, grow clumps of basil, yellow heads of dill and orange marigolds.

Between the cannabis grow the plants a grower’s guide, Joshua Mezher’s at a shop that sells grow kits, says grow well beside it. What each one is supposed to do is the guide’s word: a university extension service says research mostly does not back companion-planting claims, though marigolds grown as a cover crop do cut down a kind of worm in the soil. The farm grows them anyway, because they are good to grow: most of them are food, all of them flower, and none of them goes to waste. Basil: the guide says it brings in helpful insects and keeps some pests away. It goes to the café in the old dairy, and the honesty box. Dill: the guide says it draws caterpillars away from the cannabis. It goes to the café in the old dairy, and the honesty box. Chamomile: the guide says it protects young plants from pests. It goes to the café in the old dairy, as tea. Coriander: the guide says it keeps aphids and spider mites away. It goes to the café in the old dairy, and the honesty box. Alfalfa: the guide says it feeds the soil. It goes to the farm's animals and the sanctuary's residents. Marigolds: the guide says they keep pests away above ground and below it. They go to the honesty box, as flowers. Lavender: the guide says it keeps some pests off and brings bees in. It goes to the honesty box. Yarrow: the guide says it brings in ladybirds and hoverflies. It goes to the honesty box, dried. Sunflowers: the guide says they draw insects away and shelter the beds. They go to the honesty box, and the birds.
Many neurodivergent folks have hyper-reactive nervous systems. Anxiety and sensory overwhelm flood the senses. A substance that eases this flood offers relief and escape.
Harm reduction recognizes and honors the myriad of ways survivors cope, recover, and heal.
Harm Reduction, our own glossary, quoting Healing Justice Lineages, edited by Cara Page and Erica Woodland (North Atlantic Books, 2023).

Stimpunks’ Executive Director, Chelsea, also works at a cannabis dispensary in Colorado, and she meets a lot of neurodivergent and disabled people across that counter. Ryan, who builds this street, has a neuromuscular disease that responds well to cannabis. That is his body’s answer, and nothing on this page is a promise about anybody else’s. Our own Addiction entry puts it in the first person: That entry collects Autistic people writing about cannabis, and what happened to prescriptions where medical cannabis became legal, under Autism and Cannabis and Cannabis and Harm Reduction. It is where this farm comes from. So is harm reduction, which grew out of the War on Drugs and the HIV and AIDS years, and meets people where they are rather than where somebody thinks they should be:
Nobody here is going to tell you not to. These are the things public health says help people stay safe, in plain words, each with where it comes from.
Edibles take a while, so start low and go slow
Take from 30 minutes to 2 hours to feel intoxicating effects, so some people may eat too much, which can lead to poisoning and/or serious injury.
“Cannabis and Poisoning”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the public domain.
Edibles take a while, so start low and go slow

Colorado sells edibles in servings of 10 milligrams of THC or less. If you do not know how one will affect you, Colorado says to eat less than one serving and wait at least 90 minutes, and up to four hours, before having more. From “Safety with edibles”, Colorado's official cannabis site and “Cannabis and Poisoning”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the public domain.
If you intend to drive, the safest option is not to use any alcohol or drugs, including cannabis.
“Cannabis and Driving”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the public domain.

Colorado says to wait at least six hours after smoking up to 35 milligrams of THC before driving or riding a bike, and at least eight hours after eating up to 18. From “Driving and traveling”, Colorado's official cannabis site and “Cannabis and Driving”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the public domain.
Not with alcohol, and tell whoever prescribes for you

Colorado says cannabis and alcohol together impair you more than either one alone, and to tell your health care provider if you take prescription medicines, because they can interact. From “Mixing cannabis with other substances”, Colorado's official cannabis site.
Smoked cannabis, regardless of how it is smoked, can harm lung tissues and cause scarring and damage to small blood vessels.
“Cannabis and Lung Health”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the public domain.

Eating it, or a vaporiser for flower, keeps smoke out of your lungs, though Colorado says the research on vaporising is not settled yet. From “Cannabis and Lung Health”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, in the public domain.
Vape carts only from a licensed store
Vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to the EVALI outbreak.
“Outbreak of Lung Injury Associated with the Use of E-Cigarette, or Vaping, Products”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (archived, 2020), in the public domain.

In 2019 and 2020 an outbreak of lung injuries was traced to vaping products, most of them containing THC and bought from friends, family or dealers rather than stores. From “Outbreak of Lung Injury Associated with the Use of E-Cigarette, or Vaping, Products”, U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (archived, 2020), in the public domain.

Colorado says concentrates can be up to 90 per cent THC, and that making them at home with flammable solvents has caused explosions and deaths. From “Safety with THC concentrates”, Colorado's official cannabis site.
Use of synthetic cannabinoids is associated with severe, potentially life-threatening health effects.
“Cannabis (Marijuana)”, U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse, in the public domain.
They are not cannabis, whatever the packet says. From “Cannabis (Marijuana)”, U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse, in the public domain.

CHS only resolves when a person stops using cannabis completely.

Some people who use a lot of cannabis for a long time start vomiting and cannot stop. From “Cannabis (Marijuana)”, U.S. National Institute on Drug Abuse, in the public domain.
Locked up, away from children and pets

Colorado says to keep cannabis in child-resistant packaging, locked, where children cannot see or reach it, and that vets are seeing more pets that have eaten it. Poison Help is 1-800-222-1222, and 911 if it is serious. From “Safe storage”, Colorado's official cannabis site.

You have to be 21. Buy only from a licensed store, an ounce at a time; you can have two ounces and give up to two ounces to another adult, never sell it, and never share it with anybody under 21, which is a felony. Not in public, and not on federal land. From “Laws about cannabis use”, Colorado's official cannabis site.

Solar panels on posts high enough to walk under, peppers in their shade, sheep between the rows, and the power for the land and much of the street. It is noon, and the sun is straight overhead. The panels take the top of the light, and you can see it lying along the top edge of every one as a hard white line. Under them it is shade, and in the shade there are peppers, tomatoes and basil, doing better there than they would out in the open, and the sheep from the farm next door come in between the rows to graze. What the panels make runs everything on this land and much of the street, though every place out here has panels and a battery of its own as well, so none of them goes dark if another does.

In words: a pale blue sky with a small white sun straight overhead. Three rows of dark blue solar panels on tall grey posts, tilted, each with a bright white line of sun along its top edge. Under each row the soil is in shade. Under the first row, bushy chiltepin plants hung with small red peppers; under the second, jalapeño plants with long green peppers; under the third, cherry tomatoes in cages and low clumps of basil. Two sheep graze in the sun between the rows, and at the end there is a small pale battery shed.
Shade tolerance is not a property of the plant. It is a property of the plant and the place, and it changes when the place does.
Two Peppers, Stimpunks Zine No. 87, Stimpunks Foundation × More Realms, 2026-09-04, CC BY-SA 4.0.
There is no unsuitable crop. There is a ratio nobody adjusted.

Grow two kinds of pepper under the same panels and they answer the shade two different ways. That is what Star Stuff’s Two Peppers is about, a zine of ours, built from a field experiment outside Tucson where three crops were grown under panels and in the open beside them and measured. The point it ends on is not about peppers at all: So the farm does not ask which crops are suited to shade. It asks how much shade each one wants, and sets the panels for that: The panels over the crops in that field ran about 8.9 degrees Celsius cooler in daylight than panels over bare ground, and the soil under them stayed wetter. From Barron-Gafford and others, Nature Sustainability, 2019; the whole citation is in the liner notes.

Nut trees with crops between them, the Three Sisters, sheep, goats and chickens, and everything the farm grows going to the café in its old dairy and the honesty box on the street. The sun is going down on one side of the farm and the full moon is coming up on the other, both on the horizon at once, so everything here is lit by two lights: warm on its west side and silver on its east. The trees shelter the crops, the animals graze under the trees, the chickens follow the animals, and what comes out of one goes into another.

The USDA names five practices. Four of them are on this farm, and the fifth says why it is not:

Linear plantings of trees and shrubs to enhance, protect, and benefit people, livestock, and soil and water conservation. A line of trees along the north and west edges, between the farm and the weather.
Natural or re-established streamside forests made up of tree, shrub, and grass plantings. Along the brook, where it runs down to the sanctuary's wetland.
Agricultural crops grown simultaneously with long-term tree crops. Rows of walnut and hazel trees with the crops grown in the alleys between them.
Combines trees with forage and livestock production. The sheep and the goats graze under the nut trees in the shade, and the chickens follow them.
Silvopasture is the deliberate integration of trees and grazing livestock operations on the same land.

Cultivation of high-value crops under the protection of a managed forest canopy. Not here. The farm has no woodland of its own: the wood belongs to the campgrounds, and nobody has drawn a map of it. Every practice’s first line is the USDA National Agroforestry Center’s, word for word.

Corn, beans and squash, planted together. They are Indigenous agriculture, and the story of them belongs to the nations that tell it, so it is not told here. The Onondaga Nation publishes a book of its own about them, by Dehowähda·dih – Bradley Powless, and the Oneida Indian Nation says almost every Native nation has its own telling. Read them there. What this farm does is plant them the way the Onondaga Nation’s book describes the Haudenosaunee planting them: together, but not all at once. Corn goes in first, on a mound of earth; the beans go in beside the corn once it is up, and climb it; the squash goes in around the mound, and its leaves keep the mound shaded and damp and the weeds down, while the beans feed the soil the corn grows in. On this farm the mounds stand in the alleys between the nut trees.
Sheep, goats and chickens. Some of them are raised for meat, and the farm says so on the honesty box’s board; none of the residents at the sanctuary next door ever is.

Food and flowers from seed thrown on a windy day and left to come up how it likes, with a bench in the middle of it. It is a bright, clear day with a wind blowing across the garden from the left, and everything in it leans the same way: the stems, the flowers on top of them, the grass, and the seed still in the air. There is no cloud anywhere and nothing in a row. Nobody decided where any of it would go: a mix of seed was thrown into the wind, what came up came up where it landed, and what did best this year is what gets thrown again next year.

In words: a clear blue sky over a green garden with no paths and no rows. It is crowded with flowers on thin stems of every height, red, orange, yellow, pink, blue, violet and white, daisies, cups, spikes and round heads, smaller towards the back and larger at the front, and every stem and every blade of grass bends to the right, the way the wind is blowing. Little tufts of seed are blowing across the sky in the same direction.

At its core, chaos gardening is the practice of mixing a wide variety of seeds, often including leftover packets, wildflower mixes, or cut flower favorites, and scattering them over a planting area with minimal planning.
Deryn Davidson, Colorado State University Extension, “Chaos gardening: Wild beauty or just a mess? A sustainable landscape specialist explains the trend”, The Conversation, 2025-08-19, CC BY-ND 4.0.
But chaos gardening isn't the same as ecological restoration, pollinator meadow planting or native prairie establishment.
Deryn Davidson, Colorado State University Extension, “Chaos gardening: Wild beauty or just a mess? A sustainable landscape specialist explains the trend”, The Conversation, 2025-08-19, CC BY-ND 4.0.

A sustainable landscape specialist at Colorado State University Extension put it this way: She was just as clear about what it is not, and so is this garden. It is somewhere to grow food and flowers with very little fuss, not a nature reserve: The land next door has a wildlife sanctuary and a wood kept for what lives in it. This is a garden, and it says so.
Some wildflower mixes, especially inexpensive or mass-market ones, claim to be native but actually contain non-native species that can spread beyond your garden and become invasive.
Deryn Davidson, Colorado State University Extension, “Chaos gardening: Wild beauty or just a mess? A sustainable landscape specialist explains the trend”, The Conversation, 2025-08-19, CC BY-ND 4.0.
The mix is half things to eat and half things to look at, and it is checked before it is thrown, because a cheap mix can carry something that will not stay in the garden:
salad leaves, radishes, peas, nasturtiums, kale and dill.
blanket flower, black-eyed Susans, blue flax, Rocky Mountain bee plant, cosmos, zinnias, sunflowers, California poppies and bachelor's buttons.

chicory, dame's rocket, oxeye daisy and yellow toadflax, the four noxious weeds J. E. Klett, R. A. Cox, I. Shonle and L. G. Vickerman, “Wildflowers in Colorado”, Colorado State University Extension fact sheet 7.233 says to keep out of a seed mix.

You can only see as far as your headlights. Everything on this road is lit from one low, level direction and goes black an inch past the beam, which is why the signs below have a bright face and no back. It is also why this page tells you what is down each turning rather than showing you: out here, a sign is the honest thing and a picture would be a claim. A sign with no road behind it is still a sign. Some of what is named here is not built. Those ones are lit and say so, plainly, on their own board — because an area that quietly listed rooms you cannot get into would be the street lying about its own architecture, and a website pretending it has no unfinished edges is doing something every actual outskirts knows better than. Each premises is its own world and shares nothing with this road. The verge is cold and dead and painted by hand. What is down the turning is not, and the sign says what you are walking into so that walking in is a decision rather than a surprise. Nobody was sent out here. Two people met in Sacramento in 1972 over a shared devotion to collecting records, decided that the obvious next step was to form a band, and then spent thirty-three years refusing every single opportunity to become a different one. That is the whole story, and it is a better model for a life than most of the ones we were handed. They moved to Akron, then to New York in 1975, and turned up in the early scene at CBGB alongside the Ramones, Blondie, Television, Patti Smith and Suicide. Lux Interior sang. Poison Ivy played guitar, and wrote, arranged and produced a great deal of what the band actually sounds like — which is worth saying at the top rather than in a footnote, because the singer is the one who gets remembered and the guitarist is the one who built it. The lineup around the two of them changed constantly. The two of them never did. The band was formed in 1976 and was active until 2009, when Lux died and Ivy did not carry on without him. There was no bass player. Not for years, and not by accident: two guitars, a drum kit, and a deliberate hole where the bottom end goes, which is why an early Cramps record sounds like something coming through a wall rather than out of a stage. It is one of the great examples of a limitation chosen on purpose and then defended for a decade, and if you have ever been told that the thing you do without is the thing you need, it is a useful noise to have in your ears. What they made out of that is usually filed as psychobilly — they are credited as the progenitors of it — and the recipe is simpler than the label: 1950s rockabilly, played at punk volume, about monster movies, with no wink anywhere. That last part is the part everybody gets wrong. The Cramps are funny, but they are never ironic. Nobody in these records is standing outside the material being clever about it. They loved the drive-in, they loved the cheap single nobody bought, they loved the rubber suit, and they played all of it absolutely straight, for decades, at cost. Sincerity about disreputable things is a much harder position to hold than a joke, and it is the reason this band has outlasted most of their contemporaries. And they were archaeologists. Half of Psychedelic Jungle is other people’s forgotten singles, dug out of a collection and handed back to an audience that had no idea they existed — a garage record from Texas, a novelty side from 1962, a rockabilly cut nobody had reissued. Their real argument, underneath the rubber masks, was that the good stuff had already been made and then dropped on the floor, and that somebody ought to go and pick it up. This street is largely built out of that same conviction, so we owe them the acknowledgement.
The Napa show, and how it usually gets told

In June 1978 the band played a free concert for patients at the state mental hospital in Napa, California. It was filmed by the San Francisco video collective Target Video on a portable camera and later released as a live tape, and it is one of the most-circulated pieces of footage they ever appeared in. There is no stage to speak of. The audience is right up against the band, people take the microphone, and nobody is managing the room. It is almost always told as a joke, and the joke is at the patients’ expense. The standard line — you will find some version of it wherever that tape is written about — is that you cannot tell the lunatics from the band. That framing is very old, it is extremely easy to repeat, and it is the exact thing this organisation exists to refuse: psychiatric patients used as the punchline that certifies how wild somebody else is. We are a Disabled people’s organisation. Some of us have been the people in that room. So here is the version we will stand behind, which requires no joke at all: a band went to a locked institution and played for people who do not get played for, for free, with the barrier between performer and audience removed rather than reinforced, and let those people do whatever they wanted for the duration. That is a booking decision, and it is a good one. Whether anybody in that room had a good evening is not ours to narrate — we were not there, they were not asked on camera, and every account in circulation is somebody else’s. We will not speak for them, and we would rather leave the gap visible than fill it with a nice sentence.
The door policy at the water’s edge

Nothing plays until you press play. Same rule as every other room on this street. No request reaches YouTube before you press something, and every record on a post says how long it runs before you do. The screen is the one control here that cannot say, because it is a playlist we keep adding to — so it says that instead. Nothing here flickers, at any setting. A drive-in screen is a flickering object; that is practically its defining feature, and building one without the flicker took more work than building one with it. It has none, at Gentle, Regular or MAX GLITTER, for the reason the punk club three doors up has no strobe: a light that can put somebody on the floor has no business in a room whose whole argument is come as you are. The dial governs everything else out here. There is simply nothing in this room for it to flash. None of these words are theirs. Every note on every post is ours, about what the record does. Not one line of any song is on this page, here or anywhere else on the street, and the tool that builds this room refuses a note shaped like verse. A room built on one band, whose words are half of why anybody loves them, is exactly where that rule would have been broken affectionately. Nothing is ranked. There is no best, no greatest, no countdown, no essential nine. They are in the order they were made, 1978 at the top and 2003 at the bottom, and that is the only ordering principle in the room. Not a costume you have to keep on. It is always Halloween here, which means you may arrive as anything and nobody asks what you came as or when you are taking it off.

Billboard counted United States on-demand streams going from about 2,500 a week to over 134,000. It is the same song it always was. Nothing about it improved; the room it was being played in changed.
