A hillock inhabited by fairies A ring of earth and whitethorn standing in a field, which you can walk all the way round and will not be going into. That is not coyness and it is not an unfinished room. The outside is the part of a fairy fort that anybody has ever actually seen. The inside is the part the stories are careful never to show you, and a page that flung the door open would be making up the one thing the tradition declines to.
What the name is, and whose it is not

Sithen is a real word and it was checked rather than assumed. Scottish Gaelic sìthean — a hillock inhabited by fairies — from sìth, fairy, with the diminutive ending; there is a dictionary behind it rather than a vibe. The Irish is sídhe, in the reformed spelling sí, which is the mound itself, and is where aos sí — the people of the mound — comes from. This mattered enough to look up. Two novel series are what sent us here, and one of them uses this exact spelling for the fae court, so a room taking the name while claiming to owe those books nothing would be advertising a debt it does not otherwise have. It turns out the word is older than both. It is said here so that nobody has to assume either way.

This half is earthworks and a motorway, and it is kept apart from the folklore below on purpose, because the two are not the same kind of claim and a reader should not have to tell them apart by tone. A fairy fort is a ringfort: lios or rath, a circular earth bank, sometimes a ditch, sometimes stone. People built them from possibly the late Iron Age into early Christian times, and because the buildings inside were not durable, what is usually left in a field now is a vague circular mark and whatever has grown on it. As of 1991 there were between thirty and forty thousand identifiable fairy forts in the Irish countryside. The oldest of them possibly date back as early as 600 BCE. This is not a rare or sacred handful of sites. It is an ordinary feature of the landscape, in enormous numbers, that people have declined to plough. Believers in the fairies did not alter them, and even cutting the whitethorn growing on one was reputed to be the death of whoever did it. The tradition is specific about the thorn. Sceach, whitethorn, hawthorn: the tree of the ring, and the one you leave. In 1999 a whitethorn at Latoon in County Clare stopped a motorway. The folklorist Eddie Lenihan campaigned to save the tree from being cut down for the M18, calling it a meeting place for the supernatural forces of the region. It was spared in May 1999 and still grows there, on a strip of land between the motorway and a slip road.
A country that routes around a tree

Hold those together for a second, because it is the most interesting thing on this page. Tens of thousands of these rings are sitting in fields, and people decline to plough them. A motorway was rerouted around a single thorn bush. The stated reason is the Good People, and the actual mechanism is that leaving it alone matters to people and the paperwork required for that is a shrug. We are usually asked for a diagnosis, a letter and a business case before anybody will move a desk. There is no version of this room that does not notice the difference. A whole culture can make an enormous, expensive, permanent accommodation on the strength of this matters and I am not going to justify it to you — and the same culture will ask a Disabled person to evidence a chair.
The rules, which nobody will say out loud

Everything in the left-hand half of these is traditional and says where it comes from. Everything under what it is like is ours, written for this room, and is not claimed to be in the folklore. That split is the whole page: these taboos are a catalogue of consequential rules that nobody will state, where breaking one is punished and no one explains — which is the ordinary weather of neurotypical convention for a great many of us. Nothing here tells you how to behave. There is no advice, because a page about unwritten rules that ended in tips for following them would be a social skills curriculum with thorns on it. 01

Accept a meal inside the hill and you may not be able to leave it. Traditional · A standard motif of the Otherworld visit in Irish and Scottish fairy tradition. What it is like: The invitation that cannot be declined without a cost. The coffee, the team lunch, the quick chat that is not quick and was never optional. Hospitality is the mechanism, not the kindness: once you have taken it you are inside an arrangement you did not read. 02

Thanks implies the debt is settled, which is an insult, and a slight from a mortal is not taken lightly. Traditional · A widespread motif in fairy etiquette across Irish and Scottish tradition. What it is like: The rule where the polite thing is the wrong thing. Every autistic person has been punished for a courtesy delivered correctly, in good faith, to somebody who wanted a different courtesy and would not say which. There is no version of this you can work out from first principles, which is the entire complaint. 03
Do not give your true name.

A name is a handle. Give the real one and it can be used to call you, bind you, or hold you. Traditional · The power of the true name is a widespread motif in European fairy tradition. What it is like: Disclosure. Tell an employer what you are and you have handed over something that can be used to help you or to manage you out, and you will not find out which until afterwards. This is why so many of us are careful about the word, and why nobody should be told they are being paranoid about it. 04
Do not accept a gift you cannot return.

An unanswered gift is a debt, and the debt is collected at a time of the giver's choosing. Traditional · Reciprocity and its dangers are a recurring feature of fairy dealings in the tradition. What it is like: The favour economy, which is most workplaces. Being helped puts you in a ledger nobody shows you, and the entry is called in later as though it had been agreed. An accommodation offered as a favour rather than as a right is this exactly. 05
The bargain is kept to the letter.

What was agreed is delivered precisely, and precisely is not what you meant. Traditional · The literal-minded bargain is one of the oldest and most consistent motifs in fairy tradition. What it is like: The accommodation granted on paper. Yes, you may have the software. No, not the training, the licence, the time, or the colleague who stops scheduling meetings in it. Every word of the agreement was honoured. None of it worked, and the record shows you were given what you asked for. 06

The tree on the ring is left standing, and no one is obliged to explain why. Traditional · Documented tradition; the whitethorn taboo is specific and is still observed. What it is like: The accommodation with no justification attached. A whole country routes around a tree because leaving it alone matters to people, and the paperwork for that is a shrug. We are usually asked for a diagnosis, a letter and a business case before anybody will move a desk. 07

A night of dancing, and everybody you knew is old or gone. Traditional · The supernatural lapse of time is a central motif of the Otherworld visit. What it is like: Burnout, and any long illness. You go in for what you are told is a short thing and you come out having missed a stretch of your own life, with everybody else further along the road and nobody quite able to say where it went. Nothing was stolen from you. It is simply gone.
Why the door is not opened

Every other warm underground place on this street is an interior with one small flame in it — a burrow with a lamp, a candlelit tent, panelling, a curtained cave. There is no interior here and there is no flame. Staying outside is what keeps this from being those rooms again with thorns on, and it is also the honest shape of the thing: a fairy fort is an outdoor object, and its whole character is that it is bounded, visible, and not entered. And it suits the argument. Half the rules above are about hospitality as a trap — the meal, the gift, the debt, the bargain honoured to the letter. A room that then insisted you come inside and accept what is offered would be doing the thing it spent the page describing. You are not obliged to go in anywhere. You can stand on the bank in the cold and look, and leave, and nothing about that is a failure to engage. If a door is ever opened here it becomes its own world behind this one, the way the Jungle Room grew a den, with its own light and its own rules. It does not become this page with rooms added to it.
What pointed us here, and what is not in this room

Laurell K. Hamilton’s Merry Gentry books and Seanan McGuire’s October Daye books are why this turning exists, and they are named here rather than quietly absorbed. Nothing in this room is drawn from either of them. Not a court, not a character, not a politics, not a cosmology, not a line. Those are invented worlds belonging to living authors, and the difference between being pointed somewhere and helping yourself is the whole of what this site means by attribution. That refusal is enforced rather than remembered: tools/make-sithen.py will not build this page if a rule’s source names either series or either author. The friendly edit here is a real one and it will arrive — the folklore is thin in exactly the places a novel is rich, so the most useful material lying around is the one thing this room may not pick up. Two rock faces, a stage between them, and a great deal of very old stone that was here long before the stage was. Set amidst towering rock faces, Looming Rocks impose with their immense solidity. They give off an ancient and alive aura. Some say the rocks are sentient and full of lore from centuries of hosting storytellers and stages. They possess an unknowable intelligence that long pre-dates the humans drawn to them. The rocks saw the Sithen emerge, eons ago.

The rocks are covered in lichen. In modern times, folks discovered that UV light made them fluoresce in a dazzling display. Charged during the day by a solar array with batteries, the stage production at Looming Rocks includes UV spots and floods that make the rocks glow at night. The floods stand on the ground and point upwards, which is why everything out here is brightest at its foot and goes dark towards the top, and why there is nothing overhead at all. The lamps are violet. What comes back is not.

The door policy at the foot of the rocks

Tuning is not playing. While the stage is dark, previous and next are silent — the screen names the act and its runtime and nothing is fetched. You can walk the whole bill without a single request going to YouTube. Once something is on, the desk changes the picture instead. Every control says how long before you press it, and the desk names the act it is about to move to as well. The shortest thing here is nearly an hour. Nobody should find out the length of a thing after committing to it. The bill is a list and not a verdict. Nothing here is ranked, rated or counted. The shows are in an order, and the order is not an argument about which is better. Nothing in the rig flashes or strobes, at any dial setting. A venue is exactly the kind of room that would grow a lighting effect, and this street settled that question in the punk club: a light that can put somebody on the floor has no business in a room anybody is meant to enjoy. The rocks glow steadily or not at all. You are allowed to sit down and you are allowed to leave. There is no standing, no queue and no crowd here, which is the one thing a web page can genuinely offer that the real venue cannot — and the reason a room like this is worth having on a Disabled people’s site rather than being a poster of somewhere most of us would struggle to get round.

The real venue is Red Rocks Amphitheatre, an open-air amphitheatre near Morrison, Colorado, about ten miles south-west of Denver, owned and operated by the city of Denver. It is formed by two enormous sandstone monoliths — they have names: Ship Rock and Creation Rock, with the smaller Stage Rock between them — and it seats 9,525. Read off Wikipedia’s article on it on 2026-09-22. The room started there and is for outdoor music anywhere now, so the bill says where each show was played, and every one of them was played outdoors. Austin City Limits Music Festival is held in Zilker Park in Austin, Texas, and is a different thing from the television series it is named after, which is taped indoors — those sessions are on the desk in The Live Room, the street’s room for music played in a studio. Looming Rocks is not Red Rocks, or any other real place. It is a room on a made-up street that is extremely fond of the real ones — our executive director goes to Red Rocks whenever she can — and Stimpunks has no connection to any of these venues or festivals, is not endorsed by them, and is not describing them. The amphitheatre in Colorado is a real thing that belongs to a city; this one is a room on a street that rearranges itself for whoever turns up. None of these artists, their labels or the channels hosting these recordings is affiliated with Stimpunks, and none of them endorses us. The full running order with channels and links is in the liner notes.
← back to The Outskirts turning 04 · runway unlit · bring nothing Turning 04, and you cannot hear it from the road

A silent disco on the old airstrip. Three channels, one crate, a headset each, and the volume in your own hand. The quietest thing on this road is also the biggest crowd on it. Out past the last streetlight there is an airstrip nobody lands on any more, long and flat and wide enough for everybody, and on it a great many people are dancing to three different things at once without a sound reaching the verge. From the road you see a field of small coloured lights bobbing about in the dark. That is the whole party, and it is lit by the headsets and nothing else.
The loudest room you can turn down

A silent disco hands everybody their own music, on their own headset, at their own volume. The dancefloor is still a crowd — you can see everybody, move with everybody, be right in the middle of it — but the sound only goes where somebody asked for it. Take the headset off and the runway is quiet: tarmac, somebody laughing, the wind. Nobody on this airstrip can make anybody else’s night louder. That is the dial this whole street runs on, built as a venue. Everywhere else here, how loud it gets is something the visitor holds rather than a property of the page. Out here it is something the dancer holds rather than a property of the room. A loud room is an access barrier, as Club Chronic says about itself on the street, and a silent disco is one of the ways a crowd gets round that without anybody having to leave it. Some of us dance to the same song forty times in a row — stim listening, one song or one list over and over, which is what our playlists are for. And some of us move because joy has to go somewhere. Our Autistic Joy entry quotes Authentically Emily on what it can feel like, and one line on that list is needing to move and stim to release the feeling. A runway is a lot of room to release it in.

Three channels, and they are one crate started in three places. The crate is Dance, Punks, a playlist Stimpunks keeps on YouTube. Each channel opens on a different song in it and plays on in order from there. A real silent disco has a DJ on every channel; this one has a starting point on every channel, and the room would rather say so than borrow a word for something it is not doing. It is not shuffle either. The player has no such button. Nothing is fetched from YouTube until you put the headset on. While it is off, choosing a channel only changes the colour of the band and what the headset says it will open on — you can try all three without a single request going to YouTube. Once it is on, changing channel changes the music, because by then you have asked for a headset. No channel says how long it runs, because the crate is a list we keep adding to and today’s total would be wrong next week. It runs until you take the headset off, and the volume is on the player, where nobody else can reach it. THE HEADSET IS OFF CH 1 · Blue Opens on Daft Punk Is Playing at My House by LCD Soundsystem, and plays on through the crate from there. The top of the crate, where the playlist itself begins. A song about a party that got out of hand, which is the one kind of party this runway cannot have: nobody here can hear anybody else's music. or open channel 1 on YouTube → CH 2 · Orange Opens on Wild Child by Shopping, and plays on through the crate from there. About a third of the way down the crate. Somebody on the Blue channel will not reach this song until they have danced through everything above it, and nobody on this channel has to. or open channel 2 on YouTube → CH 3 · White Opens on Starstruck by Sorry, and plays on through the crate from there. About two thirds of the way down, and the palest headset on the runway, which makes it the easiest one to find across a dark field. That is a perfectly good reason to be on it. or open channel 3 on YouTube →

Nothing strobes, flashes or pulses, at any dial setting. No lasers, no smoke, no mirrorball swinging a beam across anybody’s eyes. The headsets glow steadily or not at all. A dancefloor is the room on this road most likely to grow a light show, and a light that can put somebody on the floor has no business at a party anybody is meant to enjoy — the punk club on the street settled that first. The channels are told apart by more than their colour. Every headset says its number and its name, and the three colours are at least 1.5 to 1 apart in brightness from each other, so they stay three different headsets in greyscale and to anybody who does not see those colours as different. That bar is ours rather than a standard’s, and make-dance-punks.py refuses a channel under it. Take the headset off whenever you like. The runway is quiet underneath the music, and standing in a silent crowd watching everybody dance is a perfectly good way to be at this party. Nobody has to dance. Sit on the tarmac, lie on it and look up, walk the centre line out to the far end and back. There are no seats because there is nowhere you are supposed to be. Nothing is counted. Not songs heard, not time on the floor, not which channel is most popular. Nobody is keeping a list of who danced. Come on your own. Most of the crowd did. That is what a crowd on different channels looks like from the road.

The crate is ours and the music is not. Dance, Punks is a playlist Stimpunks Foundation keeps on YouTube, read off its own page on 2026-09-23. Every song on it belongs to the people who made it and is on somebody else’s channel. Nothing is hosted by us, and none of those artists, their labels or the channels carrying them is affiliated with Stimpunks or endorses us. The three opening songs, who made them and whose channel each is on, are in the liner notes. The crate takes suggestions. If a song gets you moving, send it through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community. It goes in as a link to wherever it already lives, because nothing musical is hosted here, and it is checked first to see that it plays and can be shown on this page. No lyrics go on this page either way. The airstrip is invented. Silent discos are not, and neither are the headsets that glow the colour of the channel they are on.
← back to The Outskirts turning 05 · open · the tubes do not flicker Turning 05, and the lights are on

An all-night diner for bodies that keep other hours. It is open, and nobody is going to ask why you are up. Open whatever time it is where you are. This is the last lit thing on the road. You see it a long way off: one long low building with a band of window all down its side, bright as a lamp, and the light from it lying out across the car park in pale rectangles. Out here you are standing in the dark looking in. Everybody in there is in the light, and nobody in there is looking out at you. The door is the one on the right, and it is not locked.
The clock over the counter has no hands
Rather than bend disabled bodies and minds to meet the clock, crip time bends the clock to meet disabled bodies and minds.
Alison Kafer, Feminist, Queer, Crip, as our Crip Time entry quotes it
The clock over the counter has no hands
Ellen Samuels, Six Ways of Looking at Crip Time, as our Crip Time entry quotes it
The clock over the counter has no hands

Nobody in here is late and nobody is early. A great many of us are awake when the town is not — because a body takes its sleep when it can get it rather than when a day has room for it, because the rhythm it runs on is not the one a work week was drawn around, because it is the only quiet time there is, or because it simply is. Our Crip Time entry has the best sentence about this that anybody has written, and it is Alison Kafer’s: That is what the diner is. It does not ask you to arrive at a sensible hour; it has no sensible hour. It has a counter, some booths, a kettle that is always hot and a clock that does not tell anybody anything. The same entry quotes Ellen Samuels saying something shorter, which is written on the wall under the clock:
Nobody asks why you are up
The sleep-wake cycles of Autistic adults also differ, on average, from the circadian rhythms of neurotypicals, and many of us experience sleep disorders.
Devon Price, Unmasking Autism, as our Sleep entry quotes it
Nobody asks why you are up
sleep facilitating factors are in a direct contrast to the sleep hygiene recommendations
Georgia Pavlopoulou, A Good Night’s Sleep: Learning About Sleep From Autistic Adolescents’ Personal Accounts, as our Sleep entry quotes it
Nobody asks why you are up

Not the person behind the counter, not the menu, not the sign. Being awake at this hour is not a symptom anybody here is going to take an interest in. Our Sleep entry quotes Devon Price on how ordinary it is: And there is no sleep advice in this building. Not a tip, not a routine, not a leaflet by the till. The same entry quotes a study in which Autistic teenagers described what actually helped them sleep, and what they described was the opposite of the advice they were usually handed. Georgia Pavlopoulou, who wrote it up, put it in one line: So the diner keeps its opinions to itself and keeps the kettle on.
they’d sit me at the small table they’d put next to their bed and hand me some crayons so that I could blissfully colour while they watched over me in semi-consciousness.
Sarah Kurchak, I Overcame My Autism and All I Got Was This Lousy Anxiety Disorder, as our Sleep entry quotes it

Written on the board behind the counter. There are no prices, because this is a website and a price would be the one thing on it that was certainly made up. Breakfast, whenever it is for you Eggs any way and toast cut however you like it, at any hour. It is breakfast because it is the first thing you have eaten since you woke up, and that is the only clock the kitchen goes by. The same as last time Say it and it arrives exactly as it did before, down to where things sit on the plate. Nobody suggests you try something new. A safe food is a perfectly good reason to come back. Our Safe Food entry. A booth to yourself For as long as you like. Nobody is waiting for the table, and nobody will stand near it looking as if they are. Something warm in a heavy mug Refilled without asking, or never refilled at all, whichever you said when you sat down. Either is remembered until you leave and not a minute after. Crayons and a paper placemat On every table, for the reason quoted under the menu, and there is one waiting in the window below. Colouring at a small table while somebody keeps you company is a thing the small hours have been for since long before this diner. The quiet end of the counter Furthest from the kitchen and the door. The stools down there do not spin; the ones at the other end do, for the people who asked for that instead. Nothing at all You can sit here without ordering anything. Nobody brings the bill over to make a point. About the crayons. Our Sleep entry opens with Sarah Kurchak remembering the nights she did not sleep as a child, and what her parents did about it:

Every table has one: a paper placemat printed in one colour, and a paper sleeve of crayons beside it. Pick a crayon, then press a shape to colour it in, or switch to scribbling and draw wherever you like. Over the lines is fine. Nobody here minds. Every part of the placemat can also be coloured in by name, from the list underneath it, with a keyboard or a screen reader; scribbling needs a pointer or a finger. The red is the booths’ vinyl, the teal is the counter’s formica, and the white does next to nothing on white paper, the way it does in every box. The crayons red orange yellow teal blue purple brown black white What a press on the placemat does Colour in: press a shape and it fills Scribble: draw wherever you like Colour it in by name, one part at a time Nothing on it is marked and nothing is kept. When you leave, the placemat goes in the bin and nobody looks at it first. If you want it, take it home: that saves a picture of it to your own device and sends it nowhere else.
Insomnia is a research priority for autistic communities. At Stimpunks, we keep the hour-of-the-wolf.
Our post, The Neurodivergent Experience in Josephmooon’s “So Far So Good”

Josephmooon · lyrics by Ronan Boren, a Stimpunk There is one record in the jukebox that everybody in here puts on sooner or later, because it is about them. “Up All Night” is a song about Autistic insomnia, from Josephmooon’s first album, and its words are Ronan Boren’s. When we wrote about that album in 2021, we said this about it: Track 4 of So Far So Good · runs 2:41 Ronan Boren all lyrics Bill Paige vocals, guitar Ronnie Nice guitars, keyboards, bass, drums, programming Ian Nice piano, keyboards, backing vocals
The whole album is on the jukebox below and on its own page on the band’s site.

Both of Josephmooon’s albums, every track, played from the band’s own site. Nothing loads until you press something, every button says how long the song runs before you press it, and only one song plays at a time: starting another pauses the one before. The album buttons play straight through from the top; they say how many songs and how long first, because a press that starts several things has to say so before it does.

It does not close. There are no last orders and no time you are expected to leave by. The sign does not read your clock, either: a diner for people up at odd hours is the last place that should be keeping an eye on the time. Nobody asks why you are up, and nobody gives you advice about it. The tubes do not flicker and do not hum. A fluorescent light that buzzes and stutters is the sound of half the waiting rooms we have ever sat in, and it is gone from this one. You can sit without ordering, stay as long as you like, sit in a booth on your own or at the counter next to somebody you have never met and not say a word. Nothing is counted and nothing is kept. Not what time you came in, not how often, not how long you stayed, and not your placemat unless you take it home yourself. Nobody here is keeping a record of how many nights you were awake.

Every quotation here names who wrote it and is linked to the page of ours that quotes it. Each was read word for word off that page, and every author was checked against a library record rather than remembered — which is how the crayons passage got its right author: our Sleep entry links the book without naming who wrote it, and the name this room was nearly given from memory belonged to somebody else. The full list is in the liner notes. The diner is invented. Crip time is not, and neither is being up at an hour a town has decided is for sleeping.
← back to The Outskirts turning 06 · up the track · the highest point on the road Turning 06, and as far as the road goes

A radio mast on the ridge, as far from everything as the road goes, and the easiest place on it to be reached. At the very end of the road a track goes up, and at the top of it there is a ridge with a mast on it and a hut at the foot of the mast. Nothing up here is lit. The cloud above is, a little, from underneath: every lit thing on this road and the whole town past the last streetlight throws a glow up onto it, so from the ridge you see the mast, the hut and the hill as black shapes against a sky the colour of somewhere else’s light. Two small red lamps on the mast are the only lights of its own, and they do not blink. A repeater is a radio station that listens on one frequency and sends what it hears straight back out on another, louder and from higher up, so that two people who could never reach each other directly can talk. It stands where nobody lives because that is where it can hear everybody.
The mode of connection carried by signal rather than proximity — a voice note, a thread, a call left open in the background, a message typed and read across distance.
No mode sits at the top.

This road has turnings for crowds and turnings for staying out late, and it has this one for wanting to be as far off as you can get. Far off is not the same as cut off. Our Shared-Signal Space entry names what a lot of us already live in: For a great many Autistic, ADHD and otherwise neurodivergent people that is where connection comes easiest — away from the masking and the noise a room asks for — and the entry is careful to say it is not a stand-in for being in the same room. It is a mode in its own right, beside shared-air space rather than under it. The written word is a channel, not a lesser one; in the study our entry cites, by Howard and Sedgewick, phone calls came last among Autistic adults’ preferences and written channels came near the top. AAC is real communication, and so is a message that took a long time to send. The shape of it has a name: the Autistic Rhizome, which DGH Neurodivergent Consultancy gave to the network of Autistic communities growing on Discord, and which Helen Edgar has written about at Autistic Realms. Connection that spreads sideways, with no single origin and no correct path, and online spaces that work like watering holes, where turning up is enough. Our entry puts the whole argument in six words, and they are painted on the door of the hut:

One of the things on that entry’s list is a call kept open in the background while two people just exist near each other. So the hut has a line you can open and leave open. There is nobody on the other end. It is the quiet hiss of an open line and nothing else, made in your browser when you press the button, for keeping you company while you get on with something else. The line fetches nothing, sends nothing and listens to nothing: the page never asks for your microphone and could not use one if it had it. THE LINE IS CLOSED How loud A steady noise with no tone in it. It does not beep, pulse, fade in and out, or change on its own. The slider only goes as loud as a line left open in the background should.

Radio operators send each other a card to confirm a contact happened. The log in this hut confirms that every kind of contact counts, and it keeps no count of any of them — no totals, no awards for how many, no list of who reached whom. These are the kinds it has cards for: VOICE NOTE Contact confirmed Left for later and played back twice. The breath in it arrived as well as the words. THREAD Contact confirmed Picked up again days afterwards, mid-sentence, and nobody asked where anybody had been. OPEN LINE Contact confirmed A call nobody hung up. Two people getting on with separate things, near each other, saying nothing for an hour. TYPED Contact confirmed Drafted, read back, rewritten and only then sent, so what arrived was what was meant. LETTERBOARD Contact confirmed Spelled out one letter at a time. It took longer to arrive and it is no less a voice for that. LURKING Contact confirmed Read everything and said nothing for months. That was being there the whole time. ONE REPLY Contact confirmed A single answer after a long quiet. It counts the same as a conversation.

The lamps are steady. A lot of the lights on masts flash, and these are the kind that do not. Nothing on this page blinks, pulses or moves on its own at any dial setting. Nothing here sends anything anywhere. There is no form, no message box, no call-in, and nothing that listens. The line you can open is made where you are and stays there. Nobody has to talk. Listening counts. Reading and saying nothing counts. So does coming back after a long time away without an explanation. Nothing is counted. Not contacts, not time on the line, not who turned up. A place for being reached should not be keeping score of who reached it. If you want the real watering holes rather than a hut on a made-up hill, the Stimpunks community is where ours are, and our online space page says how they are built.

The argument is our own Shared-Signal Space entry, and the two lines quoted from it are ours. The Autistic Rhizome was named by DGH Neurodivergent Consultancy and has been written about by Helen Edgar at Autistic Realms; neither is folded into our “we”. The study on communication preferences is Howard and Sedgewick’s. Details are in the liner notes. The ridge and the mast are invented. Radio repeaters are not: they stand on hills all over the world, passing on the signals of people who could not otherwise reach each other.
← back to The Outskirts turning 07 · a lay-by · leave your headlights on Turning 07, and the only free market on the road

A ring of cars in a lay-by with their headlights on, and everything laid out in the middle is free. Take what you need, leave what you can, and nobody is counting either. The Outskirts is lit by your headlights. This turning is lit by everybody’s. Nobody who came out here brought enough light on their own, so everybody pulled into the lay-by in a ring, nose in, and left their lamps on, and the middle is as bright as a room. No two of those lamps match — an old estate on halogen, a newer van on LEDs, a hatchback running on one yellow fog lamp — so everything laid out in the middle throws a whole fan of shadows, one for every car, each with a slightly different colour at its edge. Everything on the tables is free. It is the only free market on the road, and the only one where the word means that.
Mutual aid is not charity. It is not a handout or an act of pity. It is a profound, ongoing, messy practice of loving each other into the future.
Sparrow, Mutual Aid: How We Survive, How We Transform, as our Mutual Aid entry quotes it
showing up for each other, laterally, with no proof of worthiness required.

That phrase is the mutual aid movement’s rather than ours, and our Mutual Aid entry quotes it from a talk about Autistic mutual aid. The difference it names is the whole of this lay-by. Charity comes down, from somebody who has to somebody who has been judged to deserve it, and it wants to know you deserve it first. Mutual aid goes sideways. Sparrow, writing at Unstrange Mind, puts it like this: And our own Mutual Aid page ends its opening on the thing that actually helps:
Knowledge is infrastructure. Access to it is mutual aid.

Everything laid out here is ours, and every one of them is free by its own page’s account, which was checked table by table before anything went on one. Our library says why the tables are here at all: BOOKS

Books from the edges, music, bookmarks, and reading lists by and for neurodivergent and disabled people. First table, because the library page is where the argument for all the others is written down. START HERE
The Autism and Neurodiversity Starter Pack
A download: foundational ideas, why so many of us are burnt out, and ways forward. By David Gray-Hammond and Helen Edgar. LEARN
Made out of surviving bad systems and building better ones, including free training for educators who want to stop replicating harm. PRINT A STACK
Single sheets made to be carried, handed over and pinned up in rooms where nobody is going to open a laptop. CC0, so print as many as you like and give them away. PIN IT UP

Walls of declarations: short lines, one idea each, made to be read fast by somebody who has not got long. Two things of ours are not on a table, on purpose. Our mutual aid grants are not take-what-you-need: they have an application, limits on who can apply and a waiting list, and a lay-by that suggested otherwise would be promising something they cannot do. They are on our Mutual Aid page, which also says why they exist. And our Things Library argues for a library economy — tools, clothes, furniture, everything held in common — without yet listing anything to borrow, so there is nothing of it to lay out.

Nothing here is for sale, and nothing is a swap. Taking something does not put you in anybody’s debt, and nobody will ask for anything back. Out at Sithen there is a whole page about the old rule that eating what the fair folk offer leaves you theirs; this lay-by is that rule turned inside out, on purpose. Nobody asks what it is for. No form, no proof, and no question about whether you need it enough. Leave what you can, and nothing is a perfectly good amount. Nothing is counted. Not what anybody took, not what anybody left, not who came. Leave your headlights on if you have them. If you walked, there is light enough. That is what a ring is for.

Every table is ours, and every quotation names who wrote it. The starter pack is David Gray-Hammond’s and Helen Edgar’s. The line about mutual aid not being charity is Sparrow’s, at Unstrange Mind. Solidarity, not charity belongs to the movement. Details are in the liner notes. The lay-by is invented. Free shops, free tables and mutual aid networks are not, and they are mostly run by the people who need them.
← back to The Outskirts turning 08 · hangar 8, by the airstrip · read the walls first Turning 08, in the old hangar at the end of the airstrip road

Peak Sensory Seek That Goes to Eleven An aircraft hangar at the end of the airstrip road, taken over by the sensory seekers in our community who wanted somewhere to stim loudly and brightly. The ceiling is a very long way up, the walls are scaffolding, tier on tier of it, and the rig is bolted to every deck. This is the one place on the street where you will see a strobe: switched on by you, twice over, and off again the moment you say.
You come in through a small room first, with the hangar doors shut behind it. It is lit plainly and evenly, and everything you need to decide is on its walls before you open them.

The hangar’s rig has a strobe in it: flashes of bright white light, from one to eleven a second. Flashing light can cause seizures in people with photosensitive epilepsy, and it can bring on migraine, dizziness, nausea or disorientation in people without it. Every rate the knob has is inside the range that can trigger a seizure. The Epilepsy Society says flashing between 3 and 30 times a second is the common range, varying from person to person, and 16 to 25 a second the most likely. It also says the UK’s Health and Safety Executive recommends that a strobe in a club or at a public performance flashes no more than four times a second. The knob starts at four. Everything above four is faster than that recommendation, and the knob says so as you turn it. It is off, and it stays off until you switch it on and then say yes to a second question, which tells you the rate before you answer. Nothing on the rig starts by itself, and nothing is remembered: it is off again every time you come in. Escape switches everything off at once, and so do the Stop buttons, going to another tab, and leaving the page. The festival films on the big screen have their own lighting in them, strobe and lasers included. The rig cannot reach inside somebody else’s video, so none of its limits apply there.

You hold the rig. The lasers and the strobe are two separate switches, the rate is a knob, and you choose whether the rig stays in its picture or takes the whole screen. The dial does not switch any of it on or off: nothing on the rig runs until you ask, at any setting, and it stops when you ask, at any setting. It goes to eleven, and it stops there. Eleven is a joke about amplifiers, and it is also where the knob ends. There is no twelve. Seekers and avoiders share the floor. Nobody has to switch anything on, and nobody on this floor is too much. Leave the rig off and dance to the screen, or just sit at the edge. Ask before you touch anybody. A dance floor is shared and a body is not. You can leave whenever you like. The Cooldown Room is through the other door in here, and the rig does not reach it. Nothing is counted. No number on the door, no streak of nights, and no board of who went to eleven.

Water, cold or at room temperature, in paper cups or into your own bottle, free and as much as you like. Beside it, a basket of foam earplugs, a hook of ear defenders, and a box of dark glasses for anybody who wants the dance floor without the rig in their eyes. Through the other door: The Cooldown Room →

The ceiling goes up and keeps going. It is all open floor, with tables and chairs round the edges and nothing in the middle but room. The DJ booth stands two floors up on its own tower at the back. Scaffold decks climb every wall, with the rig bolted to them: moving heads, speaker stacks and laser heads. The lift in the corner stops at every deck, so the stair beside the booth is not the only way up. The light in here is light you can see in the air. The haze catches every beam along its whole length, so a laser is a line drawn across the room rather than a spot on a wall, and the strobe is light in time rather than in space: all of it, then none of it.
Two switches and a knob. Nothing here runs until you press it, and everything stops on Escape. Strobe rate 4 flashes a second

On the shared screen over the floor: three films that play on into YouTube’s own mix and one playlist somebody keeps. Nothing is fetched from YouTube until you press something. While the screen is dark, previous and next move along the channel list without loading anything at all. Once something is on, they change the picture, because by then you have asked for a screen. Every film on this screen has a festival’s own lighting in it, flashing included, and a video a moderator puts up from the CB may flash too: the rig’s limits do not reach inside somebody else’s video. None of it is synced to the rig either: a page cannot see into another site’s player. THE SCREEN IS DARK The channel list — four channels, every one of them festival footage Every channel says how long it runs before you press it, or says that it has no end. Nothing is hosted by us: each is on somebody else’s channel, and that channel is named. The titles are quoted as their channels wrote them. CH 01

Somewhere small and soft to come down in. A room the size of a living room, through the wall from one the size of a hangar. Couches, armchairs, floor cushions and low tables everywhere, the doors shut on the noise, cold water on tap, and a vending machine along one wall where everything is free and made by people from round here.

Most of the light comes out of the front of the vending machine: one tall, steady, pale panel at the side of the room, at about the height of your head. Every couch has a pale edge on the side that faces it and soft shade on the side that does not, and there is a pool of it on the floor in front of the glass. It is the same light all night, and nothing in here is switched. Next door the light is yours to set going. In here there is nothing to set.

Press a slot and it drops into the tray. Everything in it is free, and you can take as many as you like: it does not run out and it does not ask. Every slot says what is in it and how it feels before you press, because crunch, cold and sour matter more than usual in a room like this one.

A cooler by the machine, with cold water and water at room temperature, paper cups and a tap low enough to fill a bottle at. A bowl of ice beside it. Free, like everything else in here, and as much as you like.

Stay as long as you like. Nobody asks why you are in here and nobody asks when you are going back. You do not have to go back. The rig does not reach in here. Nothing next door can flash, sweep or sound in this room. The walls are thick and the doors shut. Nothing in here moves and nothing makes a sound, at any dial setting. The machine drops a snack and says so in words. Nothing is counted and nothing is kept. Nobody writes down what you took or how often you came in. The tray empties when you leave. Lie down if you want to. The floor cushions are for exactly that, and so are the couches.

The snacks and the people who make them belong to this road: the orchard off the verge, the crisp fryer behind the old control tower, the overnight bakers by the fuel pumps, the sweet shed, the pretzel oven, the lolly van and the Tuesday jam club. Under the street there is rock nobody dug, and a way down into it that anybody can take. The weather stops at the top of the shaft. The daylight stops too, and the clock is up there with it. What is down here is here because it needs things to stay the same, and down here they do. We are glad of it, which is half the name.

The deeper you go, the steadier it gets. A cave keeps its weather out. At the real Carlsbad Caverns, the National Park Service measures the Big Room at an average of 56°F (13°C), moving a little with the seasons, and the lowest point at a constant 68°F (20°C) with the air close to saturated all year. So everything down here needs something to hold still: a cellar, a crop that grows in the dark, a light that only shows without one, warm water that holds you up, and a room at the bottom that is simply the steady part. The only light is the handrail. It runs at hand height along the one route, from the lift to every door, and the rock is lit where the path goes and nowhere else. There is no sky down here and no lamp overhead. Down here the only colour is the light; each room brings its own. The lift is the ordinary way down. The stair comes down beside the shaft, and every landing has the same names painted on it as the lift’s panel, so neither one is the other’s alternative. If you came down in the lift, you came the usual way. Nobody was sent down here. Underground, here, is a direction and not a place to keep things out of sight. A cellar is under the street because a cellar is always under the street; a mushroom farm is in a cave because that is where mushrooms have always been grown. Down is not the same as hidden. Nothing down here moves on its own. The dial still works and each room sets its own noise, but the passage has no ambient layer at any setting. The rail does not flicker, because it is the one thing you are holding.

A percentage is how much of the drink is alcohol, by volume. It is on every pour, before you take it, the way every play button in this street’s rooms says how long it runs before you press it. Alcohol-free, for a beer or a wine, means under 0.05%. That is the same drink with the alcohol taken out after it was made, and a brewed drink with the alcohol taken out can keep the faintest trace of it. If you need none at all, the kombucha’s alcohol-free pours have none. Kombucha is never quite zero, and ours says so. It is fermented, so there is always a little alcohol in it, and how much varies from one batch to the next. So its fermented pour gives the most it can be, under 0.5%, rather than a number that would be wrong half the time. Its alcohol-free pour is the same tea and fruit, not fermented.

A thin plastic tube with a glass capsule inside. Bend it until the capsule cracks, and the two liquids mix and light up. Bend it once and it glows until you leave. It is chemistry, not stored light, so it cannot be charged again.

Down here a glow lasts seconds, not the hours a real one can, so that you can watch one go from start to finish. Green lasts longest, and red and orange go first, which is true of the real pigments. Green glow is the brightest and longest-lasting there is. Red and orange are the dimmest: partly because the pigments that glow those colours are weaker, and partly because your eyes are least sensitive to red in the dark. The order of the colours in between is ours, not measured. The glow stick is the odd one out. It is not charged by light at all: bending it cracks a capsule inside, two liquids mix, and they glow until they are spent. It only goes once, so ours glows until you leave.

Why it is always the same down here

The caverns are named after Carlsbad, so this room keeps Carlsbad’s number. The National Park Service’s own words for the lowest point of Carlsbad Cavern are that “this lowest point remains a more constant and warmer 68°F (20ºC) and closer to 100% relative humidity”. The rooms above move a little with the seasons. This is where the moving stops. The air down here is close to saturated, so the rock is damp, and the only light that gets this far is the handrail’s. It does not arrive as a lamp. It arrives as a small point in every bead of damp on the wall, and that is all the light there is.

Anybody whose body does not keep the temperature a building assumes it will. Plenty of us run hot, run cold, or only find out we were too warm once it is already too much. Our own Interoception entry lists temperature among the signals from inside the body, and says that when our attention is taken over we may not notice them at all. In here there is nothing to notice. It is the same on the way in, the same while you are here, and the same when you leave. That is the whole of it. This room is not treatment and it is not a test of anything. Nobody here is going to tell you what it will do for your bodymind.

The temperature. 68°F (20°C) , and it was that before you came in. Nothing moves, at any setting. The dial on this page still works, and it changes nothing in this room, because there is nothing here for it to change. Nothing in the room makes a sound, and nothing is waiting to play. The CB stays upstairs: if you are signed on to it, the radio does not come down this far. There is no clock. Nothing on this page knows what time it is or how long you have been here. “Even in a 68°F room, I need a fan blowing on me. I love fans. I love the spill of air over me. I love the steady hum.” Ryan Boren, who asked for this room

A hall full of fans, for anybody who loves moving air and the noise it makes. Pick one off the floor and switch it on, switch on as many as you like, or take a room of your own with its own ceiling fan and a table to perch one on. How loud the hall is Switching more fans on makes the hall fuller, never louder than the slider says. A fan keeps going while you look at another tab, like a fan does, and stops when you switch it off or leave.
Every fan here says what it feels like and what it sounds like before you switch it on. Nothing makes a sound until you do. Each one has three speeds, and the middle one is where it starts.

Feels like: A slow, wide push of air coming down on the whole hall at once, the kind you only notice when it stops. Sounds like: A low, soft whoosh with a slow beat in it from the blades going round, and almost no motor at all.
Feels like: A flat, square wall of air, straight at you, all of it at once. Sounds like: A broad, even rush like steady rain on a roof, with the motor humming underneath it.
Feels like: Air that arrives, leaves and comes back, sweeping across you and away on a long slow turn. Sounds like: A bright whir that swings from one side of the room to the other and back again.
Feels like: A tall, soft sheet of air with no blades to look at, from the floor up to about your shoulders. Sounds like: A smooth, dark hiss with no beat in it at all, as steady as a held breath.

Feels like: Two streams of air side by side, drawing in from one side of the room and pushing out the other. Sounds like: A deep, doubled drone with a slow beat in it, the two fans never quite in step.

Feels like: A strong, wide gale off a big round fan on wheels, the kind that keeps a workshop moving. Sounds like: A heavy, rushing roar with a low motor growl in it, the biggest noise on the floor and still under the hall's ceiling.
Desk fan in a wire cage
Feels like: A small, close breeze aimed at your face, cool on whichever side it is pointed at. Sounds like: A quick, light whir with a thin hum in it, the sound of a fan a foot away.
Feels like: A narrow stream of air from wherever you clipped it: on your hands, your neck, the back of your head. Sounds like: A high, tidy buzz, one of the smallest voices in the hall.
Feels like: A breeze about the size of a hand, from a fan about the size of a mug. Sounds like: A faint, fast whir, very close and very quiet.

A room off the hall with a partition round it, its own ceiling fan, and a table to perch a fan on. It has a door, so switching anything on in here switches the hall’s fans off, and switching a fan on out on the floor opens your door again.

Feels like: A ceiling fan of your own, smaller than the big one in the hall, turning over your own table. Sounds like: A soft whoosh close over your head, with a quicker beat than the big fan in the hall.
Desk fan in a wire cage

Feels like: A small, close breeze aimed at your face, cool on whichever side it is pointed at. Sounds like: A quick, light whir with a thin hum in it, the sound of a fan a foot away. Perched on your table

Nothing makes a sound until you switch it on, and every fan says what it sounds like first, in words. Every ceiling fan’s lamp hangs below its blades, so the blades never pass between you and the light. Nothing in here flickers or flashes, at any setting. The dial keeps its promise and the fans keep theirs. At Gentle the blades stay still and the fan keeps running, because the sound is the thing you asked for. At Regular they turn once you switch a fan on. At MAX GLITTER the ribbons on the fans flutter too. No fan here is named for who made it. They are named for what they are. Your usual is kept in your own browser, and nowhere else. The speed you last set on each fan, which fan is on your table, and which fans you last had on. It never switches anything on by itself: your speeds come back when you arrive, and the fans only start when you press Switch on my usual. Forget my usual clears it. Nothing is counted, and the sound is made here and sent nowhere. You do not need a reason to love a fan. None of these is a sleep aid or a way to get more done. They are fans. Ryan’s words are his own. The fans are ours, drawn and made in the browser; none of them is a recording. Credits are in the liner notes.

Who made this noise. This street dropped almost every careful habit our other sites have — careful palettes, careful hedging, the balanced tone. It kept exactly one, and this is the page where it lives. Attribution is not a house style here. It is a licence, it is the cheapest thing on the page, and it is the only one of our habits whose absence is a legal problem rather than an aesthetic one. So the credits are loud instead of hidden: scrawled in the margins of the rooms, and collected in full here. Credits are about the people who made this street. What it keeps about the people who visit it, which is very little, is on the privacy page.

A meeting place, and a shopfront on the street: a kitchen in the afternoon with one window open and the good china out, not one cup matching the next. That mismatch is the subject of the room sitting on the table, because a covenstead is where a group meets — several people who do not entirely agree, meeting on purpose anyway. It began as turning 03 in The Outskirts and was moved. Ryan’s call, 2026-09-22, and the reasoning is about what each area is for: the campgrounds are for people who want to be somewhat apart from each other, at peace in nature, with the street still in reach; the road out of town is for night revelry and for being as far off as you can get. A covenstead is neither — it is a group that meets regularly, which wants a premises with a door on a street where people already are. Helen Edgar’s observation sharpened the split: that everything out on that road could sit on the campsite if it had planning permission, which turns out to be a useful test for anything placed in either area. It changed worlds when it moved rather than being relocated with the same paint on it. Out there it was a dark room lit by several lamps that did not match — the only room on the street lit by more than one source. Here it is daylit, warm and domestic, and the argument moved with it: the thing carrying several people who do not match, meeting anyway is now the china. That device is load bearing, and if the crockery is ever made to match, the room has lost its subject and kept its wallpaper. Terry Pratchett’s words are on that page, and they are the point of it. First Sight and Second Thoughts are his, named in the Discworld books, and the sentences that define them are the tenets — the way the Rede’s couplet is. An earlier draft named the concepts and linked out for the words; it described the thing instead of showing it, and it gutted the room. Ryan’s call, 2026-09-22. Every quotation names its author, its work and its year and links to the edition, which is the habit this site keeps when it drops all the others. What is not there is the scene. The lines about storing things in other people come out of a long exchange running to several hundred words, and that stays quoted properly, at length and in context, on our own philosophy page — the better thing to read, linked rather than raided. tools/make-covenstead.py sets its own cap rather than borrowing the Zibaldone’s: thirty words is right for a quote bank, where the danger is drift, and wrong for a room quoting a handful of named passages it is actually about. Sixty fits a defining sentence and refuses a scene. The Rule of Three is argued about inside the tradition, and the room says so instead of settling it. It is not a universal article of faith: there are Wiccans who read it as an over-elaboration on the Rede and others who consider it a modern innovation built on Christian morality, with a possible prototype in a 1949 novel of Gerald Gardner’s. A page stating it flat, as the witch law, would be deciding a live argument inside somebody else’s religion on their behalf, from the outside, in passing, for atmosphere — and the flattened version is always the one that travels. The tool refuses a tenet marked contested that does not say what is contested about it. Rede means counsel, not commandment, which is the hinge the room turns on: Middle English for advice, first publicly recorded in its best-known couplet in a 1964 speech by Doreen Valiente, and still counsel sixty years later rather than a code somebody can be expelled for breaking. make-covenstead.py refuses a tenet written as an order — which is the opposite of the rule one turning up the road, where make-sithen.py refuses advice outright. Two rooms in one area holding opposite rules about the same vocabulary, for the same underlying reason, and they must not be made to agree. Nobody is initiated and nothing is counted. No degrees, no levels, no test at the door, no record of how often you came. The Wiccan material is somebody else’s religion, treated as such, and read off the Rede and the Rule of Three on 2026-09-22. Peer support by and for people in burnout and people on the far side of it, and a shopfront on the street: a borrowed room after hours with the big lights off and the door left ajar. The name is a play on Dead Poets Society (1989, directed by Peter Weir, written by Tom Schulman; read off Wikipedia’s summary on 2026-09-23), a film about a group resisting the conformity of the school it meets in. The room takes the shape of the name and nothing else — no line, no scene, no character, no still, no motto — and tools/make-dead-tired.py refuses the film’s characters, its school and its two famous lines anywhere on the page, because the most famous parts of somebody else’s screenplay are exactly the parts most tempting to borrow for atmosphere. The light comes from outside the room, and nobody sits in it. The only light is a corridor’s strip lights through the gap in a door, lying across the floor as one hard wedge, and every word on that page stays in the shade on purpose: masking is performing under a light, and this is the room where nothing has to. The drawing places everything — a beanbag, a mug, a chair with a coat over it, a mattress, a pair of shoes, an armchair — outside that wedge, and draws nobody at all, because nobody in there is on display. The corridor’s tubes do not flicker, at any setting, for Club Chronic’s reason. Every line on a peg is somebody else’s and says whose. Each was read off our own glossary entry for that peg on 2026-09-23 and is credited to the source the entry credits, never to the entry. Where an entry named only a title or only initials, the authors were resolved rather than guessed: Botha and Frost against Crossref’s record for their DOI, and Kramer, Jones and Broadbent against the journal’s own citation metadata, because Crossref has no record for that one. The definition of burnout at the top of the room is the title of Raymaker and others’ paper in Autism in Adulthood, 2020, also checked against Crossref. The line under each quotation is ours, written for this room. Nothing there gives advice nobody asked for, counts anything, or praises anybody for how much they can take. The tool refuses the vocabulary of all three in the room’s own voice, with a window so the room can still say it will not — and skips the quotations, because two of them are the sharpest things anybody has said against resilience, and a quotation criticising a word has to be allowed to contain it. The page is not a meeting and does not pretend to be one: it has no times, no sign-up and no facilitator, and it points at our community, where the people are, and at mutual aid. The type is Sorts Mill Goudy, Barry Schwartz’s revival of Goudy’s Oldstyle, for the society’s name and headings — set like a founding charter for a society whose members are lying on the floor — and Lexend, by Bonnie Shaver-Troup, Thomas Jockin, Santiago Orozco, Héctor Gómez and Superunion, for everything that is read. Lexend was drawn to reduce visual stress and ease reading fatigue, which is the whole reason a room for the dead tired sets it. Both under the SIL Open Font License, read off their own records in google/fonts. An old aircraft hangar by the airstrip, turning 08 in The Outskirts, Ryan’s brief of 2026-09-27: somewhere for the sensory seekers in our community to stim loudly and brightly. It is the one room on this street with a strobe in it, and that reverses a rule the street has held since Club Chronic, which every room with a light show in it has repeated since. The reversal is an opt-in and nothing else: the rig is off on every visit, the strobe takes two presses and the second answers a question that names the rate, and Escape, the Stop buttons, another tab or leaving the page switch everything off at once. tools/make-rave.py refuses the page if the warning moves below the rig, if the rig stops shipping hidden, if the knob goes past eleven or starts anywhere but four, if the flash has any colour in it, or if rave.js stores anything or can start without a press. The flash rates in the warning are the Epilepsy Society’s, read off its page on photosensitive epilepsy on 2026-09-27: 3 to 30 flashes a second the common range, 16 to 25 the most likely to trigger a seizure, and the Health and Safety Executive’s recommendation, which that page reports, that a strobe in a club flashes no more than four times a second. The knob starts at four and goes to eleven, and everything past four says so as you turn it. “Goes to eleven” is Nigel Tufnel’s amplifier in This Is Spinal Tap (1984), directed by Rob Reiner and written by Reiner with Christopher Guest, Michael McKean and Harry Shearer. The Adventurer’s Guild said that Club Chronic’s rule held everywhere on this street, and it does not any more. That sentence is in its house rules and was rewritten the day this room opened, which is the claim-about-one-room-in-another-room’s-copy problem this street keeps finding. What this room takes from the books is the architecture: thirteen of everything and no two alike, a low ceiling with fans in it, windows at the pavement, mirrors, carved columns, a player piano and no screens, a wood-burning stove, ale never served cold, and lemonade with lemonade ice. A shopfront on the street: a fridge door covered in word magnets, where a sentence is built one word at a time. The game is our community’s, after the sentence builder in the Collaborative Nonsense channels of our Discord, and every word on the door came from somebody in it. Word magnets on a fridge were Dave Kapell’s idea, in 1993, and the kits are sold as Magnetic Poetry; none of their words are here. Read off Wikipedia’s article on 30 September 2026. The name is a joke on the Bridge of Sighs, in Venice. The door and the magnet at the foot of it are drawn for this room. A picture house on the street where every screening is a relaxed screening: the house lights stay up, the captions are on, and anybody can move, stim, sit on the floor or leave. The name is borrowed from a film, Lightbulb Moments: Being Autistic, by Thriving Autistic, which is on the first screen. Every screen is one of our own playlists, put on whole, and carries no runtime because it is a list we keep adding to. The first two were read off their own playlist pages on 2026-09-23 and every film on them was checked on its own watch page the same day, and every film on Screen Three was checked the same way on 2026-09-28 — playing, embeddable, and none behind an age gate. Every film belongs to the people who made it, named below wherever the film’s own description names them, and to the channel that published it. None of them is affiliated with Stimpunks and none of them endorses us, and nothing is hosted by us. The words on the rack are ours, written from the films rather than from their titles. Fourteen of the fifteen were read from their captions; the fifteenth, whose captions could not be fetched, is described from its maker’s own description and from our Autism Pathway, which already carries it. Every card says what is in its film before the press, beside the runtime — a panic attack, a bullying scene, jokes about suicide, a sponsor segment — and tools/make-picture-house.py refuses a card nobody checked for that. No maker’s pronouns are used anywhere on the rack, because not one of the films says what they are, and the tool refuses one. Screen Two has a rack too, carded the same way on 2026-09-28: from each film’s captions, read in full, and its own description. One webinar’s captions mangle names badly enough that its card names no product. Screen Three is everything we have watched at Campfire Learn Together, our Sunday watch-along, newest first, and the campfire rack has a card for every film on it linking the post we wrote for that campfire. The campfires were read out of our own posts: every one tagged Campfire Learn Together. One film is on the rack and not in the programme, because YouTube would not let it be added to the playlist, and its card says so. The cards were written from each film’s captions, read in full, except where a film has none or YouTube would not give them up: the Dystopia documentary, the Screaming Females cover, the farruca, the 1980 two-pianos concert and the Wonderstruck audiobook preview are described from their own descriptions and from our posts, and the Dystopia card’s note about what is in it has not been checked against the film. Three campfires watched nothing that can be on a YouTube playlist — a film since made private, and films on Vimeo and on their makers’ own site — and the room lists them under the rack rather than leaving them out. Nothing in the building is blue, and the tool reads the room’s palette and refuses a blue: a lightbulb theater in a neurodiversity room, lit blue, would be the Light It Up Blue campaign, which autistic people have spent years refusing. Lynch’s at NeuroClastic, whose byline came out of that page’s own metadata because our entry credits only the site, and Kari Burroughs Kraakevik’s at Thinking Person’s Guide to Autism. The two lines from the book could not be checked against a copy of it from here, and the room says so beside each of them rather than letting them sit among the checked ones looking the same. Title, subtitle, author, publisher, year and ISBN were read off Open Library’s edition record on 2026-09-23 rather than typed. The regulars’ samefoods belong to the people whose names are on the trays, and are written down exactly as they were given: nothing capitalised, glossed, corrected, sorted or merged, and nothing counted across the trays. Ryan’s, Helen’s and Ronan’s arrived in the brief for the room on 2026-09-23, Helen’s and Ronan’s relayed by Ryan as they gave them, and each tray carries a bowl of that person’s samefood of the moment; the rest are being collected in the community’s Discord. Ronan’s ketchup is in a ramekin of its own because that is how Ronan has red things, and it is Ronan’s way rather than the house’s: the café defaults to structure, separation and predictability and accommodates every guest individually, so nobody’s way is imposed on anybody else. The tool holds Ronan’s food, and only Ronan’s, to Ronan’s ask. The combos, their names, the notes on them and every drawing in the room are ours, and each combo is assembled out of that pantry: tools/make-vital.py refuses one that brings in anything it does not keep. The room was briefed as Ital Plant Livity, and both words are Rastafari’s. Ryan’s call, 2026-09-24: Rastafari has been a big influence on him, and the room takes a more general name, because this kitchen cooks with salt, MSG, soy sauce and processed food, which many people who keep Ital do not, and because how Ital is kept varies from person to person and is not ours to settle from outside. What the room says about Ital was read against Wikipedia’s article on it the same day: that the word is vital with the v taken off, that many Rastafari avoid food with additives and some avoid added salt, and that practice varies widely. The menu never calls a dish Ital, and the tool refuses the word there. The playlist on the stereo still carries the old name, and the word stays in the songs’ own titles, which are the musicians’. The songs belong to the musicians named beside them, and the list was read off the playlist’s own data on 2026-09-24, with every one checked on its own watch page the same day.
