A quiet room on the street in sage lime plaster, with one window facing north onto a hillside and a deep seat built in under it, and the only door the CB is behind. Its look answers a request from our community for something softer, lower in stimulation and more of a refuge, in the biophilic direction Ryan chose, and leans on 14 Patterns of Biophilic Design, by William Browning, Catherine Ryan and Joseph Clancy for Terrapin Bright Green (2014): a view of a living hillside, prospect from the window, refuge in the seat, soft and diffuse light, and lime, ash and wool. The window, the hill and the seat are drawn by us. The CB is Ryan’s idea, from his brief of 2026-09-24: a simple chat patterned after citizens band radio, a shared password rotated periodically, no alerts (notifications came later, on 2026-10-18, when the community asked), a short history cleared daily (two days of it since 2026-10-18, for the people in other timezones who were missing it), reachable only by signing on here, and a radio that floats in the corner of the screen once you are on. The radio, its drawing on the front desk, the house norms and every word in the room are ours. The house norms stand on the Stimpunks Covenant, which is ours and lives on stimpunks.org, and which itself adopts the Contributor Covenant, version 2.1, published by the Organization for Ethical Source, whose name is the one its own pages carry. The room links both and quotes neither; the norms in it were written for a channel that forgets. The type is Varela Round, by Joe Prince, for the room’s name and headings, and Radio Canada, by Charles Daoud, Coppers and Brasses, Alexandre Saumier Demers and Jacques Le Bailly, for everything that is read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records. The radio itself sets Bungee for its name, VT323 for its channel number and Atkinson Hyperlegible for every message, because it is furniture and keeps its own clothes in every room, the way the dial does. Getting started is Ryan’s, from his draft of 2026-10-18, the day the community moved onto the CB and the forums for everything; its steps for claiming a username are the radio’s own buttons, named as the radio names them. The radio’s themes are Ryan’s list, of 2026-10-17, and every drawing in them is drawn for the radio, in colours measured on their own case. Solarized is Ethan Schoonover’s palette, with a darker bar on dark and darker inks for words on light, because its accents fall under 4.5 to 1 as words; its eight accents are in the stripe as he lays them out. Biophilic takes queering.earth’s paper, moss, rust, lichen, verdigris, marigold and coral, and grows its ivy and mushrooms after the garden in Helen Edgar’s Faery Yurt, drawn again for the radio. Star Stuff takes starstuff.earth’s night, purple, gold, pink, cyan and green. LCARS is after the computer screens Michael Okuda designed for Star Trek: The Next Generation ; Star Trek is a trade mark of CBS Studios, and no screen, lettering or symbol of theirs is copied. Biomechanical is after H. R. Giger’s biomechanics and copies nothing of his. Greeble is after the model-making of Star Wars ; Star Wars is a trade mark of Lucasfilm. The faces for the themes’ names and headings are on the street already: JetBrains Mono, Fraunces, Space Mono, Anton, Shrikhand, Macondo, Syncopate, Oxanium, Martian Mono, Sour Gummy and Caveat, each credited where the Foundry shelves it. The radio’s Winamp skins are after skins in the Winamp Skin Museum, Ryan’s picks of 2026-10-17, and each skin’s maker is named as its own readme names them, read in the Museum that day: LuigiHann (Zelda Amp III), Vad3K (Microchip 2), Pabo Wakataeo (ASCII-Amp 2.0), ronz (Super Mario Land Amp), sasso (deviantAMP), Arne Olav Storflor (hpcalc_hp49g), Kuki (the Cube v2), shadesmaclean, also Neko-Sen’nin, of Spooky Door Productions (Fallout Pip-Boy 3000 Green) and bLy, Erik Waldner (TI-82 v1.1). Dig Dug Amp’s readme names its maker only by an email address, which we do not publish, and winamp_mario and gameboy have no readme at all. Their colours were looked at and their bitmaps were not used: every drawing is ours, and draws nothing from the games and machines the skins were after, which are their companies’ trade marks. Kuki asked that nothing of the Cube be republished, and nothing is. The faces for their names and headings are on the street already: Cinzel, B612, Courier Prime, Press Start 2P, Titan One, Exo 2, Michroma, Lilita One, Unbounded, VT323, Doto and Chakra Petch. The radio’s GeoCities pages are after homepages kept in Restorativland’s GeoCities archive, Ryan’s picks of 2026-10-17, read there that day. Each is credited as the page names its maker: Paula (Paula’s Page), Fran and Charlotte (Shop Til U Drop!), Benjamin T. Marotta, who designed the Beatnik Termites’ unofficial home page, Aaron Ortiz (The Green Room) and Sarah (Sarah’s Room). Divine Louise Brooks, mansnhomepage and Dat’s double U for W!!! name nobody, and are credited by title and address. Their colours were looked at and nothing on them is used, and nothing about anybody on them is repeated. The faces for their names and headings are on the street already: Yellowtail, Sansita, Bowlby One SC, Gloria Hallelujah, Permanent Marker, Yanone Kaffeesatz, Libre Franklin and Playfair Display. The radio’s favourite games are Ryan’s, of 2026-10-17: Castle Crashers (The Behemoth), Dragon Age: Inquisition (BioWare), Metroid (Nintendo), Mega Man (Capcom), Fable III (Lionhead Studios), The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim (Bethesda Game Studios), Doom (id Software), Portal (Valve), The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt (CD Projekt Red), Grand Theft Auto V (Rockstar North), The Legend of Zelda (Nintendo) and Middle-earth: Shadow of Mordor (Monolith Productions), whose rune medallions are after the game’s runes, as the Shadow of War wiki shows them, with every mark made up for the radio. Each theme takes a game’s palette and the shapes of its world, and draws no character, logo, emblem or symbol of any of them; the games and their names are their makers’ and their trade marks, as the CB guide sets out. The faces for their names and headings are on the street already: Bagel Fat One, Marcellus SC, Press Start 2P, Righteous, Della Respira, Forum, Rubik Dirt, Inter, Cinzel, Gravitas One, Amarante and Eczar. The profile effect called Black Leather Lagoon is after the street’s Black Leather Lagoon and The Cramps, the band of Lux Interior and Poison Ivy, at Ryan’s ask of 2026-10-18, and it is their world and not them: nobody real is drawn, and nothing of the band’s is used, no lyric, no logo, no album art and no photograph. The drive-in screen in black water, its glow and the reeds are the Lagoon room’s, in that room’s own colours; the poison ivy round the edge is a nod to Poison Ivy’s name; the leopard print and the finned hot rod are the band’s world, drawn here; and the sea serpent rising out of the water is our own, nothing of anybody’s film monster. Like the Lagoon, nothing in it flickers. Three things pair with it, for Halloween, and are the same world: the radio theme Black Leather Lagoon, in that room’s own colours, with a drive-in screen glowing over black water, reeds, cattails and bats along its trims; the Graveyard gate frame, iron railings with cobwebs and spiders in the corners; and the Jack-o’-lanterns decoration round an avatar. Nobody real is drawn in any of them. Every other frame and effect on a profile card is drawn here too, in the card’s own theme. The profile effect Otters in the kelp, the Kelp Forest theme, the Kelp fronds frame and the Otters in kelp decoration are after the Arcade’s Otterly Adorbs, at Ryan’s ask of 2026-10-18, and so after what that cabinet is built on: Stimpunks Solidarity and Otters by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms, 2026), and Star Stuff’s zine No. 58, The Stone You Keep. They keep its rules. Floating fills nothing: no meter, nothing earned, no word saying rest is for anything. No otter is ranked against another. The kelp does the holding, so the otters float among it, and the one anchored in it has a strand across its belly; no two otters hold paws, a story the internet tells and the zine does not; and nobody keeps a favourite stone in a pouch, or any stone at all. The otters, the kelp and the theme’s colours are drawn here, and nothing of the cabinet’s pixels is pasted in. The profile effect Flying Fairy and the Fairy Lights theme are Ryan’s ask of 2026-10-19. The theme is the Fairy lights frame for profiles grown into a radio theme: the same strings of bulbs, swagged across a plum night in gold, rose, mint, sky, lilac and peach, along the radio’s trims and sides, as a profile’s banner and as a nameplate on Who’s online, with the radio’s name in Leckerli One, which the street already sets on the Doom Scoop’s door. The faeries that fly across the profile are the Faery Yurt’s, the small woodland faeries drawn for Helen Edgar’s room at her ask, in that room’s own colours, with their flower crowns, long hair, mossy cloaks, posies, gauzy wings and little curled horns, no two dressed alike, redrawn here for the radio. The big fairy is our own drawing, after the look of the profile Helen wears on Discord: red hair under a crown of roses, a cloak of moss, a posy of red and pink roses, petals falling and sparkles over the top, to which we gave butterfly wings. The artwork on that profile is not ours and nothing of it is copied. Like every effect, it moves only at MAX GLITTER or after Let my theme move, and nothing in it flashes. The profile effects Howling Wolf, Starward Dreaming, Leaping Dolphins and Autumn Falls are Ryan’s asks of 2026-10-19, and every drawing in them is ours, drawn for the radio after nobody’s picture: the wolf is nobody’s emblem, the dolphins and the children are nobody in particular, and the clearing is any clearing. Each is in colours of its own, measured on its own scene’s ground. Starward Dreaming’s flames keep the rule the candles behind the door marked E keep: each sways on its own time, never faster than two and a half times a second, and dims by a tenth at most. The member map on the wall is Ryan’s brief of 2026-10-22, moving our map of where our community lives off Google My Maps: its 175 pins were brought over that day, each only a place, and how many of us are in each place is shown, Ryan’s call. The world is Natural Earth’s 1:50m land, version 5.1.2, which is public domain, simplified by us and drawn in the Equal Earth projection, of Bojan Šavrič, Tom Patterson and Bernhard Jenny; Natural Earth’s country borders said which country each of Google’s pins is in, on our own machine. New places are looked up with Nominatim, on OpenStreetMap’s data, © OpenStreetMap contributors, under the Open Database License. The pull-down map is drawn in the hall’s own paint, and nobody’s name is anywhere on it. Zoomed in (Ryan’s question, 2026-10-23), it shows Natural Earth’s 1:50m lakes, borders between countries and lines between states and provinces, the same version and public domain too, simplified by us. The Cloud City theme and profile effect, the Portholes frame and the Cloud cars decoration are Ryan’s ask of 2026-10-23, made for the profile of Rando Calrissian, a test user on the CB. They are after Cloud City, the city in the clouds of Bespin in The Empire Strikes Back (Lucasfilm, 1980), the city Ralph McQuarrie painted for the film: a disc crowded with towers, standing out of the cloud on a long stalk, with twin-pod cloud cars round it. Star Wars is a trade mark of Lucasfilm. Every drawing is ours, the city, its windows, its cloud cars and the striped sun, and nobody from the films is drawn, nor any ship, emblem or lettering of theirs. The colours, navy, cream, gold, peach and rose, are those of randocloud.cloud, Rando’s site, whose mark is a cloud in front of a striped sunset. The radio’s name and headings are in Jost, which the street already sets in the Rabbit Hole, and it is offered for your name on your card. Like every effect, it moves only at MAX GLITTER or after Let my theme move, and nothing in it flashes. The channel runs on Netlify Functions and Netlify Blobs, on the same host as the rest of the street. What it keeps and for how long is on the privacy page.

A boutique on the street for dopamine dressing. The room and its name are Helen Edgar’s idea, and the rails are Ryan’s brief of 2026-09-25, written from it: his own wardrobe, then Helen’s, relayed, then the rest of our community, some of whom take it further than either. The valet stand, every garment on the rails, every print and colourway, the crystal in the window, the curtained doorway at the back and every word in the room are ours. The looks with somebody’s name on them are in their words, as given: Ryan's usual: Thai fisherman pants almost exclusively, in bold florals, bold block patterns or patchwork; button-down shirts of various colours; a haori on top, more subdued than the pants but still often patchwork and bold blocks of colour; and beanies and slouchy beanies in a staggering array of colours and patterns. — Ryan, in the brief for this room, 2026-09-25. Helen's: Helen loves cardigans and flowing dresses and has a witchy style. — relayed by Ryan in the brief for this room, 2026-09-25. Helen’s look was relayed by Ryan rather than given by her, and the moons, the midnight and the plum on it are the house’s guess at witchy; she has the final say on every one of them. The full show is nobody’s in particular, because the brief gives it to others in our community without naming anybody. What dopamine dressing is comes from our own Dopamine Dressing entry, which sets it beside our Masking entry and quotes From the Slow Lane; the room says it in its own words rather than quoting either. Why black is a colour in there comes from our Dress Codes entry. How each garment feels and comes off follows Ryan’s own field guide page on dressing and our Why Sheet for a hoodie. The rainbow colourway’s name, all the colours there are, is borrowed from the title of our course Neurodiversity and Gender: You Hit So Hard With All the Colors That There Are. All of these were read in the Knowledge System mirror on 2026-09-25 rather than fetched live. The haori and Thai fisherman pants are described from Wikipedia, read on 2026-09-25: a haori is a Japanese jacket worn over a kimono and usually tied at the front with two short cords, and Thai fisherman pants are made wide in the waist so that one size fits all, wrapped round and tied. The brief spelled the jacket hoari; the rail says haori, which is how it is spelled. Crocs is a trade name and belongs to Crocs, Inc., which has no connection with Stimpunks and does not endorse us; the pair on the rail is our own drawing of the shoe, on Ryan’s ask of 2026-09-25, and no logo of theirs is on it. The type is DynaPuff, by Toshi Omagari and Jennifer Daniel, for the sign and the headings, and Plus Jakarta Sans, by Tokotype, for everything that is read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records.

A fancy dress shop through the curtain at the back of the Dopamine Dress-Up Den, for your bodymind. It is Helen Edgar’s idea, asked for on 2026-10-15: faery wings big and small in every colour, jewellery, beads and rings, onesies, tiger, bear, dragon and unicorn outfits, and animal ears, tails and paws. Every piece is worked out again from the bodymind it is put on, on its feet or sitting down, in avatar.js, so wings, ears, tails, paws, jewellery and suits go wherever that bodymind goes on the street: into the Dress-Up Den, into a Profile on the CB, and onto a sticker. The back of the shop, its sheers and its rail of stock, is ours too, drawn in the room’s own declared colours, and so is the loose wing on the guild’s board. The Bodymind Booth: an idea from our community, written up as a proposal by Ryan, 2026-10-14. A camera obscura on the street, painted black inside, where a chimera made out of two animals appears on a round white table under a lens in the roof. It began with Norah asking for an otteraccoon, and it is built on the chimeras stimpunks.org’s About page has had for years, which take features and colouring from one animal onto another’s body. Chimera Obscura: Ryan’s brief, 2026-10-18, after Norah asked for an otteraccoon. Bearmouse, Pandillo and Bunnybadger are Becky Hicks’s, drawn for stimpunks.org’s About page and hung here under CC BY-SA 4.0 with her yes. Every part on the shelf is drawn as code by Claude. The street’s room for asking, and a shopfront on the street: its channel on the CB is where anybody signed on asks for mutual aid, peer support and any other help, and where anybody who can offers it. Ryan’s brief of 2026-10-22. It is built out of three pages of ours: Community Care on stimpunks.org, our glossary’s Peer Support, and Tapping the Radical Roots of Peer Support, which is Tuesday Ferguson’s, on our blog under CC BY-SA 4.0. The umbrellas are our Community Care page’s. Its sign is an umbrella and its photograph is umbrellas in every colour hanging on strings over a street, so the room is that street in the rain, with everybody’s umbrellas tied to one another into one roof. The drawing is ours, made as code by Claude to Ryan’s brief. tools/make-community-care.py draws it from the room’s data and refuses an umbrella with no tie to the next, because nothing else holds the roof up; the ties are loose, after Sophie K. Rosa’s line about no single knot tied too tight. Every quotation was read off one of those three pages on 2026-10-22 and is checked against them word for word on every build where our copy of stimpunks.org is on the machine. Each is credited to whoever said it, and somebody else’s line says it was read on our page. Where our page names nobody’s work for a line, the room names none either: bell hooks’s and Larry Mitchell’s lines are credited to them and to nothing else. Vivian Ly’s talk at Autscape 2020 is on Autscape’s own channel and plays only when pressed; the presenter’s name was read off the video’s own description, because our page names the talk and not who gave it. Nobody who asks is sorted, owes anybody or proves anything, and nothing is counted. The tool refuses the vocabulary of all four in the room’s own voice, with a window so the room can still say it will not, and skips the quotations, one of which argues against charity by naming it. It also refuses the page without its paragraph saying the channel is not a crisis line, and a form or a box anywhere on the page: nothing in the room takes words, and the channel does. The Foundation’s grants are named and linked and promised nothing: they are by application, in scheduled rounds, and cannot cover anything urgent, which the tool holds against the grants page itself. The type is Agbalumo, by Raphael Alẹ́gbẹ́lẹ́yẹ̀ with Sorkin Type and Eben Sorkin, for the room’s name and headings, and Ysabeau Infant, by Christian Thalmann, for every word that is read, cut here to the Latin and Vietnamese letters so the line before this one sets in it. Both under the SIL Open Font License, read off their own records in google/fonts. A shopfront on the street in the eye of the storm. Ryan’s brief of 2026-10-24: a room that synthesizes and summarizes three pages from our Regulation and Coping hub on stimpunks.org, Seeds of Cope, The Science of Cope and Cope Is Not an Insult, with its channel on the CB under Community on the chat page, and doors to the rooms on the street for coping, regulation and peer support. All three pages are Stimpunks’, and the summaries round their lines are ours, written for the room as a way into the pages and never instead of them. The eye of the storm is ours, after our pages’ own words: seeds you can plant ahead of time or grab in a storm, and micro-worlds of safety inside hostile terrain. The storm stays in plain sight, all the way round and at both edges of a wide window, because the difference between coping and denial is that the storm is still there. The drawing and the doors on the floor of the eye were made as code by Claude to Ryan’s brief. tools/make-coping.py draws the cloud wall from a fixed seed, and draws every door in the room’s own inks, told apart by its form, because a door is this room’s sign for a room and not the room. Each door says what its room is for in words that room’s own page still says, and the tool stops when one of them stops saying it. Every quotation was read off one of those three pages on 2026-10-24 and is checked against them word for word on every build where our copy of stimpunks.org is on the machine; so are the cope map, the words to borrow, the groups the doors stand in and the works The Science of Cope names. The room has not read those works and says so beside them: it summarises our page, which is the place to start. Nothing in the room is grit, a sneer, clinical, counted or cheerful at you. The tool refuses the vocabulary of each in the room’s own voice, with a window so the room can still say it will not, and skips our pages’ own words, which argue against several of them by naming them. It refuses the page without its paragraph, before the first heading, saying it is not clinical advice and not a crisis line, with our page’s line about danger and links to our Help page and to the crisis lines. Nothing in the eye moves by itself at any setting, MAX GLITTER included. The type is Funnel Display for the room’s name and headings and Funnel Sans for every word that is read, both by NORD ID and Kristian Möller, cut here to the Latin letters with their weight axis kept. One family at two sizes, because a room for steadying yourself does not change its voice between the sign and the page. Both under the SIL Open Font License, read off their own records in google/fonts. Coping: each quotation in the room, which page of ours it was read on, and how long it is The line Read on our page Length This is a coping toolkit for getting through hard moments in a hard world. Seeds of Cope 14 words Struggling in unjust conditions is not a personal failure. You are not broken. The system is. Seeds of Cope 16 words Pick one. Do it imperfectly. Tiny is valid. Seeds of Cope 8 words If you only do one thing: reduce inputs. Lower sensory load first. Everything is harder when your nervous system is on fire. Seeds of Cope 22 words Not everything is psychological. A lot of it is sensory, social, and systemic. Seeds of Cope 13 words These are small, repeatable interventions. You can plant them ahead of time, or grab them in a storm. Seeds of Cope 18 words Stim is regulation. Let your body do its job. Seeds of Cope 9 words Permission to leave. You don’t need to justify your nervous system. Seeds of Cope 11 words Sometimes you’re not “overthinking.” You’re stuck in a loop because your attention won’t release and your body won’t downshift. Seeds of Cope 19 words Pressure: weighted blanket, tight hoodie, firm hug (if wanted). Seeds of Cope 9 words If your life is being squeezed by paperwork, punishment, sorting, surveillance, and “standards,” you may be reacting normally to abnormal conditions. Seeds of Cope 21 words After a meltdown/shutdown/panic spike, your job is gentle recovery — not “getting back to normal.” Seeds of Cope 15 words Plan one lily pad. What makes the next transition safer? Seeds of Cope 10 words Use these as-is. Edit them. Make them yours. The point is to reduce effort in the moment. Seeds of Cope 17 words Small distribution is care infrastructure. Seeds of Cope 5 words Coping is not imaginary. It is neurobiological. The Science of Cope 7 words These are not personality flaws. They are adaptive responses. The Science of Cope 9 words That is physiology, not weakness. The Science of Cope 5 words Trauma symptoms are not random. They are adaptations that once increased survival probability. The Science of Cope 13 words Coping behaviors often emerge to lower allostatic load. The Science of Cope 8 words They are not “malfunctioning.” They are regulating. The Science of Cope 7 words If removing fluorescent lights reduces shutdown, the problem was lighting — not character. The Science of Cope 13 words If written communication reduces panic, the problem was phone culture — not fragility. The Science of Cope 13 words Coping behaviors frequently expose structural flaws. The Science of Cope 6 words Coping is not delusion. It is prerequisite to change. The Science of Cope 9 words Coping is not the enemy of change. It is what keeps people alive long enough to build it. The Science of Cope 18 words They turned cope into a sneer. Cope Is Not an Insult 6 words Cope is not denial. Cope is not fantasy. Cope is not failure. Cope Is Not an Insult 12 words Cope is what living nervous systems do under pressure. Cope Is Not an Insult 9 words Stimming? Cope. Parallel play? Cope. Mutual aid? Cope. Lowering the lights? Cope. Leaving the room? Cope. Naming the harm? Cope. Cope Is Not an Insult 20 words Coping is applied knowledge of reality. Cope Is Not an Insult 6 words That is not coping. That is submission. Cope Is Not an Insult 7 words We cope to reduce harm. We cope to stay alive. We cope so we can build something better. Cope Is Not an Insult 18 words Creating micro-worlds of safety inside hostile terrain Cope Is Not an Insult 7 words Then yes. We inhale that. Cope Is Not an Insult 5 words You are not escaping reality. You are refusing to let reality erase you. Cope Is Not an Insult 13 words Coping is resistance scaled to the nervous system. Cope Is Not an Insult 8 words Coping is not evidence of weakness. It is evidence of strain. And strain tells the truth about the structure. Cope Is Not an Insult 19 words We reclaim cope from mockery. We reclaim cope from neoliberal grit narratives. We reclaim cope from shame. Cope Is Not an Insult 17 words Cope is survival. Cope is intelligence. Cope is resistance. Cope is care. Cope Is Not an Insult 12 words And we are not ashamed of surviving. Cope Is Not an Insult 7 words Coping scales from breath to policy. A shopfront on the street, down on the floor with the animals at the end of the day. Ryan’s brief of 2026-10-24: a Pets room, its channel on the CB in the Community section of the chat page, saying how important co-regulating with pets is for many Autistic people and for humans in general, because mammalian co-regulation is a thing, and linking every room on the street with animals in it, presented as doors. tools/make-pets.py writes the room out of data/pets.json. The floor at dusk is ours, drawn as code by Claude to Ryan’s brief: a dog, a cat and a rabbit asleep, the window going dark, and the lamp off because getting up would mean moving somebody. The animals are nobody in particular, and nobody is drawn. The doors are pet flaps, because on a floor at an animal’s height that is what a door is, each this room’s drawing and not the room’s it opens onto. There is one for every room tagged Pets, and the tool will not build without one for a new one. Most of the words quoted are other people’s, read on our own pages: Trauma Geek’s definition of co-regulation and Helen Edgar’s on being with, both on our Co-regulation entry; NDConnection’s lines about mammals on our Polyvagal Theory entry; a video’s line on our Body Doubling entry; Julie Bjelland’s on our Glimmers entry; and Midwest FurFest’s on our Event Access Guide. Nobody read the originals for this room, and each quotation says where it was read. They are checked against our pages word for word on every build where our copy of stimpunks.org is on the machine. Nothing in the room is clinical, ranked, counted or for sale. A garage on the street with the door rolled up, where the work of folks in our community is shown before it is finished. Ryan’s brief of 2026-10-23: a room led by our show your work philosophy and how we practise it, its channel on the CB under Community on the chat page, and Show your work in the forums as the longer-term, longer-form place for the same work. It is built out of our own pages: Show Your Work, our Infodumplings post Show Your Work, One Card at a Time, Default to Open, and our glossary’s Scenius. The idea is Austin Kleon’s, from his book Show Your Work!, which our Show Your Work page is built round, and the word scenius is Brian Eno’s. The book is in copyright, so every line of it in the room is short, read on our page, and credited where it stands; the long passages stay on our page. The created serendipity line is credited to the blog our page names, The Principal of Change, and to nobody’s name, because our page gives none and the room does not fill one in from memory. The garage is ours, made as code by Claude to Ryan’s brief: the day comes in off the street through the open door and runs out before the back wall, so whatever is brought into the light is lit from where you stand. A card is pinned over the bench for every piece of work on it, a box of cards stands with their backs to you because nobody has turned them over yet, and nobody is drawn. The bench holds only what its maker turned over, after our post’s line that turning a card over is the consent: every card names whose the work is as they asked to be named, who said yes and when, where it lives and what state it is in, and says whose words describe it. To start it, the bench holds two unfinished things of our own, Cavendish Cards and this street. A card can carry a photograph of the work under the polaroid wall’s rules (Ryan’s call, the same evening): each is a record on that wall’s own list, kept off Enid’s wall and naming this room, with a description of what is in it in its maker’s words and the yes of whoever took it and anybody in it, no camera data, and gone, not hidden, when its maker asks. Nothing on the bench is ranked or counted, nobody is pitched to or called a genius, and nobody’s draft is marked. tools/make-show-your-work.py refuses the vocabulary of each in the room’s own words, with a window so the room can still say it will not, and skips the quotations. A broadsheet press on the street, in the side of a ship: manifestos and mementos served across your bow. Ryan’s brief of 2026-09-25, a press that prints broadsides the way whysheet.press does, with an introduction to this street as its first sheet. The form is the Stimpunks broadsides’, and every number the press prints to is theirs, written up in the field guide’s notes on print: one sheet, both sides, ink on white in both media, borders rather than backgrounds, two spot inks darkened until they clear on white and no two sheets sharing a pair, and no display serif on the paper. The page, 208 × 277 mm at 9 / 7 / 7 mm margins, is whysheet.press’s, the largest that fits both A4 and US Letter. Theirs is Alfie Kohn’s Why Sheet, a single double-sided sheet laying out a case briskly, and the Stimpunks broadsides say so first. tools/make-broadside.py refuses a sheet that breaks the form, and tools/check-print.py renders the room to a real PDF and refuses anything but two pages a sheet in the sheet’s own inks. Both meanings of broadside are Wikipedia’s, in print and at sea, read on 2026-09-25, and so is the Nelson chequer, the Royal Navy’s bands of black and yellow broken by black gunports, modelled on the scheme Admiral Horatio Nelson used in battle. The drawing of the ship is ours; it is no ship in particular, and it carries no guns. Danny the Street, named on the first sheet’s reverse, is DC Comics’, credited in full on a page of its own. The type is Bodoni Moda, by Owen Earl, for the ship’s name and the room’s headings and nothing on the sheet, and Atkinson Hyperlegible Next and Atkinson Hyperlegible Mono, by the Braille Institute, Applied Design Works, Elliott Scott, Megan Eiswerth and Letters From Sweden, for every word on the sheets and the room’s prose — the faces the Stimpunks broadsides are set in. All three are under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records. The sheets are dedicated CC0 1.0, Ryan’s call of 2026-09-25, like the Stimpunks broadsides: no permission needed and no credit required, and every one says so on the paper and asks for its credits anyway, in a line generated by the tool so that it cannot be left off. The dedication covers the sheets’ words and layout and nothing that is not ours; the room around them stays under this street’s CC BY-SA 4.0, and LICENSE says which is which.

The third area, and the first one under the street rather than past an end of it: a cavern reached by a lift beside the stoop and the stair beside that, lit only by a strip in its handrail. The name is a play on Carlsbad Caverns, with a glad spin and with ARLES in it, the Stimpunks Design Method, whose ladder starts at the bottom, where a person actually is. The caverns take the name and not the method’s shape: no room down there is a rung, and nothing on the page borrows the look of any ARLES poster or deck. Its two numbers are the National Park Service’s, off the weather page for Carlsbad Caverns National Park, read on 2026-09-26: the Big Room averages 56°F (13°C) and moves with the seasons, and the lowest point holds a constant 68°F (20°C) with the air close to saturated. Stay Frosty, at the bottom of the caverns, takes the second one. The rooms down there are not open yet; each one gets its own credits here when it is. Level B3 of Arlesglad Caverns: glow-in-the-dark toys and trinkets in every colour glow comes in, blue included, Ryan’s call. The toys, the drawings and every word about them are ours, and nothing is for sale. Every toy starts dark, is charged by being held up to the rail, and gives the light back; down here that takes seconds rather than hours, so it can be watched. What the room says about how long each colour lasts was checked, and it says which half was. Green glow pigment is the brightest and longest-lasting, with afterglow reported in hours by pigment makers such as Techno Glow’s notes on strontium aluminate. Red and orange are the dimmest and first to go: the pigments are weaker, and the eye is least sensitive to red in the dark, which the introduction to a study of red afterglow phosphors sets out. The order of the colours in between is the room’s own, and tools/make-glow.py refuses a green that does not last longest and a red or orange that is not among the first to fade. The type is Baloo 2, by Ek Type, for the names, and Poppins, by Indian Type Foundry, Jonny Pinhorn and Ninad Kale, for everything that is read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records.

Level B1 of Arlesglad Caverns: a brewery and cellar for wine, beer and kombucha, lit from behind its own glass. Try our house styles is Ryan’s line from the brief; the house styles, their names and every word about them are ours, and the drinks are fiction. Every rule in it is about the people who do not drink: every pour says how strong it is before the pour, and the alcohol-free pour of every style comes first and the same size. tools/make-big-steep.py refuses a pour without its strength, a style whose first pour has alcohol in it, a kombucha that claims a fixed strength, the vocabulary of pressure and of calling an alcohol-free drink an imitation, health claims, a count of drinks, and wood in a cellar of glass and steel. The cellar videos are other people’s, picked by Ryan and played from their uploaders’ own YouTube channels: Tranquility Through Flames, Relaxation Ambience, Serene Ambience, Quiet Ember, Fireside Glow Ambience, Velvet Dark Ambience, Here While You Sleep, Sleepy Soundscaper, Sound eScapes and Elisirium. Their titles are quoted as they wrote them, and every one was checked on its own watch page before it went up: public, not age-gated, on its uploader’s channel, with its length measured. None of them is affiliated with Stimpunks, and none endorses us. The type is Zilla Slab, by Typotheque, for the names, and Red Hat Text, by MCKL, for everything that is read and every strength, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records.

Level B2 of Arlesglad Caverns: a mushroom farm with a restaurant at the end of the growing rooms. The three house specialities are Ryan’s, named in his brief: crispy fried oyster mushrooms, lion’s mane nuggets and mushroom steaks. Every other dish, every drawing and every word about the mushrooms is ours, written for the room. The one line quoted in it is ours too, from The Mycelial Worldview Is Punk, our post for a Campfire Learn Together, and tools/make-mycelium.py checks it against that post word for word wherever the Knowledge System mirror is on hand. Nothing is named in Latin, nothing here is a field guide, and nothing is a supplement. The tool refuses a list of genera and any name shaped like a binomial, the vocabulary of foraging and identifying wild mushrooms, the vocabulary of brains, focus, immunity and medicine that lion’s mane is sold with, and the wood wide web stated as fact. It also refuses a dish with a mushroom the farm does not grow, a crop no dish serves, anything served raw, and a dish that does not say what is in it. The type is Caprasimo, by The DocRepair Project, Phaedra Charles and Flavia Zimbardi, for the names, and Schibsted Grotesk, by Bakken & Bæck and Henrik Kongsvoll, for everything that is read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records. The videos are Derek Sarno’s, on his own YouTube channel: his Mushroom Masterclass - How to cook Mushrooms! playlist on one press, and the most recent videos in it in a rack, chosen by upload date because the playlist is not in date order. Every one was checked before it went up: public, embeddable, not age-gated, on his channel, with its length measured. His titles are quoted as he wrote them. The rack is a copy of the playlist taken on the date printed under it, and a new video is on the whole-playlist press straight away and not in the rack until somebody reads the playlist again. The growing link is North Spore, a shop, with its guide How to Use a Mushroom Fruiting Block Kit, both linked plain with no affiliate code. Neither Derek Sarno nor North Spore is affiliated with Stimpunks, and neither endorses us. Level B5 of Arlesglad Caverns, the bottom, and a quiet place to chill: chill as in calm, not cold. Its one number is the National Park Service’s: the weather page for Carlsbad Caverns National Park, read on 2026-09-26, says the cavern’s lowest point remains a more constant and warmer 68°F (20ºC) and closer to 100% relative humidity, and the room keeps that number because the caverns are named after Carlsbad. It is written once, in data/stay-frosty.json, and tools/make-stay-frosty.py writes it into the room and onto the room’s plate on the lift panel, so the two cannot disagree. The room is not for anything, and its tool holds it there: it refuses a sentence saying what the room will do for you, the vocabulary of cold as a treatment, a count, a clock, a button, a player, a script of its own and any motion in its stylesheet. The CB stays upstairs, the Healing Checkpoint’s way. The type is Geologica, by Monokrom, Sindre Bremnes and Frode Helland, for every word in the room, under the SIL Open Font License and read off its own record.

The room behind Stay Frosty, at the bottom of Arlesglad Caverns: a hall full of fans. It is Ryan Boren’s, and his words for why are on the page, credited to him. Every fan is ours: drawn for the room, named for what it is and never for who made one, and sounded by stay-breezy.js in the visitor’s own browser out of noise, a filter, sometimes a motor’s hum and sometimes a slow beat. None of it is a recording and nothing is fetched or sent. One thing is kept, in the visitor’s own browser: their usual, the speeds they set, the fan on their table and the fans they last had on, under love-breezy, listed on the privacy page. It never switches a fan on by itself. tools/make-stay-breezy.py builds the floor and the room of your own out of data/stay-breezy.json, and refuses a fan without words for how it feels and sounds, two fans that sound the same, a maker’s name, a fan that is for sleep, focus or treatment, a ceiling fan whose lamp is not below its blades, a keyframe that flashes, and a hall that could get louder than the Repeater’s ceiling. The type is Comfortaa, by Johan Aakerlund, for the names, and Urbanist, by Corey Hu, for everything that is read, both under the SIL Open Font License and read off their own records.

An open-air stage at the foot of enormous rock faces, turning 03 in The Outskirts. The real venue is Red Rocks Amphitheatre, near Morrison, Colorado, owned and operated by the city of Denver, formed by two sandstone monoliths named Ship Rock and Creation Rock with the smaller Stage Rock between them, seating 9,525 — read off Wikipedia on 2026-09-22. The room started there and is for outdoor music anywhere now (Ryan’s call, 2026-09-25): every act says where it was played, and tools/make-looming.py refuses one that was not played outdoors. That rule arrived the same day as ten Austin City Limits videos, nine of them taped for the television series in a studio, so only the festival set, in Zilker Park, is on this bill, and the other nine are on the desk in The Live Room, which refuses a set played outside. Looming Rocks is not Red Rocks, or any other real place: it is a room on a made-up street that is fond of the real ones, Stimpunks has no connection to any of these venues or festivals and is not endorsed by them, and the sentient rocks, the solar array and the ultraviolet rig are this street’s own invention. The lichen is real and the room says so without making a lesson of it. Fluorescence under ultraviolet light is a genuine property of many lichens and a genuine field technique for telling species apart. An earlier draft split the page into what is real and what is invented, and Ryan cut it — this is a street named after a genderqueer, shape-shifting road, and a disclaimer explaining that the sentient rocks are fiction is a page apologising for being the thing it is. What still needs saying is the part about somebody else’s property, which is a different job and lives in the credits. The guard stayed even though the paragraph went. tools/make-looming.py refuses anything shaped like a species name anywhere in the file: the room must never say which lichen glows which colour, because nobody here has checked and a confident binomial beside a colour is the format most likely to be believed. That is the herbarium’s refusal arriving in a light rig — but not the herbarium’s check, which does not survive the move. A bare shape test works on a page of short labels and matches the start of nearly every sentence in prose; its first run here refused “Rocks that”, “Once something” and “Ferrell sings”. It is a shape in a place now: sentence starts are ignored, and it only reads sentences that are about lichen at all. Verified in both directions — a real binomial in a lichen sentence is caught, and a band name in a note is not. Every id was checked on its own watch page before it went up — status, playableInEmbed and length — and the runtimes below are measured rather than typed. That matters more here than anywhere else on the street: these are full concerts, none of them under the hour and the longest over two, so a wrong number in front of a press breaks the street’s promise at the largest scale it can. Nothing is hosted by us and every act names the channel it is on — most of them the artist’s or the band’s own, which is the most durable shape of upload this site carries. The count and the range printed in the room are generated from this same file, because both were typed by hand at first and both were wrong within a day. The stage is the Hermitage’s set on a rock face, and it keeps that set’s promises because they are the street’s rather than that room’s: while the stage is dark, tuning is silent and nothing is fetched; once something is playing, tuning changes the picture. looming.js is a separate file from hermitage.js on purpose — the two sets look alike and are not the same object, and a shared widget would be the harmonising instinct arriving through a script tag. What is shared is love-embed.js, still the only thing on this site that builds a YouTube iframe. The running order is a <details> and opens and closes with no script at all. A fairy fort seen from the outside, turning 02 in The Outskirts. Two novel series are what pointed us at it and nothing in the room is drawn from either: Laurell K. Hamilton’s Merry Gentry books and Seanan McGuire’s October Daye books are named and linked in the room as the reason it exists, and not one court, character, politics or cosmology of either is used. Those are invented worlds belonging to living authors, and the difference between being pointed somewhere and helping yourself is the whole of what this site means by attribution. The refusal is enforced rather than remembered — tools/make-sithen.py will not build the page if a rule’s source names either series or either author. The name was checked rather than assumed. Scottish Gaelic sìthean, a hillock inhabited by fairies, from sìth plus the diminutive — cited to Colin Mark’s Gaelic–English Dictionary (Routledge, 2003, p. 530) by way of Wiktionary, read 2026-09-22. That mattered because one of those two series uses this exact spelling for the fae court, and a room taking the name while claiming to owe the books nothing would have been advertising a debt it does not otherwise have. The word is older than both. The documented half is kept apart from the folklore on purpose, because they are not the same kind of claim and a reader should not have to tell them apart by tone. Ringforts, the thirty-to-forty thousand of them identifiable in 1991, the whitethorn taboo and the 1999 campaign that saved a thorn bush from the M18 at Latoon in County Clare were read off Wikipedia’s article on fairy forts and its article on the Latoon fairy bush. The rules are traditional and the readings beside them are ours. Every taboo says where it comes from; every line under what it is like was written for this room and is not claimed to be in the folklore. Nothing on that page tells anybody how to behave, and the tool refuses the vocabulary of advice, because a page about unwritten rules that ended in tips for following them would be a social skills curriculum with thorns on it. The Raven is Edgar Allan Poe’s, first published in the Evening Mirror, New York, 29 January 1845, and out of copyright everywhere. Our text was transcribed from Project Gutenberg ebook #1065, transcribed 2026-09-21. The twenty-six engravings are Gustave Doré’s, made for the 1884 edition and published after his death in 1883, so they are out of copyright everywhere. Ours came from Project Gutenberg’s ebook #17192. Where each one sits is our decision and the room says so: that edition printed the poem straight through and the plates after it, and here each plate stands at the lines its own caption quotes. The captions are printed verbatim, which is how a reader can see that the 1884 text is not quite the one we set beside it. The scanned book is The Raven, Philadelphia: Tyndale, Mitchell & Co., 1865, with illustrations engraved on wood by Scattergood — digitised by Lehigh University and published by the Internet Archive under the Public Domain Mark 1.0. The whole book is there; three leaves of it are shown in the room. A separate facsimile of the poem in Poe’s own hand is linked and not copied, at the Library of Congress: that printing was made in 1949 and carries a reproduction notice on its own first leaf, and this site does not relicense other people’s assets by copying them. One explicit licence and one notice saying no; the room shows the first and points at the second. The typefaces in the picker belong to their own designers, under the SIL Open Font License or Apache 2.0 face by face, and are listed above.

The rooms named after things other people made. None of these people or estates are affiliated with Stimpunks, and none of them endorse us. The rooms are homage, not licence — we took the shape of the idea and wrote our own words in it. Danny the Street A character from DC Comics’ Doom Patrol, created by Grant Morrison and Richard Case, first published in August 1990. A sentient street who turns up wherever somebody needs shelter and rearranges what is on them to suit whoever has arrived. The whole architecture of this site is stolen from Danny, and we would like that on the record — which is why the credit is no longer only in a scrolling marquee that a screen reader never reaches. There is a page about it now: where the name came from, what Danny has been since, the television version, and why the Danny in our marquee uses they/them. Nothing of DC’s is reproduced there; every drawing on it is of a road. Pee-Wee’s Playhouse Created by Paul Reubens. Where the idea of a room in which every object is alive and clickable comes from, and the Playhouse’s secret word too: whenever anybody said it, everybody screamed, and in our room when a toy says it the room screams. The secret word did not start there: Groucho Marx had one on You Bet Your Life, where a duck came down instead, and crediting only the most recent hand is how an idea’s history gets shorter every time it is retold. Pink Pony Club, and Chappell Roan A song by Chappell Roan, and now also a subroom of thirteen videos from the same catalogue. Both take the shape of the work and none of the words — not because a lyric is untouchable, but because this room never needed one to make its point. Where we do quote a song we follow how we quote: a line or two, never the chorus on its own, and the songwriter named separately from the performer. The smial, and J.R.R. Tolkien The Latibulum is drawn as a hobbit-hole — round door, brass knob in the middle of it, thick walls, lamplight, a hill on top — and that shape is Tolkien’s. Smial is his word for it too, which is why it is in this list rather than in a comment. The Tolkien Estate is not affiliated with Stimpunks and does not endorse us. What the room takes is the silhouette and the argument that a hole in the ground is a good place to live; no name, character, place or line of his is used, and the room is named in Latin for that reason. Latibulum — Walkabout Saga The word came to Ryan from A New (Very Old) Word and What It Means for Today, which is where anybody who wants the essay rather than the dictionary should go. The room checks the sense against Lewis and Short rather than restating the post, so that the two can be read against each other. Enid Sinclair A character in Netflix’s Wednesday. Colorful goth, and the patron saint of not matching the house. Riot grrrl A movement rather than an author. The zine table takes its form — xerox, ransom note, staples, free — and none of its text. Quantum queering Barad’s argument, carried into physics education by Alexis Buzzell and Ramón Barthelemy, and read from Autistic experience by Helen Edgar. Esmx the Porkypine — Kaya Oldaker Not borrowed, and in this list anyway. Esmx is the Stimpunks Foundation’s mascot, commissioned from Kaya Oldaker and ours to use; the artist is credited here, in the Arcade and on the drawing itself, because holding the rights to a commission is not a reason to stop naming the hand that drew it. “Esmx” is CC BY-SA 4.0 with an invitation attached — feel free to customise! Make variants of Esmx to represent your community — and the Esmx in the cabinet is us taking our own invitation rather than pasting in the original. Kaya also asks that anybody sharing Esmx include alt text. Esmx’s own page has the originals, every official variant and the blank template. Carlsbad Caverns A national park in New Mexico, looked after by the National Park Service, and the pun in Arlesglad Caverns’ name. We took the pun and two of the Park Service’s published measurements, credited on the page and above; the lift down is ours, although Carlsbad has one too. The park and the Park Service are not affiliated with Stimpunks and do not endorse us. Sonic, and Pokémon Named on Esmx’s own page as the inspiration behind the design, due to their popularity within the Autistic community. No character, sprite, sound or mechanic of either is used here; what the Arcade takes from them is the fact that the mascot already came from that shelf, which is the reason there is an arcade at all. Penguin pebbling — Amythest Schaber Not borrowed and not ours either. Penguin pebbling is one of the Five Neurodivergent Love Locutions, coined by Amythest Schaber (Neurowonderful) and documented by Stimpunks in 2022. The line most people meet it through is @brainsandspoons’: “I thought about you today. I remembered this thing about you. Here’s something I want to share with you specifically.” Helen Edgar wrote it up at Autistic Realms in 2023 — a pebble, a twig, a flower, a photograph from a walk, and explicitly not spending money. The cabinet is built on the locution and on nothing else. Penguin Pebbling, the card game — Helen Edgar & Ryan Boren There is already a Penguin Pebbling game and the cabinet here is not it. Penguin Pebbling: A Game of Creating Belonging, Building Connection and Understanding Autistic Identity is thirty cards across all five locutions, by Helen Edgar (Autistic Realms) and Ryan Boren (Stimpunks), 2026, with Helen’s artwork. Go and play that one — it is the better thing and you can print it. The cabinet takes nothing from it: no cards, no prompts, no artwork, no five-locution structure. The reason is a licence rather than modesty. The deck is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and this site is CC BY-SA 4.0; an adaptation would carry the non-commercial clause onto a page that cannot hold it, and share-alike means that is not a thing we could quietly absorb. Relicensing is not ours alone to do either — half the authorship and all the artwork are Helen’s. What the penguins are actually doing Adélie and gentoo penguins build nests out of stones, carry them about, and steal them from each other. The tidy romance is the popular retelling — one penguin choosing the perfect pebble and presenting it to its beloved — rather than the finding, and the cabinet says so on its own face. The locution is named after the image and is not weakened by that: a metaphor does not have to be a finding. Otterly Adorbs, and the otters — Helen Edgar Not borrowed either, and here for the same reason. The Stimpunks Solidarity Session leaves an otter cam running every Saturday while the conversation drifts in and out, and Helen Edgar wrote down what that was doing for her in Stimpunks Solidarity and Otters (Autistic Realms, 2026) — the otters as parallel play, a cave and a watering hole in one animal. Otterly Adorbs is built on her reading, and it is hers: credited to her by name and not folded into our “we”. Helen is at Autistic Realms. What the otters are actually doing The mechanics come from The Stone You Keep (Star Stuff No. 58), which took Helen’s reading to the primary literature and sources every finding. The three the cabinet states on its own face: Tinker, Bentall & Estes, PNAS 105(2) 560–565 (2008), on individual dietary specialisation — there is no standard otter; Hall & Schaller, Journal of Mammalogy 45(2) 287–298 (1964), Point Lobos, thirty instances over six days, a mussel taking a mean 35.5 blows with a range of 6 to 88; and Law et al., Science (2024), 196 tagged otters, tool use varying enormously between individuals and the users showing less tooth damage. One thing the zine corrects and this cabinet follows: the lifelong favourite rock kept in a pouch under the arm is a popular retelling, not a finding. The primary supports a stone kept and reused across successive food items within a bout of feeding, and that is all the game does with it. Quill Drift’s one rule That a porcupine cannot shoot, throw or fire a quill is the correction on card No. 3 of the Quillery, which sources it to Uldis Roze, Porcupines: The Animal Answer Guide (Johns Hopkins University Press, 2012). It is the cabinet’s whole mechanic and not a note at the bottom of it.

The board is community show-and-tell, and almost nothing on it is ours. Pebbling is Amythest Schaber’s locution, documented by Stimpunks in 2022 and written up by Helen Edgar at Autistic Realms in 2023. Every pin credits whoever made the thing and, where we know it, whoever brought it. Summer 2026: “Things We Collected” — Norah Hobbs Collected at a gathering on 2026-06-25 and assembled by Norah, Stimpunks’ Program Director, in the block editor on stimpunks.org; rebuilt as a standalone page with Claude in June 2026 and carried onto this street on 2026-09-21. The edition’s paper is hers — the cream, the tape, the tabbed drawers, the scatter, the wording of every card, and the decision to set the memorial on its own dark spread at the end. Two of her three typefaces were substituted, and this is the note about it Norah set the board in Caveat, Special Elite and Atkinson Hyperlegible. Atkinson Hyperlegible stays: it is the Braille Institute’s low-vision face, so replacing the body text would have been an access regression rather than a style choice. The other two had to go, because both were already spoken for — Caveat is the Faery Yurt’s glimmer hint and Special Elite is the Zine Table’s typewriter, and a punk-paper noticeboard set in the zine’s own typewriter is exactly the collapse this street exists to refuse. Gloria Hallelujah and Josefin Sans in their place, Ryan’s call on 2026-09-21. Written here rather than left in a diff, for the same reason the one colour of Helen’s that this repo changed is written up in four places. The artwork — Treebeard, PalePixel, NewPartingtonPower A watercolour spread, a lighting study, a trace study, four symmetry doodles and a station ident, all made by members of the community and published here with their permission recorded in data/pebble-board.json. Sharing a drawing at a gathering is not the same as agreeing to have it published on a public site, so the tool refuses a piece whose maker has not agreed. If any of them wants their name spelled differently, linked, or the piece taken down, that is one line in the data and a rebuild. The photographs Governed by the same terms as everything in photos/ and carrying no onward licence. They do not hang on Enid’s wall — a consent record is not a booking for somebody else’s room — but the record and the withdrawal work identically: say so once, and they are deleted rather than hidden. The board is also why the young-person policy was rewritten on 2026-09-21: a flat no-children rule would have taken a teenage volunteer’s own activity off the page and left the adults beside her on it. See the changelog. Four things came off, and one had already gone Two widely-reproduced memes were dropped for having no attributable source. A screenshot of the City of Austin’s Facebook post, a screenshot of an Instagram story, and a foundation’s product render came off because they are other people’s images of other people’s things — the cards themselves stayed, with the stories in our own words. And OK Go’s “And the Adjacent Possible” had gone private between the gathering and publication; the entry is kept in the data with what was measured, the way the Jungle Room keeps its dead cams.

The trope is somebody else’s — the guild hall with the inn over it and the board of posted jobs by the door, ranked by difficulty class, which turns up in more games and shows than anybody could list and is catalogued on TV Tropes. What is ours is what it was pointed at. The Adventurer’s Guild. The job board, the markers standing in every room, and the codes that join them are built from data/quests.json by tools/make-guild.py. The guild sets Rye, a woodtype face for posted bills, and Public Sans, the typeface of the United States Web Design System — a civic form face, because the joke of that room is that it is the one tidy room on a street that refuses tidiness. Both are under the SIL Open Font License. Every question on the board is answered by a sentence already published on the page its marker stands on, and each was read off that page rather than remembered. Where a question asks for a name it is a name one of our own pages already credits. The guild’s badges were asked for by people in our community, and they borrow from three places, each named on the board: the merit badges of Scouting America, a patch for a list of requirements; Open Badges, the format for digital badges that its own site calls verifiable and portable; and video game achievements, which Wikipedia dates, as a system across many games, to the Xbox 360’s Gamerscore in 2005, and before that to the iron-on patches Activision posted in 1982 to players who photographed a high score. What the guild kept of each and what it left is on the board. The drawings are ours, and they are built by the same tool as the jobs. The candle stub on the Faery Yurt’s windowsill is ours, not Helen Edgar’s. That room is her design and this repository does not redecorate it; the only other design change we have made to it unasked is the one colour noted above. On 2026-09-23 Helen gave a standing yes to maintenance that changes nothing you can see, and the first of it is the width and height on her two photographs, so the page no longer jumps while they load; anything that changes how her room looks is still hers to decide. The marker was added with Ryan’s say-so so that her pitch is not the one room on the street with no job in it, it is drawn in her own declared colours, and it is written down here for the same reason the colour is — a change to a contributor’s room should be visible somewhere other than a diff. Helen has the final say on whether it stays. The fractal window’s switch in the Faery Yurt’s sign-off is ours, and Helen Edgar asked for it. Every room on the street has one; hers waited, switched off, until she said yes on 2026-09-27. The picture it opens is drawn only in her room’s own declared colours, the room itself is unchanged, and it is written down here for the same reason the candle stub is. Helen has the final say on whether it stays.

The patches. Every patch for the battle jacket is ours, drawn for this street by tools/make-patches.py out of data/patches.json and lettered in its own room’s face, so each typeface is the one already credited for that room above. Lone wolfing, on the Cave’s patch, is Betsy Selvam’s word for being alone well, and Kindness Is Punk, on Club Chronic’s, is from our own Rules of Punk. A future with dirt behind our ears, on Brighter Days’ Solarpunk patch, is after Adam Flynn’s “Solarpunk: Notes toward a manifesto” (Project Hieroglyph, 2014): “Solarpunk is a future with a human face and dirt behind its ears.” Our glossary credits the line to a video; Star Stuff’s Shared Air zine traced it to Flynn, and the line was read in his piece for this patch. A battle jacket is a punk and metal tradition that belongs to nobody, and nothing of anybody else’s patches is copied here.

The object is somebody else’s: a split-flap indicator board is a Solari di Udine machine, the kind that stood in railway stations and airports for decades and the reason a particular clacking noise still means something has changed. The one in that room is drawn from nothing in CSS, is not one of theirs, and makes no sound. Solari are not affiliated with Stimpunks and do not endorse us. What is on the board One wire per site, read off each site’s own RSS feed by tools/pull-arrivals.py into data/arrivals.json, and drawn by tools/make-arrivals.py. Which feed belongs to which site was read off each sibling repository’s own feed.xml — the self link its generator writes — rather than guessed from the domain. Two of those sites publish more than one feed, so which one a wire carries is a decision recorded in the data file, named on the board and linked. Whose words they are The room holds none of them. A row is a title, a date and a link, and there are no summaries, excerpts or opening paragraphs anywhere on that page — make-arrivals.py refuses a row carrying one. Every title belongs to whoever wrote the page it points at. Several of those sites were built with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms, who is named rather than folded into our “we”; Penguin Pebbling is hers and Ryan Boren’s together. The running order Not ours to choose. It is the order our sites appear in on stimpunks.org’s own feeds page, which is the one place they are already collected by somebody deciding. Re-sorting them here — alphabetically, or by which wire had something newest — would be this room overruling a decision made somewhere else, which is the rule the Jungle Room keeps about its cams. Why it says the minute it was set None of those hosts sends a browser the header that would let our page read its feed, so the board cannot be live, and the ways round that are a proxy we do not run and a third-party reader we would be handing visitors to without asking. So it is a snapshot and it says so: every plate carries the minute its own wire was read, generated from the same file the rows come out of. This is make-jungle.py’s refused runtime upside down — a live camera has no length to give, and a board has a time it was set. What arrives between two settings is said on the room’s CB channel by The Feed itself, read from our server, where no browser’s rule stands in the way. Nothing is ranked No busiest, no quietest, no rows-per-week, nothing saying which of our sites has been getting on with it. make-arrivals.py refuses the vocabulary in the room’s own copy. A board that showed that would turn publishing into a race between our own people, most of whom are Disabled and several of whom are one person. The typefaces Michroma sets the room’s name and the nameboard over each machine and nothing else — a very wide squared face is what machined signage looks like and what a paragraph must never be. Space Mono sets every row, date and plate, because a flap board is a grid of cells with one character in each. Both are under the SIL Open Font License. The prose is the street’s ordinary sans, so only the machine has an accent. This street is on its own board stimpunks.world’s changelog feed is fetched over the network like every other wire rather than lifted out of the file next door, which means the board can be out of date about this site too. A board that listed every sibling and left itself off would be claiming to be the station rather than a platform in it.

The hill is ours, drawn in tools/make-the-source.py from a fixed seed. What it is after is somebody else’s and much older: travertine terraces, the white stone a warm spring lays down on everything it runs over, which stand at Pamukkale in Turkey and at Mammoth Hot Springs in Yellowstone. Neither is drawn, and the room names neither; the hill is nowhere, and nothing in it is a picture of a real place. What is in the pools One pool for every repository whose commit feed stimpunks.org’s own feeds page lists, in that page’s order, read off GitHub’s public commit feeds by tools/pull-source.py into data/the-source.json and drawn by tools/make-the-source.py, which checks the list and its order against the Knowledge System’s copy of that page. A deposit is a commit’s first line, its short id, its day and whose hands made it; the rest of every message stays on GitHub, where it was written, one press away. Whose hands Every name a commit gives: its author as GitHub names them, and anybody its message credits in a Co-Authored-By line, which on these repositories is very often Claude, working with Ryan Boren or Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms and More Realms. GitHub names an author only when the address a commit was made with is an account’s; where it does not, the deposit says somebody GitHub does not name made it, and the address is never read. The morning timers’ own commits are left off. Nothing counts anybody’s commits or ranks a repository, and the tool refuses the vocabulary. GitHub The repositories are kept on GitHub, whose commit feeds these are. GitHub is a trade mark of GitHub, Inc., which is not affiliated with this street; nothing of its design is used here. The channel’s bot The Feed’s and The Source’s CB channels hear each new arrival from a function on our server, runFeedBot in netlify/cb/lib.mjs, after the feed bots people run on Discord; Ryan’s ask, 2026-10-23. What it keeps and who it tells are on the privacy page. The typefaces Philosopher, by Jovanny Lemonad, sets the room’s name, every pool’s name and the headings, and nothing at reading size. Spline Sans, by Eben Sorkin and Mirko Velimirović, carries every word that is read, and Spline Sans Mono, by the same two, sets every short id, day and plate, because those are what a repository writes for itself. All three are under the SIL Open Font License, cut here to the Latin letters, and their records are in fonts/_sources.json.

The knowledge garden is stimpunks.org’s own idea and its own page, and the argument this room is built on — that ideas spread sideways, that nothing needs to be read in order, and that a garden with no fallow ground is a catalogue — is that page’s. What is ours here is the drawing of it. The Garden. One bed per site we publish, built from data/garden.json by tools/make-garden.py. Which sites are in it is not decided in either of those files: the roster and the running order are read out of data/arrivals.json, whose order is the one our sites appear in on stimpunks.org’s own feeds page — the same list The Feed runs on, and the same reason: re-sorting it here would be this room overruling a decision made somewhere else. What each site is was read off that site’s own pages, and where one of them describes itself in a phrase worth keeping, the phrase is attributed to it rather than absorbed — Star Stuff calls itself the public flowering of this garden, which is its sentence and not ours. The notes here are written for this room: The Feed says what has arrived from a site and this says what grows there, because two rooms holding one paragraph is one room with two doors. Every bed says whose hands are in it, on the face of the bed. Half of these sites were made with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms; Star Stuff is a collaboration with More Realms; the Cavendish model is David Thornburg’s three primordial spaces by way of Steve Silberman’s NeuroTribes; monotropism is Dinah Murray, Wenn Lawson and Mike Lesser’s; the pebbling locution is Amythest Schaber’s. A credit filed only here and not in the room is a credit nobody reads, so the generator refuses a bed with nobody on it. The garden next door is Helen Edgar’s and is not a bed. Autistic Realms and More Realms are hers, so the only way to plant them would have been to write them into the roster above — which would put them on The Feed as our own wires and claim her work as ours in the one file this room is not allowed to invent anything in. They are through the ivy instead, and the grammar inverts to say so before the words do: a bed shows its soil and most of them show what is under it, and a plot stops where the ivy runs, because we do not get to draw the ground of somebody else’s garden. Nothing over there casts a shadow either — the sun has not moved, the floor is past the ivy. What each of them is was read off its own pages, and the phrases in quotation marks are theirs. It was a woven fence for an afternoon, and Helen asked for ivy and stars instead. Her call, on a drawing of her own gardens, and she was right about more than the picture: a fence says kept out and ivy says this is as far as we can see. What that line marks is the edge of what we know and never the edge of where anybody may go, which is the opposite reading and the correct one on a page about somebody else’s work. The stars are glimmers caught in the ivy rather than a sky — this room is still midday, nothing is lit by them and nothing was added to the page — and threads, glimmers, and soft, weird spaces is More Realms’ own line about itself, which is where the word comes from. They are limewash white carried by an outline, because white on this path measures 1.07 and what has to separate is the edge: the ghost pipe’s answer in Queering.Earth’s bed, in a star. The drawings are ours, and each one is a different habit of growth — a rhizome, an umbel, a plant with no chlorophyll in it, a frame with seedlings under glass, a runner, a dry seed head, a scramble, a tendril. That is the campground’s grammar inverted on purpose: out in the field each pitch gets one lit colour of its own, and there are not many kinds of light. Every habit is also written out in a sentence beside its bed, because the drawings are decoration a screen reader never reaches and the habit is the argument. The Garden Spider is ours too, and it is an orb weaver rather than anybody’s mascot. The spider’s own words are stimpunks.org’s. That a spider is a guide to the garden and never a replacement for it, and that its best answer is an entrance, are lines from our Ask page, quoted from ourselves rather than paraphrased into something softer. The typefaces are Faustina and Mulish, both under the SIL Open Font License, and this is the one room on the street that sets no display face at all.

The object is nobody’s invention of ours. A zibaldone is a notebook people have been keeping since the fourteenth century, the English word for it is a commonplace book, and our own glossary has had an entry for one since 2022. The room was asked for by somebody in our community — a quote bank, quotes for any state of mind. What is ours is the desk, the drawings and the rules. The good lines belong to the people who wrote them, which is the entire point of the room and the reason its generator refuses so much. The Zibaldone. Built from data/zibaldone.json by tools/make-zibaldone.py, which refuses more than any other generator here: a quotation over its word limit, a song, a line naming a title but no printing, one with no record of how it was checked, a public domain claim that does not clear for the translator as well as the author, a margin note carrying a second quotation, and the vocabulary of ranking. Nothing in that room is ranked, counted or voted on. Every quotation names its printing, and the room prints how it was checked. The public domain lines were read out of the transcriptions named on each card rather than recalled — which is how the Dickinson turned out to be in the second series and not the first, and how the Thoreau kept the sentence he actually wrote instead of the one everybody quotes. A line still in copyright was read off one of our own published pages, or read in the book itself by the person its card names, who gives the page. Michel de Montaigne by way of Charles Cotton’s English, Walt Whitman, Emily Dickinson, Henry David Thoreau, Marcus Aurelius by way of Meric Casaubon’s English, Karen Barad, Helen Edgar, Louisa May Alcott, Simone de Beauvoir by way of H. M. Parshley’s English and Sylvia Plath. A translation is a copyrightable work of its own, so it has to be out of copyright too, and its translator is named on the card. Lines people sent in say who sent them: Betsy. The room quotes lightly and refuses songs. The word limit is a number in the generator and the page prints it; a quote bank is the shape of thing that becomes a book one entry at a time. No song lyrics at all, refused by the tool rather than by care, because nothing musical is hosted on this street and this is where that promise would have been broken in the way that looked most harmless. The typefaces are EB Garamond, Newsreader and Lora for the quotations and Kalam for the hand, all under the SIL Open Font License, and the tool refuses a quotation set in the hand. The drawings are ours, one pressed thing per leaf, and each is described in a sentence beside it because a drawing is decoration a screen reader never reaches. The attribution slip copies to your clipboard and sends nothing anywhere — its fields are Creative Commons’ TASL with the three a quotation also needs.

Seven more facades and six engravings, down the shaft at the end of the street, and a fifth data file because they came from a fifth place: our own glossary entry, Rabbit Hole. Every video below is one of that page’s own embeds, in that page’s order, which interleaves them with the quotations they sit under — so the running order is an argument somebody made and not a list to re-sort. Titles, channels and runtimes were read off YouTube’s own watch pages on 22 September 2026, along with whether each one plays and whether its owner allows it to be embedded; none of them was written from memory. Three are published by a rights holder and four are re-uploads on individuals’ channels, which the room says on every plate, because that changes how long a link lasts. Not one second of it is hosted by us. The words to White Rabbit are not on that page and will not be. Our glossary entry prints them; this one does not. Song lyric reproduction is a minefield in the United States in a way prose is not — music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel — which is the same reasoning that makes the Zibaldone refuse a song outright. So the recordings are offered, Grace Slick’s own published account of writing it is quoted, and tools/make-rabbit-hole.py refuses a lyric field and any value shaped like verse rather than leaving that to anybody’s care. The two headings on that page that are her phrases are credited to her where they stand. The engravings are John Tenniel’s, cut for the first edition of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland in 1865. Tenniel was born in 1820 and died in 1914, so they are out of copyright everywhere; each scan below is one that Wikimedia Commons carries an explicit public domain statement for, which is exactly what the Mopery’s Library of Congress facsimile did not have and the reason that one is linked rather than shown. Every file was re-encoded to greyscale here and written out with no metadata carried over. Nothing was cropped, tinted or filtered. Which engraving sits beside which paragraph is our reading — the 1865 edition captioned none of them — and the room states that rather than letting a reader assume they are looking at the book’s own arrangement. The hole itself is Lewis Carroll’s. One performer is not named and we did not guess. The trailer edit describes itself as an edited remix of the Jefferson Airplane recording and credits no remixer in its title, its description or on its channel, so the plate says what the upload says and says that the hand is unnamed there. The drawing at the top of the room — the shaft, seen from inside it — is ours and is abstract on purpose, because the engravings further down are the real thing.
