Room 429 is built out of one page of ours: the glossary entry for Rest, read out of the Knowledge System mirror on 22 September 2026 rather than fetched live, because on stimpunks.org a 301 is a failure and not a pass. Three lines are quoted from it, each under the thirty-word limit tools/make-checkpoint.py enforces and the room prints, and each one names the page it came from and the day it was checked. Two things on that page are named here and deliberately not copied onto this street — a poem, and three illustrations of Disabled people resting — because a page built out of somebody else’s page should say what it did not take rather than leave it to be noticed. Nothing in that room says what rest is for, and that is a refusal in a tool rather than a habit. Star Stuff’s zine No. 58 spends a spread refusing “rest so you can produce”; otterly.js already holds that line for one cabinet, where floating fills nothing. This is the room where the whole street says it, so the generator sweeps its own data and the published page for the vocabulary of rent — earn, deserve, recharge, productive, bounce back, so you can — with a negation window, so the room can still say out loud that it will not. The friendly edit here arrives from somebody being kind, because every wellness page on the internet is written the other way round, and one sentence of encouragement would turn rest from a thing owed into an investment. Nothing in it is counted and nothing is stored. No total, no streak, no visits, no local storage, no server — which is the pebbling cabinet’s refusal of a tally arriving where a counter is the most obvious improvement anybody could propose, and one floor above a job board that does keep a list in your own browser. A checkpoint that remembered you would be keeping a record of how often you needed one. The Retry-After slips send nothing anywhere: each one is a <details> that works with scripts off, and checkpoint.js only adds a copy button that ships hidden — the Zibaldone’s slip and the guild marker’s arrangement, in a room that cannot afford a dead control. The status code is the joke and it is load-bearing. 429 Too Many Requests was added to HTTP by Mark Nottingham and Roy Fielding in RFC 6585, April 2012, and it says the rate is wrong rather than that the sender is. The room quotes it because a rate is a property of a situation and not of a person. The bed, the alcove and the light in the floor are ours; the trope is TV Tropes’ name for a thing games have always had, and belongs to nobody. The typefaces are Quicksand and Rubik, both under the SIL Open Font License, and they are the only two rounded faces in the room because it is the only room on the street with no hard edge in it. The first three are quoted; the last two are named precisely because their work is not in that room.

The yarn is Helen Edgar’s: her own playlist, Faery Yurt’s Yarn, on her AutisticRealms channel, put on whole in her Music Room, and since 2026-10-18 a second playlist of hers beside it there, Strange things will happen, with a shelf of its own. A third, Library Music, is on the gramophone in her Reading Room the same day, with a shelf of its own there, and the same tool writes it. Every song on it is its artist’s, named on every card, and the channel’s that published it. At Helen’s ask, on 2026-10-13, the songs went on a rack under the phonograph, each playing where it hangs or up on the phonograph in place of the whole yarn, each saying how long it runs before you press it; and at her ask on 2026-10-18, when she had added a good deal to the playlist, the music went through to the Music Room and nowhere else, and the yurt kept its phonograph with a songbook under it listing every song, each line a link to that record next door. The book’s and the rack’s few working sentences are ours, and hers to change. All of it is built from data/yurt-yarn.json by tools/make-yurt-yarn.py, which refuses a song with no runtime, a runtime on the playlist, because she keeps adding to it, and the yarn or a record on the yurt’s own page. One upload on the yarn has embedding switched off by its channel, so its sleeve is a door to YouTube rather than a record that plays here, and says so. The phonograph is ours, and Helen asked for it. It is drawn after a photograph she sent of a reproduction gramophone, brass horn with pressed petals, carved case, turned columns and a crank, and drawn only in colours her room already had: her own, the browns of her portrait frame and shutters, and two of her book spines, the amber one for the brass and the red one for the label. It replaced the small record that used to sit beside her paragraph, and like that record it turns at MAX GLITTER and nowhere else. The moon and star on its label are ours too. Stimpunks.World is a website built as a street. Every shopfront is a door, and behind every door is a room that is its own world, with its own light, its own lettering and its own colours. It is made by Stimpunks Foundation, which builds accessible infrastructure and public tools for Disabled and neurodivergent people. This is the one of our sites that gets to be loud, and it was built to show that loud and accessible are not opposites.
A film, thirty seconds long and silent. It plays only when you press play, and everything it shows is written out underneath.
What the film says and shows

0:00 “As neurodivergent and Disabled people, we’re often told we live in our own worlds.” Then, in yellow capitals: “We said why not.” Small lights come on along the bottom of the screen, one at a time. 0:05 “So we built a street of them.” The stimpunks.world sign lands, and a row of dark shopfronts rises out of the lights onto a pavement. 0:09 “No two rooms alike. Each brings its own light, its own type and its own colours.” Walking past the shopfronts, each door lights up in its own colours with its own name in its own lettering: Pink Pony Club, Club Chronic, The Arcade, The Mopery, The Jungle Room, The Adventurer’s Guild, Laughingstock and Samefood Cafe. 0:16 “How loud it gets is yours to hold.” The street’s dial, asking how loud you want it, turns from Gentle to Regular to MAX GLITTER. At Gentle the doors stand still, at Regular they lift a little, and at MAX GLITTER they sway and sparkles rise slowly past them. “Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words.” 0:22 “Difference is the layout, not the exception. The street rearranges itself for whoever walks down it.” The doors lift and swap places. 0:26 The stimpunks.world sign again, over the lit doors, and: “Nobody has to earn the right to walk in.”

Walk in anywhere. There is no right order, nothing to finish and nothing keeping score. The Map shows the whole street, and the foot of every page has a Where am I? that opens it at the page you are on. Turn the dial. Every page carries it, and the one at the foot of this page works too. Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words, and MAX GLITTER turns everything up. Press play only if you want to. Nothing from anybody else plays or loads until you press it, and every play button says first how long it runs, or that it runs until you stop it. Rest. Some rooms are for nothing else, like the Healing Checkpoint and Stay Frosty. Rest is owed here, not earned. Find people. The Community Center is where to start if you want company.

Because a street can hold rooms that have nothing in common. Every other site we make is careful and consistent; this one has no house style on purpose, because here difference is the layout rather than the exception. The rooms share a dial and a set of promises, and the Mission writes each promise down beside the page that keeps it. The idea of a street that rearranges itself for whoever turns up is not ours. It is Danny the Street’s, a character in DC Comics’ Doom Patrol, created in 1990 by Grant Morrison and Richard Case. The street is not mutual aid. It pays no rent and gives no grant. The foundation does those things, at stimpunks.org.
What is Stimpunks, and where does Stimpunks.World fit in?

Stimpunks offers Disabled- and neurodivergent-led mutual aid and access infrastructure: free tools, language and guides for surviving bad systems, building dignity and living authentically. Stimpunks.World is part of that work. Why we built it, and what it is for, is in the Mission.
How did it start, and how has it changed?

Stimpunks.World started as a way for Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, our Co-Creative Directors, to have fun. So much of what we do is very serious, hyper-diligent, and carefully curated and designed. We wanted a way to tell our stories in a more relaxed and fun way that also invited community. We took inspiration from Danny the Street, created our first few rooms, and ran with it from there. It rapidly grew and morphed into a third space for our community to gather in. Helen and Ryan and others hang out in the world often, chatting in text and video, watching videos together, and building more rooms around our interests and advocacy.
Why does it look like the old web, and what does AI make possible?

This answer is Ryan Boren’s. The throwback to Web 1.0, “the web we lost”, and GeoCities is intentional — a sort of love letter to the early days of the web. Unlike GeoCities, Stimpunks.World has some rules regulating its mayhem: everything must still be accessible, particularly contrast. AI makes Stimpunks.World possible. Without AI, it’d all be a dream still in the can. AI opens all of this to folks who aren’t web developers. Even for experienced web developers like myself, it frees me to focus on being a creative director instead of a programmer. I’m retired from software development and have no desire to go back to slinging code. Generative AI agents are better at it and more up-to-date on the latest conventions, techniques, and tools than I ever was anyway. Leveraging AI, we can use things like HTML5 animations and modern CSS and JS techniques, all while keeping it accessible. One of our primary motivations with Stimpunks.World is to use open source software, publish everything we build for the site in the open under CC BY-SA 4.0, and own as much of the resulting software stack as possible. We want to be less reliant on third party platforms. We are getting tired of platforms succumbing to enshittification and executives at those companies revealing that they are fascist, bigoted assholes. We seek to escape rentier technofeudalism with deliberately boring technology and generative AI. We keep third parties few, and we name them. The site is hosted on Netlify. Hosting our own video serving infrastructure is beyond us, so our calls run on Jitsi, an open source video and audio stack, on a platform hosted by 8x8, a company we currently trust. Most films on the street are YouTube embeds, the music players are Spotify, Apple Music and TIDAL, and nothing from any of them loads until you press play. How the site runs lists every outside service it contacts. Everything is designed so that we can swap out third party parts if necessary.
Has the technology helped bring lived experience online?

The tech has greatly enabled expression of our humanity and lived experiences. Coding and full-stack web development knowledge are no longer necessary to tell your story in interesting, interactive, and accessible ways on the open web. Samefood Cafe, about samefoods, safe foods and food aversions, is one of those stories.
What are you hopeful about with AI, and what worries you?

We list our many reservations about AI in our AI Hub. We acknowledge and confront the many downsides of generative AI, while at the same time exploring how AI can assist constructionism and access. AI is at its most helpful when enabling constructionism and helping us build and leverage knowledge gardens. Many of the problems with AI are not intrinsic to it, but rather are very human political problems resulting from our extractive and exploitative systems that are currently failing us all, including the planet. The biggest danger of AI is our lack of political will to harness it safely in service to the commons.
Where’s a good place to start?
Start on the front pages at stimpunks.org and stimpunks.world and take it from there. They both reward freestyle exploration.

I could not live in any of the worlds offered to me – the world of my parents, the world of war, the world of politics. I had to create a world of my own, like a climate, a country, an atmosphere in which I could breathe, reign, and recreate myself when destroyed by living. — Anaïs Nin,
The Diary of Anaïs Nin, Vol. 5: 1947–1955

As neurodivergent and Disabled people, we’re often told we live in our own worlds. We said why not and built Stimpunks.World. It’s infused with fantasy and hopeful longing, but also rimed with hard lessons in hard reality. You don’t have to explain reality to us. We live closest to it. We’ve found better ways, and present them here. Read off the front page of stimpunks.org, which quotes it, and not checked against the Diary from here. That page’s copy prints the pronoun as a vertical bar, a slip from reading the words off an image; it is an I here. What follows is the street’s mission. Every aim names the page where it is already being kept, and the failure that would show we had quietly stopped, because a list of values you cannot check against the work is only a list. The argument underneath it is the manifesto, Ribald Songing, printed as a broadside you can pin up. Last updated 2026-10-22. Every change to it is dated in the changelog.
THE WHOLE OF IT, IN ONE SENTENCE

Stimpunks.World is the Stimpunks Foundation getting wild, wacky and loose on purpose: a street of rooms that share nothing but a dial and a set of promises, built so that difference is the layout rather than the exception, and so that nobody has to earn the right to walk in.

Belonging comes before anything else. The street is Danny’s, and it rearranges itself for whoever turns up, so it has no wrong side and no outside to push anybody to. Even the road past the last streetlight, The Outskirts, is a direction and not a verdict. We would have stopped the day a page calls any corner of the street the place where the people who do not fit end up. No two rooms alike. Every room brings its own light, its own type and its own colours, even where they argue with the room next door, and that repetition of ideas in different clothes is the product. How this site is made says why. We would have stopped the day two rooms share a palette because it was tidier.
What we owe whoever walks in

How loud it gets is yours to hold. Every page carries the dial, and Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. A checker renders every page at every setting to hold us to it. We would have stopped the day Gentle shows somebody less, or anything moves before they asked. Nothing from anybody else plays or loads until you press it, and every play button says, before the press, how long the thing runs or that it runs until you stop it. We would have stopped the day a video frame loads on arrival. Clashing is not the same as illegible. The colour under every word is measured, and a pair that fails stops the build. We would have stopped the day a colour ships because it looked fine. Rest is owed, not earned. The Healing Checkpoint and Stay Frosty are for it, and neither says what rest will do for you afterwards. We would have stopped the day a room calls rest a way to recharge for more work. Nobody is counted, ranked or scored. No tally in the pebbling cabinet, no score on the Adventurer’s Guild’s board, where a badge is a set of things done that go together and nothing counts how many anybody has, no headliner on any bill. The numbers on the street belong to nobody: Pando Calrissian’s, how many times we have watered one tree together, and Count Me In’s, the step we have climbed to together and the highest it has reached. None of them says who. The street counts people in three places. The World room’s Most active order, Ryan’s call of 2026-10-18, puts the rooms with the most people seen in them and in their calls first, works it out each time, and shows no number and names nobody for it. And a poll in the forums, his call of 2026-10-22, says how many picked each choice, in the poll’s own order, never sorted by it and with no winner marked: a show of hands with the names of who picked it, and a sealed ballot only once it closes, with nobody’s pick kept. And the member map on the Community Center’s wall, his call of the same day: how many of us live in each place, by our own choosing on the Join form, never with anybody’s name. Behind the street, the people who look after it count. The desk in the Moderators’ room says how many usernames there are and how many are seen in a room now, his call of 2026-10-22 after moderators asked for it for safeguarding, because this rule is about what everybody sees; nobody else is shown it, and nobody has a total of their own there either. We would have stopped the day anybody on the street has a total of their own, or anything grows a progress bar. Your face and your voice stay yours. A photograph goes up only with its subject’s own consent, stays outside the site’s licence, and is deleted when they say so, as Enid’s wall promises. A recording of a voice says whose it is on the press. We would have stopped the day a photograph is still up after somebody said no. We keep as little about you as we can, and the privacy page says exactly what that is. We would have stopped the day something is kept that the page does not name.

The credits get louder, not quieter. Every writer, printing, typeface and drawing hand is named, in the room and in the liner notes, because attribution is the one careful habit this street kept when it dropped the others. We would have stopped the day a quotation goes up without the printing it came from, or a song without its writers. In the open, errors included. Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar build the street, and either of them can change anything in it. Changes are dated in the changelog, and a correction to something we published stays on its page, where the person who read the mistake will see it. We would have stopped the day a mistake is quietly swapped for the right answer.
What a street has to do with Stimpunks

Stimpunks builds accessible infrastructure and public tools that support disabled and neurodivergent people to live with dignity, challenge dehumanizing systems, and design environments that honor difference as strength. — We, Stimpunks, Mission
What a street has to do with Stimpunks

The Stimpunks Foundation is created by and for neurodivergent and Disabled people, and its mission begins with direct support and mutual aid. It also says this: This street is the last part of that sentence, built rather than argued: an environment where difference is the architecture. It is also the only one of our sites that gets to be loud, and it was built to show that loud and accessible are not opposites.

This street is not the foundation’s mutual aid. It pays no rent, buys no groceries and gives no grant. The foundation does those things, and the street says so and sends people there. What the street has is a room where people ask each other: Community Care’s channel on the CB is for asking our community for mutual aid, peer support and any other help, and that room names the foundation’s grants without promising them. A page of loud rooms that let anybody blur the two would be doing the thing we exist to name. It also does not speak for every Disabled or neurodivergent person, and it is not finished: the street keeps growing, and if the rooms stop matching this page, the page is what is wrong.

The opening is Ryan Boren’s, in the foundation’s own voice. Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, drafted the rest of this page and the manifesto to Ryan’s brief of 2026-09-29, from what the street already does. How we use AI is written up on its own page. Ryan and Helen Edgar have the final say on every line.

If what the street is for changes, this page changes with it, the date at the top moves, and the change is written up in the changelog on the day, where the feed will pick it up. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.

Every other Stimpunks site has a design system. This one has a street instead, and every room on it refuses to look like the one next door. This page says what is shared, what is not, what gets checked, and who makes it, including how we use AI. Last updated 2026-10-18. Every change to it is dated in the changelog.

No design system, on purpose. Every room is its own visual world, and no two are alike. One thing every room shares is the dial, so how loud the street gets is up to you. Loud is allowed. Illegible is not. Contrast is measured on every page. Nothing from anybody else plays or loads until you press it. The credits are loud, because attribution is the one careful habit this street kept. Most of the building is done by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, working to briefs from Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar. What that means is below.

Queering Earth is drawn as a herbarium sheet in daylight. Star Stuff has a design system page with a palette you can copy. Both are careful, and so is every other site we run. This one started from Ryan’s brief of 2026-09-19: “All of our sites are so careful. Careful color palettes, careful fact checking, careful sourcing, careful attribution. I wanna get wild and wacky and loose.” So here the street is the system and the rooms refuse to share one. Each room brings its own ground, its own typefaces and its own palette. What does the most work is that each one is lit differently. The Faery Yurt is candlelight in canvas. The Latibulum has one low lamp in a burrow. The Community Center gets north light through one window onto a hill, with a seat built in under it. The Healing Checkpoint is lit from under the floor. The Outskirts has nothing but headlights, and the Adventurer’s Guild is lit like a photocopy, from nowhere at all. When two rooms are about the same feeling, something structural keeps them apart: where the light comes from, what the room is built of, which way round the words sit. A nudge to a colour will not do it. The instinct to tidy all that up, with one type scale, one palette and shared components, is the right instinct on every other site we make. Here it would delete the thing the street is for. The rule we work to is short: if a change would make two rooms look more alike, it is probably wrong. You will not find a count of the rooms anywhere on this site. The street keeps growing, and a total written into a dozen places goes out of date in eleven of them the day a room opens. A small checker refuses any sentence that states one.

One stylesheet, love.css, holds the whole street. It opens with a small shared base: the typefaces, a few ground rules every page needs (the skip link, the focus ring, making sure a hidden thing stays hidden), the dial, and some shared furniture. That furniture is the press-to-play plate, the job marker from the Adventurer’s Guild, the fractal window and the sign-off at the foot of every page. It carries layout and no colour of its own, so it turns up in each room wearing that room’s ink. After the base, every room gets a section of its own, free to contradict all the others. Those sections duplicate each other’s ideas in different clothes, and that duplication is the point. The pages that have a job to do and no room to be, like this one, Privacy, the liner notes and the changelog, share one quiet look and otherwise get out of the way.

Every page has a dial with Gentle, Regular and MAX GLITTER on it. It starts wherever your device says about reduced motion, and once you pick a setting your browser remembers it (that is love-intensity on the privacy page). Gentle stills everything. Regular moves things when you hover over them or focus them. MAX GLITTER turns on the ambient layers, like the mirrorball over the dancefloor and the sparks at the guild. Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. No content is kept behind a louder setting, and nothing you can read at MAX is missing at Gentle. A checker loads every page at all three settings and measures both halves of that. Games keep a speed control of their own, separate from the dial, so Gentle never hands anybody a lesser game. Nothing on the street flashes or strobes, with one exception. The Rebellion Rave Room has a strobe for the people who stim with one, and it sits behind a warning and two presses. This is a Disabled people’s organisation. A glitter-maximalist site that overwhelmed the people it is for would be the kind of self-own we exist to name. We did not fix that by toning the site down. We made loudness something the visitor holds. Access is the premise of this design, not the brake on it.

Clashing is not the same as illegible. All text on the street is held to WCAG AA contrast against every ground it sits on, and two different checkers do the holding. The first is a list of every text colour and ground somebody chose, each with its ratio and the reason beside it. The second renders every page in a browser and measures each piece of text against the colour actually behind it, because the colour that renders is not always the colour that was written down. Each checker has caught failures the other could not see. Decoration that carries no words is listed with its measurement rather than ignored, and every room chooses its own focus ring, because a ring picked for a dark street disappears on a pale one. The one change this repository made to Helen Edgar’s design for the Faery Yurt was a single grey, which failed contrast on every ground it sat on. That change is written up in the liner notes and the changelog rather than left in a diff.
Nothing plays until you press it

Every video and player on the street is a plate standing in for the real thing. Until you press it, this site has made no request to that service for you. Every plate says how long it runs before you press it. A live camera or a playlist has no length to give, so its plate says that instead. Every typeface, script, stylesheet and image is served from this site, so opening a page talks to nobody but our host. The full account is on the privacy page.

Every typeface is self-hosted, and a room only downloads the faces it sets. The Foundry holds every face on the street, with who drew it, what licence it travels under and which rooms set it, all read from each family’s own record in Google Fonts’ public repository rather than typed in. Most are under the SIL Open Font License and a few are under Apache 2.0. We know that because a tool read those records and found our own credits saying every face was OFL.

Every page has a share card, the picture that shows up when somebody posts a link. Each one is rendered in a headless browser from the page’s own markup and stylesheet, with a design for each room rather than one template, and none is written without alt text. A new room will not build until it has a card of its own. A room with somebody else’s face on its card would be the street tidying itself up somewhere nobody looks.

The site is plain HTML files, one stylesheet and some small scripts, with no framework and nothing to compile before it can be served. Next to them sits a workshop of Python tools. Some generate the parts of a page that have to agree with a data file: a jukebox’s track list, a credit, the sitemap, a share card. Others check things we have got wrong before: a page left out of the sitemap, a photograph still carrying its location, a colour nobody measured, a quotation longer than a room allows, a credit with nobody’s name on it. The tools refuse rather than guess, and when one refuses, we fix the cause and leave the tool alone. It is hosted on Netlify. The only code that runs on a server is the CB radio, together with its chalkboard, its pebble bowls and the Slake. Everything else is files. The source and its whole history are on GitHub. Architecture has the code and the hosting in full: the deploy, the generators and checkers, the CB’s server side, the morning timers and every outside service. Our words and design are under CC BY-SA 4.0. Photographs, recorded voices, songs, typefaces and borrowed names keep their own terms, the broadside sheets are given away under CC0, and the licence file says which is which.
Who makes it, and how we use AI

Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar make this street. They decide what each room is, what it argues, what it refuses and where on the street it goes. They write the briefs that the rooms quote, and they correct the rooms when they are wrong. The Faery Yurt is Helen’s own design, from a mockup she built. Most of the building is done by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, in Claude Code sessions that Ryan or Helen directs. Claude writes nearly all of the code: the pages, the stylesheet, the scripts, and the generators and checkers described above. It also drafts most of the words in the rooms, working from the briefs, from our own pages on stimpunks.org, and from the sources each room credits. Nearly every change in the site’s public history names Claude as a co-author, so you can see which parts it wrote. Some specifics, so nothing here has to be guessed at: The drawings are code. The pictures you see in the rooms, from the shopfronts to the chairs, are SVG shapes and CSS, and Claude writes that code to a brief. No image generator made any picture on this street. Stimpunks does not use generative AI for art on stimpunks.org. These drawings are made by a language model writing code, and we would rather say that plainly than call them hand-drawn. The one film on the street, on the About page, is code too: Claude wrote it in Claude Motion, as shapes and type moving over time, and it was exported from there as a video. The three chimeras on the wall in Chimera Obscura are the exception: Becky Hicks drew them by hand for stimpunks.org’s About page, and they hang here with her yes. Every chimera made on that room’s bench is code, like the rest. The photographs and the old engravings are not AI-made. The photographs are of real people and real things, published with consent and credited. The engravings and plates are public domain scans, each one credited to its artist. In the Collection Collection, Claude describes the photographs by looking at each one, so that nobody has to write a title, a description and a caption before they can send in a picture. Every cabinet says so on its label. No voice on this site was made by an AI. Every recorded voice belongs to the person named beside it. When the CB reads messages aloud, it uses your own device’s voice. Nothing you do here is sent to an AI. No page on this street calls an AI service. The Garden’s spider links out to Ask, the generative search on stimpunks.org, and says what that is before you go. What an AI gets wrong, and how this site catches it. A language model’s most common mistakes are exactly the ones this site’s tools are built to refuse: a quotation, a credit or a number written from memory, a book link that points at a different book, a framing borrowed because it sounded right. Many of those mistakes were Claude’s, and many are written up in the changelog along with how they were found. Quotations are checked against a source, and each one says how it was checked. Where one could not be checked, the page says that too. Checkers catch what can be checked. People looking at the page catch the rest, and several faults on this street were found by Ryan simply pressing the buttons. Stimpunks’ policy on all of this is AI Collaboration at Stimpunks, and the thinking behind it is at AI at Stimpunks and AI, Disability Justice, and the Ethics of Making. Those pages name the tensions honestly, the energy and water costs included, and we carry the same tensions here. Generative AI is built from knowledge taken from communities, so what we make with it goes back to the commons. That is one reason everything we write here is under an open licence.

If how this site is made changes, and especially if how we use AI changes, this page changes with it, the date at the top moves, and the change is written up in the changelog on the day, where the feed will pick it up. Every page is a hand-written HTML file at the repository root, complete before any script arrives, styled by one shared stylesheet and plain scripts with no framework and no dependencies. There is deliberately no design system: each room is its own visual world, and the code is arranged so that stays true. A page. Its <body> class names the room, and that class is the hook for the room’s section of love.css and for its share card. Gentle, Regular and MAX change motion and sparkle only, never content. §3’s reset carries !important, and rooms scope their own tilts with :where() so the reset can win. check-gentle.py measures every page at all three settings. Then love-embed.js checks the address against its list and swaps the button for a youtube-nocookie.com frame, or another origin on the list. A room styles the pressed state on the container, because the button’s classes do not survive the swap. What your browser keeps. Only localStorage, and only in your browser: love-intensity (the dial), love-cb (your CB pass and handle), love-cb-guest (the guest panel left open), love-quests (the Guild’s list), love-rescues (animals you rescued) and love-breezy (Stay Breezy’s usual fans). Privacy says the same. Every read and write is wrapped so a private window still works. Machine-readable files, all generated: sitemap.xml, llms.txt, feed.xml (from the changelog), cb-rooms.json, search-index.json, /.well-known/security.txt, /.well-known/api-catalog and the agent skill under /.well-known/agent-skills/.

The pages are hand-written, but any part of a page that restates a list, a credit or a fact held somewhere else is generated from a JSON file by a Python script, so the two cannot drift. The scripts are local tools in tools/; none of them runs on a server. The usual path is data/<room>.json to tools/make-<room>.py to the room’s page, between markers, and usually to the liner notes as credits too. Marker regions. A generator only ever rewrites text between a pair of comments such as <!-- jukebox:begin --> and <!-- jukebox:end -->. Everything outside the markers is hand-written. Every page has at least the sign-off and the structured data between markers. A room somebody built with their own AI and brought in through Your Room sits between import:<slug> markers. Generators refuse rather than guess. Each one checks its data against the promises its room makes before writing: a runtime on every track, a credit on every quotation, a consent record on every photograph, an allowed origin on every player. A refusal stops the build and nothing after it runs. Kind Tools What they write Room builders make-<room>.py, one per room with data That room’s marker regions, and usually its credits in the liner notes Readers of the rooms make-now-playing.py, make-map.py, make-signoff.py, make-structured.py Now Playing, the map, every sign-off, every page’s structured data. They read the published pages, so they run after the builders. Site files make-sitemap.py, make-search-index.py, make-feed.py, make-agent-files.py, make-security.py sitemap.xml, llms.txt, cb-rooms.json, search-index.json, feed.xml, /.well-known/* Headers make-csp.py The policy line in _headers, from love-embed.js’s origin lists and the pre-paint snippet’s hash Images make-webp.py, make-og.py, make-icons.py WebP only where it is as faithful (SSIM 0.98 or better) and at least 10% smaller; a share card per page in og/; the favicons Network pulls pull-arrivals.py, pull-doom-scoop.py, pull-vital-rack.py, pull-notebook-month.py, pull-large-month.py, pull-cookin-month.py, pull-green-latest.py, pull-club.py, pull-foundry.py A data file refreshed from feeds or GitHub. That covers feed.xml, sitemap.xml, llms.txt, cb-rooms.json, search-index.json, everything in og/, data/og-prints.json, the policy line and anything between markers. On a merge conflict in one of them, take either side, fix the source and run the build again. Share cards. make-og.py drives headless Chrome to photograph a scrap of markup on the page’s own body class with love.css attached, and lifts the page’s heading word for word. There is a card design per room and no template. It keeps the committed picture when nothing that decides it has changed, because two Macs draw the soft edges of letters differently.

tools/check-all.sh is the build and the test suite in one. It runs every generator and every checker in the one order that works, stops at the first refusal, and changes nothing on a clean tree. It runs before every commit; Netlify does not run it. The Node tests. netlify/cb/lib.test.mjs races writers against each other and fails if any write that was told it worked is missing. tools/fractal.test.mjs counts flashes in what the fractal window paints. Images, before anything refers to one. The room builders, each from its own data file. The things that read the rooms: Now Playing, the map, sign-offs, structured data, the sitemap, the search index, the feed, the policy line, the agent files, share cards, icons and security.txt. The checkers, against what was just written. Checker Refuses Renders in Chrome check-contrast.py A text and ground pair under WCAG 1.4.3, and any colour on :root that is neither measured nor exempted with a reason no check-contrast-live.py Rendered text against the ground it actually sits on. It declines rather than guesses on a gradient. yes check-focus.py A focus ring that cannot be seen against its ground yes check-gentle.py Rotation, skew or ambient motion left at Gentle, and content that changes between dial settings yes check-print.py A zine page that is not one sheet, a broadside that is not two pages a sheet, an ink not on the allowed list yes, to PDF check-weights.py Two of the Foundry’s weights that render the same letters yes check-headings.py A skipped heading level, or other than one <h1> no check-ids.py An id used twice on a page, or a script asking for an id no page has no check-classes.py A class claimed by two rooms, a custom property declared twice, a section number out of order no check-counts.py A sentence stating how many rooms, pages or typefaces the street has no check-quests.py A job code that disagrees between a room and the Guild’s board no check-faces.py A typeface in fonts/ missing from the Foundry or the Mopery’s picker no check-teleport.py The room search drifting apart between the radio, the guest bar and the finder no Left out of the build on purpose: anything that needs the network. check-jukebox.py asks YouTube’s watch page whether every play button’s video still plays and still embeds, and it is run by hand. A gate that fails on a train is a gate people learn to skip. When a tool refuses, the cause gets fixed. Loosening a check, or adding an exemption to quiet it, is the one change the repository’s rules forbid outright.

The CB, a chat channel patterned after citizens band radio, is the only server-side code on the site: Netlify Functions in netlify/functions/ sharing one library, netlify/cb/lib.mjs, and one Netlify Blobs store. Every promise on Privacy is kept in that library. How it runs. Each function is a JavaScript module whose config gives its address and a Netlify rate limit. A request carries the pass from the browser, readPass() checks it, and a change is written only if the stored copy has not changed since it was read, so people writing at once never lose a message. Three functions are scheduled, two of them every hour. cb-midnight sweeps whatever has expired; it runs hourly because everything it sweeps goes at its own time, a message two weeks after it was sent, a note at the end of its week, and its name is older than that, from when the channel was cleared at midnight in Colorado. cb-recur makes the task each recurring task owes on its day, by the same clock. cb-office-daily runs late each evening in Colorado, keeps the office’s line for that night (how many grant requests, cases and tasks were open, counts only, sealed) reads our QuickBooks books, if the office is connected, and reads our Givebutter account, if its key is set. The radio only asks while it is open and in front. One function in cb.js decides; folded, or in a background tab, the radio sends nothing. Open, it listens every four seconds. Tuned to World it says nothing about where it is; tuned to a room it names that room. Area Addresses What is kept, and for how long Signing on /cb/signon, /cb/join, /cb/account, /cb/account/recover, /cb/account/admin, /cb/invites A pass is an HMAC keyed by a secret, kept only in your browser. Joining takes an invite and claims a username: a salted scrypt hash, a version and a lock, filed under a hash of the name, and an email address for recovery only if somebody gives one, sealed with the office’s key and sent nowhere but a reset code they ask for, through the team mailbox. An invite counts its uses and never who used it. No list of accounts. The channels /cb/channel, /cb/transmit, /cb/moderate, /cb/edit, /cb/react, /cb/image A hundred messages per channel (World, or one per room), each gone two weeks after it was sent, unless an administrator sets the channel otherwise at the desk (/cb/channel-rules); a message is stamped with its channel’s time when it is sent, and a listen sends the latest hundred and only when something changed. Whoever sent one can edit its words, and the words it replaces are not kept. Pictures are redrawn in your browser, refused if they still carry metadata, and deleted with their message. Being seen, and watching together /cb/here, /cb/here/leave, /cb/online, /cb/beacon One record per visit, shown for 30 seconds after its last check; Who’s online is read from those records, and from the call records the rooms whose calls have somebody in them, and nothing records who looked. A host’s beacon is replaced, never added to. Calls /cb/call, /cb/call-events, /cb/call-settings Nothing about a call. It signs an 8x8 token for one handle and one room, or for the World call, which is one more call under its own name, and reads 8x8’s webhooks for who is in a call. Boards /cb/chalk*, /cb/pebbles*, /cb/brass*, /brass-tacks.xml The chalkboard and the pebble bowls: a week. The Brass Tacks Board: until a moderator takes a post down. Forums /cb/forum, /cb/forum/file Topics in categories, for claimed usernames only, each gone a week, three or six months after its last post, or kept, as its category says. A post’s author is kept as a hash of the username and when it was claimed, and never sent. Pictures, redrawn in your browser, and files, checked against their first bytes, are fetched with the pass by readers of their topic only, and go with their post; an upload no post took goes after a day. An @mention tells a device that asked, from the server, when the post is made. Nothing about who reads. Tasks /cb/tasks The team’s to-do list, for directors, board members and administrators only: every task in one record, each kept until somebody deletes it, with who it is assigned to and who changed it last. Its recurring tasks are kept beside them, and each makes its task on its day. Nothing about who reads. The office /cb/office Contacts, grant requests and cases, moved from EspoCRM, and mailing templates and mailings, for directors, board members and administrators only: every contact in one record, every grant request in another and every case in a third, each encrypted with AES-256-GCM under CB_OFFICE_KEY, which only the functions hold; without it the office is shut. Nothing about a contact, a request or a case is logged, and nothing about who reads. On a director’s press on a join request, and never otherwise, it sends Givebutter a name, an email and the mailing lists they said yes to, with CB_GIVEBUTTER_KEY, and adds their line to stimpunks.org’s Members page, or their organization and its logo to the Organizations page and its media library, through WordPress’s own REST API, as one WordPress user with an application password in CB_WP_USER and CB_WP_APP_PASSWORD, asking for those pages and nothing else. A logo is fetched only from the Join form’s own uploads on stimpunks.org, and goes with its camera data taken off. The office’s intake /cb/office/intake stimpunks.org’s forms, posted one entry at a time by a WordPress plugin on stimpunks.org’s server, each signed with an HMAC of the time and the body under CB_OFFICE_INTAKE_KEY, which the two servers share and which is never sent. It finds or adds the contact by email and makes the grant request or case, never twice for one entry. Nothing about an entry is logged. The office’s mailbox /cb/office/mail The team mailbox’s email with our contacts, posted one email at a time by a Google Apps Script inside the mailbox, each signed with an HMAC of the time and the body under CB_OFFICE_MAIL_KEY, a key of its own. The script asks for a keyed hash of every contact’s address and sends only email with a contact, and adds a contact, with only the name and address off the email, when the team puts a label on one of their emails in Gmail; it also asks for the outbox, the emails of a mailing a director confirmed, which is the one answer with anybody’s address in it, sends each from the team mailbox, and says each went; the office files it whole, sealed like the rest, on each contact it is with, never twice, and never one deleted from the office. Attachments stay in Gmail. Nothing about an email is logged. Shared games /cb/pando*, /cb/fridge*, /cb/stair*, /cb/shelter*, /cb/pets*, /cb/adopted A tree’s count, finished sentences and a stair’s step, kept with no name in them. Adopted pets, under a hash of the handle, until Forget Me. Profile /cb/avatars*, /cb/jobs*, /cb/patches* Avatars, kept as lists of choices; the jobs you keep from the Adventurer’s Guild and the patches on your battle jacket, which ones and nothing about when; all under a hash of the handle until Forget Me. A badge is worked out from the jobs and kept nowhere. The Slake /cb/mud/here, /cb/mud/say, /cb/mud/leave, /cb/mud/moderate Presence per visit, replaced on moving. Each place’s talk goes two weeks after it was said. The sweep cb-midnight, scheduled Deletes what has expired across all of the above Recurring tasks cb-recur, scheduled Makes the task each switched-on recurring task owes, on its day in Colorado, never twice The office’s way back from Intuit /cb/office/quickbooks Where Intuit sends a director after they connect the office to QuickBooks. It keeps the tokens, sealed, only if the state the office handed out is the one kept, unused and under ten minutes old; reads the books once; and sends them back to the dashboard. The office only reads our books, from quickbooks.api.intuit.com, with the app’s id and secret in CB_QB_CLIENT_ID and CB_QB_CLIENT_SECRET. Nothing about the books or the tokens is logged. The office’s night cb-office-daily, scheduled Late each evening in Colorado, how many grant requests were open in each pipeline, and cases and tasks, as one sealed line for the dashboard’s trend lines, numbers only, 400 nights; then QuickBooks’ last 30 days of money in and this year’s profit and loss, if the office is connected, and Givebutter’s last year of gifts, its recurring plans and its campaigns, with nobody who gave named, from api.givebutter.com with CB_GIVEBUTTER_KEY Never stored: an IP address (Netlify’s limiter counts them and never hands them over), anything a person types in a log line, an email address, or a list of who has signed on. Who’s online is worked out from the thirty-second records Be seen here keeps, each time somebody asks. Roles. CB_MODS says which handles hold which roles, and it is read on every request. The server decides who may enter each private room in the Town Hall, in one function. A page that hides its radio from the wrong person is only keeping quiet; it is not the lock. Calls are 8x8’s Jitsi as a Service. The CB signs a token with CB_JAAS_KEY for one room, and nobody joins without one. Guests get a token, never a moderator’s, only for the rooms Cavendish Coworking keeps open to the world. love-embed.js builds the call’s frame, and 8x8 is the only origin given the camera, microphone and screen.

The rooms that show other sites’ feeds are snapshots refreshed by Ryan’s laptop each morning, not live pages. None of those hosts lets a page read its feed from another site, and the alternatives were a proxy we do not run or a third-party reader. Each room prints when it was last set, so a missed morning leaves an honest page rather than a wrong one. The task. A Claude Code scheduled task, arrivals-board-daily, runs at 06:10 local time on Ryan’s machine. Its instructions are tracked in .claude/scheduled-tasks/arrivals-board-daily/SKILL.md, and tools/install-scheduled-task.sh installs that copy and reports drift. The schedule itself lives in the scheduler, not the repository. Each script does the same five things. It refuses unless the tree is on main and its own files are clean. It pulls, which is the only network step; redraws its room; runs the fast offline checkers as a gate; then commits only its own files under a fixed subject and pushes. A failed push is left for a person. The scripts never rebase or force. Script Room Commits Subject daily-arrivals.sh The Feed data/arrivals.json, the-feed.html daily arrivals board reset daily-scoop.sh The Doom Scoop data/doom-scoop.json, the-doom-scoop.html, now-playing.html daily doom scoop edition daily-vital.sh Vital Plant Living’s telly data/vital-rack.json, vital-plant-living.html daily vital telly refill daily-notebook.sh The Open Notebook data/open-notebook-month.json, the-open-notebook.html daily open notebook refill daily-large.sh Learning Large data/learning-large-month.json, learning-large.html, now-playing.html daily learning large refill daily-cookin.sh Hey, Good Cookin’ data/hey-good-cookin-month.json, hey-good-cookin.html, now-playing.html daily good cookin refill daily-green.sh The Green’s search rack data/the-green-latest.json, the-green.html daily green refill They run in that order, each whatever the last one returned, so one failing feed leaves the others filled. Every push deploys, so the morning makes a run of deploys. The commit subjects matter: the tool that writes Ryan’s weekly changelog skips exactly these. Consequences. Before editing any of those files in the morning, pull first. If the laptop is asleep, the boards keep yesterday’s date. The build never pulls anything; the network tools run by hand are check-jukebox.py, pull-club.py and pull-foundry.py. The only job on Netlify’s side is the CB’s hourly sweep.

A page load contacts nobody but stimpunks.world. The security policy makes that a property of the site rather than a habit: default-src, script-src, font-src, img-src and connect-src are all 'self', so there is no analytics, no CDN and no third-party script to remove. Every outside origin below is reached only after somebody presses something. Origin Used for Allowed by Contacted when www.youtube-nocookie.com Videos and playlists in every room with a play button, rack or set frame-src; the player’s features in Permissions-Policy after a press open.spotify.com Club Chronic’s stage frame-src after a press embed.music.apple.com Club Chronic’s Apple Music deck frame-src after a press embed.tidal.com The records in Words, Bud, Beats frame-src after a press videopress.com Ryan’s own grass video in Swaying Sweetgrass frame-src after a press 8x8.vc A room’s voice and video call frame-src; camera, microphone, screen and autoplay in Permissions-Policy after a press, with a token the CB signed josephmooon.wordpress.com, its uploads folder only The Small Hours’ jukebox, streamed from the band’s own site media-src after a press Adding an origin is one edit. It goes in a list in love-embed.js, then make-csp.py runs. The policy line in _headers is never edited by hand: the next run puts it back, and the local server sends no headers, so the mistake only shows on the live site. Playing is not the same permission as embedding. A service can refuse to be framed (stoat.chat, music.apple.com) or publish no player at all (Qobuz), and a video can have embedding switched off or be age-gated. Those become links shaped like doors, never frames, and check-jukebox.py asks YouTube for every play button whether it may still be embedded. Other outside traffic, none of it from your browser: Netlify hosts everything, runs the functions and holds the store. Linked pages are read once by the forums’ function, when a post with a link on a line of its own is made or edited: the page’s title and description, or a YouTube video’s own page and oEmbed for its title and length. Only a public address, three redirects and five seconds at most, and never when somebody reads the post. 8x8 calls /cb/call-events and /cb/call-settings as webhooks, and both are signature-checked. Ryan’s laptop reads YouTube’s channel feeds and watch pages and our sibling sites’ RSS each morning, and pull-foundry.py reads Google Fonts’ public repository when it is run.

Ryan Boren and Helen Edgar both commit straight to main, one at a time, each working through their own Claude, and they agree outside the repository whose turn it is. A push is a deploy and nothing reviews it, so the routine is the safeguard: Pull before touching anything; the morning task will have pushed. Run tools/check-all.sh before every commit. Files it changes are generated files catching up with a source, and they go in with the change that caused them. Commit and push when you stop. Uncommitted work blocks the other person and the morning task, which refuses to run over anybody’s edits. Never hand-merge a generated file. Take either side, fix the source and run the build again. A new changelog entry goes at the top with its own id, because the id is the feed item’s permanent address. What a machine needs For Python 3 Every generator and checker Google Chrome The rendering checks, the print check, icons and share cards, all headless Node The local preview, the Node tests, and netlify dev for the CB cwebp, ffmpeg A new JPEG arriving ffprobe A new recording, because runtimes are measured off the file Pillow intake-collection.py The Knowledge System mirror Optional, and on Ryan’s machine only. Tools that read it say so and carry on without it. Where decisions are written. CLAUDE.md holds the rules sessions get wrong and why. DECISIONS.md lists what is open and what is settled. The changelog is the public record and feeds feed.xml. Privacy is the CB’s promise to the people on it. The liner notes hold every credit. SECURITY.md and /.well-known/security.txt say how to report a vulnerability privately. Licence. Our words, markup and design are CC BY-SA 4.0. Photographs, recorded voices, songs and borrowed names keep their own terms, typefaces keep their own OFL or Apache 2.0 licences, and nothing musical is hosted here. The licence file says which is which.

Read from the repository on 2026-10-04: README.md, netlify.toml, _headers, _redirects, package.json, love.js, love-embed.js, the section headings of love.css, netlify/cb/lib.mjs and the config of every file in netlify/functions, tools/check-all.sh and the head of every checker, tools/daily-arrivals.sh, and the morning task’s instructions. When any of those changes in a way this page describes, this page changes with it, and the changelog says so. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.
What this site knows about you is very little, and this page is all of it. Last updated 2026-10-24. Every change to it is dated in the changelog.

No cookies. This site sets none, on any page. No advertising, no trackers, nothing sold, and no email unless you give us an address. There is nobody to sell anything to. The CB takes an invite, from a moderator or from our community’s join form, and joining with one claims a username of your own with a password of your own. That username is your account: the username, its password, and an email address only if you give one, which is used for nothing but sending you a reset code you ask for. Moderators can see a list of every username, how many there are and who is seen in a room now, and nothing else about anybody. More below. A few things are kept in your own browser, each because you asked for it. Only one of them is ever sent anywhere, and only to us, and only by the CB: the radio, the chalkboard, the pebble bowls, the suggestion box, Pando Calrissian’s tree and its fence, the Fridge of Sighs, Count Me In’s stair, the cat and dog shelters and Profile, the forums, and the Slake. The CB is the one thing on this site that sends anything, and only while you have it open. What is said on it is kept for two weeks, a hundred messages a channel at most, unless our administrators set a channel otherwise, and then deleted, unless somebody copies it into a forum topic. A room’s call is run by 8x8, and only people signed on to the CB can join one, except the three public calls behind Cavendish Coworking’s meeting doors, which a guest joins under a name they type. While somebody is in a call we keep their name in it, from 8x8, and it goes when they leave. There is also a World call, which anybody signed on can join from any room. The radio’s Who’s online names the World call and every room whose call has somebody in it, and never who or how many. More below. You can choose to be seen. Signed on, Be seen here puts your handle and the room you are in on the radio’s Who’s online list, for anybody signed on to the CB, and shows you and anybody else seen in the same room to each other, with who is in its call. Nobody who has not chosen it is shown, and nothing is counted. In a room that keeps to itself, being seen shows you only to people seen there, and never on Who’s online. More below. Hosting a film is the CB too. If you press Host this film, everybody signed on sees which film you are watching, in which room, and where it has got to, until you stop. More below. The chalkboard on Plural Mural is the CB’s too, and it is public. Only people signed on to the CB can write on it, anybody at all can read it, and every note is rubbed out after seven days. The World room is a list of every room on the street, and anybody can read it. Signed on to the CB, it also shows which rooms are active now: who has chosen to be seen in each, whether its call has somebody in it, and when its channel last had a message today. Its Most active order is the one place on the street that counts people, to put the busiest rooms first; it never shows the numbers. More below. The forums are the CB’s too, and only claimed usernames can read them. Topics in categories, each kept for a week, three months, six months or for good after its last post, with your username on what you write. Nothing about who reads is kept, and a link on a line of its own is previewed by our server reading that page once, when the post is made. Messages copied from the CB last as long as their topic, and whoever sent one can take it out again. More below. Tasks, the team’s to-do list, are the CB’s too, and only our directors, board members and administrators can read them, with the usernames of who each task is assigned to. Each director’s saved filters are kept under their username, for them alone. More below. The office holds the people and organisations we are in touch with, our grant requests, and the connection requests and volunteer applications that come in, moved here from EspoCRM, and only our directors, board members and administrators can open it. Most of them never signed on to the street, so everything in it is encrypted where it is kept, nothing about it is ever logged, and nothing records who looks. More below. The suggestion box in The Sandbox is the CB’s too, and it is public. Signed on, you can drop in a suggestion, a feature request or a bug report, with your handle on it, and screenshots or other pictures with it, which are public too. Anybody can read it, our moderators reply under it with their own usernames, you can reply too, anybody signed on can say it affects them too, and it stays until you or a moderator take it down. More below. Pando Calrissian’s tree is the CB’s too. Signed on, you can water it. It keeps how many times it has been watered, for good, and never who watered it. The fence beside it holds notes on the chalkboard’s rules. More below. The Fridge of Sighs is the CB’s too. Signed on, you can put up one word of a sentence. Finished sentences are kept for good and no word says who put it up. More below. Count Me In’s stair is the CB’s too. Signed on, you can take the next step, by number or by the lift. It keeps the step it is on and the highest it has reached, for good, and never who took any step. More below. Rescue A Cat, Rescue A Dog and Rescue Small Animals are the CB’s too. Signed on, you can rescue an animal and name it, and adopt one into Profile on your radio. The shelters and the list of everybody adopted never say who rescued or adopted anybody. Your pets, your avatars, your chimeras, your battle jacket’s patches, your crystal pouch, your herb basket and, if you ask it to, the jobs you hand in at the Guild are the things the street keeps under a person, filed under a scrambled form of your handle, and Forget me under Account deletes them. More below. Avatars are the CB’s too. Signed on, you can keep a bodymind you drew at the Bodymind Booth, or an outfit from the Dress-Up Den, as an avatar in Profile, and with a claimed username wear one beside your name on Who’s online. An avatar is a list of choices, never a picture, and Forget me under Account deletes them. More below. Chimeras are the CB’s too. Signed on, you can keep a chimera you made in Chimera Obscura in Profile, name it, and send it as a sticker. A chimera is a list of choices, never a picture, and Forget me under Account deletes them. More below. Props are the CB’s too. With a claimed username, you can open a Props tab on your profile, where anybody else with a claimed username can give you props: a sentence or a short paragraph thanking you. Each waits until you confirm it, and only then can anybody else read it. Forget me under Account deletes them. More below. The Slake, out the back of the MUD Room, is the CB too. Signed on, you can choose to be seen out there, on each visit, and only then does it send anything: where you are and what you say. You meet people in the place you are in; nobody gets a list of who is out there, and nothing is counted. Nothing from anybody else loads until you press it. Every video and player on the street waits for a press. Our host keeps ordinary server logs, the way every web server does.

These are stored with localStorage in your own browser. All but love-cb are never sent to us or to anybody else, and we cannot read them. love-cb only exists once you have signed on to the CB, and it is sent to us, and only to us, each time the radio checks the channel, when you write on the chalkboard, leave a pebble, drop something in the suggestion box or answer it, water Pando Calrissian’s tree, pin a note to its fence, put a word up on the Fridge of Sighs, take a step on Count Me In’s stair, rescue or adopt an animal, open Profile or Account, read or write in the forums or tasks or look at the World room, and every few seconds while you have chosen to be seen on the Slake. Each one only remembers something you asked this site to remember, which is why there is no consent banner here: there is nothing a banner would be asking about. Clear this site’s data in your browser settings. love-low The low-stimulation mode you escaped to from the dial or the bodymind break: Warm Light, Cool Dark, Plant Green or Red Light, and nothing else, so every page opens in it until you leave it. Press the mode again, Back to the rooms’ own colours, or a level on the dial, or your browser settings. love-quests The jobs you have handed in at the Adventurer’s Guild, so the board can show them as done and work out your badges. It is only written when you rescue one, it is never sent to us, and the shelters do not know which were yours. (It was called love-cats for its first day, and the rooms move an old one across.) The animals you adopt are not here: they are your pets, kept by us, below. The Forget the ones I rescued button in each room, or your browser settings. love-cb Your CB handle, the pass that lets the radio onto the channel, if you are a moderator the roles the site last told the radio you hold, where you last put the radio on your screen, whether you left it folded away, what size you made it, which theme you chose for it and whether you let its drawing move, whether you chose to be seen in the rooms you visit, whether it is tuned to World or to the room you are in, whether it passes new messages to a screen reader, whether it speaks them aloud, the rooms you follow for Unreads or that you follow every room, whether you left Who’s online open, the order you chose for the chat page’s channels under tags, and, while it is in a window of its own, that it is. It is only there once you have signed on at the Community Center. The pass is sent to us each time the radio checks the channel and when you write on the chalkboard, leave a pebble, use the suggestion box, water the tree, pin a note to its fence, put up a word on the fridge, take a step on the stair, rescue or adopt an animal, open Profile or Account or use the forums or tasks, is checked and not kept, and stops working the moment the password changes. Sign off on the radio, or your browser settings. love-forum For the forums: which topics you have opened and when you last looked at each, so they can mark what is new to you since; the colours you chose for them, if not your radio’s; and a post you started and have not sent yet. It is never sent to us. It remembers a thousand topics at most, dropping the longest quiet first, and a topic that has gone drops out when you next go to it. Forget what I have read in the forums, or your browser settings. love-world In the World room: whether you chose to show every room, the active ones or the quiet ones, and which order you put them in. Nothing else, and it is never sent anywhere. Your browser settings. love-notice That you put away the notice along the top of the street’s front page, the Community Center, the forums and the office’s dashboard: a short code worked out from its words, and nothing else, so it stays away on all of them until a new notice goes up. It is only written when you press Put it away, it is never sent anywhere, and it clears itself once that notice is no longer up. Wait for the next notice, or your browser settings. love-familiar Your familiar, if you took a chimera with you from Chimera Obscura or from Profile: which animal gave each part, its name, its sayings, which of your kept chimeras it is if you took it from Profile, whether you let it move by itself, roughly where in the window you last put it down, and where in the window it was when you left the last page, so it can walk in from there, each as two fractions of the window. Never which room you were in, so it is no record of where you have been; nothing is counted, and this is never sent anywhere. Every page reads it to draw your familiar again when you arrive. Bringing it into rooms for other people to see is a separate switch on the radio, below. Press your familiar and Send it home, or your browser settings. love-cb-guest That you left the CB bar’s panel open, before signing on, so it stays open on the next page. It holds the word open and nothing else, and is never sent anywhere. Fold the panel away, or your browser settings. Nothing else on this site stores anything: no session storage, no IndexedDB, no service worker. The site’s own security policy lets its pages send data to this site and nowhere else (connect-src ’self’) and never lets them submit a form (form-action ’none’), and the only thing on any page that sends anything at all is the CB, with its chalkboard, its pebble bowls, the suggestion box, Pando Calrissian’s tree, the Fridge of Sighs, Count Me In’s stair, the shelters and Profile, the forums, tasks, and the Slake. Opening Plural Mural asks this site for what is on the board, once, opening Pando Calrissian asks for the tree and its fence, once, opening The Sandbox asks for what is in the suggestion box, once, and opening the street’s front page, the Community Center, the forums or the office’s dashboard asks for the notice, once; none of those requests carries anything of yours.

This site is served by Netlify. Like any web server, it receives what every browser sends with every request — your IP address, your browser’s user-agent string, the address you asked for and the time — and it keeps logs of that under Netlify’s own privacy policy, which also says how long. We need that to run and secure a website, which is the legal basis for it (legitimate interests). We have not switched on Netlify’s analytics, we do not add anything to those logs, and we do not use them to find out who anybody is. Every typeface, script, stylesheet and image on this site is served from this site, so opening a page makes no request to anybody but Netlify.

The search box on the street and on the Map does its searching in your browser. The first time you type in it, it fetches two files from this site, the list of rooms and the words on every page, and nothing else. What you type is never sent anywhere, to us or to anybody, and it is not kept: not in your browser and not in the address. Following a result is an ordinary link on this site.

The jukeboxes, screens and players on the street are press-to-play: until you press one, this site has made no request to that service on your behalf. When you press, your browser loads that service’s player, and from then on the service receives what any website receives from you — your IP address, your browser details, and that you came from stimpunks.world (the site’s address only, not the page) — and may set its own cookies. What it does with that is covered by its own policy, not ours: The services a press-to-play control loads, and their privacy policies Service Where on the street Its privacy policy YouTube, through youtube-nocookie.com Most of the videos, songs and live cameras Google’s privacy policy Spotify Club Chronic’s stage Spotify’s privacy policy Apple Music Club Chronic’s stage Apple’s privacy policy TIDAL Words, Bud, Beats’ records. Its player also loads Datadog, which TIDAL uses to watch how the player is working, in about one visit in ten. TIDAL’s privacy notice Vimeo The Faery Yurt’s Moon Spoon Pebbling Pot, whose window plays Vi Hart’s Moon Spoon. The player is asked not to track the visit. I need a bodymind break, in the dial’s box at the top of a page, on the CB’s radio, and on the CB bar for anybody not signed on, opens a calm screen over the page you are on. It keeps nothing and sends nothing: the first press fetches its own script and stylesheet from this site, and that is all. The forest and the jellies on it are YouTube’s, and like every player on the street, nothing reaches YouTube until you press one; closing the break stops it. If something on the page is playing, the break offers to pause it, and pauses nothing by itself. While it is up, the radio reads nothing aloud. Its links to our Help page and to crisis lines and warmlines are ordinary links to stimpunks.org.
When you follow a link away

A lot of this site is links to other places. When you follow one, the site you arrive at learns that you came from stimpunks.world — the address of the site, never the page you were on — and from then on you are covered by that site’s policy.

Some pages carry photographs of people, recordings of people’s voices, and the names of the people we credit. Every photograph of somebody, and every recording of somebody’s voice, is published with that person’s consent, recorded in our files with a date — the readings in Hear Queer Here included — and it comes down when the person in it says so: one message, no reason needed. A young person who is doing the work and has said yes themselves is published and credited like anybody else; a parent’s yes does not stand in for theirs, and a child too young to give that consent is not published at all. The whole of that is on the Polaroid Wall’s page. The photographs are excluded from this site’s CC BY-SA licence precisely so that taking one down is something we can actually do.

The CB is a chat channel, patterned after citizens band radio. You join with an invite, on the joining page, which claims a username of your own with a password of your own, and after that you sign on at the Community Center or on the bar in the corner of any page. Until you sign on, the radio is not on any page and nothing is sent. Until 21 October 2026 the CB took a starter password the community shared, and a username was claimed only if you chose to; that password signs nobody on now, and a radio still on with it can only claim the username it is on. Before you sign on. A folded bar in the corner of each page, with a teleporter and a way to find out how to get on the CB. It is not the radio: it sends nothing to the channel, knows nothing about who is on it, and shows nothing that is said. Opening the teleporter fetches this site’s list of rooms, from this site, and nothing else is fetched. If you leave its panel open, your browser remembers that under love-cb-guest, and folding it away deletes it. You can sign on from it too, with your username and your password: that sends exactly what the front desk sends, only when you press Sign on, and then the radio takes its place. What it sends. While the radio is open on your screen and the tab is in front of you, it asks this site for the latest messages every few seconds, and the first time it does, or the first time you open its teleporter, it also fetches the list of rooms on the street, so that a room named with a # can be shown as a link and the teleporter knows where it can take you; that request carries nothing about you. With a claimed username it also asks us, once, which categories in the forums you can read, because each of them is a room on the CB that the public list does not name; that request carries your pass, the answer names only categories you can read, and nothing records who asked. Teleporting to a room is an ordinary link on this site: it sends nothing to the channel and tells nobody where you went. Typing an @ into it asks us who is online, once, and narrows that list in your browser, so what you type after the @ is not sent. More below. Closed, folded down, or in a tab you are not looking at, it sends nothing. When you transmit, your handle and your words come to us. World, or this room. The radio hears one channel at a time. World is the one everybody shares, and listening to it tells us nothing about where you are on the street. This room is the room’s own channel, and to hear it the radio has to tell us which room it is, each time it asks. We do not keep that: nothing records who listened to which room. The radio starts on World, and it remembers which you chose, in your own browser. In the forums, this room is the category you are reading (Ryan’s call, 2026-10-21): a category’s page, a topic in it, or a new topic you start in it, and a category inside another is the room of the one it is in. Each category’s room is a room in every way, with its own channel, Be seen here, call and Follow this room, and only the claimed usernames that can read the category can hear it, be seen in it, call in it or be told about it, so a staff category’s room is its staff’s, as its topics are. The forums’ home, Latest, Mentions and Search are the forums’ own room. Going from one category to another tells us the new one the next time the radio asks, as walking into another room does. On the chat page (since 2026-10-22) the radio is docked into the page, and the channel you pick there is the one it hears, with that room’s Be seen here and call: picking one tells us which, the next time the radio asks, as walking into the room would, and nothing records it. The page keeps your pick only in its own address, after a #, which your browser never sends. It marks what is new in the other channels from what Unreads already asks, and asks nothing more. If you sort the channels under tags by Recently active or Most active (Ryan’s ask, 2026-10-24), the page asks us once when it opens, when you choose the order and when you press Sort again, never as messages come in: we look at the channels you can hear and answer with two orders, newest message first and most messages in the last two weeks first, never a time or a number, leaving out any room that keeps to itself and any room you cannot go into, and counting none of the street’s bot’s messages. Nothing is kept for it and nothing records who asked. Which order you chose is kept in love-cb, in your own browser. A to Z, where everybody starts, asks nothing. If you choose My own order (Ryan’s call, 2026-10-24, so it follows you from one device to another), the order you arrange the channels into, group by group, is kept on our server under a scrambled form of your claimed username: which channels, in which order, under which group, and nothing about when, not when you arranged them nor how often. Arranging sends your pass and the whole of your order; opening the page with My own order chosen asks for it. A room that keeps to itself is never kept in it. Nobody else is sent it or told you have one, a moderator included. Forget me and deleting your username delete it. A place in a film. Somebody can put a place like @34:12 in a message, and on every radio it is a button that moves the film on your page to that place. It never presses play, and nobody else can move your film: only your own press does. Add my spot reads where the film on your page has got to, and the film’s title and the room you are in, and writes them into your message box. The room’s name in a spot links to that room with the spot on the end of the address, after a #, which your browser never sends to any server, ours included; arriving that way gets that film’s play button ready to start at the spot, and nothing plays until you press it. The radio and the film talk to each other inside your browser. That sends nothing, to us or to YouTube, until you transmit it like anything else you type. What we keep. The latest hundred messages on each channel, World and every room’s, each with its handle, its words, the handles it @mentions, which message it replies to, if it is a reply, the time it was sent, the time its sender last edited it, if they did, whether it came from the base station or from a claimed username (since 2026-10-21 every username is claimed, so the radio no longer shows that one), the picture sent with it, if there was one, and its description, and the sticker, if it was one: a copy of what one of your pets looks like and is called, or of one of your avatars, its name and what you wrote about it, or of one of your chimeras, which animal gave each part and its name, or which patch, or which patches were on your battle jacket, taken when you sent it. Reactions are kept on the message they were pressed on: which reaction and the handle that pressed it, shown to everybody on that channel by handle and never as a number, and deleted with the message.
