Once a channel is full, the newest pushes the oldest off, picture and all. Every message is deleted two weeks after it was sent, unless the channel is set otherwise (below). That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-25, after requests from our community for more to scroll back through, in channels like Pets above all; from 2026-10-18 it was 48 hours, because people on the street live in timezones all over the world and were missing what was said while they slept, and before that everything on every channel was deleted every day at midnight, Colorado time. A message keeps the time it was sent under: one sent on or before 2026-10-25, Colorado time, still goes at its 48 hours. Whoever sent a message can delete it sooner with Take off, picture, reactions and all, and a moderator can delete any message. Taking one off sends your pass, which message and which channel. There is no archive and no backup, and the only copy is one somebody makes into a forum topic. A picture. A screenshot or a photo sent on the channel is redrawn in your own browser before it leaves it, which takes off everything a camera or a phone writes into the file, where it was taken first of all; this site refuses a file that still carries any of it. It is kept only with its message and deleted when the message goes, and one that was never sent is deleted within the hour. It has no public address: only a radio signed on to that channel can fetch it, and a picture sent in one of the Town Hall’s private rooms only by the people that room is for. Download saves the copy your radio already holds onto your own device, which is yours; it asks us for nothing more. An @mention. Typing an @ into the message box offers the people who have spoken on the channel and the people on Who’s online, and the first one asks us who is online, once. A message keeps the handles it mentions, at most ten, so every radio draws them as names: your radio says who it means, and we keep only the ones the words really name. Who is told about a mention is unchanged, and only a device that asked is. A link to another site. An address on another site in a message is a link that opens in a new tab and says which site it goes to, and so is one with words of its own, [words](an address), whose site is written after the words. Following it sends that site nothing from here: no referrer, so it is not told which page of ours you came from, and nothing about the channel. What it does once you are there is up to that site. Copy. Copy on a message puts its words on your own clipboard, in your browser. It sends nothing, to us or anybody. Sealed at rest, in the staff rooms (since 2026-10-25, Ryan’s call). The channels of every room only some of us may enter (the moderators’, directors’ and board rooms, Executive Session, and every forum category with roles), the words of every call for a moderator left on the desk, and every picture sent on any channel are encrypted where they are kept at Netlify, with the staff key Tasks and the forums use, so somebody who got at the stored files alone could not read them. Every picture, not only the staff rooms’, because a picture is stored under a name that does not say its room. The World channel and the public rooms’ channels are not sealed: everybody signed on reads them. None of this is end-to-end: our server opens them for whoever may read the room. Without that key those channels and the pictures are shut rather than written in the clear, and anything written before that day is sealed within the hour. Replies (since 2026-10-21). A reply keeps which message it answers, and nothing else of it: not its words and not who sent it. Every radio draws the line above a reply from what is on the channel at that moment, so when the message answered is edited the line changes, and when it is taken off or its two weeks are up, the line says it answered a message no longer on the channel. Replying sends your pass, your message, which channel, and which message it answers, which must still be on that channel. It tells whoever sent that message only if they switched on When somebody replies to me. Edit. Whoever sent a message can change its words with Edit; a moderator can edit only their own, like everybody else. The words it had before are not kept, by us or anywhere: the message is rewritten where it is, says edited and when, keeps its picture, sticker and reactions, and still goes two weeks after it was first sent. Editing sends your pass, which message, which channel and the new words. An edit tells nobody about it unless it @mentions somebody it did not name before, and then it tells only them, if they asked to be told about mentions. Take to the forums. With a claimed username, Take to the forums on a message lets you tick messages on the channel and start a forum topic with them. Our server copies them from the channel itself, words, handles, marks and times exactly as they are on the channel, with edited on any their sender has edited, and they then last as long as the topic does. Pictures and stickers stay behind. Whoever sent a copied message can take it out of the topic again, and a moderator can. Ask everybody in the conversation first, as you would before a screenshot. How many messages a day. For our directors’ dashboard in the office, every message sent on World or in a room adds one to a count for its day: three numbers a day, for World, for the rooms, and for the rooms only some people can hear: the moderators’ rooms, and since 2026-10-21 the rooms of the forum categories only staff can read. No handle, no room, no words and no time go with it, so it says how busy the channels were and nothing about who was on them or where. Direct messages are not counted. Each day’s three numbers are kept for 400 days. What we do not keep. Your IP address is not stored with a message or anywhere else by us, and we do not write handles or messages into any log. We keep no list of who has signed on. Where it is kept. Netlify, our host, stores the channel for us and runs the small program that answers the radio, under Netlify’s privacy policy. Netlify’s ordinary logs record that the radio made a request, the same as for any page. Netlify also limits how often one address can try the password; it does that itself, without handing the address to us. Who can read it. Anybody signed on, which means everybody who has joined. That makes it a room full of people rather than a private line, so say on it what you would say in a room. A username signs on only with its owner’s password, so a name says whoever holds that password sent it, and nothing more about who they are. A moderator’s is marked BASE: our moderators’ usernames, and which of them hold the board, director or administrator role, are on a list that is not published. A username on it is claimed only with the moderators’ password as well as its owner’s own. The list is read each time a pass is checked and never written to by the radio, and the only thing a radio is told about it is its own roles, so that it can keep out of the Town Hall’s rooms it cannot use. The radio in a window of its own. Pop out moves the radio into a browser window of its own, which stays open while you go from room to room in the window you came from. It is the same radio with the same pass, and it sends what the radio on that page would have: it reads which page you are on, its address and title and what it says about itself, straight from that window, inside your own browser, to know which room you are in. Your other pages learn that it is out, and ask it to come back, over a channel that stays inside your own browser, and love-cb notes that it is out until the window closes. Nothing more about it is sent to us or kept. Links in a message become cards (since 2026-10-24, a request from our community). A bare address in a message on the channel, up to three of them, gets a card under the message. Our server reads each link once, just after the message has gone out, for words: the page’s title, its description and its site’s name, or what the site’s own oEmbed answer says (who made it, the site’s name and, for a post on X, Bluesky or the like, the words of the post), and for a video how long it runs. For a YouTube video it first asks YouTube’s own Data API, sending it only the video’s id, for its title, its channel, how long it runs and whether it may play here. The site sees a request from Netlify, our host, and never from you or from anybody reading the channel. The card is kept with the message and goes when it does. No picture is fetched from anywhere, and nothing a site sends to put on a page is ever put on ours. A YouTube or Vimeo video is a press-to-play player like every other on the street: nothing from YouTube or Vimeo loads until somebody presses it, and then only for whoever pressed. A link written in angle brackets, <https://…>, a link with words of its own, and a link to a room on the street get no card. A card is read again only for a link new in an edit. What is new to you, with a claimed username. The radio marks a channel or a conversation where something has been said since you last read it, and lists them under Unreads: a dot, never a number. So that reading on one device clears the dot on the others, we keep, for your claimed username, when you last read each channel and each conversation, and nothing else: not what you read, not how often, and nothing about anybody else’s reading. Each time is dropped once it is two weeks old, because nothing that old is left on the channel. A room that keeps to itself is never recorded. Nobody but you is ever sent it, a moderator included. Forget me and deleting your username delete it. To tell you what is new, the radio is sent the time of each channel’s newest message, as the World room shows anybody signed on, and never their words; which rooms you follow for it, or that you follow every room, is kept in your own browser. What it does not do. No chimes, no badges, no number of anything; what is new is marked, above. If the radio is closed, nothing reaches you from it and nothing is saved up for later. A device you switch on for notifications is told about what you chose for it, and nothing else, and since 2026-10-25 what your devices are told is kept for you for 30 days. Speaking aloud. If you switch on Speak new messages aloud, the radio reads each new message out, handle first, using a voice built into your own device. It only uses voices your device says are on the device itself, so the words are not sent to a speech service anywhere else; some browsers also offer voices that are, and the radio will not use those. If your device has no voice of its own, nothing is spoken. Each message comes with a burst of radio static before it and the tail of static after, made in the page and not fetched from anywhere; at the Gentle setting the words come without it, and there is no static without a message being spoken. It is off until you switch it on, it only reads what arrives while the radio is open, and folding the radio away stops it mid-word. Read aloud, under a message’s three dots, reads that one message the same way when you press it, with the same voices only, and sends nothing anywhere either. We keep a message because you sent it for other people on the channel to read, and keeping it for two weeks is what that takes. Transmitting is your consent to it, and you can take that back by asking us to delete what you said.

Since 2026-10-25, Ryan’s call, our administrators can set how many messages a channel keeps and for how long, at the desk in the Moderators’ room: World, any room’s channel, every channel not set otherwise (the Slake’s places too), and direct messages, each on its own. A channel can keep 50, 100, 200, 500 or 1,000 messages, each for a day, two days, a week, two weeks, 30 days, 90 days, a year or for good. Unless it is set otherwise, a channel keeps its latest 100, each for two weeks. The radio says what the channel you are on keeps, as the first line under In this channel, so you know before you say anything. A longer time never reaches what was already said. Every message is marked, when it is sent, with how long its channel kept messages then, and it is never kept longer than that, whatever the channel is set to later. One exception was made, for the Pets channel on 2026-10-25: its two writers, Ryan and Norah, both said yes to what they had already said there being kept as long as the channel now keeps it. Nothing else has had that, and nothing will without everybody who wrote in a channel saying yes. A shorter time, or fewer messages, reaches everything at once: what no longer fits is deleted when the change is made. What the desk keeps about it: for each channel set, how many and how long, and which administrator set it last and when. Nothing about who read what. For good means as long as the channel keeps it: the newest still pushes the oldest off once the channel is full, Take off still takes a message off, and Forget me and deleting your username still delete what they always did.

Anybody signed on to the CB can host the film they are watching, with Host this film on the radio, so that everybody else on the channel can see where it has got to and catch up. It is off until you press it, it is never remembered, and a new page starts with nobody hosting. What it sends, and when. Your pass, your handle, the room you are in, the film’s title, its YouTube id and how long it runs, the place in it and whether it is playing, and, when the film is one song or video in an album or a playlist, that list’s YouTube id. For a live video it sends that it is live, in place of a length and a place. The id is what lets everybody else’s radio find that film’s own play button on the page, when several films have nearly the same name, and the list’s id is what lets it find that album’s and go on through it with you, and how long it runs is what a play button says when a radio has to put one up (below). It goes when you start hosting, when the film plays, pauses, jumps or changes, and every half minute besides, and only while the radio is open and the tab is in front of you. Put the tab behind another and it stops sending until you come back; fold the radio away or leave the page and you stop hosting. What we keep. One record for each room somebody is hosting, holding exactly that and the time it was last heard. Every update replaces it rather than adding to it, so there is no history of what you watched or where you were in it. It is deleted the moment you stop hosting. If you go quiet instead, by folding the radio or leaving, it is shown to nobody seventy-five seconds after it was last heard, and it is gone for good at the next update from any host or at the hourly sweep, whichever comes first. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. Who can see it. Anybody signed on, on every page: their radio shows who is hosting which film in which room, and where it has got to. Everybody’s radio is sent every host on the street with the channel, so nobody’s radio has to tell us which room they are in to find the host for theirs. A room that keeps to itself is the exception: its host is sent only to radios tuned to that room’s own channel, and to nobody else. What it does not do. It moves nobody’s film. Catch up is a button on each person’s own radio, and only their press moves their film, the same as a place in a message. Follow, beside it, keeps your film in step with the host’s, playing, pausing and moving with it, on to the next song of an album with it, but only once you have pressed it yourself; it sends nothing, it is never remembered, and your own pause ends it. One person hosts a room at a time, and only the base station can take a room over. A moderator’s own video. A moderator can paste the address of one YouTube video into Screen a video on the radio, and it goes up on the first screen of the page they are on. It plays on their page and nowhere else, and nothing is sent to us until they host it. If they do, pressing Catch up or Follow beside them puts that video’s play button on the first screen of your page, in place of what it had, saying how long it runs and who put it there. Nothing reaches YouTube until you press it, and the screen’s own controls put back what was there. On a set you tune, like the Solarpunk Hermitage’s television, Looming Rocks’ stage or the Rebellion Rave Room’s big screen, it is tuned on the set, which stays off until you press play. Only a moderator’s hosting can do this, and our server, not their radio, says whose hosting is a moderator’s. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who watched. We keep that you are hosting because you pressed Host this film so that other people could see where you are, and keeping it while you are hosting is what that takes. Pressing it again takes that back.

Signed on to the CB, the radio has a switch, Be seen here, in every room on the street. It is off until you press it, and once pressed your browser remembers it, so you are seen in each room you open with the radio until you switch it off. Since 2026-10-07, being seen puts you on the radio’s Who’s online list, for anybody signed on to the CB, with the room you are in. Before that it showed you only to people seen in the same room. If you switched it on before then, it now does more than it did when you pressed it, and switching it off takes you off the list at once. What it sends, and when. Only while you are seen, the radio is open, and the tab is in front of you: every few seconds, your pass, which room this page is, and a random number the page makes up for this visit, which nobody else is shown. Switch it off, fold the radio away, put the tab behind another or leave the page, and it tells us you have gone and sends nothing more. Who can see you. Anybody signed on to the CB, seen or not, on Who’s online: your username, whether it is the base station, and the room you are in. Anybody else seen in the same room sees you there too, and only they are shown who is in that room’s call. Names come in alphabetical order and nobody is shown a number. A room the base keeps, and the room of a forum category only staff can read, is named only to the people it is for, and somebody seen only there is on nobody else’s list. A room that keeps to itself is named to nobody: being seen there shows you only to people seen there. Moderators see the same, by the same rules, on their list of every username, with how many are seen now. What we keep. While you are seen, one record: your handle, whether you are the base station, whether your handle is a claimed username, which room, the time of your last check and the visit’s number. Opening another room replaces it rather than adding to it, so which rooms you have been in is not kept. It is shown to nobody thirty seconds after your last check, and deleted when you stop being seen, or within two minutes by anybody else’s check, or by the hourly sweep at the latest. We keep that you are in a room because you chose to be seen there, and keeping it for as long as you are is what that takes. Pressing Be seen here is your consent to it, and pressing it again takes that back.

Who’s online, beside World and This room on the radio, lists everybody seen in a room and which room, with a link to go there, and, beside a claimed username, the avatar its owner wears on the CB, if they wear one (below), and the chat status they chose, if they chose one (below), except a room that keeps to itself, which is never on it. While its panel is open, the radio is open and the tab is in front of you, it asks us every few seconds, sending your pass and nothing else. Typing an @ in the teleporter asks the same once and narrows the list in your browser, so the letters you type are not sent. Nothing records who looked, or when.

Signed on to the CB, Your chat status, under Who’s around on the radio, says whether you would like to be talked to, with one of the interaction badges: come say hi, people i know or not right now. It is not Be seen here: being seen says you are in a room, and a chat status says whether you want to be talked to, wherever you are. It starts as none. Nothing is shown beside your name until you choose a badge, and it stays until you change it. Nothing changes it for you: it never goes to idle or away when you stop typing, and it never runs out. Who can see it. Anybody signed on to the CB: beside your name on Who’s online and to people seen in the same room as you, on your profile, and at the top of a conversation with you under Messages, so it can be checked before anybody writes. It is a sign and not a lock: it stops nobody writing to you. What it sends, and when. Your pass and the badge, when you choose one. The radio’s own ask of what is new to you, while it is open, brings your badge back, so one chosen on another device reaches this one. What we keep. Which badge you chose, under a scrambled form of your username, and nothing else: not when you chose it, not how often you change it, and nothing about who looked. Choosing none takes it away at once, and so do Forget me and deleting your username. We keep your chat status because you chose it so that people could see it, and keeping it is what that takes. Choosing none takes that back.

People signed on to the CB can join a voice and video call for the room they are in, with Join this room’s call on the radio, and in the rooms behind Cavendish Coworking’s doors from the room itself. Three of those calls are open to anybody; see below. The rooms off the Town Hall for our directors, our board and our moderators are the other way round: anybody can walk in, and their channel, their call and any film hosted in them are handed to the base and to nobody else, so nobody else’s radio hears anything about them. The call is run by 8x8’s Jitsi as a Service, not by us, and it opens in a window of its own at the foot of the page. What we send, and to whom. Pressing the button asks this site for a pass into that room’s call, which carries your handle and whether you moderate that call: the base station moderates every call, and since 2026-10-24 everybody signed on moderates the three public calls below. We sign it and send it back; your browser hands it to 8x8 when the call opens. 8x8 sees your handle, as your name in the call, an id we make from your handle so that 8x8 counts one person once, and which room it is. What 8x8 gets. Whatever any video call gets: your IP address and browser details, and, once you join and switch them on, your camera, your microphone, what you type in the call’s own chat and any screen you share. What 8x8 does with that is covered by 8x8’s privacy notice, not by this page. Camera and microphone. Both start off. Opening the window may make your browser ask about them, so the call’s first screen can show you a preview; nothing goes to the call until you join on that screen. The call is the only thing on this site allowed to ask for a camera, a microphone or a shared screen, and our pages never ask for any of the three themselves. Sharing a YouTube video in a call. Anybody in a call can share a YouTube video for everybody in it to watch together, from the call’s own menu. That is Jitsi’s feature, and when somebody uses it, Jitsi loads the video from YouTube itself (youtube.com, not the no-cookie address our own players use) in the call window of everybody in the call, so YouTube gets what it gets from any of its players, and may set its cookies, under Google’s privacy policy. Jitsi’s analytics, its avatar lookups and its animated-picture search stay switched off. The public calls, and guests. The calls in the rooms behind Cavendish Coworking’s Events, Operations and Editorial doors are open to anybody, not only people signed on to the CB. Somebody who is not signed on types the name they want to be called, and that name comes to us with the room, is signed into their pass and sent back, and goes to 8x8 as their name in the call; we do not keep it. 8x8 also gets an id we make from that name, so that 8x8 counts one person once. A guest knocks and waits in the lobby until a moderator lets them in. Since 2026-10-24 everybody signed on to the CB joins those three calls as a moderator, because 8x8 lets nobody else past the lobby, so they come straight in and can let a guest in; recording and transcription are still the base station’s alone. Before each of those meetings 8x8 asks us whether it has a lobby, and all we answer is yes or no. Recording and transcripts. The base station can record a call or turn on live transcription, and nobody else can. Jitsi shows everybody in the call when either is on. A recording or transcript is kept by 8x8, under its notice. Sharing a file. Anybody in a call, guests included, can share a file there, a screenshot or a photo, from the call’s own Share file. The file goes to 8x8 and to the people in the call, never to us, and we keep nothing about it. 8x8 does not publish how long it keeps a file shared in a call, so share nothing there you would not want kept, and nothing with somebody else in it who has not said yes. For anything to be kept, or kept to the people it is for, the forums are the place. The CB’s own channel forgets everything after two weeks. Who is in a call is shown before anybody joins. 8x8 tells us when somebody joins or leaves a room’s call, and when the call opens and closes, and the radio of anybody signed on who has chosen to be seen in that room shows the names of everybody in its call: handles, and the names guests typed, in alphabetical order, with no number. A room the base keeps, and a staff category’s room in the forums, shows its call only to the people it is for. What 8x8 sends is checked against a secret we share with 8x8, and what does not match is not believed. The World call. Since 2026-10-13 there is one call that is no room’s: Join World call on the radio opens it from any room, for anybody signed on to the CB, and never for a guest. It is a room’s call in every other way, run by 8x8, with the same pass, the same record while you are in it and the same deletion when you leave. Since 2026-10-18 it is the call of the World room too, so, as in every room, somebody seen in the World room is shown who is in it; nobody else is shown who is in it before they join, and like every call it hangs up when you leave the page, a move to another room included, unless it is popped out. A call in a window of its own. Pop out on a call moves it into a browser window of its own, which stays open while you go from room to room. That window asks for a new pass into the call with your CB pass, exactly as joining does, and keeps nothing; which call to open is in the part of its address after the #, which your browser never sends to us. The radio on your other pages learns which call the window holds, and asks it to hang up when you press Leave, over a channel that stays inside your own browser. Nothing about it is sent to us or kept. Which calls are going is shown to anybody signed on. Since 2026-10-13 the radio’s Who’s online names the World call and every room whose call has somebody in it, for anybody signed on to the CB, seen or not: the room and nothing else, not who is in the call and not how many, guests included. A room the base keeps is named only to the people it is for, and a room that keeps to itself is never named. It is read from the records below, nothing more is kept for it, and nothing records who looked. What we keep. While you are in a call, one record: your name in the call, whether you are a moderator, the time you joined, and 8x8’s id for you, scrambled so it cannot be looked up. No email, and nothing else 8x8 sends. It is deleted when you leave, when the call closes, or by the hourly sweep once it is older than a pass into a call can be. Somebody’s leaving is remembered, without their name, for an hour, so that a late message from 8x8 cannot put them back. We do not keep who was in a call once they have left, when they joined before, or for how long. The pass is signed and handed back, and not stored. Leaving. Leave the call, or leaving the page, hangs up.

The World room, past the Garden, is every room on the street on one web, and anybody can read the list. Signed on to the CB, you also see which rooms are active now. The World room’s own channel is the CB’s World channel, and its own call is the World call. What it shows, for every room you may go into: who has chosen Be seen here in it, as Who’s online already shows; whether its call has somebody in it, as Who’s online already says, and never who; and the time of the latest message on its channel, which keeps two weeks, and which until now only somebody tuned to that room could see. Never the words. Nothing at all is shown about a room that keeps to itself, and the Town Hall’s private rooms only to the people they are for. Most active, Ryan’s call. Sorting by most active puts first the rooms with the most people seen in them and in their calls. To work that out, our server counts them each time somebody asks, and sends the order and never the numbers; but the order itself says which rooms have more people in them than others. It is the one place on the street that counts people. Nothing is kept for it. What it sends. While the World room is open and in front of you, signed on, it asks us every half minute and when you come back to it. Each request carries your pass and nothing about where you are, and nothing records who asked. Its call is the World call. As in every room, if you choose to be seen in the World room you are shown who is in its call, which is the World call, and so is everybody else seen there.
The Feed’s and The Source’s channels

Since 2026-10-23 (Ryan’s ask, after Discord’s feed bots), the CB channels of The Feed and The Source hear each new arrival as it comes in: every quarter of an hour our server reads the feeds on The Feed’s boards and the commit feeds on The Source’s terraces, and says anything new on that room’s channel, under the room’s own name and marked BOT. What it reads. Our own sites’ public feeds, and GitHub’s public feed of commits for each of our repositories, from our server. Nothing about you goes with those requests, and nobody’s visit to the street causes one. What it says. A new item’s site, its name and where it goes, and for a commit its short id, its day and the names it gives for who made it, never an email address. Never the words of the thing itself. It is a message like any other: on its channel for two weeks, with reactions and replies, and our moderators can take one off. Nobody can edit it, and its name, The Feed or The Source, cannot be anybody’s username. What we keep for it. For each feed, the ids of the items it last carried and the version our server last read, so nothing is said twice. Nothing about anybody. It never pushes a person’s message off a channel. When a channel is full, the bot’s oldest go first, and it keeps at most thirty of its own on one. Who is told. A device that follows that room by name under notifications is told about each new arrival there, with its site and name unless the words are switched off. Follow every room does not take them in: that switch is for people’s talk, and a phone that pressed it did not ask to be told about every commit to the street.

Plural Mural has a chalkboard leaning against the foot of its wall, for leaving a note to whoever comes by next. It was Helen Edgar’s idea. It is part of the CB and runs on the same rules, with two differences, both written above the box you write in: anybody can read it, and a note stays up for seven days, where a message on the channel stays two weeks. Who can write on it. Only people signed on to the CB. Writing sends your handle, your note and your pass to us, the same as transmitting on the radio. Who can read it. Anybody who opens Plural Mural, signed on or not. That makes it a board in the street rather than a room, so write on it what you would write on a board in the street. A username says whoever holds its password wrote it, and nothing more about who they are. The board’s answers ask search engines not to index or archive it; that is a request they honour rather than a lock. What we keep. The latest thirty notes, each with its handle, its words and the time it went up. A thirty-first rubs out the oldest. Every note is deleted seven days after it was written, and the base station can rub one out sooner. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who wrote or who read. Where it is kept. Beside the channel, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep a note because you chalked it up for passers-by to read, and keeping it for the week is what that takes. Writing it is your consent to that, and you can take it back by asking us to rub it out.

The Solarpunk Hermitage and the Faery Yurt each have a bowl by the door for leaving a pebble: a line of your own, and a link if the thing is somewhere else. It was Helen Edgar’s idea. Each bowl is part of the CB and runs on the chalkboard’s rules: anybody can see what is in it, and a pebble stays for seven days. The basket beside it, of things the host has put out to take, is part of the page and sends nothing: taking one is following a link, and nothing records that you did. Who can leave a pebble. Only people signed on to the CB. Leaving one sends your handle, your words, the link if you gave one, which room it is for, and your pass to us, the same as transmitting on the radio. Who can see it. Anybody who opens that room, signed on or not, so leave in it what you would leave by a door somebody else walks through. A username says whoever holds its password left it, and nothing more. The bowls’ answers ask search engines not to index or archive them. What we keep. For each room, the latest thirty pebbles, each with its handle, its words, its link and the time it was left. Every pebble is deleted seven days after it was left, a thirty-first lets the oldest go, and the base station can lift one out sooner. There is no archive, no backup and no copy. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who left or who looked, and nothing about what anybody took from a basket. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep a pebble because you left it for whoever comes to that door, and keeping it for the week is what that takes. Leaving it is your consent to that, and you can take it back by asking us to lift it out.

Pando Calrissian has one tree on a hillside, which anybody signed on to the CB can water, and a fence beside it for notes. Both are part of the CB. The tree is kept for good, and what it keeps is a number. Who can water it. Only people signed on to the CB. Watering sends your pass to us, so the tree knows somebody signed on is holding the can. The pass is checked and not kept, and nothing about who watered is written down: not your handle, not when you watered, not how often. What the tree keeps. How many times it has been watered, and the time of the last watering, so it can tell everybody when the ground will take more. Nothing else. That number never expires and is never reset. It is not personal information about anybody, because it cannot be traced to anybody. The fence. The chalkboard’s rules exactly. Only people signed on can pin a note, which sends your handle, your words and your pass to us; anybody who opens the room can read it; the latest thirty are kept, each with its handle, its words and the time; every note is deleted seven days after it went up, and the base station can take one down sooner. A username says whoever holds its password wrote it, and nothing more. Its answers ask search engines not to index or archive it. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who watered, who pinned a note or who looked, and no copy or backup of the tree or the fence. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep a note because you pinned it up for whoever comes up the hill, and keeping it for the week is what that takes; pinning it is your consent to that, and you can take it back by asking us to take it down. The tree’s number is kept because it is the tree, and it holds nothing of yours.

The Fridge of Sighs is a fridge door covered in word magnets, where a sentence is built one word at a time by whoever comes in. It is part of the CB. Finished sentences are kept for good, and that is only simple because none of them holds anything about who wrote it. Who can put up a word. Only people signed on to the CB. Putting one up sends the word and your pass to us. The pass is checked and not kept. The one thing kept about anybody. To stop anybody putting up two words in a row, the fridge keeps a mark saying the last word was yours: your handle, scrambled with a secret kept in the site’s settings on Netlify, so it cannot be looked up from a handle without that secret. It is replaced by the very next word, from anybody, and it is never shown to anybody, sent to any page, or stored with a sentence. Nothing records who put up any other word. What the fridge keeps. The words on the line so far, the finished sentences, and the time each one was finished. The newest forty stay on the door, and older ones are filed by month into the drawer. They are kept for good, with no names in them, and the base station can take a word or a sentence down. Who can read it. Anybody who opens the room, signed on or not. Its answers ask search engines not to index or archive it. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who put up words or who looked. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. A word you put up is part of a sentence that belongs to everybody who added to it, which is why it is kept with no name on it. If something on the door should not be there, ask and we will take it down.

Count Me In is a stairwell everybody climbs together, a number to a step, with a chairlift beside the stair. It is part of the CB, and what it keeps for good is two numbers. Who can take a step. Only people signed on to the CB. Taking a step sends your pass to us, and the number you typed; riding the lift sends your pass and no number. The pass is checked and not kept. The one thing kept about anybody. To stop anybody taking two steps in a row, the stair keeps a mark saying the last step was yours, the same kind of mark as the Fridge of Sighs: your handle scrambled with that secret. The very next step replaces it, and it is never shown to anybody or sent to any page. Nothing records who took any other step, or whether anybody came up by the stairs or the lift. What the stair keeps. The step it is on, the highest step it has reached, and where it had got to the last time it went back to one, with the time. The highest step is kept for good. None of it is personal information about anybody. Who can read it. Anybody who opens the room, signed on or not. Its answers ask search engines not to index or archive it. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no list of who climbed or who looked, and nothing about who put the number that sent the stair back to one. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy.

The Brass Tacks Board is for posts meant to last: news, notices, events and celebrations. Anybody can read it, and it has a feed of its own, so its posts reach feed readers and search engines may find them. Who can post. Only our moderators, signed on to the CB as moderators. Posting sends their pass, the title, the words and the picture, if there is one; the pass is checked and not kept. What we keep. Each post’s title, its words, the moderator’s username, when it went up and when it was last edited, and its picture and description. The username is public on the post, on purpose, so anybody can see who put it up. Posts are kept until a moderator takes them down; there is no other copy and no archive, and nothing about who reads the board is kept or counted. Pictures. A picture is redrawn in the moderator’s browser before it is sent, which takes off everything a camera writes into a file, where it was taken first, and the board refuses one that still carries any of it. It must have a description, and the moderator says that everybody recognisable in it has said yes to it being on the board. It is served to anybody from this site, and deleted when its post is taken down or its picture changed; one that never made it onto a post is deleted after a day. If you are in a picture on the board and want it down, ask any moderator, and they will take it down. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy.

Our moderators can put up one line along the top of the street’s front page, the Community Center, the forums and the office’s dashboard, for news everybody should see. What opening those pages sends. Each asks this site for the notice, once, with nothing of yours in the request: no pass, nothing you typed, nothing from your browser’s storage. Nothing is kept about who asked, and nothing is counted. Putting it away. The notice has a Put it away button. Pressing it keeps a short code worked out from the notice’s words in your own browser, under love-notice, so it stays away on every page it is on until a new notice goes up, and changing even a letter of the words counts as a new one. That is never sent to us, and nothing tells us who put a notice away. Who can put one up. Only our moderators, from the desk in their room, signed on to the CB as moderators. Doing it sends their pass and the words; the pass is checked and not kept. What we keep. The notice up now, or that there is none, and which moderator put it up or took it down last, and when. The pages show only the words; the moderator’s username and the time are shown to the other moderators at the desk. There is one notice at a time, and a new one replaces the old: there is no archive. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy.

The suggestion box in The Sandbox is where anybody signed on to the CB can drop in a suggestion, a feature request or a bug report, and where our moderators answer them. Anybody can read what is in it, signed on or not, the way anybody can read the Brass Tacks Board; its answers ask search engines not to keep them, and it has no feed. Who can drop something in. Anybody signed on to the CB. Dropping one in sends your pass, what kind it is, its title and its words; the pass is checked and not kept. What we keep. Each one’s kind, title and words, your handle, public on it, on purpose, when you dropped it in, and the mark your pass gave it: BASE for a moderator, which nobody can set themselves. (A box from before 2026-10-21 may also say a suggestion came from a claimed username; every username is claimed now.) Under it, every reply from you or a moderator (since 2026-10-25 a suggestion has a thread of them, where it had one answer): its words, the username on it, public, when it was sent and last edited, and whether a moderator’s reply marked it done, not doing or open again. Where a suggestion stands is worked out from those replies and kept nowhere else. A suggestion and a reply can each carry pictures, below. Me too: the handle of everybody signed on who pressed it, to say a suggestion affects them too, public on the suggestion, alphabetically, and never shown as a number. It is not a vote, and nothing in the box is sorted by it. A device can be told when there is something new in the box for it, only if it switched that on: see notifications. Nothing about who reads the box is kept or counted, and nothing in it is counted, ranked or voted on. How long. Until it is taken down: by you, from the box, or by any moderator, with every reply and Me too on it. A reply stays until whoever wrote it or a moderator takes it down, and a Me too until whoever pressed it presses it again; editing a reply keeps nothing of what it said before. A suggestion from a claimed username comes down only for that username’s own password, the same as a message on the channel. There is no other copy and no archive. The box holds a few hundred at most; a full box refuses the next one and says so, rather than quietly pushing the oldest out. Pictures. This reverses what this page said when the box opened, that it takes words only, because a screenshot of a bug is a picture of somebody’s screen: Ryan’s call, 2026-10-25, so a bug report can show what went wrong. A suggestion can carry up to four pictures, and so can every reply under it. Each is redrawn in your own browser before it is sent, by the same code the CB uses, which takes off everything a camera or a phone wrote into it, where it was taken first of all; our server refuses one that still carries any of that. Each needs a sentence saying what it shows, which is what a screen reader says in its place. A picture in the box is as public as its words: anybody can see it, signed on or not, at an address of its own that asks search engines not to keep it. A screenshot shows whatever was on your screen, so the box asks you to say you have looked at all of it: no messages but your own, no faces from a call, nothing from your other tabs, emails or notifications, and that anybody recognisable in it has said yes. We keep each picture, its description, when it was added, and a scrambled mark of the username that added it, which is never shown to anybody and is how only you can put your picture in the box. A picture goes the moment its suggestion is taken down, or the reply it is on is edited without it or taken down. One you added and never dropped in is never shown to anybody, and is deleted after a day. A browser that has shown somebody a picture may keep its own copy of it for ten minutes. Not for a security problem, which everybody could read there: report it privately, as below. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy.

Notifications, under Your radio on the CB, can switch a device on to be told about the CB, even with stimpunks.world closed. It reverses what this page used to say, that there were no notifications at all. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-18, after several requests from our community, and especially from our staff, as more of our chat and work moves onto the street. Sealed at rest (since 2026-10-25, Ryan’s call): every device’s record, its delivery address and keys included, is encrypted where it is kept at Netlify, with the staff key Tasks and the forums use, because a delivery address works like a password for sending that device a notification. Without that key no device can be switched on or off, and nothing is written in the clear. What can notify you. These, each off until you switch it on: somebody @mentioning your handle on a channel you can hear, or in a post in the forums that your claimed username can read; somebody replying to one of your messages on a channel you can hear (since 2026-10-21); somebody giving you props, which wait in Profile for you to confirm or reject; somebody sending you a direct message; any message on a room you follow, and on The Feed’s and The Source’s channels each new arrival, but only if you follow that room by name; a call starting in a room you follow, or the World call; every message on World; and, for our directors, board members and administrators, something new in your Notifications in Tasks (since 2026-10-21); and events, one you said you are interested in starting, and a new one on World or in a room you follow (since 2026-10-23); and the suggestion box (since 2026-10-25, Ryan’s ask and Norah’s): a moderator replying to a suggestion you dropped in, and, offered only to our moderators, something new in the box, a suggestion dropped in or a reply from whoever dropped it in, so whichever of them switch it on know without watching the box. One more switch, Everything, and anything added later, switches on every one of them at once and any kind of notification we add after you press it, so a new kind reaches you without asking you first: that was asked for by somebody in our community, and is Ryan’s call, 2026-10-19. It leaves the words and the rooms you follow as you set them. Follow every room (Norah’s ask, 2026-10-21) follows every room your pass can go into at once, rooms that open later included, instead of one at a time; it is not a kind of notification, so Everything leaves it as you set it too. You are never told about your own messages. An edited message tells only somebody it @mentions that it did not name before, and nobody who follows the room again. A room that keeps to itself tells only the devices that follow it there, by name and never by Follow every room, so a mention or a reply there tells nobody else. A reply to a message sent under a claimed username tells only the devices switched on as that username. Calling a role. Since 2026-10-23 (Ryan’s ask), @moderator, @director, @board and @administrator call everybody who holds that role, the way an @ before somebody’s handle calls them: on a channel, in a post in the forums, and in a task or a comment in Tasks or the office. Anybody signed on can call @moderator, which is how to ask our moderators for help; the other three can be called by our moderators, directors, board members and administrators. On a channel or in the forums, a call tells the devices of the people holding that role that switched on When somebody @mentions me, and says which role, only where their pass can go now, and never in a room that keeps to itself; in Tasks and the office it goes into the Notifications in Tasks of everybody there who holds it, as an @ before their handle would. Nobody is ever told who holds a role, or how many people a call reached: not whoever called it, and not the radio’s @ list, which offers the role’s word and says only what it calls. Nothing new is kept: a message or a post keeps which roles it called, as it keeps which handles it mentions, and goes when it goes. Those four words cannot be anybody’s username. A call for a moderator leaves a note on the moderators’ desk. Since 2026-10-23 (Ryan’s call), when somebody who is not a moderator calls @moderator on a channel or in a forum post, a note goes on the desk in the Moderators’ room as well, so a call made while no moderator was listening is still waiting for one. It holds who called, when, where (the room’s channel, or the topic and post), and the words they called with, as they were then; an edit leaves one only if it newly calls. Nothing is left from a room that keeps to itself, or from one only some people may enter. Only moderators signed on as the base can read the notes. A moderator closes one once the call is answered, which deletes it, and nothing records who closed it; one nobody closes is deleted after thirty days. A note stays if you take the message off the channel, edit it, or delete your username, as a report does, because it was said to the moderators. The desk keeps two hundred at most, and past that the oldest goes. A moderator calling the others leaves no note. What a notification says. Who sent the message and where, and its first 180 characters, unless you switch Show the words of a message, a post, props or a task off for that device. For a mention in the forums, who wrote the post and its category, and, unless the words are off, the topic’s title and the post’s first 180 characters. For props, who wrote them and, unless the words are off, their first 180 characters, and never how many are waiting; pressing it opens the street with Profile open at Your props. For a direct message, who sent it, whether it is asking to start a conversation, and, unless the words are off, its first 180 characters; pressing it opens the street with Messages open. For a task, who did it and why it is yours (assigned to you, put on it, taken off it, mentioned in it or in a comment on it, or one you are on, made or commented on), and, unless the words are off, the task’s name and the words of a box ticked; for a comment in the office, who wrote it and whether it is on a contact, a grant request, a case, a mailing, a template or an email, and never which one by name, whatever the words switch says; never what a description or a comment says, and never how many are unread; pressing it opens the task in Tasks, or the comment. It is sent only once the change is in your Notifications in Tasks, and only while your pass can read Tasks. For an event, where and when, the event’s title unless the words are off, and for a new one who scheduled it; never who else is interested, and never how many; pressing it opens the chat page at Events, on that event. For the suggestion box, who did it and whether they dropped a suggestion in, replied, or marked yours done, not doing or open again, and, unless the words are off, the suggestion’s title and the first 180 characters of what they wrote; never how many are waiting, and never anything to whoever wrote it; pressing it opens the box on that suggestion. Anybody who can see your screen can read a notification, so switch the words off where that matters. A call’s notification says only that a call has started in a room, never who is in it, because that is shown only in the room itself (see calls). Private rooms. A device is told about a room only if the pass it was switched on with could hear that room now. Before anything is sent, our server checks that pass by the same rules as the radio, so a changed password, a claimed or deleted username, or a moderator taken off the list stops that device’s notifications at once. What we keep. For each device you switch on: the push address and the two keys your browser made for it; the handle it was switched on as, which kind of pass that was and a scrambled form of the pass, not the pass itself; and what you chose. Nothing about what was sent to the device itself, and nothing in any log; what your devices are told is kept for you, apart from them, in your past notifications. It is kept beside the channel, at Netlify. Your browser’s push service. A notification travels through the push service your browser comes with: Google’s for Chrome, Edge on Android and most Android browsers, Mozilla’s for Firefox, Apple’s for Safari, and Microsoft’s for some Edge on Windows. It is encrypted to your device’s own keys, so the push service cannot read who sent it or what it says, but it sees that a notification went to your device, when, and how large it was. Our server sends to those services and nowhere else. What we cannot take back. Once a notification has reached your device it is your device’s, and it stays in your notifications until you clear it. A message taken off the channel, or gone at its two weeks, is not taken off a device it has already reached. Your past notifications (since 2026-10-25, Ryan’s ask: notifications come and go, and Tasks already kept its own for 30 days). It reverses what this page used to say, that nothing about what was sent to a device is kept. Each time one of your devices is told something, our server also keeps it for you, once however many of your devices were told: what kind of notification it was and why, who it was from, where, which message, post, task, suggestion or event it was about, and when, and never its words. Only a notification a device was actually sent is kept, so what you switch on decides what is in it. Your page shows them, newest first, for 30 days and 500 at most, and marks the ones you have not seen there yet, never how many. The words on Your page are read again each time you open it, whether or not your devices showed them, from wherever they still are and only if your username can still read them there: a message while it is still on its channel, a post while it is still in the forums, a task’s name while you can read Tasks, a suggestion’s or an event’s title while it is there. A message gone at its two weeks, or taken off, is gone from Your page too, and only that there was one is left. Direct messages and props are never shown there in words; they are where they always were, under Messages and in Profile. It is kept under a scrambled form of your username, and nobody else is shown it, a moderator included. Opening Your page marks everything in it seen, which only your own list knows. Clear my past notifications on Your page deletes the whole of it at once, and Forget me and deleting your username delete it too. Switching it off. Switch off on this device in the tray, or signing off the CB on that device, deletes that device’s record and takes the subscription off it. Forget me and Delete my account under Account delete every device switched on as your handle. A device your browser’s push service says has gone is deleted the next time anything is sent to it. Who can switch it on. Anybody signed on to the CB, as their own username, and nobody else can be told about yours: every username is claimed, and a device is told only while the pass it was switched on with still works. On an iPhone or iPad, a website can only send notifications once it has been added to the Home Screen and opened from there, and stimpunks.world only from iOS or iPadOS 26, which opens every site added to the Home Screen as a web app. We keep a device’s record because you switched notifications on there and asked to be told, and keeping it is what that takes. Switching it on is your consent to it, and switching it off takes it back.

The forums are the CB’s place for conversations that need to last longer than two weeks: topics in categories, each kept for a week, three months, six months or for good after its last post. Only a claimed username can read them, so they are not public: they have no feed, and every answer from them asks search engines not to keep it. Since 2026-10-25 every topic, every category’s list of topics, and every picture and file posted or waiting to be posted is sealed at rest, Ryan’s call: encrypted where it is kept at Netlify, with the same key of their own as Tasks, which neither the office nor direct messages use, so somebody who got at the stored files alone could not read them. Every category is sealed, not only the staff ones, because a topic moved out of a staff category must never be left in the clear. They are not end-to-end encrypted: our server opens them for whoever may read the category. Without that key the forums are shut rather than written in the clear, and anything written before that day is sealed within the hour. Who can read and write. Anybody signed on to the CB with a claimed username, moderators included once they have claimed theirs. A few categories are for our moderators, directors or board, by the same roles as the Town Hall’s rooms. A category you cannot read is never sent to your browser, and nothing tells you it is there. Reading sends your pass and which category, topic or search you asked for; the pass is checked and not kept, and nothing records who read what. Each category is a room on the CB. Ryan’s call, 2026-10-21: reading a category, or a topic in it, tunes the radio’s This room to that category’s own room, with its own channel, Be seen here, call and Follow this room, and a category inside another is the room of the one it is in, so all of Team Docs is one room. Its room is for exactly the people who can read the category: a claimed username, with the category’s roles, checked by our server for everything the radio does there, and by nothing kept in your browser. Somebody seen in a staff category’s room, or in its call, is shown only to the people that category is for, and a notification about its room goes only to a device whose claimed username can read it. A category’s room is not on the street’s public list of rooms, and the World room shows its people, its call and its latest message on the forums’ own line, to the people who can read it. It cannot be your favourite room on your profile card, which everybody signed on can see. What we keep. Each topic’s title, its category, its tags, when it was started and last posted to, and whether a moderator has pinned or closed it. Each post’s words, your username, shown to everybody who can read that category, the mark your pass gave it (BASE for a moderator), when you posted it and last edited it, which post it answered, its reactions (who pressed which, by username, and never how many), the previews of the links in it, its pictures and files, below, and the usernames it @mentions, so they can be shown as names. With every post we also keep a scrambled mark of the claimed username that wrote it, which is never shown to anybody, ourselves included: it is how only you can edit or take down what you wrote, and not somebody who claims the same name after you have deleted yours. The Wiki. Ryan’s call, 2026-10-19: a category of how-to pages, kept for good. The post that opens each topic there is a wiki page, which our moderators can edit whoever started it, and the page shows the username of whoever started it and of whoever edited it last, which we keep with it. Nothing else about earlier versions is kept: an edit replaces the words. Team Docs works the same way (Ryan’s call, 2026-10-20, for the team’s documents moving out of Google Docs): it and everything in it, its Field Guide, Notes, Meeting Minutes and Templates, can be read only by our moderators, directors, board and administrators, is kept for good, and the post that opens each topic there is a page any of them can edit. Everywhere else in the forums, and on every reply in the Wiki and Team Docs, only whoever wrote a post can edit it. A wiki page goes only with its whole topic. Templates. A topic in Team Docs’ Templates is offered to anybody who can read it when they start a new topic, and choosing one copies its title and words into the new post in their own browser. Nothing records who used which template, and its pictures stay with it. Grantmaking and tags. Ryan’s call, 2026-10-22, moving the Grants table out of Notion: a topic can carry up to five tags, words you choose, which anybody who can read it sees and which a category’s page can show it by. Every grant round is a topic in Grantmaking tagged grant-round, kept for good, and the post that opens one is a page any of our directors and board can edit, so each can add their name to its approvals; it shows who edited it last. A grant round names the people being considered for a grant, links their entries on stimpunks.org, and can hold what our team noted about each of them, their circumstances included, as the Grants table did. Grantmaking is read only by our directors, board and administrators, but it is kept the way the rest of the forums are, not sealed the way the office is. The rounds made in Notion were brought in once, each under the username of whoever made it there and at the time they made it, with the id of its Notion page kept so it could be brought again without a second copy, and each says it was brought from Notion. Nobody was told when they arrived. What we do not keep. Anything about who reads: no views, no read receipts, no list of who has seen what, and nothing counted but a poll’s votes, below. There are no badges and no unread count. What is new to you is marked by your own browser, below, and never by us. Polls. Norah’s ask, Ryan’s calls, 2026-10-22: whoever starts a topic can open it with a poll, or add one to it later, as can the editors of a wiki like Grantmaking and our moderators, and a poll is the one place in the forums that counts: how many picked each choice, in the poll’s own order. A poll keeps the username of whoever added it, shown on it. It is one of two kinds, chosen when the poll is made and never changed. A show of hands keeps, for each vote, your username, which choices you picked and a mark from your pass, and shows your username under your choices to everybody who can read the topic, as the votes come in; you can change your vote or take it back while the poll is open. A sealed ballot keeps how many picked each choice and, apart from that, that you have voted, as a code made from the topic and your pass that differs in every poll, so you cannot vote twice. Nothing we keep says what you picked, so nobody can see it, our moderators and Ryan included, and a sealed vote cannot be changed or taken back, because we could not find it. Nobody is shown any of a sealed ballot’s numbers until it closes, on its date or when whoever added it, the topic’s starter or a moderator closes it, and then everybody who can read the topic sees them, and it cannot be opened again. With only a few votes, the numbers can still say who picked what, which the poll says before you vote. A vote tells nobody, and a poll goes with its topic. Pictures and files. This reverses what this page said when the forums opened, that they take words only: Ryan’s call, 2026-10-18. A post can carry pictures and files. A picture is redrawn in your own browser before it is sent, by the same code the CB uses, which takes off everything a camera or a phone wrote into it, where it was taken first of all; our server refuses one that still carries any of that, and refuses a picture sent as a file. A description is offered and never required. A file goes exactly as it is, so anything written inside it goes too, such as the author’s name a word processor puts in a document: check it before you post it. The forums take only PDFs, plain text, Markdown, CSV, RTF, and Word, Excel, PowerPoint and OpenDocument documents and EPUB books, each checked against what its first bytes say it is, never a web page, a script, an SVG or a document with macros in it, up to 5 MB each. Neither has a public address: each is fetched with your pass, only by somebody who can read the topic it is in, so a topic moved to a staff category takes its pictures and files with it, and a file is only ever saved to your device, never opened in the forums. Ask anybody recognisable in a picture before you post it. A picture or file goes the moment its post, its topic or your edit lets go of it; one you added and never posted is deleted after a day. @mentions. This reverses what this page said when the forums opened, that they send no notifications: Ryan’s call, 2026-10-18. Typing @ offers the people in the topic, anybody with a claimed username on Who’s online, and anybody who started or last posted in a topic you can read (and, if you can open Tasks, everybody Tasks can assign), which your browser asks for once, the first time you type an @. They are names you can already see; there is no list of every username. A post keeps the usernames it mentions, to show them as names. Mentions lists the topics where somebody has mentioned you: our server works it out from the posts each time you look, and nothing records who was mentioned where. A mention tells you on a device only if you switched on When somebody @mentions me there (see notifications), and only if your claimed username can read the category it is in. How long. Every category says how long its topics stay after their last post, and every topic says the date it goes. When it goes, everything in it goes with it: every post, reaction, vote, preview and copied message. A topic a moderator has pinned stays while it is pinned. Whoever wrote a post can take it down sooner, a topic’s starter can take the whole topic down while nobody else has posted in it, and a moderator can take down any post or topic. There is no archive and no backup. Previews of links. A link on a line of its own in a post becomes a preview. For a page on another site, our server reads that page once, when the post is made or edited, for its title, its description and the site’s name, or for what the site’s own oEmbed answer says about it (who made it and, for a post on X, Bluesky or the like, the words of the post), and keeps those with the post. For a YouTube video it asks YouTube’s own Data API, sending it only the video’s id, or reads the video’s own page, for its title, its channel and how long it runs, and the preview is a press-to-play player like every other on the street: nothing from YouTube loads until somebody presses it. Either way the site sees a request from Netlify, our host, and never from you or from anybody reading the post, and nothing is fetched again when somebody reads it. No picture is fetched from anywhere. A link to a room on the street shows that room’s own name and description, from this site. Copying from the CB. Anybody with a claimed username who can hear a channel can tick messages on it and start a topic with them. Our server copies them from the channel itself, so the words, the handles, the marks and the times are exactly as they are on the channel, with edited on any their sender has edited, and nobody can put words in somebody else’s mouth; pictures and stickers are not copied. Once copied, they last as long as the topic. The house norm is to ask everybody in the conversation first, as for a screenshot. Whoever sent a copied message can take it out of the topic at any time, and so can a moderator. Nothing can be copied from a room that keeps to itself, and from one of the Town Hall’s private rooms, or a staff category’s room, only into a category no wider than that room. In your browser. love-forum, in the table above: which topics you have opened and when, the colours you chose for the forums, and a post you have started and not sent. It is never sent to us. The tab’s own history keeps, beside each address it already holds, how far down that view you were and the address of the view before it, so going back one step puts you where you were (going back, since 2026-10-21); it goes with the tab’s history, and nothing of it is sent to us. What the link back says and which link you followed are kept only while the page is open. Deleting your username. Your posts stay up with your username on them, and from then on only a moderator can take them down. If you want them gone, take them down yourself first, or ask a moderator. A vote in a show of hands stays too, with your username under it, until the topic goes, so take it back first if you want it gone; a sealed ballot never had your name on it. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep a post because you wrote it for the people in the forums to read, for as long as its category says. Posting is your consent to that, and taking a post down takes it back.

Tasks are the team’s to-do list, moved here from EspoCRM (Ryan’s call, 2026-10-20). They are the CB’s too, and they are not public: only our directors, board members and administrators can read or change them, and only once they have claimed their username. Nobody else is sent a task, or told that there are any. Since 2026-10-25 they are sealed at rest, Ryan’s call: every task, its comments, its activity, everybody’s Tasks notifications and saved filters, the recurring tasks and the templates are encrypted where they are kept at Netlify, with a key of their own that neither the office nor direct messages use, so somebody who got at the stored files alone could not read them. They are not end-to-end encrypted: our server opens them for whoever may read Tasks. Without that key Tasks are shut rather than written in the clear, and anything written before that day is sealed the next time it is written, or within the hour. What we keep, for each task. Its name; its status and priority; the day it starts and the day it is due; when it was finished, if it was; its description, written in Markdown; the username of whoever it is assigned to, and of anybody else working on it; its tags; the username of whoever made it, and when; and the username of whoever changed it last, and when. A task brought over from EspoCRM also keeps EspoCRM’s id for it, so bringing tasks over again updates them rather than making them twice; and when one of those is deleted here, its EspoCRM id is kept on its own, so bringing tasks over again leaves it deleted. A task brought over from our Tasks in Notion (since 2026-10-21) keeps the id of its page there in the same way, and when it was made there; Notion does not say who made it or when it was finished, so neither is kept. Nothing else about the Notion page comes over, and nothing is sent to Notion. Activity and notifications (since 2026-10-21, after EspoCRM’s stream and notifications). Every change somebody makes to a task is kept as part of its Activity, on its page: who made the change and when, and for each thing it changed (its name, status, priority, days, who it is assigned to, who else is on it, its tags) what it was before and after. A change to a description is kept as only that it changed, never its words; a tick keeps the words of the box ticked. A task a recurring task makes is kept under nobody’s name. A task’s activity keeps its newest 200 changes and goes when the task is deleted. Each change is also put in the Notifications of everybody it concerns, except whoever made it: whoever the task is assigned to and whoever else is on it, before and after the change, whoever made the task, and anybody the change newly @mentions in its description. A comment is kept in the activity and the notifications as only that somebody commented, and which comment, never its words. A comment in the office is put in these notifications too, naming only what kind of record it is on and its id. Your notifications are kept under a scrambled form of your username, each with whether you have read it, for 30 days and 200 at most, and nobody else is shown them. Nothing is sent anywhere for them: they are there when you open Tasks. Comments (since 2026-10-21, after EspoCRM’s stream posts and Notion’s comments). A comment on a task keeps its words, written in Markdown; the username of whoever wrote it; when it was written, and when it was last edited; and a scrambled form of the writer’s username and when they claimed it, which is never sent to anybody, so that only they can edit it, and somebody who claims the same name after it was deleted cannot. They, or an administrator, can delete it. A task also keeps when it was last commented on, so the Feed can put it first. A comment goes in the Notifications of whoever the task is assigned to, anybody else on it, whoever made it, anybody who commented on it before, and anybody it @mentions, except whoever wrote it, as only that there is one and on which task; an edit tells only anybody it newly @mentions. A task holds 500 comments at most, and after that a new one is refused rather than an old one dropped; they go when the task is deleted. A comment brought over from a task’s page in our Notion (since 2026-10-21) also keeps Notion’s id for it, so bringing comments over again changes it rather than adding it twice, and when one is deleted here that id is kept on its own so it stays deleted; it keeps who wrote it, as their username, and when, and tells nobody. Nothing is sent to Notion. What we do not keep. Anything about who reads: nothing records who looked at a task, or when, and marking a notification read is known only to your own list. A description’s or a comment’s earlier words are not kept anywhere. The Feed (since 2026-10-21) is worked out from the tasks and their activity each time it is opened, and keeps nothing of its own. How long. A task stays until a director or an administrator deletes it. Finished tasks stay too, as a record of the work. Recurring tasks. Each is kept like a task: its name, which can carry the week, the year or the month; its description; whoever its tasks go to and anybody else on them; their priority and tags; how often it comes round; the next day it makes a task, and how many days after that day each task starts and is due; whether it is switched on; who made it and when, and who changed it last and when; and, for one brought from EspoCRM, EspoCRM’s id for it. On its day the site makes the task by itself, under nobody’s name, and the task keeps which recurring task made it and for which day, so it is never made twice. A recurring task stays until a director or an administrator deletes it; deleting it makes no more tasks and leaves the ones it made. Templates (since 2026-10-22). A template is a task to start from, kept like a recurring task: its name and description, which can hold fill-ins such as {name} for somebody’s name and links to their records in the office; whoever its tasks go to and anybody else on them; their priority and tags; how many days after a task is made it starts and is due; and who made it and changed it, and when. A director making a task from one replaces the fill-ins themself. When somebody fills in stimpunks.org’s Join form, the office makes their onboarding task from a template by itself, under nobody’s name, with their name in its name and links to their join request and their contact, which are in the office, sealed; nothing else of what they wrote is put in the task. A task made from a template keeps which one. A template stays until a director or an administrator deletes it; deleting it leaves the tasks made from it. Your saved filters. When you save a list or a board as a saved filter, we keep, under a scrambled form of your username, its name and the address that holds its filters, order and columns, and nothing about when. Nobody else is sent them or told you have any, an administrator included. You delete one with Delete beside it; Forget me and deleting your username delete them all. Deleting your username. Your saved filters and your notifications go, and so they do with Forget me. The tasks, their comments and their activity stay, because they are the organisation’s work, with your username on them as words. In your browser. Nothing of the tasks. The tab’s own history keeps, beside each address it already holds, how far down that view you were and the address of the view before it, so going back one step puts you where you were (going back, since 2026-10-21); it goes with the tab’s history, and nothing of it is sent to us. What the link back says, which can be a task’s name, is kept only while the page is open. How you filter and sort the list or the board lives in the page’s address, which you can bookmark or share with another director, and nothing is stored there; a saved filter is kept with us, above, so it is on any device you sign on with. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. Every answer asks search engines not to keep it.

The office holds the people and organisations Stimpunks is in touch with, our grant requests, and the connection requests and volunteer applications that come in, which EspoCRM called cases, moved here from EspoCRM, where they were kept until now (Ryan’s call, 2026-10-20), and the email between them and our team mailbox. Most of the people in it never signed on to this street: they wrote to us, asked us for something, or were introduced to us. So it is held more tightly than anything else here. Only our directors, board members and administrators can open it, and only once they have claimed their username; nobody else is sent anything from it, or told whether anybody is in it. What we keep, for each contact. Their first and last name; an email address and a phone number, if we have them; whether they have asked not to be emailed or not to be called; notes, in Markdown; the username of whoever added them, and when; and the username of whoever changed them last, and when.
