A contact brought over from EspoCRM also keeps EspoCRM’s id for it, so bringing contacts over again updates them rather than adding them twice; and when one of those is deleted here, its EspoCRM id is kept on its own, so bringing contacts over again leaves it deleted. EspoCRM’s address and payment fields were empty on every contact, so they are not kept. What we keep, for each grant request. Its name; which of our grants it is for (Mutual Aid or Creator Grants) and the stage it is at, which says whether it is open, granted or denied; the amount, in dollars; the day it was submitted and the day it was decided, which is set when it is granted or denied; the contact it is from; the number of the stimpunks.org form entry it came in as; a description, in Markdown; the username of whoever added it, and when; and the username of whoever changed it last, and when. One brought over from EspoCRM also keeps EspoCRM’s id for it, kept on its own if it is deleted here, as a contact’s is. The history of its stages that EspoCRM kept was not brought over. What we keep, for each case (a connection request or a volunteer application). Its number; its name; which of the two it is; its status, which says whether it is still open, and its priority; the day it was submitted and the day it was closed; the contact it is from; the number of the stimpunks.org form entry it came in as; a description, in Markdown; the username of whoever added it, and when; and the username of whoever changed it last, and when. One brought over from EspoCRM keeps EspoCRM’s number and id, as a contact or a grant request does; the HubSpot ids EspoCRM still held from before it, and its history of status changes, were not brought over. The highest number given is kept too, so a number is never given twice. How an entry from stimpunks.org arrives. When somebody fills in one of stimpunks.org’s forms to ask for a grant, to connect, to volunteer or to join our community, stimpunks.org’s server sends their entry here, signed with a key the two servers share, so nobody else can send one. The office finds them as a contact by their email or adds them, with their name and phone number, and makes the grant request or case, with every other answer they gave, their address among them, in its description. A Join entry makes a join request, which is a case, and since 2026-10-22 also a task in Tasks to welcome them, which carries their name and links to their join request and contact, and none of their answers. This replaced EspoCRM on 2026-10-20, and nothing goes to EspoCRM any more. The entry also stays on stimpunks.org, under its own privacy policy. Email with the team mailbox. A script inside our team’s Gmail sends the office every email between the team mailbox and somebody who is a contact, as it arrives or is sent, signed with a key the two share. It is filed on that contact’s page whole: who it is from and to, its Cc, and its Bcc on what the team sent; when it was sent; its subject and its plain text; and Gmail’s ids for it and its thread, so the office can link to it there. Attachments stay in Gmail: the office keeps only their names and sizes. To know who is a contact without being sent anybody’s address, the script is given a keyed hash of each contact’s email address and compares the addresses on each email with those, so email with anybody who is not a contact never leaves Gmail, and the office keeps nothing of an email that reaches it with no contact on it. Somebody becomes a contact this way only when one of the team chooses, by putting a label on one of their emails in Gmail: the script then sends the name and address that email gives them (its sender, or whoever we sent it to), the office adds them as a contact, added by the team mailbox, with nothing else about them, and the whole thread is filed on them. The script remembers, in its own settings in the team’s Google account, which labelled threads it has handled. Writing and replying are done in Gmail; the office only opens it. A director or an administrator can delete an email from the office, which leaves it in Gmail; its Gmail id is kept on its own so it is never filed again. The email also stays in Gmail, under Google’s privacy policy. EspoCRM’s own copies of our email were not brought over. Mailings. A director or an administrator can send an email from a template to everybody at one stage of a grant pipeline. The office keeps each template (its name, subject and words, and who wrote or changed it, and when), and for each mailing the template’s words, the pipeline and stage, the day it was narrowed to requests submitted since if it was, who sent it and when, and for each email the grant request and contact it is for and whether and when it went. Until an email goes, it also keeps that person’s address and the email filled in, because the team mailbox’s script fetches them to send it: the one time the office hands that script anybody’s address, and only for a mailing a director has seen in full and confirmed. Anybody who asked not to be emailed, or has no address, is left out. The script sends each from the team mailbox’s own Gmail, one email to each person and never as a group, and tells the office it went; the mailing then drops that address and those words, and the email comes back to the office as one of the team mailbox’s, filed on its contact. Stopping a mailing takes back whatever has not gone, deleting a contact takes back theirs, and a mailing with nothing waiting can be deleted. Writing to one person with a template (since 2026-10-22). On a contact’s page, Write to them in Gmail can take one of these templates, filled in for them, and opens Gmail’s compose window with their address, the subject and the words ready, for the director to read and send from Gmail themself. The office keeps nothing for it and sends nothing: the filled email travels in the link to Gmail, so it is in that director’s own browser history, as the address alone always was, and reaches Google only as an email being written in our Gmail does. QuickBooks. A director or an administrator can connect the office to our QuickBooks company, through Intuit’s own sign-in. The office then reads our books once a day, late in the evening, and when a director presses Read the books now, and never writes to them. It keeps, sealed like every record: the permission Intuit gives it, two tokens that never leave our server and are never logged, with our company’s id at Intuit and who connected it and when; and what it last read, which replaces the time before: the money that came in over the last 30 days, each deposit, payment and sales receipt with its day, its amount, its kind, the account it went into and who it was from as our books name them, and no memo, address or email; and this year’s income, expenses and net by month, and income by account. Disconnect tells Intuit the office may no longer read our books, and deletes both. Our books themselves are at Intuit, under Intuit’s privacy statement. Givebutter. The office reads our Givebutter account, where people give to Stimpunks and where our mailing lists are kept, once a day, late in the evening, and when a director presses Read Givebutter now, with a key of ours. It writes to it in one way only, below. What it keeps, sealed like every record, replaces what it read the time before: for each gift in the last twelve months, its day, its amount, what reached us after Givebutter’s fees, its campaign, whether it was recurring and whether it went through; for each recurring plan, whether it is giving, how often and how much; and for each campaign, its name, its goal, what it has raised and how many people have given. It keeps nobody’s name, email, phone or address, and no message left with a gift, because somebody can give anonymously and the office needs nobody’s name to count. Everything about who gave stays at Givebutter, under Givebutter’s privacy policy. Joining our mailing lists (since 2026-10-23). When somebody asks on stimpunks.org’s Join form to be added to our Members Only mailing list or our Monthly Newsletter, a director can press Add them to Givebutter’s lists on their join request in the office. That press sends Givebutter their email address, their first and last name when their contact has both, and the lists they said yes to, as Givebutter’s tags for those lists, and marks them as wanting our emails. Givebutter takes a first and a last name together or no name at all, so somebody whose contact has one name goes to Givebutter by their email address alone (since 2026-10-25). Nothing else of their join request goes: not what they told us about themselves, not their city, not their profile or website, and nothing about who pressed. It happens only on that press, never when a form arrives, and never for a list they said no to. Givebutter matches somebody already there by their email address and adds the lists without taking any away, and the office tells the director who pressed whether they were there already, from when Givebutter says it made their contact, keeping nothing of its answer. The join request keeps which lists were sent and when, sealed like every record. Once there, they are on Givebutter’s lists under Givebutter’s privacy policy: every email it sends can be unsubscribed from, and taking somebody off a list, or out of Givebutter, is done in Givebutter, because deleting their join request or their contact in the office does not reach it. Our Members page (since 2026-10-23). When somebody fills in the Members page part of stimpunks.org’s Join form (a few words about themselves, a website, or both), a director can add them to our Members page, stimpunks.org’s Individuals page, from their join request in the office. The office shows the line as it will appear there: the name they asked to be shown by, or else the name or pseudonym they gave on the form, linked to their website if they gave one, and their words. The director can tidy the name, the link and the words first, and then presses Add them to the Members page. That press puts that one line at the end of the page’s list, and nothing else of their join request goes: not their email address, not their city, not what they told us about why they are joining, and nothing about who pressed. It happens only on that press, never when a form arrives, and only for somebody who filled in that part of the form. The office writes to stimpunks.org as one WordPress user, with an application password kept in Netlify’s settings and never in our code, and uses it for that one page and nothing else. Before it writes, it reads the page, and it refuses if the page has changed since a director looked, or if somebody by that name is on it already. WordPress keeps the page as it was before as a revision, under that user. The join request keeps when they were added, sealed like every record. Once there, the line is public on stimpunks.org, under stimpunks.org’s privacy policy. Changing the line, or taking somebody off the page, is done on stimpunks.org, because deleting their join request or their contact in the office does not reach it. Our Organizations page (since 2026-10-23). When somebody fills in the Organizations page part of stimpunks.org’s Join form (a few words about their organization, its website, its logo, or any of these), a director can add their organization to our Organizations page from their join request in the office, as the Members page is added to. The director types the organization’s name where the form did not ask it, and can tidy it, the link and the words; the office shows how it will look first. To show the director their logo, the office fetches it from where the Join form keeps it on stimpunks.org, takes off anything a camera or a phone wrote into it (where it was taken, the device, the time), and shows it in their browser; nothing of it is kept. The director says in words what the logo shows, for anybody who cannot see it. Then Add it to the Organizations page copies that logo, with its camera data taken off, into stimpunks.org’s media library, and puts one entry at the end of the page: the name, linked to the website, the words, the logo and its words. Nothing else of their join request goes: not their name or email address, not their city, not what they told us about why they are joining, and nothing about who pressed. It happens only on that press, never when a form arrives, and only for somebody who filled in that part of the form. The office writes as the same WordPress user, with the same application password, and uses it for that one page and the logo and nothing else; it refuses if the page has changed since a director looked, or if an organization by that name is on it already. WordPress keeps the page as it was before as a revision, and the logo stays in the media library, public, until somebody deletes it there. The join request keeps when they were added, sealed like every record. Changing the entry, or taking it or the logo off, is done on stimpunks.org, because deleting their join request or their contact in the office does not reach it. Comments (since 2026-10-21). A contact, a grant request, a case, a mailing, a mailing’s template or an email filed from the team mailbox can have comments under it, kept as a task’s comments are, and sealed like every record in the office: each comment’s words, written in Markdown, the username of whoever wrote it, when it was written and when it was last edited, and a scrambled form of the writer’s username and when they claimed it, which is never sent to anybody, so only they can edit it. They, or an administrator, can delete it. A contact, a grant request or a case also keeps when it was last commented on, so the feed can put it first. A comment is told in Tasks’ Notifications, to whoever added the record, anybody who commented on it before and anybody it @mentions, except whoever wrote it; those notifications are not sealed, so they never carry the record’s name or the comment’s words, only who commented, when, whether it is on a contact, a grant request, a case, a mailing, a template or an email, and the ids of the record and the comment. A record holds 500 comments at most, and they go when the record is deleted; an email’s go when it is deleted from the office, or with its only contact. A comment’s earlier words are not kept. The dashboard, the reports and the feed are worked out from these records each time they are opened, and the feed keeps nothing of its own. Some things are kept for the dashboard alone. One is a line each night, late in the evening, of how many grant requests were open in each pipeline and how many of those were submitted that year, and how many cases and tasks were open and how many tasks overdue, because a record does not keep the history of its stages: numbers only, sealed like every record, for 400 nights. Two more are what the office last read from QuickBooks and from Givebutter. Since 2026-10-22 there are two from the team mailbox. One is a list of the newest emails filed in the office, the twenty sent last, each with its Gmail id, when it was sent, its subject, whether the team sent it and which contacts it is filed on, and never an address or its words; an email deleted from the office, or let go with its contact, leaves it. The other is the mailbox’s counts, which the team mailbox’s script sends once an hour: how many unread conversations are in the inbox, how many emails came in and went out in the seven days before it counted and the seven before that, and how many of those were with a contact. Numbers only, so nothing about anybody leaves Gmail for them, and each count replaces the last. Both are sealed like every record. The dashboard also shows how many messages went out on the CB each day, and the forum topics posted to last, of the ones whoever is reading may read, from the forums themselves; it keeps nothing of them. Encrypted where it is kept. Every record is sealed with AES-256-GCM under a key only our server’s functions hold, in Netlify’s settings and never in our code, so the store on its own shows nothing that can be read, and a record changed without the key is refused. Without the key the office is shut: nothing in it can be read, and nothing is ever written to it unsealed. What we do not keep. Anything about who reads: nothing records who opened the office, which contact they looked at, or what they searched for. Nothing about a contact is ever written to a log. A change replaces what was there before; no earlier version is kept. How long. A contact, a grant request, a case or an email stays until a director or an administrator deletes it, and a record’s comments go with it; deleting a contact leaves their grant requests and cases, which then say their contact has been deleted, and deletes the emails filed only on them. Deleting is for good: there is no archive and no backup of it on this street. In your browser. Nothing of anybody’s. The order of a list, and which pipeline, stage, type and status it shows, live in the page’s address; a search does not, because what is searched for is somebody’s name, email or number, and the address goes into the browser’s history. It lasts only while the page is open. The tab’s own history keeps, beside each address it already holds, how far down that view you were and the address of the view before it, so going back one step puts you where you were (going back, since 2026-10-21); it goes with the tab’s history, and nothing of it is sent to us. Never a name: what the link back says, which can be somebody’s name, is kept only while the page is open, like a search. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. Every answer asks search engines not to keep it, and to be cached nowhere.

Since 2026-10-22 our member map, of where our community lives, hangs on the Community Center’s wall, and stimpunks.org’s Individuals page shows the same map as a picture of it, served from here. It used to be a Google My Maps map. It shows places and how many of us are in each, and never anybody’s name. What anybody can see. Every place on the map, where it is, how many of us are there, each country and how many, and how many in all. Anybody can see it, signed on or not, because a map of where a community is is meant to be seen. A place is only the place somebody gave when they asked to be on the map, on stimpunks.org’s Join form: a city, a region or a country. What is kept. One entry for each of us on the map: the place’s name, its country, and a latitude and longitude, and nothing about who. The entries brought over from our Google map on 2026-10-22 also keep which entry each was there. Which join request an entry came from is kept on the join request, sealed in the office, which only our directors, board members and administrators can open, so that taking somebody off the map takes their entry. Looking a place up. To put somebody on the map, a director looks up the place they gave. The words of the place, and nothing else, go from our server to OpenStreetMap’s Nominatim, under the OpenStreetMap Foundation’s privacy policy, which answers with places to choose from. Nothing goes to OpenStreetMap from anybody’s browser. A place near one already on the map joins it, so a city is one place with how many are there. Looking at the map asks nobody else for anything. We draw the world ourselves, from Natural Earth’s outlines, which are public domain; there are no map tiles, and no map service is asked anything when the map is shown, here or on stimpunks.org. Coming off it. Ask us, through the Stimpunks contact page or in our community, and a director takes you off. Deleting your join request takes your entry off too. A place stays on the map while anybody else is there. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. The map’s answers ask search engines not to keep them.

Who is a moderator, and which moderators also hold the board, director or administrator role, decides who can open the Town Hall’s private rooms, the staff forum categories, Tasks and the office. Since 2026-10-21 our administrators keep that list at the desk in the Moderators’ room (Ryan’s call), where until then it was only in the site’s settings. Sealed at rest (since 2026-10-25, Ryan’s call): the list our administrators keep is encrypted where it is kept at Netlify, with the staff key Tasks and the forums use. Without that key the desk’s roles are shut, and only the break-glass list in the site’s settings counts until it is back. What we keep, for each moderator. Their username; which of board, director and administrator they hold; and the username of whoever changed that last, and when. Nothing else, and no history: a change replaces what was there. The break-glass list. A few names are kept in the site’s settings at Netlify instead, so that nobody can lock everybody out of the desk. The desk shows them, and cannot change or remove them. Who sees it. Only our administrators, at the desk. It is never published, never sent to anybody else, and never written to a log. A radio is told only its own roles. The rules it keeps. Only an administrator changes it; the board role is given or taken only by somebody on the board or on the break-glass list, because Executive Session is the board without staff; and nobody can be left without an administrator. A change reaches every page within half a minute, and the radio of the person it changed is handed their new pass by itself, which is the pass signing on again with their own password would give them. Where it is kept. Beside the CB, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy.

Since 2026-10-21, after Notion’s links and backlinks (Ryan’s ask and calls): typing [[ in a message on the CB, a forum post, a task, a comment, or a record in the office finds a forum topic, or for our directors, board members and administrators a task, a grant request, a case or a contact, and puts a link to it in the words. A task, a topic and an office record each say, under Linked from, what links to them. A link is never a name. What goes into the words is what kind of thing it is and its id, nothing else, so a copy of the words, a search, a notification or a page somebody saved carries no name. The name is filled in each time the words are read, for whoever is reading: a task or a grant request linked from a topic everybody reads shows its name only to the people who could open it, and everybody else sees that it is one they can’t open, never whether it exists. A notification says only what kind of thing a link is. What the [[ menu sends. The letters you typed after [[, to our server, in the body of the request and never in an address, so they are in no browser history or log; it answers with what you could open whose names hold them. Nothing about what was searched for is kept. What Linked from keeps. For each task, task comment, forum post, contact’s notes, grant request, case and office comment that holds a link, which things it links to and when that last changed. The office’s are sealed, like every record there. It changes as the words change and goes when they go: an edit that takes a link out takes it out of Linked from, and deleting a task, a topic, a record or a comment takes it away. Linked from shows a reader only the places they could open themselves. A chat leaves no trace. A message on the channel or between two people can hold a link, and it shows in it as anywhere else, but it is never in anything’s Linked from, and nothing about it is kept, because the CB keeps its messages for two weeks. A single message is not something to link to, for the same reason; taking a chat to the forums is the way to keep it. In your browser. Nothing kept. The radio remembers the names it has been told only while the page is open.

Everybody on the CB has a username of their own, claimed with a password of their own. You claim yours when you join with an invite, on the joining page, and from then on the username signs on with its own password and nothing else, so nobody else can sign on as you. That is Ryan’s call of 21 October 2026, which retired the starter password the community shared: until then claiming was optional. A radio still on with that password, or with the moderators’ shared one, can do one thing now, claim the username it is on, and it asks you to before anything else. Invites. A moderator makes an invite at the desk in the Moderators’ room and passes on its link, which has the code after a #, so your browser never sends it to any server as an address. An invite is its code, a note saying what it is for, which moderator made it and when, when it runs out, how many times it may be used and how many times it has been. Nothing records who joined with which invite: joining takes one use off it, and that is all it knows. Only moderators see the invites, and a moderator can delete one, which stops it at once; an invite that has run out is deleted a month later. Since 2026-10-23 a director can also make one from the office, when they write to somebody in Gmail with a template that has an invite in it, from that person’s contact or join request: one press makes an invite that works once and runs out after thirty days, and puts its link in the email for the director to read and send from Gmail. Its note says only that it was made in the office for one person, and it is not written down anywhere whom it was for, on the invite, the contact or the join request, so the office does not become a record of who came in through which invite either. Joining. The joining page sends the invite, the username you would like, the password you chose twice over, and an email address if you gave one, only when you press Join; before that it asks us whether the invite works and whether the username is free, which sends those two and nothing else. A moderator’s username needs the moderators’ password as well, and no invite. What we keep. The username as you claimed it; your password and a recovery code, each only as a salted scrypt hash, from which neither can be read back; when you claimed it; a version number that moves whenever the password changes, so every other device is signed off; and a count of wrong passwords with the time the username is locked until after five of them. If a moderator gives you a reset code, its hash, for a day; if you ask for one by email, its hash, for an hour. Your email address, only if you give one, below. And only while a moderator has timed your username out or banned it, until when. No other name, and nothing about what you do. It is filed under a scrambled form of the username, so the store’s own list of what it holds does not show usernames; moderators can see a list of them. An email address for recovery, if you give one. It is optional, offered when you join and under Account on the radio, where you can add it, change it or take it off with your password. It is used for one thing: sending you a reset code when you ask for one at the front desk in the Community Center, with your username and that address. It is kept sealed, encrypted with a key kept in the site’s settings on Netlify, and shown to nobody but you, moderators included. Asking for a code tells nobody anything: the desk gives the same answer whether or not the address is the one on the username. The email is sent from our team’s mailbox at Google, by a small script in it that collects it from us within ten minutes, so Google handles the address and the code to send it, under Google’s privacy policy, and the email stays in that mailbox’s sent mail, where the people who look after the mailbox could see it; that is why the code works for an hour and not a day. We forget the email as soon as the script says it went, it is never filed with our contacts in the office, and at most one goes for a username in a quarter of an hour. The address goes when your username does. Your password. We never see it again once you have typed it, cannot tell you what it is, and it is never logged. The ways back in are the recovery code you are shown, once, when you join; a reset code by email, if you gave an address; and a reset code from a moderator, who will want to be sure it is you first. Any of them is used at the Community Center, and gives you a new recovery code. On the channel. Until 21 October 2026 a message from a claimed username was marked CLAIMED. Every username is claimed now, so nothing marks it; BASE is still a moderator’s, put there from the pass, and nobody can set it on a message themselves. Your pets, your avatars, your chimeras, your jobs, your patches, your crystals, your herbs and your profile card. The pets you adopt, the avatars and chimeras you keep, the jobs you keep from the Guild, the patches on your battle jacket, the crystals in your pouch, the herbs in your basket and your profile card and profile sets are kept under your username, and only your password reaches them. Deleting it. Delete my account under Account deletes the username, its password, its email address, your pets, your avatars, your chimeras, your jobs, your patches, your crystal pouch, your herb basket, your profile card and its sets, your props, your chat status, your saved filters for tasks, your own order for the chat page’s channels and every direct message and conversation you are in at once, and anybody with an invite can claim the name afterwards. A moderator can do the same, if you ask them to or if the covenant needs it. Your adopted animals stay on the list of everybody adopted, where nothing connected them to you. Your forum posts stay up, with your username on them. Moderators. A moderator’s username is claimed the same way, on the joining page, with the moderators’ password as well as their own, and after that only their own password signs on as them. We keep exactly the same record for them as for anybody: which roles they hold is not in it, and is kept on the moderators’ list. The desk will not reset, delete, kick, time out or ban a moderator’s username, or clear its card. What moderators can do. Make and delete invites; see the list of every username; look up one username, give it a reset code, delete it, clear its profile card without deleting it, or kick, time out or ban it. That is all: they cannot read your password or your email address. The moderators’ list of every username. Since 22 October 2026, Ryan’s call after moderators asked for it for safeguarding, the desk in the Moderators’ room lists every username on the CB, says how many there are and how many are seen in a room now, and shows who is seen and where, by exactly Be seen here’s rules: only if you pressed it, never in a room that keeps to itself, and a room only to a moderator it is for. Each name opens its profile, which anybody signed on can already open from the channel. It shows nothing else: not when you joined, not your email address, not anybody’s roles beyond moderator. It is fetched when a moderator presses for it, nothing is kept for it, and nothing records who looked. Until that day there was no list of everybody, for moderators or anybody, and it is still shown to nobody else: the street’s rule against counting people is about what everybody sees, and this list is for the people who look after our community. Kick, time out and ban. A moderator can sign your username off every device at once (kick), which you can sign straight back on from with your own password; keep it off the CB for ten minutes, an hour, a day or a week (time out); or keep it off until a moderator lifts it (ban). Each signs every device off, so your notifications stay off until you switch them on again. While a time out or a ban holds, nothing that needs signing on works for your username, reading included, and signing on tells you a moderator timed you out and for how much longer, or banned you, and where to reach us; it says so only after the right password, so nobody else who tries your username learns anything. We keep until when it holds, and nothing else: not which moderator did it, not why. A time out that has ended is taken off the next time you sign on. Your username, and everything kept under it, stays yours throughout, and a ban keeps anybody else from claiming the name. If you think one was a mistake, reach us privately. Where it is kept. Beside the channel, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. We keep your account because you asked us to, so that your username is yours; joining is your consent, giving an address is your consent to that too, and deleting your username takes both back.

Since 2026-10-26, Ryan’s call, anybody with a username can turn on two-step sign-in under Account: after your password, signing on asks for a six-digit code from an authenticator app on your phone, or a passkey (your fingerprint, your face or the screen lock on your device). From 2 November 2026 it is required for our moderators and staff; a staff username without it is on the CB as an ordinary member, with nothing else shut, until it is set up. Somebody who learns your password still cannot sign on as you. What we keep, on your username’s record and nowhere else. For an authenticator app, its secret, sealed at rest with the staff key, and the last half-minute a code was used in, so each code works once. For each passkey, its credential’s id, its public key, which kind it is, its signature counter and the name you gave it; never your fingerprint or your face, which never leave your device, and nothing that could sign on as you. Your backup codes, each kept only as a scrambled form of it, each good once. Nothing about when any of it was added. The QR code is drawn in your browser, from the key, so the key never goes to anybody else to be turned into a picture. The key is shown to you once, to put into your app, and not again. Signing on. Your password earns a ticket good for five minutes, and the second step is checked against it; nothing is stored for it. A wrong code counts as a wrong password, and five lock the username for fifteen minutes. Adding or taking off a step signs every other device off. Taking one off, and new backup codes, ask for your password. If you lose your steps. A backup code signs you on once. Your recovery code, or a reset code we email you, changes your password and still asks for the second step. A reset code from a moderator takes the second step off, because the moderator has made sure who they are talking to.

Rescue A Cat, Rescue A Dog and Rescue Small Animals are shelters where animals turn up at random, and the first person signed on to the CB to press brings one in and can name them. Anybody signed on can adopt one, who then lives in the Profile on their radio. Both are part of the CB. Who can rescue or adopt. Only people signed on to the CB. Rescuing sends your pass, which animal, and the name you typed, if you typed one; adopting sends your pass and which animal. The pass is checked and not kept, and nothing records who rescued any animal. What each shelter keeps. The animals waiting for a home: each one’s looks, where they were found, their name and when they came in; and when the next animal is due, which is random and never sent to any page. An animal stays until somebody adopts them. The base station can take a name off an animal, wherever the animal is. The list of everybody adopted, kept for good. Each adopted animal’s looks, name, and when they came in and were adopted, and, once their person has renamed them, the name they came in under. It never says who adopted or renamed anybody, and anybody who opens the rooms can read it. Showing your pets, if you choose to. With a claimed username, Show my pets on the CB in Profile lets anybody signed on to the CB press your handle on the channel and see your pets: what they look like and what they are called, not when they came in or were adopted. It is off until you switch it on. We keep only that it is on, and when you switched it on; switching it off, Forget me and deleting your username delete that. Showing them lets people find them on the list of everybody adopted, which still says nothing itself. Pressing somebody’s handle sends your pass and their handle, and we keep neither. Stickers. Sticker on the radio sends a drawing of one of your own pets, with its name, to the channel you are tuned to. It is a message like any other, kept and deleted with the channel’s messages, and it says nothing more than the drawing and the name. Renaming. Once adopted, a pet can be renamed from Profile, as often as you like. That sends your pass, which pet and the new name; the name changes in your pets and on the list of everybody adopted, and the base station can take a name off there as it can in the shelter. Your pets, which with your avatars, your chimeras, the jobs you keep from the Guild, your battle jacket’s patches, your crystal pouch, your herb basket, your profile card and your username, if you claim it, is all the street keeps under a person. When you adopt, the animal is filed under your handle so that your Profile shows them on any device you sign on with. The record is filed under a scrambled form of your handle, not the handle itself, so the store does not list handles; it holds your pets’ looks, names and dates, and nothing else about you, and beside it, only if you switch it on, that your pets are shown, and, only while you have let one out, a copy of that pet in the room. Only your password reaches them: nobody else can sign on as your username. Opening Your pets in Profile sends your pass to us, once, to fetch them. Forget me. The button under Account, on your radio. It deletes your record there and then, your avatars, your chimeras, the jobs you keep from the Guild, your battle jacket, your profile card and its sets, your props, your chat status, your saved filters for tasks, your own order for the chat page’s channels, your messages and when you last read each channel and conversation with it, and takes home any pet you have let out. Your animals stay on the list of everybody adopted, where nothing ever connected them to you. It cannot be undone. What your browser keeps. The animals you rescued, under love-rescues, as listed above. That is on your device and never sent to us. It is also why the Guild’s Rescue Ranger badge is shown only on the board and in your own Profile: nothing here knows who rescued, so nobody else can be shown it. The cat café and the dog park. Pekoe and Purrs and the Run read their shelter’s list when they open, the same way anybody opening the shelter does, with no pass, and that list now carries the pets people have let out there. Otherwise they keep nothing: the animal on your lap or beside your chair, and what is on your table, live in the page and are gone when you leave it. A film on either telly loads from YouTube only when you press it, like every film on the street. Letting your own pet out, if you choose to. Signed on to the CB, you can let a cat you adopted out in the café, or a dog you adopted off the lead on the Run, a few of yours at a time. The part in the room that does it sends your pass once when the room opens, to see which of your pets are out, and then only when you press: your pass, which pet, and out or home. While a pet is out we keep a copy of them in that room’s list: what they look like, where they were found, their mood and their name, filed beside the scrambled form of your handle and nothing about when. Anybody who opens the room can meet them, with no pass, and the room says they have a home and never whose; their name is the one already on the list of everybody adopted. Renaming them changes the copy, and the base station can take a name off it. Taking them home deletes the copy, and so do Forget me and deleting your username. The animals waiting for homes come first: when the room is full, yours stay home, and if the shelter fills up while yours is out, the last pet let out waits outside until there is a place. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who rescued, who adopted or who looked. Where it is kept. Beside the channel and the chalkboard, at Netlify, under Netlify’s privacy policy. The shelters’ and the pets’ answers ask search engines not to index or archive them. We keep your pets because you adopted them and asked the street to remember, and keeping them is what that takes. Adopting is your consent to it, and Forget me takes it back.

An avatar is a bodymind you drew at the Bodymind Booth, dressed or not at the Dopamine Dress-Up Den, or an outfit on the Den’s valet stand with no body in it. Drawing one, changing it and walking it next door happen in your browser and send nothing: next door, it travels in the address, after the #, which never reaches any server. Avatars are the second thing the street keeps under a person, after pets, and only when you press a button that says it keeps. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-14, made knowing it. An avatar is a list of choices, never a picture. What is kept is the choices you made, every one a word out of the booth’s and the Den’s own lists, which our server checks against those lists and refuses anything else; its name, if you give it one; and what you wrote about it, if you write anything. There is no camera in the booth, nothing to upload, and nothing an image could be. The drawing is made fresh from the choices wherever it is shown. Keeping one. Signed on to the CB, Keep it in the booth or the Den sends your pass, the choices, the name and what you wrote. Changing or deleting one from Profile, or keeping the changes, sends your pass, which avatar and what changed. We keep up to 24 at once. Opening your strip. Signed on to the CB, Open my strip in the booth, the Dress-Up Den or Fantasy Fancy Dress sends your pass and brings back the avatars you kept, so you can change one there. It sends nothing else and keeps nothing, and nothing in Fantasy Fancy Dress is kept: what you change there is kept back in the Dress-Up Den, when you press Keep. Where they are kept. Under a scrambled form of your handle, the same as your pets, so the store does not list handles, at Netlify, beside the channel. Only your password reaches them: nobody else can sign on as your username. Wearing one on the CB, if your username is claimed. Profile lets you wear one avatar at a time, and change which whenever you like. The one you wear is shown beside your name on Who’s online to anybody signed on to the CB, while you are seen in a room, and large in your profile, which anybody signed on to the CB opens by pressing your handle on the channel or your name on Who’s online, with what you wrote about it. To do that, a copy of its choices and what you wrote is kept where Who’s online can read it, under the same scrambled form of your handle, and it is shown only beside a claimed username, a mark we take from your pass. Taking it off, deleting it, Forget me and deleting your username take that copy away first. Showing the rest, if you choose to. With a claimed username, Show my avatars on the CB in Profile shows all your avatars in your profile, the one you wear first, with their names and what you wrote. It is off until you switch it on. We keep only that it is on, and when you switched it on; switching it off, Forget me and deleting your username delete that. Opening somebody’s profile sends your pass and their handle, and we keep neither; the answer never says whether somebody has avatars they have not shown. What a screen reader hears. Only what you wrote about it. The drawing is silent if you wrote nothing, and nothing on the street ever describes your body for you. As your familiar. Take it with you in the room, or Take it with me on a chimera in Profile, makes it your familiar, which follows you from room to room and sits wherever there are no words. That is kept in your own browser, under love-familiar above, and never sent to us: we do not know who has a familiar or which one, and nobody else sees it, unless you bring it out. Its sayings. A chimera can have up to five sayings, a line each, which you write beside its name on the bench or in Profile. They are kept with the chimera when you keep it, shown under it in your profile if you show your chimeras, and said by it as your familiar: when you press it, and now and then in a speech bubble while it may move by itself. Bringing your familiar out, if you choose to. With a claimed username, Bring my familiar under Be seen here on the radio sends us a copy of your familiar: which animal gave each part, its name and its sayings. The people seen in the same room as you see it there, walking about the room, while you are seen there, and you see theirs; nobody else does, it is never on Who’s online, and we keep nothing about when or where. It is off until you switch it on. Switching it off, sending your familiar home, Forget me and deleting your username delete the copy; taking a different chimera with you changes it. Nobody is told who looked. Chimera Cozies. Some rooms have a cozy, a spot drawn for a familiar to sit in, and your familiar sits in a free one. Nothing about that is sent or kept. Sending it home. Send it home, on the familiar, forgets it in your browser, and takes the copy in if you brought it out. As a sticker. Sticker on the radio can send one of your avatars to the channel you are tuned to, with its name and what you wrote. It is a message like any other, kept and deleted with the channel’s messages. Deleting them. Delete any one from Profile, which asks once more; Forget me under Account deletes them all with your pets, and whether they are shown; and Delete my account deletes them with your username. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who has an avatar or who looked at one. Every answer about your avatars asks search engines not to index or archive it. We keep your avatars because you pressed Keep and asked the street to remember them, and keeping them is what that takes. Pressing Keep is your consent to it, and deleting them takes it back.
Your jobs at the Guild, and their badges

The Adventurer’s Guild stamps the jobs you hand in, in your own browser, under love-quests, and works out your badges from them there; a badge is a set of things done that go together, mostly jobs, and it is kept nowhere. The jobs you hand in are the third thing the street can keep under a person, after pets and avatars, and only once you switch on Keep my jobs in my Profile on the Guild’s board, which starts off. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-14. What the board sends. Signed on to the CB, opening the Guild’s board sends your pass to us once, to ask whether your Profile keeps your jobs, and, as yes or no, whether it has a pet, for the Pet Parent badge; signed off, it sends nothing. Switching keeping on sends your pass and the jobs this browser has stamped. After that, handing a job in sends your pass and which job. The pass is checked and not kept. What we keep. Which jobs you have handed in, as a sorted list, and nothing about when or in what order: a list of times would be a record of how you spend your days. Only a job that is on the board can be in it. Your badges are not kept: the board and the radio work them out from the jobs, from whether your Profile has a pet, and from the animals your own browser rescued. Which badges other people see. In your profile, only what your jobs and your pets already show: the badges your jobs make if you show your jobs, and Pet Parent if you show your pets. Rescue Ranger is never shown to anybody but you, because nothing on the street knows who rescued which animal. Where they are kept. Under a scrambled form of your handle, the same as your pets and your avatars, at Netlify, beside the channel. Only your password reaches them: nobody else can sign on as your username. Showing them, if you choose to. With a claimed username, Show my jobs on the CB in Profile lets anybody signed on to the CB who opens your profile see your jobs and the badges they make. It is off until you switch it on. We keep only that it is on, and when you switched it on. Opening somebody’s profile sends your pass and their handle, and we keep neither; the answer never says whether somebody keeps jobs they have not shown. Deleting them. Switching Keep my jobs in my Profile off, which asks once more, deletes them and whether they are shown. So do Forget me and Delete my account under Account. The stamps in your browser are yours to forget with the board’s own button. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who keeps jobs, who has which badge or who looked. Every answer about your jobs asks search engines not to index or archive it. We keep your jobs because you switched on keeping them and asked the street to remember, and keeping them is what that takes. Switching it on is your consent to it, and switching it off takes it back.
Your battle jacket and its patches

Patches lie about the street, and some are on a counter in a shop, free to take. Each one is drawn in its own room and goes on your battle jacket, in Profile on the radio. The patches are the fourth thing the street keeps under a person, after pets, avatars and jobs, and only when you press a patch’s own button. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-14. Picking one up. Only signed on to the CB: a patch’s Pick it up or Take one sends your pass and which patch, and nothing else. Signed off, the button is not there and nothing is sent. The page itself sends nothing until you press. What we keep. Which patches are on your jacket, as a sorted list, and nothing about when you picked any of them up or in what order; the jacket sews them on in the order the street lists them. Only a patch that is on the street can be in it. Nothing counts who else has a patch: there is no list of a patch’s takers, only each person’s own jacket. Where it is kept. Under a scrambled form of your handle, the same as your pets, at Netlify, beside the channel. Only your password reaches it: nobody else can sign on as your username. Showing it, if you choose to. With a claimed username, Show my battle jacket on the CB in Profile lets anybody signed on to the CB who opens your profile see your jacket and what is sewn on it. It is off until you switch it on. We keep only that it is on, and when you switched it on. Opening somebody’s profile sends your pass and their handle, and we keep neither. As a sticker. Sticker on the radio can send one of your patches, or your whole battle jacket, to the channel you are tuned to. It is a message like any other, kept and deleted with the channel’s messages, and it carries which patch, or which patches were on your jacket when you sent it, and nothing else. A jacket sent as a sticker does not change when you pick up another patch. Downloading a picture. Download in Profile saves a picture of one of your avatars, chimeras, pets, badges or patches, or of your battle jacket, onto your own device. It is made in your browser from the drawing already on your screen, with the typefaces its words are set in fetched from this site; nothing is sent to us or anybody, and nothing is kept. Deleting it. Forget me under Account takes every patch off, with your pets, your avatars, your chimeras and your jobs; Delete my account does the same with your username. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who has which patch or who looked. Every answer about your jacket asks search engines not to index or archive it. We keep your patches because you picked them up and asked the street to remember, and keeping them is what that takes. Pressing a patch’s button is your consent to it, and Forget me takes it back.

On every card of the Crystal Wheel in Myths & Legends, behind Helen Edgar’s Faery Yurt, you can take that crystal with you, and it goes into your crystal pouch, in Profile on the radio. The pouch is the eighth thing the street keeps under a person, after pets, avatars, jobs, patches, profile cards, chimeras and props, and only when you press a crystal’s own button. That was Helen’s ask, 2026-10-26. Taking one. Only signed on to the CB: Take it with you sends your pass and which crystal, and nothing else. Signed off, the button is not there and nothing is sent. The page itself sends nothing until you press. What we keep. Which crystals are in your pouch, as a sorted list, and nothing about when you took any of them or in what order. Only a crystal on the wheel can be in it. Nothing counts who else has a crystal: there is no list of a crystal’s takers, only each person’s own pouch. The pouch shows small drawings of the stones, never anybody’s photograph, and each one links back to its card. Putting one back. Put it back in Profile takes a crystal out of your pouch, and nothing remembers it was there. Showing it. Off until you switch it on, and only for a claimed username: Show my crystal pouch on the CB puts a Crystals tab in your profile for anybody signed on. While it is off, your profile says only that you have not made it public, the same whether your pouch is empty or full. Deleting it. Forget me under Account empties it, with everything else; Delete my account does the same with your username. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who has which crystal or who looked. Every answer about your pouch asks search engines not to index or archive it. We keep your crystals because you took them and asked the street to remember, and keeping them is what that takes. Pressing a crystal’s button is your consent to it, and Forget me takes it back.

In the Herbery in Myths & Legends, behind Helen Edgar’s Faery Yurt, you can gather a herb, and it goes into your herb basket, in Profile on the radio. The basket is the ninth thing the street keeps under a person, after pets, avatars, jobs, patches, profile cards, chimeras, props and the crystal pouch, and only when you press a herb’s own button. That was Helen’s ask, 2026-10-26. Gathering one. Only signed on to the CB: Gather it sends your pass and which herb, and nothing else. Signed off, the button is not there and nothing is sent. The cauldron sends nothing. Tipping herbs into the cauldron and stirring happens in your browser, and nothing about it is sent or kept, signed on or not. What we keep. Which herbs are in your basket, as a sorted list, and nothing about when you gathered any of them. Only a herb in the Herbery can be in it. Nothing counts who else has a herb, and the brews and stews your basket could make are worked out on your screen each time and kept nowhere. Putting one back. Put it back in Profile takes a herb out of your basket, and nothing remembers it was there. Showing it. Off until you switch it on, and only for a claimed username: Show my herb basket on the CB puts a Herbs tab in your profile for anybody signed on. While it is off, your profile says only that you have not made it public, the same whether your basket is empty or full. Deleting it. Forget me under Account empties it, with everything else; Delete my account does the same with your username. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who has which herb or who looked. Every answer about your basket asks search engines not to index or archive it. We keep your herbs because you gathered them and asked the street to remember, and keeping them is what that takes. Pressing a herb’s button is your consent to it, and Forget me takes it back.

Pressing somebody’s handle on the channel, or their name on Who’s online, opens their profile: their card, and beside it their avatars, pets, badges and jobs, battle jacket, chimeras and props, each as they have chosen to show it. The card is the fifth thing the street keeps under a person, after pets, avatars, jobs and patches, and it is yours alone, because only your password signs on as your username. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-17, after requests for profiles more like Discord’s. What is on it. Only what you fill in, at Edit my profile card in Profile: a theme, a banner, a decoration round the avatar you wear, a frame round your profile, an effect over it, a face for your name and a nameplate, each chosen from the street’s own lists, which our server checks against those lists and refuses anything else; and, in your own words, your pronouns, a tagline (one line, since 2026-10-23), a few hundred characters about yourself, up to five links to your other places, and your favourite room on the street with a line on why. A part left empty shows nothing. Whether you are in the community directory is on it too, and it is off until you tick it. Who sees it. Unless you choose otherwise, whatever you fill in is shown to anybody signed on to the CB who opens your profile, the way the avatar you wear is, because you wrote it to be shown. Since 2026-10-26 (Helen Edgar’s question, Ryan’s call) your card can instead be private, shown to you and nobody else, or open to the public, on its own page, which you choose on the card. Your nameplate is shown under your name on Who’s online, while you are seen in a room; to do that, which nameplate you chose is kept where Who’s online can read it, under a scrambled form of your handle, and it is shown only beside a claimed username, a mark we take from your pass. Opening somebody’s profile sends your pass and their handle, and we keep neither. What it never says. When you claimed your username or joined, and nothing on it is counted. A room that keeps to itself cannot be named as a favourite, because naming it would list it. Links. Each must start with https:// or http://, with no name or password in it. It is shown as you typed it, with the site it goes to written after it, the way a link on the channel is, so nobody is sent somewhere it does not say. Following one opens that site, which has its own privacy policy, in a new tab with no referrer. Saving and changing it. Save my card sends your pass and everything on the card, and replaces what was there. Nothing is sent while you choose, and closing the window without saving sends nothing. Deleting it. Clear my card, which asks once more, deletes it and takes your nameplate off Who’s online and you out of the community directory first. So do Forget me and Delete my account under Account, which delete your profile sets too. Profile sets. A set is your card’s look kept under a name you give it, to wear again with one press: its theme, banner, decoration, frame, effect, name face and nameplate, and which avatar you wear, or none. Nothing you wrote is in a set, so wearing one changes how your card looks and leaves your pronouns, your words, your links and your favourite room as they are. Your sets are shown to nobody: anybody who opens your profile sees what is on your card, and is not told what sets you have, that you have any, or which one you are wearing. Save as a set and Update send your pass and the set’s name, and our server reads the look off your card as it is saved and the avatar you wear, so a set only ever holds something that was on your card. Pressing a set sends your pass and which set, and saves its look onto your card and wears its avatar, as Save my card and wearing an avatar do. We keep each set’s name, its look, which avatar and an id, under a scrambled form of your handle beside your card, and nothing about when: not when it was saved, nor when you last wore it, nor which one you wore. Up to 24 at once. Clear my card leaves them; Delete it deletes one, and Forget me and Delete my account delete them all. That was a request from our community, 2026-10-19. A moderator clearing it. If a card breaks our covenant, a moderator can clear it from their desk, which deletes it and takes your nameplate off Who’s online and you out of the community directory exactly as Clear my card does, and leaves your username, its password, your pets, avatars, chimeras, jobs and patches as they were, so you can fill in a new card. We keep nothing about it: not who cleared it, not when, and not what the card said. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-18; until then a card could only go with the whole username. Where it is kept. Under a scrambled form of your handle, the same as your pets, at Netlify, beside the channel. Every answer about a profile asks search engines not to index or archive it. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no time the card was saved, and no list of who has a card or who looked at one. We keep your card because you filled it in and saved it to be shown, and keeping it is what that takes. Saving it is your consent to it, and clearing it takes it back.
Your profile’s own page, and who may open it

Every claimed username’s profile has a page of its own, at stimpunks.world/profile.html# and the username, so you can share it wherever you like. That was Helen Edgar’s question and Ryan’s call, 2026-10-26. You choose who may open your card, on the card itself, under Who can open your card, and nobody else can choose it for you: The community. Anybody signed on to the CB, on the radio and on your page. This is what every card was before, and it is what yours is until you choose something else. Only me. Your card is shown to you and nobody else, on the radio and on your page; anybody else who opens your profile is told you keep your card private. It also takes your nameplate off Who’s online and you out of the community directory. The avatar you wear is still shown, as it is beside your name on Who’s online, and so is each tab you have switched on to show on the CB, by its own switch. Anybody with the link. Your page shows your card, the avatar you wear and each tab you have switched on to show on the CB (your avatars, pets, badges and jobs, battle jacket, chimeras, crystals and herbs) to anybody who opens it, signed on or not. It never shows your props, your chat status or a way to message you, to anybody: those are the community’s and stay on the radio. BASE, for a moderator, is shown only to people signed on. What the page sends. The username is after the # in the address, so it never reaches our server in the address. The page sends it to us in the body of one request, with your CB pass if you are signed on, and we keep neither. To somebody signed off, our server answers the same thing for every username it will not show, whatever the reason: private, for the community, nothing on the card, or nobody by that name. So the page cannot be used to find out which usernames exist. Search engines. A search engine reads every address after a # as the one page, profile.html, which says only what the page is, so no profile is ever indexed or listed, open to the public or not. Every answer about a profile asks search engines not to index or archive it. No profile is in the sitemap, the street’s list for AI agents, or anywhere else we publish. Somebody you give the link to can still pass it on, as with any link. Animations. Everything on your card is drawn on your page as on the radio. What moves moves at MAX GLITTER, or after the reader presses Let it move, which lasts for that visit and is kept nowhere, not even in their browser. What is kept. Which of the three you chose, on your card, and nothing else: no list of who has a public card, nothing about who opened anybody’s page, and no IP address or log, the same as the radio. Taking it back. Choose another and save your card, and the page shows the change straight away. Clear my card, a moderator clearing it, Forget me and Delete my account put it back to the community, with nothing on it. We keep your choice because you made it, and showing your card to the people you chose is what that takes. Choosing is your consent, and choosing again changes it.

The community directory lists everybody on the CB who has chosen to be in it, so people can find each other. That was Ryan’s ask, 2026-10-23. Nobody is in it until they choose to be: Show my profile in the community directory, on your profile card, starts off, and only you can tick it, because only your password signs on as your username. What it shows of you. Your username, BASE if you are one of our moderators, which we take from the moderators’ list, your nameplate, your tagline, your pronouns and the avatar you wear, each as it is on your card and on Who’s online. Your name there opens your card, as it does anywhere on the CB. Who sees it. Anybody signed on to the CB, the same people who can open your card. Nobody else: the page itself is public, and the list is only sent to a pass. Opening it sends your pass, and we keep nothing about who looked. What it never says. How many people are in it, and when anybody joined or was last on. It is in alphabetical order and in no other. Its search box narrows the list in your browser and sends nothing. What is kept. Whether you are in it, on your card; and, while you are, a copy of your username, nameplate, tagline and pronouns in one list our server reads the directory from, under a scrambled form of your handle, at Netlify, beside the channel. Save my card brings the copy up to date. Every answer about the directory asks search engines not to index or archive it. Coming out of it. Untick it and save your card, and your line is deleted. Clear my card, a moderator clearing your card, Forget me and Delete my account all take you out of it too. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, no time you were listed, and no list of who looked. We keep your line because you ticked the box to be listed, and listing you is what that takes. Ticking it is your consent to it, and unticking it takes it back.

A prop is a sentence or a short paragraph thanking somebody, acknowledging them or celebrating them, usually for something they did for you or for the community. Props are the seventh thing the street keeps under a person, after pets, avatars, jobs, patches, profile cards and chimeras, on a Props tab in their profile. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-18, after the forums’ Props & Gratitude category. Your Props tab is shut until you open it. Show my props on the CB in Profile opens it, and only you can confirm a prop, because only your password signs on as your username. While it is shut, nobody can give you props and your tab shows none of them. What you confirmed is kept, and comes back when you open it again. Giving somebody props. Open their profile, from their handle on the channel or their name on Who’s online, and write it on their Props tab. Anybody signed on can, and a prop carries their username on somebody else’s profile, which only they can sign on as. Sending one sends your pass, their handle and your words, at most 500 characters. One of yours waits for each person at a time. Nothing goes up until its person says yes. A prop waits, read only by the person it is for, in Profile, and by whoever wrote it, until they press Confirm, which puts it on their Props tab, or Reject, which deletes it. Nobody is told it was rejected: it simply stops waiting, which its writer can see. Being told. If you switch on When somebody gives me props under Notifications, a device switched on as your claimed username is told when somebody gives you props: who wrote them, and their first 180 characters unless you switched the words off for that device. It never says how many are waiting, and the writer is never told anything: not whether you were notified, nor whether you read, confirmed or rejected what they wrote. Nothing about the notification is kept. Pressing it opens the street with Profile open at Your props. Without it, props wait for you there until you next open Profile. Who reads it once it is up. Anybody signed on to the CB who opens that person’s profile, with the writer’s username on it and whether they were the base station, which we take from their pass. Opening somebody’s Props tab sends your pass and their handle, and we keep neither. Taking one off. The person it is for can take any prop off their tab, from Profile or from the tab; whoever wrote it can take it back, waiting or up; and a moderator can take one down. Each asks once more, and nothing is kept about it: not who took it off, not when, and not what it said. What is kept. Whether your tab is open, and each prop waiting for you or up on it: its words, its writer’s username, whether they were the base, a scrambled mark of the claimed username that wrote it, so that a username deleted and claimed again by somebody else cannot take back what its owner wrote, and an id. Nothing about when, and nothing is counted: nobody is shown how many props anybody has, or has waiting. Up to 100 on a tab and 20 waiting at once. Where it is kept. Under a scrambled form of your handle, the same as your pets, at Netlify, beside the channel. Every answer about props asks search engines not to index or archive it. Deleting them. Forget me and Delete my account under Account delete your Props tab, everything on it and everything waiting for you. Props you wrote for other people stay up on their tabs, with your username on them, the way a forum post does; take each back from their tab first if you want them gone. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no list of who gave whom props or who looked at a tab. We keep props because somebody wrote them to be shown and the person they are for confirmed them, and keeping them is what that takes. Confirming one is your consent to it, and taking it off takes it back.

Events on the CB are times somebody has scheduled for something: a coworking hour in a room’s call, a film in a room, a meeting at a link off the street. They came on 2026-10-23, Ryan’s ask and calls, after Discord’s scheduled events. They are under Events on the radio, and at the top of the channels on the chat page. Who can see one. An event is in a channel. On World, everybody signed on to the CB can see it; in a room, whoever may go into that room can, so an event in one of the Town Hall’s private rooms, or in a staff category’s room in the forums, is seen only by the people who can go in. A room that keeps to itself has no events, because an event is listed and announced outside its room. Scheduling one. Anybody signed on can, on World or in a room they can go into: in its call, in the room itself, or at a link off the street. It carries your username for everybody who can see it, and whether you were the base. Sending one sends your pass, its title, what it is about if you write anything (up to 2,000 characters), where, the date and time you typed, your device’s time zone, how long it runs and how it repeats. The time zone is kept with it, because a repeating event keeps to its maker’s clock when summer time starts or ends. Up to 20 at once each. Changing or cancelling one. Whoever scheduled it, and any moderator who can see it, can change it, cancel one time a repeating event would happen, or cancel it altogether. A change keeps who scheduled it and who is interested. Nothing is kept about who changed it, when, or what it said before. Saying you are interested. Anybody who can see an event can say they are interested, and take it back. Your username is then on it for everybody who can see the event: an event names who is interested, in alphabetical order, and never how many, the way a reaction names who and never counts. Whoever schedules one is interested in it from the start, and can take that back too. Each list holds up to 500 names. Being told. Two switches under Notifications, each off until you switch it on. When an event I’m interested in starts tells a device switched on as you, up to five minutes before it starts: its title unless the words are off for that device, where and when. New events on World and in rooms I follow tells a device about an event scheduled on World or in a room it follows: who scheduled it, its title unless the words are off, where, and when it first starts. Never who else is interested, and nobody is told about an event they scheduled. Pressing one opens the chat page at Events. Add to my calendar. Makes a calendar file of the next time an event happens, in your browser, and hands it to your device. Nothing is sent to us, or to anybody, for it. What is kept. For each event: an id, its title, its words, its channel and where in it, its link if it is off the street, when it first starts and in which time zone, how long it runs, how it repeats and any times of it cancelled, its maker’s username and whether they were the base, and the username of everybody interested; and, for its maker and everybody interested, a scrambled mark of the claimed username, so that a username deleted and claimed again by somebody else is not them. Nothing about when it was scheduled or changed, or when anybody said they were interested. So that each start is told once, which starts have been told, kept for a day. All of it is at Netlify, beside the channel, and every answer about events asks search engines not to index or archive it. How long. An event that happens once is shown to nobody once it has ended, and is deleted within the hour. A repeating one is kept until whoever scheduled it, or a moderator, cancels it. Deleting them. Forget me and Delete my account under Account delete every event you scheduled, and take your username off every event you said you were interested in. What we do not keep. The same as the radio: no IP address, nothing in any log, and no record of who looked at an event. We keep an event because somebody scheduled it for other people to see, and a username on it because they said they were interested, and keeping them is what that takes. Taking either back, or cancelling the event, deletes it.

Messages, a part of the CB between the channel and Watching together, is for writing to one other person. That was Ryan’s call, 2026-10-18, after requests from our community as it moves off Discord. A username at both ends. Every username is claimed, so a message to one is read by whoever holds its password and nobody else. Messages are kept under the username and when it was claimed, so if a username is deleted and somebody else claims the same name, nothing of the old owner’s reaches them. Nobody new can write to you until you switch it on. Let people message me, under Messages, is off until you switch it on. While it is on, anybody with a claimed username can ask to message you: their first message waits, and they can write nothing more until you answer it, press Accept, or press Reject, which deletes it and tells nobody. A conversation already going goes on if you switch it off; you can still write to people who take messages. Every message goes two weeks after it was sent, the same as the channel, and a conversation keeps its latest hundred, unless our administrators set direct messages otherwise (How long each channel keeps). Who talked to whom is not kept a minute past the last message between them: a conversation with nothing left in it is gone, and the next message after a quiet two weeks asks again. You can edit your own messages, which shows that they were edited and keeps nothing of the words they replaced, and take them back, which deletes them for both of you. Stickers and reactions, once a conversation is accepted. As on the channel: a sticker is a copy of something of yours, made when you send it, and a reaction says who pressed it and never how many. Both go with their message, and neither can go with a first message, which is words only. Replies, once a conversation is accepted. As on the channel: a reply keeps which message in the conversation it answers and nothing else of it, and says so once that message has gone. Pictures, once a conversation is accepted. Ryan’s call, 2026-10-19, after somebody in our community could not send him a screenshot privately: a first message is words only, so nobody’s first contact with you can be a picture, and once a conversation is accepted either of you can add a picture to a message. It is the channel’s picture in every way that matters: redrawn in your own browser before it is sent, which takes off everything a camera or a phone wrote into it, where it was taken first of all, and refused by our server if any of that is still in it; a description is offered and never required; and it has no public address. It is kept beside the conversation, with which of you sent it and when, is fetched with your pass by the two of you and nobody else, and goes the moment its message goes: taken back, at its two weeks, pushed out by the fiftieth after it, or with the whole conversation when either of you blocks the other, rejects it or deletes their username. One you added and never sent is deleted within the hour. Ask anybody recognisable in a picture before you send it. Blocking. Block, under a conversation, stops that person writing to you and you to them, and deletes your conversation for both of you. They are not told: if they try to write, they are told you are not taking messages from them, the same words as if your switch were off. A block is kept in your own record, by a scrambled form of the name you blocked, so it holds if that name is deleted and claimed again, and nobody but you is shown your block list. Unblock under All messages takes it off. They are not end-to-end encrypted. Your words travel to our server encrypted, like everything on this site. Since 2026-10-25 they are sealed at rest, Ryan’s call: every conversation, every picture sent in one, your switch and your blocks, and any report copied from them are encrypted where they are kept at Netlify, with a key of their own that nothing else on the street uses, so somebody who got at the stored files alone could not read them. Our server still opens them, to show the two of you your conversation, and a report to our moderators, which is why this is not end-to-end. Without that key, Messages is shut rather than written in the clear. Anything written before that day is sealed the next time it is written, or within the hour. Nothing on the street shows a conversation to anybody but the two people in it. No moderator can read one: there is no way for them to, on the desk or anywhere else. End-to-end encryption, where only your devices hold the keys, would be a much bigger thing to build and to keep working on every device, and it is not this. Reporting a message. Report, on a message the other person sent you, is the one way a message reaches the moderators. It copies that message’s words, its picture if it has one, who sent it and when, your username and a note if you write one onto the moderators’ desk. A reported picture is shown on the desk only when a moderator presses to see it. The person you report is not told. A report stays until a moderator closes it, which deletes it, or for thirty days at most, even if either of you deletes your username, because it is how the moderators look after the street. Nothing else about the conversation goes with it. Being told. If you switch on When somebody messages me under Notifications, a device switched on as your claimed username is told when somebody writes to you. The sender is never told anything about it. What is sent. While Messages is open on your radio, and only then, it asks for your conversations, or the one on your screen, every few seconds: your pass, and the username you are talking with, in the body of the request rather than the address. Folded, in a tab behind another, or with Messages shut, it asks nothing.
