2026-09-22 — One Space Grotesk, and a bold the bench had been hiding

Space Grotesk was stored three times over, byte for byte. Same sha256, same 22320 bytes, and fonts/_sources.json recorded the same gstatic URL for all three, because the family ships as a variable font and Google serves one file for every weight. On the shared base that every page on the street loads, that cost about 45KB. It is one file now, declared three times against the weight axis, the way §1 already handles Cabin, Karla and the rest. The Feed was preloading the copy that got deleted, which would have 404’d on a published page; it preloads the one that survives. And then the interesting half: identical bytes are not an absent bold. The obvious reading of three identical files is that a weight-700 declaration renders the same drawings as the 400 — and The Foundry had been built on exactly that reading since it opened, grouping each family’s variants by the sha of the file they point at and keeping one. It is the wrong question. A variable font carries a weight axis inside the file, and the browser instances it at every @font-face declaration: same bytes, genuinely different outlines. The rule was throwing away bolds that work. Measured rather than argued about, because the premise sounded right. Rendered out of one file at 64px: Cinzel’s 700 lays down 68% more ink than its 400, Work Sans’ 600 45%, Space Grotesk’s 700 41%, Nunito’s 39%. Not one pair on the shelves came out the same. Twelve families had a weight the street holds and the bench was keeping in a drawer — Cabin, Cinzel, EB Garamond, Faustina, Jost, Karla, Mulish, Nunito, Quicksand, Rubik, Space Grotesk and Vollkorn — and every one of them is offered now. tools/check-weights.py is the check the sha was standing in for. It renders the published picker — never the generator, which is check-quests.py’s rule — and refuses two offerings of one family that come out the same drawings, a weight love.css does not declare, and a declared weight the room does not offer. Advance width alone cannot decide it: Courier Prime and Space Mono are monospaced, so their 400 and 700 share an advance to the hundredth of a pixel while the bold lays down about 40% more ink. It measures ink and advance and calls two the same only when both match. It found a bug in itself on the first run, which is why it was broken on purpose first. @font-face is lazy, so nothing is downloaded until a page sets it — and a canvas asked to draw a font it has not got silently draws the fallback instead. The first draft measured before loading anything, so every face on the street would have measured identically and been reported as the same drawings. It loads, waits, then measures, and still asks whether each face actually arrived. Fed a static face declared at two weights, it correctly calls the second one a control that does nothing; that is the protection the sha was giving, and it is still there. Nunito’s bold was not in the record at all. love.css declares that one file at 400 and 700; fonts/_sources.json listed only the 400, and nothing compared the two. The new checker reads the stylesheet the browser actually obeys, so that class of drift now refuses rather than sitting there. Two things found and deliberately not changed. Jost is still stored twice — jost-400.woff2 and jost-500.woff2 are byte-identical, the same duplication Space Grotesk had — and it is logged here rather than swept into a commit about something else. And the campground sets its emphasis in Alfa Slab One because Bitter’s bold “was byte-identical to its regular”: that reasoning is the one corrected above, so the decision rests on a premise that turns out to be false. It is a room’s own design decision and not a bug, so it stays until somebody who owns that room says otherwise.
2026-09-22 — The Foundry, and the first room whose content is the typefaces

A type foundry on the street: The Foundry. Ryan’s brief — a font play storefront, your own text or text out of The Playhouse, The Mopery and The Zibaldone, every setting the type has, and a way to print it. A grey iron workshop under a dirty roof with a bench in it. Every other room on this street uses a typeface; this is the one where they are the thing in the window. It is the first mid-grey ground here, and that is the whole separation. Every other world on the street is either a night ground with light applied to it or a sheet of paper with the room cropped away. This is the middle — the colour of the metal — and the only pale object in it is one proof lying on a bench. The four paper rooms are the obvious collapse and each one is held off by something structural: The Mopery is a cold building you stand up in whose type is impressed into the page, the guild is manila lit like a photocopy from nowhere, The Doomscroll is one unbroken roll of warm foxed newsprint, and The Zibaldone is bound leaves with a gutter and a fold. There is no fold in here and nothing is bound. It is the third daylit room, and north light is what a workshop was built for — the glazing faces away from the sun so the work has no glare on it, which means flat, cool, directionless daylight and no lit face on anything. The Hermitage has a low morning sun with long sideways shadows; the Garden’s light has come through leaves and tints every pale surface green. A furnace would have been the obvious build and would have made this the seventh warm room on a street that already has six. The only warm value in here is brass, and brass is a metal rather than a light. Nothing about any typeface was typed. tools/pull-foundry.py reads every family’s own record out of github.com/google/fonts — family name, designer, licence, copyright, repository, classification — and cross-checks the licence against which directory of that repository the family lives in. It refuses a family it cannot resolve rather than publishing a face with nobody’s name under it. It is kept out of the pre-deploy sequence with check-jukebox.py because it needs the network, and make-foundry.py needs nothing but the file it writes. Do not merge them. The first thing it found was that four of these families are not OFL, and three published pages said they were. Permanent Marker, Rock Salt, Special Elite and Ultra are under the Apache License 2.0. love.css’s §1 comment said “every family here is OFL-licensed”, the liner notes said “all are licensed under the SIL Open Font License” and again “the typefaces keep their own OFL licence”, and the Mopery’s generated credit line said it a fourth time. All four are corrected and every face now carries its own licence on the shelves. A licence nobody has checked since the file was added is a claim rather than a fact, which is the whole argument for a tool that goes and reads. The Mopery’s picker had quietly lost eighteen families, and tools/check-faces.py is why it cannot again. That room says in its own copy that the picker holds every typeface on this street and llms.txt says the poem can be set in any face on it; both had been false for a long time, because adding a file to fonts/ and adding an <option> in a room two doors away are two edits in two places and only one of them is obviously required. The picker is generated now, from the same record The Foundry’s shelves are built from — when something has to agree in several places, make the others read it rather than write it out again, which is love-embed.js’s ORIGINS lesson. The new checker reads both rooms’ published markup and never the generators, in both directions, and it was broken on purpose before being believed. An italic is not a slant, and the bench is built to show you rather than tell you. A real italic is a second alphabet, cut separately, with different letters in it. A machine slant is the upright pushed over by something that has no idea what it is looking at. Both are offered and both are labelled, and the italic is disabled where this site holds no italic file — because the browser answers a request for one it has not got by inventing it, nothing looks broken, and the room has told you a lie about somebody’s typeface. Measured rather than assumed: on Rye, a requested italic renders at the roman’s own advance widths; on Cardo, which has a real italic, oblique 12deg comes out at 399.65px against the italic’s 377.42px, so the slant really is the roman pushed over. The slant is a font setting and never a transform, deliberately. check-gentle.py reads rotation and skew out of the computed matrix and cannot tell a leaning page from a leaning letter, so a skewX() here would be reported — correctly — as this room’s decoration outranking somebody’s Gentle setting. There is no transform anywhere in §32, which is the call arcade.js made with left/top and the Oracle Deck made with its lozenge. A weight is offered only where the bytes differ. Seven of these families ship as variable fonts, so love.css declares one file against two or three weights — and a bold that renders the same drawings as the regular is a control that does nothing, which is make-chappell.py’s typo that never becomes a video arriving as a dropdown. The puller records a sha for every variant and the bench groups by it. Hashing the whole shelf also turned up Space Grotesk stored three times over, byte for byte, on the shared base that every page loads; that is logged separately rather than fixed in this commit. Four ink and paper pairs, each printing its own measured ratio on its own control, and the tool refuses one under 4.5:1. This is the one room on the street where somebody other than us picks the colour of the text, which makes it either the place contrast quietly stops being ours to keep or the place it becomes a thing you can watch being kept. There is no colour picker and there is not going to be one. The light moved rather than the palette. The north light was a fixed full-height wash to begin with, which composites the floor to #596267 — and against that the room’s link brass measures 3.14 and its fine print 3.34, both under the bar. Worse, fixed, that composite could arrive under any paragraph on the page depending on how far somebody had scrolled, which is the shape The Rabbit Hole’s scrolling ground already taught this stylesheet. It is 340px tall and absolute now: the light comes in at the top of the room and the page scrolls out from under it, which is also what happens in a building. A light that follows the viewport is not a light, it is a veil in front of the reader. The only words standing in it are the topline’s, and they are bone at 5.19 for that reason. The proof prints and the room does not, and what prints carries a colophon naming the family, the person who drew it, the licence and every setting it was pulled at — because printing somebody’s typeface is exactly where the credit should travel with it. It comes out black on white whatever pair is on the screen: paper colour is a screen decision and a printer would spend your toner on it. Measured rather than asserted: the rendered PDF is one page with two fonts embedded in it, the proof’s face and the colophon’s, which is how you can tell the shelves did not print. Nothing here describes a typeface, and that is a refusal rather than an omission. A line of appreciation beside every family on this street would mean inventing type history at scale in the format most likely to be believed — the herbarium’s refusal to name a pressed plant to species, arriving where there is one to write for every face. What the room says truthfully is who drew it, what licence it travels under and which room here sets it, and that last claim is checked against love.css: make-foundry.py refuses a line the stylesheet does not support. A derived version got it wrong on its first run, because the street letters each door in that room’s own face. Nothing is counted. Not the faces, not the proofs pulled, not the sizes tried, and there is no favourite and no ranking of one designer’s work against another’s. This is the room most likely to want to boast about how much type it holds, and the generator refuses the sentence as well as the habit. Two new faces. Anton is the street’s other condensed display face and is Club Chronic’s: solid, on a black wall, under a marker. Work Sans is the prose and is a workhorse on purpose, because a room whose content is other people’s typefaces cannot have a voice that argues with the window. Both under the SIL Open Font License. 2026-09-22 — The Rabbit Hole, and the first room that carries a song without its words

A new storefront, and it is not a room: The Rabbit Hole. Ryan’s brief. Every other door on this street opens onto somewhere you can stand; this one opens onto a shaft with no floor at the bottom of it. It leads with our own glossary entry, Rabbit Hole, and the argument is that one: for monotropic minds the rabbit hole is not a detour, it is the destination, and three hours you did not mean to spend is not a failure of discipline. It carries all seven of that page’s embedded videos, six wood engravings from 1865, a feed your head section, and a trail out. The glossary entry prints the whole lyric and this room prints none of it, which is the one place a room here deliberately does less than the page it came from. Song lyric reproduction is a minefield in the United States in a way prose is not — music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel — which is the reasoning that already makes the Zibaldone refuse a song outright. The friendly edit here is real and it will arrive: a room whose spine is one song, whose source page has the words on it already, and whose section headings are phrases from it, reads thin without them, and whoever pastes them back will be right about the page and wrong about everything else. So tools/make-rabbit-hole.py refuses a lyric field and any value shaped like verse — several short hand-broken lines, which is what a lyric looks like in a JSON string and what a sentence never does. The recordings are offered instead, with Grace Slick’s own published account of writing it, and the two headings that are her phrases are credited to her where they stand. The Latibulum is the hardest collapse this street has had, harder than any subroom, because these two rooms are literally both holes in the ground. Every earlier version of the temptation came with a structural excuse attached — it is only a subroom, an area should look like an area, they are both cosy — and this one needs no excuse at all: the floor plan is the same. What keeps them apart is that the burrow is somewhere you arrive and the hole is somewhere you keep going. The burrow has a floor, walls, furniture, a lamp at knee height and a shelf; it is horizontal, it is at rest, and almost every word in it sits dark on lit plaster. This has no floor, no walls to lean on and no furniture whatsoever; it is vertical, the light is above and behind you and there is less of it the further down you read, and every word is pale on the dark. The burrow is earth and is brown. There is no brown in this room at all — it is wet slate — and if these greys ever warm up, the two rooms have become one and it is this one that moves. The ground darkens down the document, which is a shape of ground the contrast tools had not met. The Zibaldone’s rule is a flat background-color under the gradient, and its flat colour is the darker end; here it is the lightest end, because that room sets dark type on pale paper and this one sets pale type on a dark wall. In both cases the flat colour is the worse case for the type standing on it, which is the actual rule and is what makes the live checker’s answer the pessimistic one. And because the gradient runs the height of the document rather than of a sheet, the colour under a word depends on how far somebody has scrolled — so every block that carries text sits on a flat panel of its own and the wash carries nothing but the header’s lines. Two grounds, two link decisions, made at the room. Brass measures 6.74 and up on all three dark grounds and 1.83 on the paper mats the engravings sit on, so a single room-level link colour would have shipped an illegible provenance line under every plate. That is the hole The Doomscroll left and the Playhouse had been carrying since it opened — a colour nobody decided leaves no pair for check-contrast.py to hold — caught this time before the room shipped rather than by somebody looking at the page. Six engravings by John Tenniel, 1865, public domain, shown rather than linked because each scan says so. Tenniel was born in 1820 and died in 1914 and the book came out in 1865, so they are out of copyright everywhere, and every file used carries an explicit public domain statement on Wikimedia Commons — which is exactly what the Mopery’s Library of Congress facsimile did not have and the reason that one is still a door and not a window. The 1865 edition captioned none of its illustrations, so unlike that room’s Doré plates there is nothing printed to quote: every word beside an engraving here is ours, which engraving sits beside which paragraph is our reading and the room says so, and the generator refuses a plate with no sentence of ours, no rights page, or no file on disk. Nothing was cropped, tinted or filtered, and every file was re-encoded with no metadata carried over. One performer is not named on their own upload and the room does not guess. The trailer edit describes itself as an edited remix of the Jefferson Airplane recording and credits no remixer in its title, its description or on its channel, so the plate says what the upload says and says the hand is unnamed there — which is the herbarium’s refusal to guess at a binomial, applied to a credit. And the running order is the glossary page’s own, which interleaves the videos with the quotations they sit under, so it is an argument somebody made rather than a playlist to re-sort — the rule the Jungle Room keeps about its cams. Three of the seven are published by a rights holder and four are re-uploads on individuals’ channels; each plate says which, because that changes how long a link lasts, and the generator refuses a track that does not say. The room carries our own entry’s warning as well as its argument. Be wary of the holes you rabbit, and the reason: the appetite a recommendation engine farms is the same appetite, and what changes is who chose the next thing. So there is no autoplay in there, no next-up, and nothing that decides for you what comes after — seven things, all named, and nothing reaches YouTube until you press it. Nothing in that room moves at any setting, and it has no transform in it anywhere. Not a tilt, not a rotation, no flicker and no strobe; at MAX GLITTER the wash of daylight from the mouth of the hole is a little stronger and that is the whole of it. A rotation is indistinguishable from a tilt to check-gentle.py, which can only read the computed matrix, so a room with no transform in it cannot get that argument wrong — the call arcade.js and The Oracle Deck both already made. 2026-09-22 — The Zibaldone, and a quote bank that refuses to become a book

A new storefront, asked for by somebody in our community: The Zibaldone. The request was a quote bank — quotes for any state of mind and emotion, seeded by us and added to by anybody. It is built as a commonplace book, which our own glossary has had an entry for since 2022, and named for the Italian miscellany notebook: a zibaldone is a heap of things. Montaigne kept one and invented the essay out of it; the Meditations is one. A quote bank is the most dangerous shape of page this site has built, and the danger has no moment anybody could catch. Nobody decides to republish a book. They add one good line, then another, each individually reasonable, and a year later the page is the work instead of pointing at it. So tools/make-zibaldone.py refuses a quotation over thirty words, the number lives in the tool, and the room prints it — because “we quote lightly” is not something a page can promise and not enforce. Where the line is not enough, the book is linked. No song lyrics, refused structurally rather than by care. Ryan’s reply to the person who asked: song lyric reproduction is an intellectual property minefield in the US. Music publishing enforces on quotation where prose publishing shrugs, the licensing is separate from the recording, and one line is a far larger fraction of a song than of a novel. This street already says that nothing musical is hosted here, and a quote bank is exactly where that promise would have been broken in the way that looked most harmless. The first thing that check ever refused was a false positive — the word song matched Whitman’s Song of Myself — and the pattern was narrowed rather than the poem excepted, which is check-counts.py’s own first-run lesson happening for the third time. Every line names its printing, not its title, and says how it was checked and when. A title is not a source: these texts differ between printings, and a quotation nobody can trace is the thing The Doomscroll dropped a poem over. The Emily Dickinson is the proof it matters — it is in the Second Series of 1891, edited by Mabel Loomis Todd and T. W. Higginson, not the first, and the only thing that found that out was reading the title page above the poem instead of remembering it. The Thoreau is the other proof: the version everybody quotes has somebody marching to a beat, and he wrote neither word. The public domain lines were grepped out of the transcriptions each card names; the contemporary ones were read off our own published pages. A translated work has to clear the public domain twice — a trap this repository had not met before. make-doomscroll.py’s test is the author dead more than seventy years, everywhere rather than in one country; but a translation is a copyrightable work of its own, so a Roman emperor in a modern English is a modern book. The Meditations here is Meric Casaubon’s 1634, and he is credited on the card. Seneca is not in the room at all and the data file says why: our glossary quotes him on words becoming works, that wording is a modern translation the entry does not name, and the public domain one does not read that way. A gap somebody has already checked is worth more than a line nobody can place. There are no faces in that room, and that is the whole answer to “any state of mind”. The obvious build is a grid of moods you pick from, and the obvious drawing for a mood is a face — which on a Disabled people’s site is the emotion flashcard autistic people spend their childhoods being drilled with. The Playhouse settled this for its sound board and the answer is the same here: each card says what it is for in a sentence about a situation, and the tool refuses an emoji in that field. Nothing is ranked, counted or voted on either, checked with make-guild.py’s negation window so the room can still say so out loud. The quotations are set in type and only the margins are handwritten. The room varies the face per entry, which is what was asked for — EB Garamond for the oldest, Newsreader for the nineteenth century, Lora for the living — and Kalam is the hand and never carries a quotation, refused by the tool. A passage in a handwriting face is an access failure wearing atmosphere, which is the lesson The Doomscroll’s blackletter already carries one room over. The margin note on every card is ours, and the tool refuses a quotation mark in it, because margins that could hold quotations would quietly become a second uncited quote bank running down the side of the cited one. The room it could collapse into is every other paper room on this street, and the separation is that all of those are PRINTED. The Mopery is a cold building you stand up in, with type punched into the page by a press. The Doomscroll is one unbroken machine-set roll of cold grey newsprint with nothing cut and nothing rotated. The zine table is a photocopy made in a hundred copies to give away. This is one object at arm’s length, seen from above, written into by hand, and bound — there is a fold down the left of every sheet, and the fold is what makes it a book rather than a page. And where the guild is lit like a photocopy and the garden’s light has come through leaves, this is the one room lit by something in the room with you: a lamp on the left, at desk height, which is why the paper has a tooth and the fold has a shadow in it. The attribution slip is TASL plus the three fields a quotation also needs, and it sends nothing anywhere. Creative Commons’ Title, Author, Source, Licence is the right skeleton for a photograph, where the thing you point at is one file at one address; a quotation comes out of a work, in a printing, and the person copying it found it somewhere else again — and that last field is the one that catches a misquotation, because most of them are copied in good faith off something already wrong. There is no form action and no endpoint: the button writes a block of text to your clipboard and you send it however you already talk to us. Its fields are generated from the same list the cards are checked against, so the day somebody adds a field to an entry cannot be the day the form stops asking for it. A colour under the bar, and a tilt with no reset, both caught before it shipped. The pencil grey carried every citation, margin note and provenance line and measured 4.43 on a pasted leaf; check-contrast.py refuses a colour it has never seen, which is how it surfaced, and it was darkened. check-gentle.py then found all seven leaves still lying at their pasted angles at Gentle: :where() guarantees a tilt cannot be out-ranked but does not conjure a rule to outrank it, and §3’s reset names the shared tilt classes and nothing else. The room resets its own now, which is the fault that shipped on the Faery Yurt’s windowsill. 2026-09-22 — The Garden, and a palette that splits at the soil line

A gate in the wall, and a garden behind it: The Garden. Ryan’s brief. Our knowledge garden as a place you can walk: an intro to what knowledge gardening is and how this one is tended, one bed for every site we publish, the Garden Spider, and everything needed to start a garden of your own. Every bed links straight out, because each of those sites is already its own room — so it is not a door in the grid but an opening, and it is the one place on a night street where the sun is up. The roster is not in the garden’s own data file. Which sites exist, in what order, with what names and addresses, is read out of data/arrivals.json — the same list The Feed runs on, whose order is stimpunks.org’s own feeds page. So a bed cannot be invented, a site cannot be quietly left out, and re-sorting the garden would mean overruling a decision made somewhere else, which is the rule the Jungle Room keeps about its cams. data/garden.json holds nothing but our own writing about each site. The Feed is the room this one could collapse into, and both rooms list every site we run. So the division is structural rather than tonal: a board is a timetable — a title, a date, a destination and the minute it was set — and this is a planting plan: what a site is for, whose hands are in it, and nothing that changes when somebody publishes. Hence no network in tools/make-garden.py, no pull step beside it, and a refusal of dates in a bed, because that is the edit that would turn one room into the other. The drawings are told apart by FORM, which is the campground’s grammar inverted on purpose. Out in the field every pitch gets one lit colour of its own — the yurt emits, the hermitage catches, the meadow carries — and that runs out at about the fourth pitch, because there are not many kinds of light. There are as many kinds of growth as you like: a rhizome, an umbel in flower, a plant with no chlorophyll in it, a frame with seedlings under glass, a runner rooting a new plant beside itself, a dry seed head, a scramble over the path, a tendril. Each one says something true about its site, and every habit is also written out in a sentence beside its bed, because the drawings are decoration a screen reader never reaches and the habit is the argument. No bed says how much a site holds, and nothing is ranked. No glossary-term count, no sheet count, no biggest or busiest. A number like that is wrong within the week and authoritative-looking meanwhile — the fault The Feed spends a paragraph avoiding — and a garden measured by volume is an inventory. Both are refused in the generator, the ranking one with make-guild.py’s negation window so the room can still say that it does not rank anything. Green on that earth measures 1.38, and no brown can fix it. check-contrast.py put the two greens at 1.38 and 2.14 against the soil, and because they are only 1.55 apart from each other no soil colour clears 3:1 against both at once — so there was no palette fix available and the drawings changed instead. The palette splits at the soil line the way a plant does: green above it, pale below it, so every root, rhizome, mycelial thread, spilled seed and blanched shoot is drawn in the path’s own colour, which is also what a shoot looks like before it reaches the light. make-garden.py walks every coordinate of every green element and refuses one that crosses the line — broken on purpose first, with a stem pushed two pixels under and a leaf circle whose edge dipped below, and it caught both. The two rooms it could collapse into are the two other daylit ones, and the separation is physics. The Solarpunk Hermitage’s light lands on a warm plaster wall, with everything standing in front of it and the shadows falling sideways off a low sun. The Adventurer’s Guild has no light source at all, lit like a photocopy, with nothing casting anything. Here the sun is overhead and has come down through leaves: every pale surface is tinted green, and every shadow is small, hard and directly underneath the thing that made it. And the palest thing in the room is not the ground — a limewashed board is brighter than the path it lies on, where both neighbours put their panels darker than their paper. It sets no display face at all, which is the room’s one claim about type. Every other world here has something that shouts — a woodtype, a condensed grotesque, a fat slab, a blackletter, a pixel face — and a garden has no signage in it, only labels. So Faustina sets the garden’s own name and the label on every bed in the same breath, Mulish carries the notes, and the loud things in the room are the plants. Both are under the SIL Open Font License. The Garden Spider is an orb weaver and not a mascot, and its panel is careful in our own words rather than softer ones: a spider is a guide to the garden and never a replacement for it, its best answer is an entrance, it can be wrong, and every trail it puts you on ends at a page a person wrote. Those lines are from our Ask page, quoted from ourselves, with the ethics pages linked beside them and a way to reach a human instead. Every bed says whose hands are in it, on the face of the bed. Half of these sites were made with Helen Edgar of Autistic Realms; Star Stuff is a collaboration with More Realms; the Cavendish model is David Thornburg’s by way of Steve Silberman’s NeuroTribes; monotropism is Dinah Murray, Wenn Lawson and Mike Lesser’s; the pebbling locution is Amythest Schaber’s. The generator refuses a bed with nobody on it, and refuses a link inside a note that points somewhere that is neither ours nor that bed’s own site — make-hermitage.py’s rule about the Star Stuff table. The with line is the exemption, and that is the whole reason it exists. The leaf shadow is still at Gentle, drifts at Regular and drifts further at MAX. The light is never taken away, because the light is not the wobble — the campground’s own call about its grass. Both are keyframes, so §3 kills them at Gentle with !important; nothing flashes, pulses or strobes at any setting, which is Club Chronic’s rule holding in the brightest room on the street. A row is a title, a date and a destination, and the tool refuses one carrying a summary. A departures board does not read you the contents of the train — which is the metaphor and also what keeps that page from republishing everybody else’s writing onto one surface it does not own. The vocabulary is refused in the room’s own copy, with the negation window make-guild.py uses so the room can still say that it does not rank anything. Each wire names which feed it carries, because two of those sites publish more than one. “The latest from Star Stuff” is an ambiguous sentence when Star Stuff keeps a feed of the pieces and a feed of the reasoning, and a board that picked quietly between them would be answering a question nobody knew it had been asked. And this street is on its own board, fetched over the network like every other wire, so the board can be out of date about this site too. The seam through the middle of the letters had to go, twice. A real flap splits straight through the glyphs, so that is what it was: one near-black hairline at 50%. On the share card the row lettered NEVER read as a word struck through. Two solid faces with a lit fold between them fixed the card and then failed worse on a phone, where a destination wraps to three lines and 50% of a tall row lands inside somebody’s second line. The reason is structural and is not going away: a real board’s rows are one line of fixed-width characters and cannot wrap, and ours carry the titles people actually gave their pages. There is no proportion of a row that is not inside a sentence, so the lower leaf sits at the foot of the flap, where no width can push it into a word. The room it could collapse into is the Adventurer’s Guild, and this is the hardest case since The Den. Both rooms are made of ruled rows, both are square, and in both of them nothing is rotated and nothing overlaps — and that room’s own section says its tidiness cannot spread. What holds them apart is not the layout, because the layout really is the same: the guild has no light source and no depth, lit like a photocopy of a document, with nothing casting anything, and this is nothing but light and depth. A clerk filed that; an engineer bolted this together and switched it on. And the light is a third kind of transmitted light, because a neighbour already owns the idea. Swaying Sweetgrass is lit through a translucent body — diffuse, no edges, nothing with a lit face. This is lit through an aperture: a hard light behind a mask, so every letter has a crisp edge and every flap throws a hairline shadow. It exists because the pair list was blind three times, each found by a person looking: a link colour nobody ever decided, a decided colour that lost the cascade, and three hexes that had never rendered at all. Same shape every time — the colour that renders is not the colour that was written down. It found the skip link unreadable in twenty-one rooms. .skip carries its own yellow ground and near-black ink at (0,1,0); every room sets .room-x a at (0,2,0). So the first control a keyboard user meets took each room’s link colour on a yellow box: 1.26 in the chapel, 1.10 in the arcade, 1.00 — yellow on yellow — on every plain room. Nobody had seen it because it sits off-screen until focus and nobody screenshots a focused skip link. It carries !important now, for the reason §2’s [hidden] guard does. It declines rather than guesses now: a gradient in the chain makes a piece of text unmeasurable, counted and reported as such, and left to the hand-written list where those grounds are recorded with their measurements. 2026-09-21 — a sound board in the Playhouse, and a row of moods with no faces on it

The Playhouse has a sound board on the wall. Ryan’s brief: everything in that room is a button, so a three-by-three board of stimmy noise keys, with the bottom row holding mood keys that toggle between happy, sad and angry noises, and a different visual fanfare for each key at MAX GLITTER. A click, a pop, a rainstick, a chime, a purr and a squeak; then a hum, a spring and a drum with three moods each. The bottom row is not a feelings chart, and that is why there are no faces on it. A face is the first thing anybody sketches for a mood key, and a row of happy/sad/angry faces on a Disabled people’s site is the emotion flashcard — the thing autistic self-advocates spend their lives being drilled with. What a mood is here is the shape of a noise: a hum that lifts a third and stays up, the same hum sagging a tone and a half, two drones fourteen cents apart buzzing against each other. Each one is a word, a drawn waveform and a sound, and the room says so in its own copy rather than leaving the absence for somebody to helpfully fill in. It also says that a sad noise is a perfectly good thing to want, and that you can leave a key on angry and go and do something else. A mood key shows the mood it is about to play. Press it and you get that noise; the key then offers the next one. The face of a button should describe what pressing it does, which the alternative — naming what you just heard — does not. The flourish keeps the colour of the noise that just happened while the label has already moved on, which is why that button carries two attributes and not one. Every noise is synthesised in the browser and nothing is fetched, so the room’s own house rule stays true: it is silent when you walk in and silent if you never touch anything. Oscillators, filters and a buffer of white noise, built inside the click handler — the AudioContext cannot start without a gesture, which is the platform enforcing the promise rather than us making it. A bell is 880 and 2.76 times 880, which is the whole difference between a bell and a sine; a purr is a trill at twenty-two on the gain rather than on the pitch; a bubble goes up, which every first draft of that sound gets backwards. Every key says what it sounds like, in words, on the press. A board made of sounds is the one thing on this street that can lock somebody out completely, so the room’s live region gets the noise described rather than just its name — the Jungle Room’s rule that colour is never the only channel, in a room where the channel is audio. make-soundboard.py refuses a key without that line, and refuses two keys that claim to sound the same. Three files have to agree about every key and none of them is near the others, so the tool reads all three: the markup is in the page, the noise is a registered voice() in love.js, the colour and the flourish are rules in love.css. A key whose voice is missing is not an error anywhere — it is make-chappell.py’s typo that never becomes a video, arriving in a room where the press is the content. A key whose flourish is missing is quietly ordinary at MAX, which nobody would notice because nobody screenshots MAX. Both refuse now, along with two keys sharing a flourish, a mood key anywhere but the last row, and a mood set that is not the same three in the same order. Nothing on it is counted. No total, no streak, nothing kept between visits. A board of nine keys is exactly the shape of thing that grows a press counter, and the stim box one object over already counts its own presses as a joke about counting — a joke that does not survive being repeated by a second object with a straight face. The pebbling cabinet’s refusal of a tally, arriving a third time. Nine flourishes and no two alike, at MAX GLITTER only. Rings, bubbles, falling hairlines, a burst thrown eight ways, widening bars, darts, flat arcs off the bottom edge, a stretching coil, confetti — each clipped to its own key, so the flourish belongs to the button that made the noise. Everything moves with a translate or a scale and nothing rotates, which is arcade.js’s call and quest.js’s: rotation and skew are all check-gentle.py can read, and a checker must not be asked to take a room’s word for something. Nothing flashes and nothing strobes — Club Chronic’s rule, in the loudest room on the street. At Gentle nothing is built at all and the words are identical; measured at all three settings, along with the rendered boxes of the pieces themselves, because “the elements exist” is a question about the DOM and this was a question about paint. Red was the obvious colour for angry and it measures 3.06 on the mood keys’ near-black. Angry is orange at 8.03, sad is cyan at 10.7 and happy is yellow at 14.5. The mood ink is on the word as well as on the line, so these are body-text pairs rather than graphics ones. Seven new pairs. A media block written above the rules it overrides loses exactly the declarations the base rule also sets, and keeps the rest. A new failure shape here, and it renders as a layout nobody wrote: the phone block sat before .stimpad, so flex-flow and a font size lost to the base rule while a flex basis the base rule does not set went straight through. Half a breakpoint. It looked like a stale stylesheet and it was source order. And it is three across where there is room and one column on a phone. Held at three columns at 375px, a key gets about seventy pixels of text column and every blurb sets one word to a line. Hiding the blurbs to keep the grid would have been the lite-version mistake arriving through a breakpoint, so the grid gave way; the sentence describing the board’s shape is generated and carries its own caveat. New: data/soundboard.json, tools/make-soundboard.py.
2026-09-21 — The Adventurer’s Guild, and the one tidy room

The Adventurer’s Guild has opened a shopfront on the street. Ryan’s brief: the trope with the inn and the job board, jobs ranked by difficulty class, sending people on quests across the rooms; a discreet clickable drawing in each room as the quest target; a code revealed at the target and redeemed at the board; hints; and fanfare that follows the HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? dial. The room is tidy, and that is its entire costume. On a street whose architecture is that nothing matches, somebody has come in and filed everything: manila, printer’s ink, hairline rules, ruled rows, a class in the margin, a stamp. Nothing in §26 has a gradient, a shadow, a rounded corner or a rotation in it. It is the second room you can read by daylight and it has no light source in it at all — the Hermitage has a sun in it, with a direction and shadows falling away from it; this is lit the way a photocopy of a document is lit, evenly, from nowhere. And it is the second pale ground on a dark street: the Doomscroll is one unbroken roll of foxed newsprint with nothing ruled on it, and this is made of rules. It states its own link colour, at the room, which is the hole the Doomscroll left the day before: that page declared a colour for one line and every other link fell through to the base stylesheet’s pink, at about 2.4 on paper, and the contrast checker had nothing to hold a pair for because nobody had decided anything. Every room on the street carries a marker, and no two markers are alike. A staple on the zine table, a token on the arcade carpet, a spindle adapter on the den floor, a tent peg in the field. make-guild.py holds one drawing per room and refuses a room it has no drawing for — make-og.py’s refusal, for make-og.py’s reason, because the failure mode of guessing is one shared glyph quietly appearing in every room on a street whose whole point is that the rooms share nothing. Each marker is drawn in its room’s own declared colours and every one is held against the floor it lies on at the body-text threshold, the Jungle Room’s quills rule: a marker you cannot pick out of the floor is a control you cannot use. The Playhouse lost that argument to its own floor — its yellow measures 3.88 on that blue, so the block is white at 5.08. The marker is a native <details>, and the way out of a question is another one. So the code, the hints and the “give me the answer” escape all work with JavaScript off; the scripted part is only the answer box, which ships hidden and is revealed by quest.js, so a page without scripts shows no dead control. Discreet means visually quiet and nothing else: every marker is a full-size target in the tab order with a real name on it, which is The Den’s door rule. And every marker is on the floor of its room, said out loud on the board, because scattering them at a different depth in each room would have made finding one a test of eyesight and of a mouse rather than a walk between rooms. The marker is never the play button, although the example in the brief starts from one. A facade is two elements and love-embed.js replaces the pressed <button> with a bare <div class="facade">, so anything it was wearing evaporates — the fault that shipped Swaying Sweetgrass’s players at 0×0 the day before. A play button that also does a second thing hands a popup to somebody who only wanted the song, and gating a quest behind a press would put it behind consenting to a third-party frame. So the George Jones job is a spindle adapter on the den floor and its question is what makes you read the tile: who wrote She Thinks I Still Care , which the room credits to Dickey Lee and Steve Duffy on the cut itself. Nothing is scored, and the tool refuses the vocabulary. No total, no percentage, no streak, no rank you climb, nothing that expires. A job board is exactly the shape of thing that grows a score, and a score beside a walking tour of a Disabled people’s site turns a wander into a workload — the pebbling cabinet’s refusal of a tally, in the room most likely to talk itself out of it. The difficulty class is how far you walk, enumerated in the tool and defined by geography, so it says nothing whatever about the person doing it. The first thing that tool ever refused was a false positive, and the pattern was narrowed rather than excepted. “A book it points at” is the verb, and a scoring pattern that cannot tell it from a points system is check-counts.py’s first draft refusing “no two rooms alike”. A point is only a point now when it is being awarded or counted. The fanfare follows the dial and the words never do. Gentle says its piece and adds nothing; Regular chimes; MAX chimes properly and throws sparks that rise once and fade. The sentences are identical at all three, and nothing flashes or strobes at any setting — Club Chronic’s rule. The sparks move with a translate rather than a rotation, deliberately, because rotation and skew are all check-gentle.py can read and a checker must not be asked to take a room’s word for something. A marker’s link carries its code to the board and stops there. It fills the box; the visitor still presses. That press is what the fanfare is consented by, and it is the accessible path for anybody who finds typing expensive, which is most of the reason it exists. The board holds a checksum of each code rather than a second copy, and the tool says out loud that this is a courtesy and not a lock. Every code is printed in plain text in the markup of a public page — that is the mechanism. What the checksum buys is that opening the source of the board is not a spoiler sheet for every room at once. check-quests.py reads the published HTML and never the data file. The generator writes both surfaces, so they cannot disagree the moment it runs; this is about every moment after that, when a generated line sitting in a committed file gets edited by hand. That is the frame-src shape exactly. It found a bug in itself on its first run: it sliced each marker at the next </details>, the marker’s own hints are <details>, and it reported eighteen missing escapes that were all present. It slices on the generator’s end marker now. check-classes.py caught this page wearing two of the street’s classes — pavement and masthead__dial — which is the tagline leak again, and the newcomer was renamed rather than out-specified. The guild ends in its own voice, like every other room. The marker does not print. It is a control whose whole content is a code to type into a page you cannot type into on paper, and the zine room’s one-sheet promise has been broken by a single paragraph twice. Pitch 01 got a marker and it is ours, not Helen Edgar’s. A candle stub on the Faery Yurt’s windowsill, drawn in her own declared colours, added on Ryan’s call so that her pitch is not the one room on the street with no job in it — and written into the liner notes beside the one colour of hers this repository has changed, because a change to a contributor’s room should be visible somewhere other than a diff. Helen has the final say on whether it stays. Two pages carry no marker, on purpose and by name in the tool. The changelog is a dated record and writing new furniture into a log is the same instinct as rewriting a September entry to satisfy a linter; the guild is where jobs are handed in, so a marker there would be a job that sends you to the room you are standing in. Everything else refuses to ship without one. Two faces nothing else here sets — Rye, a woodtype face for posted bills, and Public Sans, which was drawn for United States government forms, which is the room’s joke set twice. Thirty-five new contrast pairs and one measured ornament. A guild is an inn as well as a board, and this one has no room over it yet. When it does it will be about rest as something owed rather than earned, which means it will owe a great deal to The Nap Ministry and Tricia Hersey and will say so in its own copy. The board says that out loud rather than leaving a gap.
2026-09-21 — Swaying Sweetgrass, and a book we are not going to serve

Swaying Sweetgrass is pitched on pitch 02, which had been open ground since the field opened. Ryan’s brief: a meadow of sweetgrass left alone, except for a natural-surface path a wheelchair can use, running to a clearing at the centre with a communal fire pit under open sky. The light is behind the grass, and that is the only thing keeping this out of a family it would otherwise join. The Faery Yurt, The Latibulum, The Den, the Hermitage’s cave and The Mopery are every one of them lit by a flame you could put your hand over. Here the sun is low, a hundred feet off and behind everything, so nothing has a lit face at all — the blades glow because the light is coming through them. That is why the greens go yellow while the ground stays dark, and it is a different warmth from tallow or varnish. There is no furniture in a meadow either; the only built things are the path and the fire ring. The fire is painted in the room’s own two golds and given no colour of its own, deliberately. A flame with an orange to itself would have made this the sixth flame-lit room on the street by the back door. Ryan’s brief pointed at 21 chapters of Braiding Sweetgrass read aloud, and they are published as doors rather than screens. The playlist is uploaded by The Anarchist Audio Library and is an unauthorised reading of a book that is in copyright — Milkweed Editions, 2013, Robin Wall Kimmerer living, publishing, and narrating the real audiobook herself. Every chapter plays and every chapter embeds, so nothing in the machinery would have stopped them going in beside the fire: love-embed.js only asks whether an id is well formed and check-jukebox.py only asks whether a video works. What stopped them is that this room’s whole argument is the honorable harvest — never take the first, never take more than you need, ask — and a page making that argument cannot serve somebody else’s entire book off its own surface while doing it. Ryan’s call once the provenance was put to him: keep both, her voice as the fire and these as a way out. make-sweetgrass.py refuses a reading marked as a screen, so the decision survives being tidied by somebody who thinks the doors look broken next to the presses. What is at the fire instead is Kimmerer in her own voice — her publisher, Bioneers, TEDxSitka, Harvard, the New York Botanical Garden, On Being, the Museum of Science, the Natural History Institute, the Commons KU — shortest first, so three minutes and an hour and a half are both a real option. Every id was resolved against YouTube on the day: status, playableInEmbed, length, title and channel, off one fetch of each watch page. That check is the only reason the two lists are two lists; the readings arrived looking exactly like the talks and the channel is what told them apart. The build refuses a talk whose channel is the readings’ channel, in either direction. The 21-strand teaching is somebody’s, and the video does not say whose. Seven generations behind, seven sacred laws, seven ahead. It was matched to its source rather than guessed at — the transcript panel was opened and read against the words, and it is Sweet Grass Teaching, published by Shawenim Abinoojii Inc., at 0:53, which was already in Ryan’s own field-guide list. The description says only “Made for Shawenim Abinoojii Inc.”, there is no name card at the end and the channel does not say, so the room credits the organisation and states plainly that the Elder is unnamed there rather than inventing a name. That is the herbarium’s refusal to guess at a binomial, applied to a person. make-sweetgrass.py counts the bundles and refuses one that is not seven — the opposite of check-counts.py’s rule and for the opposite reason: a count that belongs to somebody else is a fact to protect, not a total that goes stale. Nothing on that page teaches sweetgrass. Six teachings from Indigenous organisations, institutes and nations, Ryan’s selection, each linked and credited with one line of ours saying what it is about — and nothing anywhere instructing anybody how to harvest, braid or burn it, because that is not ours to hand out. A correction we owe is on the page rather than in a commit message. Our own glossary attributes a framework called reciprocal ethical unity to Barry Lopez and he never wrote the phrase; Star Stuff’s zine No. 72 went and read the essay. The room is quoting from the pages that carry the error, so it says so near the top instead of further down. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins. Three of the four passages were checked against the mirror and one could not be. The sheaf, the braid of stories and “becoming indigenous to a place” are verbatim on our own Nature, Place-Based Education and Offline pages. The Cajete and goldenrod-and-asters passage is on no page of ours, and archive.org’s search-inside was unreachable and Google Books rate-limited every attempt, so it is published on Ryan’s word and the liner notes say so rather than letting it sit among the checked ones looking identical. Zine No. 72’s own caveat on a fourth is still open and is recorded too. Ryan’s ten seconds of backlit bunchgrass is in there, and it is not sweetgrass. He said so when he sent it. It is already published by us on the Nature entry, underneath the line about immediate contact with the outdoors, which is exactly the argument: place-based means the ground you are standing on, not the sacred meadow somewhere else. The plant is deliberately not named to species — nobody here determined it, and a plant named on a page reads as a determination. VideoPress is the third origin this site will build a frame for, and getting it there took two goes. It was added to _headers by hand, confirmed in the file, and shipped — but that CSP line is generated by make-csp.py from a string literal of its own, so every later run put the old list back. The dev server serves no headers at all, so the room worked locally and the live site refused the frame; Ryan found it by pressing the button. The allowlist is one place now: love-embed.js’s ORIGINS array, which make-csp.py reads to build frame-src and make-sweetgrass.py reads to refuse a bad URL at build time. Both refuse outright rather than falling back to a default if the array is missing, because a silently narrowed frame-src is a room full of blank boxes and a silently widened one is a hole. Verified in a network panel: zero iframes and zero external requests on load, with eighteen presses on the page; one press produced exactly one iframe, at the right URL, with the right referrer policy, and left the other seventeen alone. The field’s sign for the pitch needed a light of its own, because the two on that board are taken. The yurt emits and the hermitage catches, so this one is carried: fireflies low in the grass, many small lights and no source you could point at, with the path going in and a thread of smoke where the clearing is. Eliot’s The Hollow Men would have sat at the top and is public domain in America; Eliot died in 1965 and it will not be in much of Europe until the 2030s. The Pebble Board is street furniture, not a storefront. A room on this street is permanent and singular; a board is defined by being replaced, edition after edition, with the old ones kept. A shop whose entire stock is swapped out every gathering is a periodical, and giving it a shopfront would quietly have made every other shopfront look temporary. So it stands on the pavement outside the shops, in the same category as the signpost to the campgrounds. Your Room also already holds the one community storefront, and that one means something exact: one person decorates one room. 2026-09-21 — Club Chronic, and the room that refuses the one effect it obviously wants

Club Chronic is open. That looks like the campgrounds’ rule and is a different rule — the field is still because quiet is what it is for, and this room is still because the obvious idea here hurts people. A room whose whole argument is come in as you are cannot have a light in it that puts somebody on the floor. MAX GLITTER buys nothing in here and the copy says that is on purpose rather than unfinished. And it says out loud that a loud room is itself an access barrier. A scene that lets anybody in and then builds the only entrance out of volume has not finished the job. The honest thing about this being a page is that you can leave mid-song and nobody notices. A song has a length; a list somebody keeps adding to does not, and storing today’s total publishes a number that is wrong next week and authoritative in the meantime. 2026-09-20 — the set said it was off while it was on, and the stylesheet was the one lying

Ryan found the television reporting the wrong thing about itself. A column of text beside the running video announcing THE SET IS OFF, overflowing its own box, and sometimes naming a different programme from the one playing. Three symptoms, and underneath them one bug and a half. The bug: [hidden] loses. The browser’s own rule for the hidden attribute is [hidden] { display: none } at specificity (0,1,0) — which any ordinary class rule that sets display ties with and then wins, because it comes later in the file. So offPanel.hidden = true did nothing visible. The script was correct and the stylesheet was overruling it, silently. The panel had never once been hidden. It was the third time in one room, which is the actual finding. The way-out link had it, the play button had it, and both were patched one selector at a time — which is exactly how the whole off panel was left still waiting to be found. The guard is in §2 now, for everything on the street, and the per-component patches are gone: doing it per component is what hid the third one. And the half: the panel was only ever written on the path that does not play. Retuning while the set was on built a new player and left the panel holding whatever had been tuned the last time it was off — so the stale text Ryan saw was not a rendering artefact, it was a real second bug wearing the first one’s clothes. What the panel says is derived from the tuned channel on both paths now. A panel that is only correct on one of two paths is a panel that will be found wrong. The overflow was real too, and the fix is that 16:9 is a floor rather than a ratio. A channel title runs to a hundred characters; at phone width that is four lines, and with the runtime and the button under it the panel wanted 215px inside a 152px screen — putting the one control that matters below the bottom of the set. Scrolling inside a television to find the play button is not a fix. The screen is a grid now whose row takes the height of the tallest thing in it, so the set is exactly 16:9 on every channel at normal widths and grows only on a phone, where 16:9 would be too small for the card to fit in. Nothing is truncated and nothing is unreachable, which matters more than a set that never moves. The runtime and the play button moved onto one line, because they are one sentence — how long it runs, and the control that starts it — and because it saves the set a whole row of height where the room is tightest.
2026-09-20 — one television instead of twelve, and two sections numbered twenty

The campfire is a room now rather than a grid. Green shag, three bean bags in colours nobody agreed on, a wooden coffee table with rings on it, and one shared television the chairs are all pointed at. Ryan’s brief. The twelve separate players are gone; the listing moved into a Channel Listing that opens and closes, and the set plays whatever you pick. Tuning and playing are two different things, and the set keeps them apart. While it is off, previous and next move the channel in silence — the screen says what it is on and how long that runs, and nothing is fetched. You can walk the entire listing without a single request leaving the page; verified in the network panel at five channel changes, zero requests, zero iframes. Once it is playing, changing channel changes the picture, because by then you have asked for a television and pressing play twelve more times would be a worse room and no more consented. The dial says where it is going before you press it. A next button that only says “next” is the one place this design could have quietly broken the rule that every control on this street names its runtime first — so the slip of paper beside the buttons names the channel it is about to tune to and how long that one runs.
