The thing keeping them apart is structural rather than decorative: the yurt reads cream on dark all the way down, and almost every word in the burrow sits dark on a lit plaster wall. One is a pitched column of canvas with lights strung across it; the other is dug into a hill and has no sky in it anywhere. Two new faces for the same reason — a planed slab and a rounded sans, because a smial is carpentry and the yurt is calligraphy. The wireless is Adriel’s and stays where he put it. Ocean Waves is by Adriel Jeremiah Wool, a Stimpunk, and he has given us permission to use it however we like. It is a press-to-play facade anyway, because a permission is not a reason to take a copy of somebody’s seventy-four-minute composition off its own shelf, and because this street does not host anything musical. It is also not a recording of the ocean and the room says so: Ryan’s own line calls it a fractal composition of the nature of the ocean, and knowing that before you press it changes what you do with it. The television is a class you can take lying down. Annette of Itstimefitness, 22:45, seated tai chi and qigong — Repulse Monkey, Parting the Horse’s Mane, Cloud Arms — chosen for our own Campfire Learn Together on somatic practice. Everything in it is seated and not as a modification: as the design. The shelf refuses to be a checklist. Stretch, flap, fidget, meditate, stim dance, body scan, eat, drink, pee — lifted from our own Bodymind Break, and not one of them is a button. No ticks, no streak, nothing that notices which ones you did. A shelf that kept score would have turned a bodymind break into a small unpaid job, which is what the break is a break from — the same argument the pebbling cabinet makes about tallies, arriving in a room with no game in it. MAX GLITTER, down here, is one lamp breathing. Nothing in the room rotates at any setting, so there was no tilt to reset; the single animation is an opacity change over nine seconds on the lamp flame. The room says that on its own face rather than leaving somebody to turn it up and wonder whether it worked. And then the interesting bug, which was in the stylesheet rather than in the room. This site is one love.css holding a set of worlds that share nothing, and a class name is global whatever section it is written in. Four of this room’s names were already taken: .scrawl belongs to the zine table, .shelf to the bookshelf in the Faery Yurt, .knob to the Arcade’s speed control, and .tagline to the street’s six-typeface masthead. Only one of them was visible — the burrow’s trail line came out in the zine’s Rock Salt, which is how it was noticed at all. The other three were quietly inheriting a timber gradient, a button’s border and display: flex from rooms on the other side of the file. So there is a checker for that now. check-classes.py refuses a class claimed by two rooms’ sections of love.css, and — the half that catches the .tagline case, where the stylesheet is innocent and the markup is not — refuses a page wearing a class name another room has claimed. It is the CSS twin of check-ids.py and exists for the same reason: the browser applies the winner and says nothing. A third check was written and thrown away: a class styled in love.css that nothing wears is real dead weight, and it cannot be told apart from a class a script builds through a helper, because svgEl('frond', …) in otterly.js puts a class on an element without the word class appearing near it. It reported seven drawings that are on the screen right now, and a checker that cries wolf is one people stop running. And it found three leaks that were already here, none of them new. Two rules belonging to the quantum room had been left stranded at the bottom of the file, after the print section, which is how the print section came to look like it was claiming .fringe; they are back in their own room. .scrawl turned out to be worn by the zine table, issue #2 and Enid’s room while living inside the zine’s section — three rooms on one class makes it furniture whichever section it was typed in, so it moved to §4 rather than being renamed twice. And the Faery Yurt’s tagline had been quietly taking display: flex and a 940px max-width from the street’s masthead since the room shipped. That one is a class name and not a design decision, so it is .yurt-tagline now; nothing of Helen’s moved, and the room renders pixel for pixel as it did. The share card is two grounds. Earth at the top with the lamp on it and the round door drawn on it, a band of lit plaster along the foot carrying dark type. That inversion is the room rather than a flourish, and a card that left it out would be advertising a different room. New contrast pairs for both halves; the brass moved from #C28F3C to #E3BB6A because a knob measured 1.93 against the lightest of the three woods behind it — a knob you could not see on the cabinet it is screwed to. The burrow’s two facades are in check-jukebox.py. A room with two of them is exactly the size at which somebody decides a list is not worth adding to a checker, and a dead station in a room built for people who are already flat is the worst place on this street to find rot.
2026-09-20 — a pebbling cabinet, and the licence that decided what it could be

Penguin Pebbling is in the Arcade. A shore, pebbles on it, three neighbours with nests. Walk into something to pick it up, carry it over, press GIVE. Every gift is taken and every one gets something different said back, because giving is how you find out who somebody is rather than a lock to pick. The first thing to say is that there is already a Penguin Pebbling game, and this is not it. Penguin Pebbling is thirty cards across all five locutions, by Helen Edgar and Ryan Boren, 2026, with Helen’s artwork. Go and play that one. The cabinet takes nothing from it — no cards, no prompts, no artwork, no five-locution structure. And the reason is a licence rather than modesty, which is worth writing down because it nearly was not noticed. The deck is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0. This site is CC BY-SA 4.0, with no non-commercial clause. An adaptation would have dragged NC onto a page that cannot carry it; share-alike means it could not be quietly absorbed; and relicensing is not ours alone to do, because half the authorship and all the artwork are Helen’s. So the cabinet is built on the locution — coined by Amythest Schaber (Neurowonderful), documented by Stimpunks in 2022, written up by Helen at Autistic Realms in 2023 — which belongs to the community. Two of our own things with two different licences is exactly the case attribution exists for, and it is the first time on this site that a licence has changed what a page is rather than what it says at the bottom. It refuses a count, and that is the locution rather than a difficulty setting. No tally of what you gave, no total, no streak, nothing at the end. The neighbours bring you things on their own clock whether or not you have ever given them anything — built as a timer rather than as a reward, because a gift that arrives because you gave first is a trade. A number beside a practice that is explicitly not about volume would quietly make it about volume. The pale screen is the only one on the street, and the contrast work is why the pebbles have shapes. Everything on a shingle beach is a mid-tone including the shingle, so nothing on this screen is carried by its fill: every pebble, penguin and nest is drawn with the same dark outline, and check-contrast.py measures that outline against the three grounds and then each fill against the outline. That is the honest reading of WCAG 1.4.11, which asks about adjacent colours rather than about a fill against a distant background. But holding the fills to 4.5 against the outline squeezes them all light — and a narrow band of light tones is a narrow band of things nobody can tell apart. So the six things you can carry are six different shapes: a round pebble, a smooth one, a shard of sea glass, a speckled stone, a feather, a broken shell. Shape carries it, and the name said out loud on every pick-up carries it again. Thirteen new pairs, 195 in the file, none failing. The card inverts too, and had to. Gold on a pale sky measures 1.9, so the type is dark on light — the only share card on this street that is. It was decided by a measurement rather than chosen. A duplicate id, and a bug that would have been much worse anywhere else. The penguin’s drawing sits in the page’s <defs> as #peng and the player’s sprite was also id="peng", so getElementById returned the definition and the game threw on the first line of start(). It took thirty seconds to find because pressing START does something visible. The same mistake in markup nobody presses would have sat there, which is why the other cabinets’ cloned sprites were built out of <use> against one definition in the first place. All four arcade pages were swept; no others. So there is a checker for that now, and it immediately found a worse one. check-ids.py refuses a page that uses an id twice, and refuses a script that asks by name for an id no page loading it has. Run against the whole site it turned up seven elements sharing id="yurt-says" in the Faery Yurt — make-yurt-sound.py had been emitting a live region inside every sound tile, so six of them were dead markup that had never received a word, and love.js only ever reached the first. It had been live since the regulation nook shipped and nothing had said so, because a duplicate in markup nobody presses does not announce itself. The generator emits one shared region now. Broken on purpose with both real bugs put back; it named both. Two things found by looking at the screen rather than by any check. Every penguin was the same size on the same line, so there was no telling which one you were steering — the neighbours are drawn smaller and staggered up the beach now, and you are the one in front. And the nests were single filled ellipses that read as puddles the penguins were standing in; a nest is a rim with a hollow, which is also what the animal actually builds. And an honest note about the penguins, on the page. Adélie and gentoo penguins do build nests of stones, carry them about, and steal them from each other. The tidy romance — one penguin choosing the perfect pebble for its beloved — is the popular retelling rather than the finding. The locution is named after the image and is not weakened by that. A metaphor does not have to be a finding. There is no stealing in the cabinet, because the game is about the locution and not about penguins.
2026-09-20 — a second cabinet in the Arcade, in which floating gets you nothing

Otterly Adorbs. You steer an otter round a kelp bay. It twirls, somersaults, dives and floats on its back; three other otters keep their own rhythms; fish come through at feeding time and go again. Ryan’s proposal, and the name is his. It turned out not to be a blank sheet, which changed the design. The Stimpunks Solidarity Session has been leaving an otter cam running every Saturday for months — cameras on or off, some speaking, some in text, nobody has to watch. Helen Edgar wrote down what that was doing for her in Stimpunks Solidarity and Otters, and Star Stuff built The Stone You Keep (No. 58) on top of it, sourced to the primary literature. So the cabinet is built out of findings rather than out of charm, and otterly.js names the paper beside each one. Floating fills nothing up, and that is the single sharpest constraint in the build. No meter, no stamina, no bonus afterwards — the cabinet says so out loud the first time you roll over. Zine No. 58 refuses rest so you can produce in as many words: the otter is not recharging in order to forage better tomorrow. The friendly version of this game rewards resting, and the friendly version would have put a sentence on this page that another of our pages spends a spread refusing. It is written into CLAUDE.md so the next well-meant improvement gets stopped. A clam takes between 6 and 88 presses, and those are the real numbers. Two observers at Point Lobos in 1964 watched thirty instances over six days: a mussel took a mean of 35.5 blows, range 6 to 88 (Hall & Schaller). The game rolls in that range unrounded and reports your number with no target beside it. The urchin opens in a couple of goes and a stone does not help with it, which is Law et al. 2024 — some otters never carry one, because they are on the prey that does not need one, and the ones who do carry one keep their teeth. Nothing ranks the other three otters. Under food limitation a real population does not converge on one best way to be an otter; it fans out into specialists, each measurably better at its own thing (Tinker, Bentall & Estes, 2008). One of ours mostly floats, one mostly dives, one mostly turns in circles, and there is no scoreboard for any of it. The kelp does the holding. Float in the fronds and you stay where you are; float in open water and you drift. That is co-regulation stated as physics rather than as a metaphor, and it is the one mechanic that is also the reason the Saturday session works. It follows the zine’s correction rather than our own changelog. stimpunks.org’s week-28 entry describes the otter keeping “a favorite stone tucked in a pouch of skin” and returning to it “again and again”. No. 58 went to the primary and found the lifelong favourite rock in an armpit pouch is a popular retelling; what Hall & Schaller support is a stone kept and reused across successive food items within a bout of feeding. The game does the second thing. When two of our own pages disagree, the one that checked wins. A twirl is drawn frames, not a rotation, and that cost real work. Rotating the sprite would have been three lines — and would have made the room’s own comment false, because check-gentle.py reads rotation out of the computed matrix and this room says in its stylesheet that there is nothing there to read. So the otter has five drawn poses and a trick is a run through them. The angled poses are rotated, inside their own <svg>, where a transform is part of the picture the way a path’s d is. Frame-swapping is also what an actual cabinet did. The contrast checker found the seabed. It measured 1.10 against the water above it — invisible — and lightening the floor until it cleared 3:1 started swallowing the cobbles and the urchin that sit on it, which are the things a player reaches for. So the boundary is carried by a line instead, at 8.44 on the water and 9.25 on the bed. The information is “here is the floor”, and a line carries it perfectly well. Nineteen new pairs; 182 in the file, none failing. Buoyancy was winning an argument the player was trying to have with a clam. An otter is buoyant, so doing nothing takes you up — at the first setting that was about eight per cent of the bay a second, and it pulled you off the bed before you could pick a stone up. It is a quarter of that now, and it stops entirely while you are working on a shell, because an otter cracking something is holding itself there. Then the room split, and the share card is what decided it. Both games lived on one page for about an hour. Which meant a link to the otter game unfurled as a picture of a porcupine — the exact fault make-og.py exists to refuse, being committed by a room against its own second game. The Arcade is a foyer now, with the cabinets standing in it under lit marquees, and Quill Drift and Otterly Adorbs are pages with a machine on each. Three cards where there was one, and the two new ones are the screens: a flat dark field with Esmx and loose quills, and a kelp bay with an otter on its back. Those three pages share a carpet, a marquee, a cabinet build and a pixel face, and that is correct here. On this street that normally reads as the tidying instinct winning, so it is written into CLAUDE.md before somebody either “fixes” the similarity or cites it as licence to harmonise actual rooms. An arcade is precisely a room whose machines share a body and differ behind the glass. The worlds here are the screens, and a dark field and a kelp bay have nothing to do with each other. The chrome moved to a .arcade class so that the thing which styles and the thing which unfurls are never the same word — each page carries exactly one class make-og.py has a card for, and no ordering inside a class attribute decides anything. Each cabinet carries its own panels, its own refusals and its own credits. A single shared sidebar stopped working the moment there were two machines: a readout headed YOUR ESMX floating above an otter game is furniture belonging to nobody. The foyer keeps only what is true of every machine in the room — no timer, nothing chasing you, no sound, no memory, nothing moving until you press start. check-counts.py gained cabinets and games while this shipped and immediately refused two sentences calling one of them “the second cabinet”.
2026-09-20 — the street stops saying how many rooms it has, and a checker to keep it that way

Ryan’s call: the number of storefronts is going to grow well past anything worth writing down, so nothing here states a total any more. Not the pages, not the stylesheet’s comments, not a generator’s published strings, not the docs. The street’s own description, its share card, llms.txt, the feed’s description, the liner notes, the campground’s lede and the empty storefront’s opening line all say something that stays true however many there are — no two rooms alike, one card per room, a row of shopfronts, a storefront with nothing in it. The change that opened the Arcade is the argument for this, and it is not a flattering one. That commit carefully updated the room count in twelve places — and shipped three sentences still carrying the old one. love.css went on describing the doors and the shopfronts by a number that had stopped being true the moment the seventh one landed, and CLAUDE.md went on giving the number of share-card designs as one fewer than existed. All three were written by the same session that was updating the other twelve, and nothing caught them, because nothing was looking. A total is a fact about the whole site that gets written in a dozen places and updated in one. So check-counts.py refuses a number or an ordinal sitting in front of a thing that grows when a storefront opens — rooms, storefronts, shopfronts, doors, worlds, card designs. It is deliberately small. The jukebox’s tracks and The Chappell’s are real counts of real data, generated from files holding exactly that many, and it leaves them alone. It starts at four, because the first draft refused its own fix. Written to catch any number from two upwards, the very first thing it flagged was “no two rooms alike” — the count-free phrasing this whole change exists to encourage — along with “two rooms turned out to be putting text on a background nobody had measured”, which is a finding rather than a claim about the size of the street. Below four, a number in front of these nouns is nearly always counting instances. A street’s total will be four and rising. Quoted text is skipped in prose and not in code, and the asymmetry is the point. A page or a doc has to be able to say what it corrected, so a count inside quotation marks there is evidence rather than a claim. In a generator every quoted string is a candidate for publication — make-og.py writes its card footers out of string literals — so there is no safe quotation, and the checker’s own docstring therefore describes the three stale counts rather than quoting them. It is the one place where a tool’s prose has to obey the rule it enforces. The first version scanned line by line and refused itself, because the quotation it makes its argument out of wrapped across two. Broken on purpose in all three shapes that actually shipped — a page’s prose (“the seventh storefront”), a stylesheet comment (“the six doors”) and a generator’s docstring (“eleven card designs”) — and it named all three with their file and line. Then the working tree was put back. One count it missed on the way, which is why it grew a word. The Arcade’s own source said the room “shares nothing with the six next door”, and the first rule sailed past it because next was not in the short list of words allowed to sit between a number and its noun. It is in the list now, and the sentence says the rooms next door. The share card changed with the street. Its footer read ONE STREET · SEVEN ROOMS · A FIELD PAST THE TREELINE and now reads NO TWO ROOMS ALIKE, which is the better line anyway: the count was never the interesting claim, and the thing it was standing in for is the one this site is actually about. The room numbers on the doors stay. room 04, room 05, ROOM 07 are addresses, and a house number has never told anybody how long the street is.
2026-09-20 — the second yell, and a duration that lies about itself

The yell button has two voices in it. The Playhouse holds a yell from Enigma, lent on 2026-09-20 — the first on that button from somebody other than the person who built the room. It is published under the name it came with, the room says whose yell it was out loud on the press, and it is credited in the liner notes as well. It carries no onward licence, unlike everything else here: CC BY-SA cannot be revoked, and a voice somebody lends us has to be one they can take back. Two tools refused it on arrival, which is what they are for. The file sat in audio/yells/ with no entry in data/yells.json, so make-yells.py stopped — a yell with nobody’s name on it is the one thing it cannot publish — and make-yurt-sound.py’s sweep of every audio file in the repo stopped on the metadata: com.apple, Core Media, and a creation timestamp to the second. Neither tool strips anything, and that is deliberate: what to do with somebody’s recording is theirs to decide, not a script’s. It was stripped once there was a decision to strip it. And the obvious way to check that strip is misleading. The instruction in both docstrings is to compare the duration before and after, because -c copy re-muxes rather than re-encodes. It went from 4.160s to 4.096s — 64 milliseconds apparently gone, which reads exactly like a bad edit. It is not. -map_metadata -1 drops the iTunSMPB tag, which is the container’s declaration of encoder padding, and the start offset went 0.044 to 0.000 with it. Decoding both files to raw PCM gives 196,608 samples each, identical at every one of them, same peak. The audio is untouched; the 64ms was never audio. Written down here because the check the tools recommend will keep producing that number, and the next person to run it should not go looking for what they cut off. The house rule rewrote itself, which is the whole reason it is generated. The Playhouse now says the button holds “2 recorded yells” rather than one. A claim a page makes about itself should not depend on somebody remembering to edit it. Verified in the network panel afterwards: zero requests to audio/ on load, one per press, and both names reached the live region.
2026-09-20 — a seventh storefront, with one cabinet in it

The street has an arcade on it. The Arcade is room seven, sixth door in the row, and it holds one game: Quill Drift, starring Esmx the Porkypine. Loose quills drift across a dark field, Esmx walks, and a quill joins the mane on contact and only on contact. No timer, no lives, no score, no streak, nothing chasing anybody and no way to lose a quill once it is in. The one rule is the mechanic, not a note at the bottom of it. A porcupine cannot shoot a quill — cannot throw, fire or launch one; it comes away in whatever touched it, and an attacker has to come to the animal. That is card No. 3 of the Quillery, sourced there to Uldis Roze. A spiky mascot invites precisely the opposite reading, so the game has no verb for it: there is nothing to aim, nothing to press but a direction, and nothing on the field but Esmx and the quills. “Non-violent” was the brief; refusing the one verb everybody expects is what it turned into. The point of the game is a variant, which is what the licence asks for. Twelve quills fill the mane, and what you are left with is a mane in an order nobody else walked into — written out in words beside the cabinet as well as drawn on the sprite, because a mane nobody can read is a mane nobody can tell anybody about. Esmx’s own page does not merely permit this: feel free to customise! Make variants of Esmx to represent your community. A correction, caught by Ryan mid-build and worth the space. The room shipped its first draft calling Esmx “our mascot and not ours”, and borrowed the framing from the Quillery, which says Kaya Oldaker’s artwork “is not ours to redraw stroke for stroke”. That is wrong about the facts. Stimpunks commissioned Esmx and holds the IP; Kaya is the artist. The credit line stays on every surface it was on — in the room, in the liner notes and in the drawing’s own markup — because holding the rights to a commission is not a reason to stop naming the hand that drew it, which is a different and better sentence than the one that was there. Attribution here is a courtesy as well as a licence, and it turns out the courtesy is the half that was doing the work. Esmx is drawn again rather than pasted in, and not because anybody needed permission. The originals are a download away and ours to use. A PNG would have been the only thing in the arcade that came from somewhere else, in a room whose whole argument is that it shares nothing with the six next door — and taking our own invitation seemed like the least we could do with it. The marks that make Esmx Esmx are kept: the pig snout, the earring in one ear, the chunk out of the other, and a mane that comes apart at the tips. An arcade in particular, because the mascot already came from one. Kaya’s notes say Esmx resembles a Sonic character or a Pokémon on purpose, due to their popularity within the Autistic community. Nothing of either is used here. The room is not a costume put on the mascot; it is where the mascot came from. The dial and the speed knob are two controls, on purpose. The dial governs the room — the cabinet glow, the marquee bulbs — and the game’s speed belongs to the player. The dial picks the knob’s starting position, Slow if you arrived on Gentle, and then stops having an opinion; all three speeds are offered at every dial setting. Tying the game to the dial would have made Gentle a different game, which is the “lite version” mistake with a joystick on it. And nothing on the playfield moves until a coin goes in — the jukebox’s consent model in a different costume, and the reason a room with a game in it does not make the dial lie. Motion the visitor started is not ambient motion. The cabinet also makes no sound at all, ever, at any setting; an arcade that is silent by choice seemed better than one that is silent until it isn’t. Everything moves with left/top, and that is a decision about the checker rather than about performance. Rotation and skew are what check-gentle.py reads out of the computed matrix, and a room that put its game behind a transform would be asking that tool to take the room’s word for something. There is nothing to take on trust if there is no transform to read. The two that are there are the sprite’s centring translate and a scaleX(-1) when Esmx turns round — both of which the tool already reads as layout, and both of which it can see. Broken on purpose with an unreset rotate(-2deg) on the cabinet marquee: it named p.cab-marquee and the matrix it found. 192 elements in the room, measured at all three settings, none tilting. Thirty-six new contrast pairs, two of them against grounds nobody chose. #0F1F24 is what the screen becomes under its scanline stripe and is the lighter of the two grounds the playfield makes, so it is the one that decides; #2D1C25 is the carpet under the cabinet’s own glow, where the headline and the eyebrow sit. The eight quills are in the list too — WCAG 1.4.3 does not reach a graphic, but a quill you cannot pick out of the background is a control you cannot use, and they are held to the body threshold rather than the 3:1 one so that nobody has to remember later which bar applied. Each quill also has a name, said out loud on contact, because colour is never the only channel here. 162 pairs, none failing; broken on purpose by dimming one grey, and the composite ground failed harder than the flat one, which is the whole argument for having both in the file. make-og.py refused the room until it had a card, which is exactly what it is for — the eleventh design, and the one that is mostly a drawing, because this is the only room whose subject is a character rather than an argument and a poster for a game showing nobody playing it would be a poster for the wrong thing. Esmx and the marquee bulbs are lifted out of the page rather than retyped, alongside the campground’s stream and the yurt’s crown, so the card cannot come to disagree with the room. The mane on it is the markup’s own default rainbow; the game only ever overwrites those twelve fills with what a player actually caught. Press Start 2P is the eighteenth family and the only face in the room. A pixel face is the one thing no other room on this street could have borrowed without turning into the arcade. 4.7KB, latin only, self-hosted like the other seventeen — verified in the network panel: every byte on the page comes from this origin, and the cabinet fetches nothing when you press anything, because there is nothing to fetch. Playtested, and the first build was over before its own instructions were. Six quills on the field at a reach of 7.5 filled a twelve-quill mane in about ten seconds. Dropping to five at 6.2 went too far the other way — a full lap of the field turned up one quill and the game went slack. Six at 7.0 fills a mane in something under a minute of walking, measured over a sixteen-leg random walk rather than guessed. “Six rooms” was written down in twelve places — the street’s description and its card alt, llms.txt, love.css’s own header, the liner notes, the campground’s lede, the feed’s description and the street card’s footer. It is seven now, and Your Room is the seventh storefront rather than the sixth. The derived files are derived, so make-sitemap.py and make-feed.py carried their own copies of the sentence and had to be edited at the source rather than in the output. The pad takes a press-and-hold or a single click, because a control that only works while a button is held down is not a control for somebody driving it with a switch or a screen reader. The arrow keys are bound to the playfield rather than to the document — arrow keys that stop the page scrolling from anywhere on it would be a trap — and Escape hands them back.
2026-09-20 — a checker for the dial, and the windowsill it caught

The dial had nothing watching it. check-gentle.py loads all fourteen pages in headless Chrome, sets the intensity to Gentle, Regular and MAX GLITTER in turn, and reads what actually moves out of 2,253 computed styles — rather than reading the stylesheet and believing it. The global half was always safe: animation and transition are killed at Gentle with !important, and nothing out-shouts that by accident. The tilts were never safe. Every room sets its own rotations and resets them room by room, unprefixed, so a reset is one selector away from being outranked — and CSS does not warn when that happens. It applies the winner and says nothing. It found the Faery Yurt’s windowsill on its first run. A book at rotate(-3deg) and a pen at rotate(24deg), both still tilted for anybody who had asked the wobble to stop, because that room shipped without a single Gentle rule in it. Twenty-four degrees is not subtle. The room was a day old and two people had read it. The sill keeps its angles at Regular and MAX — they are Helen’s and they stay; the reset is the dial, which is our plumbing and applies to every room on the street. Rotation and skew are the wobble; a mirror and a translate are not. The tool reads the off-diagonal terms of the computed matrix, which are non-zero for exactly those two and nothing else, so a vine flipped with scaleX(-1) and a positioned layer pass without needing an exception. Transforms inside an <svg> are excluded on purpose: a transform on a <g> is part of the drawing, the same kind of thing as a path’s d, and flattening one would produce a broken picture rather than a calmer page. Hear Queer Here — quantum queering, with Barad and Helen Edgar quoted and cited, and a superposition panel where “leave it open” is a real answer. Enid’s Room — colorful goth, a sticker wall wired to seven glossary entries, and somewhere to sit when the glee runs out. The Playhouse — four toys, all real buttons, all synthesised rather than fetched, all reachable by keyboard. Your Room — the sixth storefront, left empty on purpose, with the terms written down. The intensity dial — three settings on every page, defaulting to whatever your device asks for and letting you turn it up past that. Gentle takes away the wobble, never the words. Twelve typefaces self-hosted, so reading a page here makes no third-party request.

Enid’s polaroid wall has two photographs and room for more. Issue #2 of the zine has a quotation slot shaped for the last line of the course and nothing in it, because the credit that line needs is not something we will guess. All of them are listed here rather than hidden, because a room that says what it is missing is more use than one that pretends. HOW LOUD DO YOU WANT IT? Starts wherever your device says. Nothing moves, flashes, or plays until you say so.
